Due to that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the deva realm and, performing merits repeatedly, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans. In this Buddha-era, he was born into a brahmin family in the kingdom of Magadha. In due course, reaching the age of discretion and having an inclination toward renunciation, he went forth as a wandering ascetic (*paribbājaka*). While wandering after learning what was to be learned there, he heard that Upatissa and Kolita had gone forth in the Buddha's Dispensation. Thinking, "Even those of such great wisdom have gone forth under that Buddha; I think that very course is better," he went to the Teacher, heard the Dhamma, gained faith, and went forth. The Teacher taught him insight meditation (*vipassanā*). Practicing insight, he realized Arahantship before long. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

"My name was Nārada; they knew me as Kesava.
Searching for what is wholesome and unwholesome, I approached the Buddha."
234:
Having thus gone to the Buddha and heard the Dhamma, he gained faith and went forth. The Teacher showed him the practice of insight meditation (*vipassanā*). By practicing insight, that elder realized Arahantship before long. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

'My name was Nārada; they knew me as Kesava. Searching for what is wholesome and unwholesome, I approached the Buddha.

'With a heart of loving-kindness, possessing great compassion, seeing the benefit, the Great Sage (*Mahāmuni*), the One with Vision (*Cakkhumā*), that Buddha Atthadassī taught the Dhamma, giving solace to beings.

'Having gladdened my own mind, raising my joined palms to my head, and paying homage to the Teacher, I departed facing the east.

'One thousand seven hundred aeons ago, there was a powerful king named Amittatāpana, a Wheel-turning Monarch (*Cakkavatti*) of great strength.

'My defilements have been burned away... the Buddha's bidding has been done.'

When he reached Arahantship, wishing to declare his attainment, he spoke this verse:

'The five aggregates have been seen as they truly are; all existences have been shattered. The wandering in the cycle of births is exhausted; now there is no more renewed existence.'

In that verse, 'aggregates' (*khandhā*) refers to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcupādānakkhandhā*). Those aggregates should be investigated through insight by way of defining them through their individual characteristics and general characteristics, and by way of full understanding through the full understanding of the known (*ñātapariññā*), etc. 'Seen as they truly are' (*diṭṭhā yathābhūtaṃ*) means seen without distortion as 'This is suffering,' etc., by Path-wisdom (*magga-paññā*) accompanied by insight-wisdom. 'All existences have been shattered' (*bhavā sabbe padālitā*) means all kamma-processes (*kammabhava*) and rebirth-processes (*upapattibhava*) in the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*), etc., have been broken and destroyed by the weapon of Path-knowledge. Indeed, by the destruction of defilements, the kamma and rebirth processes are said to be shattered. Therefore, he said, 'The wandering in the cycle of births is exhausted; now there is no more renewed existence.' The meaning of that verse has already been explained below.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Paviṭṭha is finished.

## 8. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Ajjuna

'I have indeed been able to [tame] myself' (*Asakkhiṃ vata attānaṃ*) is the verse of the Venerable Elder Ajjuna. What is the special background? This Elder Ajjuna was also one who had performed meritorious services under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit that is a powerful foundation for Nibbāna in various existences. In the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, he was born in the lion species. One day, seeing the Blessed One sitting at the foot of a certain tree in the forest, he felt a devoted heart, thinking, 'Only this Blessed One is the Great Man, the Lion among men, superior to all at this time.' He then broke off a well-bloomed Sal branch and offered it to the Blessed One. Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans, and when our Blessed One Gotama appeared, he was born into a wealthy family in the city of Sāvatthī. The name of that merchant's son was Ajjuna. When he grew up and gained wisdom, because he was familiar with the Nigaṇṭhas, he thought, 'If I practice in this way, I shall attain Nibbāna, which is free from death.' Desiring Nibbāna, he went forth among the Nigaṇṭhas while still young, and in the practice of those Nigaṇṭhas...
235:
Having seen the Teacher and thinking with a devoted heart, "This is indeed the most excellent lion-like man at this time," he broke off a well-blossomed Sāla branch and made an offering to the Teacher. Because of that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans, and in this Buddha-era, he was reborn in a wealthy family in Sāvatthī. He was named Ajjuna. When he reached maturity, having become acquainted with the Nigaṇṭhas, he thought, "In this way, I shall attain the Deathless Nibbāna." Desiring Nibbāna, he ordained among the Nigaṇṭhas while still young, but he found no essence in that practice. Seeing the Teacher's Twin Miracle (Yamaka Pāṭihāriya), he gained faith, ordained in the Dispensation, and by striving in insight (Vipassanā), he soon became an Arahant. This matter is stated in the Apadāna as follows:

"Then, I was a lion king, of noble birth and with a fine mane. While searching through mountain ravines, I saw the World Leader, Vipassī Buddha.
'This Great Hero indeed brings peace to the multitude. What if I were to attend upon this God of gods, the Bull among men?' (I thought).
Breaking a branch of a Sāla tree, I brought the flowers along with their buds. Approaching the Sambuddha, I offered the most excellent flowers.
In the ninety-one aeons since I offered those flowers, I have not known a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of offering flowers.
Nine aeons ago from now, there were three powerful Cakkavatti kings named Virocana.
My defilements have been burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled."

Having attained Arahantship, wishing to utter an inspired word (udāna) with the surge of joy born from the attainment of supreme happiness:

"I have indeed been able to lift myself from the water to the dry land. While being carried away in the great flood, I have pierced the Truths."

He spoke this verse. In that verse, "Asakkhiṃ vata attānaṃ" means I have indeed been able to lift myself from the water to the dry land. The piercing of the Four Noble Truths is truly wonderful. Therefore, He taught the passage beginning with, "Monks, what do you think? Which is more difficult or more hard to achieve: that one should pierce the tip of a hair split into seven strands with another tip...?" "Monks, what do you think of the word I have spoken?" (He asked).
236:
In that verse, "asakkhiṃ" means "I was able". "Vata" is an exclamation of wonder. The piercing of the Four Noble Truths is indeed extremely wonderful. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, what do you think? Which is more difficult or more hard to achieve: that one should pierce the tip of a hair split into seven strands with another tip...?" and so on.

"Attānaṃ" refers to one's own internal continuity. Because it is not another, it is called "self" (atta). "Uddhātun" means to lift out; there is also a variant reading "uddhaṭaṃ". "Udakā" means from the great flood of Saṃsāra. "Thalaṃ" means the dry land of Nibbāna. "Vuyhamāno mahoghevā" means like one being carried away in the ocean.

The meaning is this: For example, a man being carried away by the force of a great flood that is very deep, wide, and without a foothold, if he obtains a sturdy boat equipped with oars and poles brought by someone desiring his welfare, he could easily lift himself out of that flood and reach the other shore. In the same way, while I was being carried away in the great flood of Saṃsāra by the force of defilements and volitional formations (kilesa-abhisaṅkhāra), I obtained the boat of the Noble Path (Ariyamagga) endowed with Samatha and Vipassanā brought by the Teacher, and thus I was indeed able to lift myself out of that flood and reach the dry land of Nibbāna.

How was I able? To show this, he said, "Saccāni paṭivijjhahaṃ" (I pierced the Truths). Since I have pierced the four Noble Truths—Suffering and so on—through the piercing of full understanding, abandoning, realizing, and developing with the Knowledge of the Noble Path, the connection is: "I have indeed been able to lift myself from the water to the dry land."

## The Commentary on the Verses of Ajjuna Thera is finished.

## 9. (First) Commentary on the Verses of Devasabha Thera

The verse beginning with "Uttiṇṇā paṅkapali" is that of the Venerable Devasabha Thera. As for the background: This Elder also had performed meritorious deeds (adhikāra) under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit that serves as a support for the attainment of Arahantship in various births. In the time of the Blessed One Sikhī, he was reborn as a pigeon. One day, seeing the Teacher, with a devoted heart, he offered a Piyāla fruit. To increase the pigeon's devotion, the Teacher consumed that fruit. Because of that, the pigeon, with an extremely devoted heart, approached and paid homage from time to time, thus clarifying his mind.
237:
(The Blessed One) consumed that piyāla fruit. Because of that, the pigeon, having a heart of supreme devotion, approached and paid homage at all times, thus purifying its mind. Due to that meritorious deed, the pigeon was reborn in the celestial realm. After performing repeated meritorious deeds and wandering through the rounds of rebirth among devas and humans, in the time of our Buddha’s appearance, he was reborn as the son of a certain Maṇḍalika king. While established in kingship from a young age and enjoying royal happiness, upon reaching maturity, he approached the Teacher. The Teacher preached the Dhamma to that young man. Having heard the Dhamma, he gained faith and, being moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega), renounced the kingship and went forth as a monk. While practicing the meditation of insight (vipassanā), he attained the fruit of Arahantship before long. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

“At that time, I was a pigeon who did not harm others,
I made my bed in a mountain cleft, not far from the Teacher Sikhī.

In the evening and morning, I saw the Buddha, the supreme leader of the world,
But I had no gift to offer to the Lord of bipeds, the Such-like One.

Taking a piyāla fruit, I went into the presence of the Buddha,
The Blessed One, the Elder of the world, the Bull among men, accepted it.

From then on, I attended upon the Guide,
With that devotion of mind, I passed away in that life.

Thirty-one aeons ago from this present age, I gave that fruit,
I have not known a miserable rebirth since; this is the fruit of offering fruit.

Fifteen aeons ago from this present age, there were three kings named Piyāli,
Endowed with the seven treasures, wheel-turning monarchs of great power.

My defilements are burnt away... etc... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.”

Furthermore, having reached Arahantship, with a joyful heart arising from the review of the abandoned defilements, and wishing to utter an inspired utterance (udāna), he recited this verse:

“The mire and the deep mud have been crossed, the abysses have been avoided,
I am freed from the floods and the bonds, all nine types of conceit are destroyed.”

In that verse, "uttinnā" means they have been crossed over. "Paṅkapalippā" refers to the mire and the very deep, wide mud. Ordinary mud is called "paṅka." A deep and vast great mud is called "palippa." In this context, sensual lust (kāmarāga) is called "paṅka" because it is like mire, as it smears the mind by causing impurity; and because it smears well in the manner described, and is difficult to cross, it is called "paṅka." Great desire-attachment (chandarāga) towards objects such as children and wives is called "palippa" because it is like a deep and wide mud. I have completely crossed over that sensual lust and desire-attachment through the Path of Non-returning (anāgāmi-magga); therefore, he said, "uttinnā paṅkapalippā." "Pātālā" are so called because they are capable of swallowing water; it refers to the low-lying areas in the great ocean. Some teachers say the realm of the Nāgas is "pātāla." In this context, (the Buddha) taught...
238:
In that verse, "uttinnā" means they have been crossed over. "Paṅkapalippā" refers to the mire and the very deep, wide mud. Ordinary mud is called "paṅka." A deep and vast great mud is called "palippa." In this context, sensual lust (kāmarāga) is called "paṅka" because it is like mire, as it smears the mind by causing impurity. Great desire-attachment (chandarāga) towards objects such as children and wives is called "palippa" because it smears well in the manner described and is difficult to cross, thus resembling a deep and wide mud. I have completely crossed over that sensual lust and desire-attachment through the Path of Non-returning (anāgāmi-magga); therefore, he said, "uttinnā paṅkapalippā." "Pātālā" are so called because they are capable of swallowing water; it refers to the very low-lying areas in the great ocean. Some teachers say the realm of the Nāgas is "pātāla." In this context, because they are difficult to enter and difficult to cross, the sixty-two types of wrong views (diṭṭhi), which are like abysses in the great ocean, are called "pātālā." I have completely avoided and eradicated those wrong views just by the attainment of the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga); therefore, he said, "pātālā parivajjitā." "Mutto oghā ca ganthā ca" means I am freed from the four floods such as the flood of sensuality (kāmogha), and from the four bonds such as the bodily bond of covetousness (abhijjhākāyagantha), through the respective Noble Paths; it means I have crossed over by way of not being scattered again and not being bound. "Sabbe mānā visanhatā" means that the nine types of conceit have been specifically destroyed and eradicated by the attainment of the Path of Arahantship. Some teachers read "mānavidhā hatā," meaning the groups of conceit. Others read "mānavisā"; in their view, it should be understood as "mānavisā" because the nine types of conceit themselves cause suffering (like poison).

## The Commentary on the Verses of the (First) Elder Devasabha is finished.

## 10. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Sāmidatta

"Pañcakkhandhā pariññātā" is the verse of the Venerable Sāmidatta. What is its origin? This Sāmidatta also, having made an aspiration under previous Buddhas, was reborn in a family home during the time of the Blessed One Atthadassī and, upon reaching the age of discretion, became wise. When the Buddha attained Parinibbāna, he made an offering of tiered umbrellas made of flowers at the stupa of that Buddha. Due to that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the celestial realm and, after performing repeated meritorious deeds and wandering through the rounds of rebirth among devas and humans, in the time of our Buddha’s appearance, he was reborn as the son of a certain Brahmin in the city of Rājagaha. His name was "Sāmidatta." That youth Sāmidatta, having gradually reached the age of discretion and hearing of the Buddha's power, went to the monastery together with the lay devotees.
239:
Seeing the Blessed One preaching the Dhamma, with a heart full of faith, he sat down in a suitable place. The Blessed One, seeing his inclination, preached the Dhamma in such a way that he gained faith and a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) regarding saṃsāra. Having gained faith and being filled with spiritual urgency, he ordained. However, because his knowledge was not yet mature, he lived for a short time being somewhat indolent. Later, being encouraged by the Blessed One with a Dhamma discourse, he took up a meditation subject for insight (vipassanā) and, while dwelling with diligent effort in that meditation, he attained Arahatship before long. Regarding this, it is said in the Apadāna:

“When the Blessed One Atthadassī, the best of men, had attained Parinibbāna, I made a tiered parasol and placed it on the stupa.

“From time to time, I came and paid homage to the Leader of the World; having made a flower ceiling, I placed it on the parasol.

“For one hundred and seventy aeons, I ruled as a king of devas; I did not go to a human state—this is the fruit of worshipping the stupa.

“My defilements are burnt away; all existences are uprooted. Like an elephant that has broken its bonds, I live without taints (āsavas).

“My coming to the presence of the Noble Buddha was indeed a good coming; the three knowledges have been attained, and the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.”

Later, when he was asked by the monks, “Friend, have you attained the superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma)?” he wished to make known to them the liberating nature of the Dispensation and his own practice in accordance with the Dhamma. By way of declaring his attainment of Arahatship, he recited this verse:

“The five aggregates have been fully understood; they stand with their roots cut. Rebirth in saṃsāra is exhausted; now there is no more renewed existence.”

In that verse, “The five aggregates have been fully understood” (pañcakkhandhā pariññātā) means: I have known, perceived, and penetrated these five aggregates of clinging by means of the three types of full understanding (pariññā), defining them as “This is suffering, this much is suffering, there is nothing beyond this.” “They stand with their roots cut” (tiṭṭhanti chinnamūlakā) means that because they have been fully understood in that way...
240:
...because the origin (samudaya), which is the root, has been abandoned in every way, those aggregates now stand with their roots cut until the cessation of the final consciousness. But with the cessation of the final consciousness, they cease without further rebirth. Therefore, he said: “Rebirth in saṃsāra is exhausted; now there is no more renewed existence.” The meaning of that verse has already been explained below.

## The commentary on the verses of the Elder Sāmidatta is finished.

## The commentary on the Ninth Chapter is finished.

## 10. The Tenth Chapter (Dasama Vagga)

## 1. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Paripuṇṇaka

The verse beginning with “Na tathā mataṃ satarasaṃ” is that of the Venerable Elder Paripuṇṇaka. What is its origin? This elder had also performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas. In the time of the Blessed One Dhammadassī, he was reborn in a respectable family. When he reached the age of discretion and the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna, he performed a grand offering of flowers and other requisites at the Blessed One’s stupa. Due to that meritorious deed, he was reborn among the devas. Performing merits in subsequent lives and wandering only in the happy realms (sugati), he was reborn in this Buddha’s era in the Sakyan royal family in Kapilavatthu. When he reached the age of discretion, he became known as “Paripuṇṇaka” because of his complete and abundant wealth.

Because he was endowed with wealth, he always consumed food known as “satarasa” (hundred-flavored). While doing so, he heard that the Blessed One consumed mixed food (missakāhāra) and thought: “Even the Blessed One, who is so delicate, still subsists on whatever food is available, having regard for the bliss of Nibbāna. Why should we be greedy for food and be those who consider only the purity of food? We should seek only the bliss of Nibbāna.” Thus, a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) arose in him regarding saṃsāra. He abandoned the household life and ordained in the presence of the Blessed One. Being urged by the Blessed One in the meditation subject of mindfulness of the body (kāyagatāsati), he established himself in that meditation. Using the attained jhāna as a basis, he developed insight (vipassanā) and reached Arahatship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

“When the Leader of the World Dhammadassī, the bull among men, had attained Parinibbāna,
I erected a banner pole at the stupa of the Noble Buddha.

“Having created a ladder, I climbed the excellent stupa;
Having taken jāti flowers, I offered them upon the stupa.”
241:
“How wonderful is the Buddha! How wonderful is the Dhamma! How wonderful is the perfection (sampadā) of our Teacher! I do not know of ever reaching the four woeful states; this is the fruit of worshipping the stupa.

“Ninety-four aeons ago, there were sixteen universal monarchs (cakkavatti) named Thūpasīkha, possessed of great power.

“My defilements are burnt... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.”

Upon attaining Arhatship, due to his great reverence and esteem for the Dhamma, he uttered an inspired utterance (udāna) released by the force of joy, reciting the verse beginning with “Na tathā mataṃ satarasaṃ.”

In that verse, in the phrase “Na tathā mataṃ satarasaṃ sudhannaṃ yaṃ mayajja paributtaṃ,” the word “tathā” means in that manner. “Mataṃ” means highly desired (abhimata). “Satarasaṃ” refers to food having a hundred flavors. It is said that “hundred-flavored food” (satarasabhojana) is food well-prepared with ghee cooked a hundred times and so forth. Alternatively, the word “sata” has the meaning of “many,” as in “sataso sahassaso” (by hundreds and thousands). Therefore, food that is complete with many curries and many side dishes is called “satarasa” because of its many flavors; it means food with various tastes. “Sudhā” itself is food, thus it is called “sudhābhojana,” which is the nutriment of the devas. “Yaṃ mayajja paributtaṃ” means that which I have enjoyed today (the bliss of Nibbāna). This phrase “yaṃ mayā paributtaṃ” should also be applied to the phrase “satarasaṃ sudhannaṃ.”

The meaning is this: The bliss of Nibbāna, which is exceedingly peaceful and sublime, and which I am now enjoying through the power of attaining the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) and the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti)—just as that bliss of Nibbāna is desired and cherished, the hundred-flavored food I enjoyed when I was a king and the divine food (sudhā) I enjoyed in the celestial realm are not so desired (not considered as cherished). Why is that? Because this bliss of Nibbāna is resorted to by the Noble Ones (ariyas), is free from worldly taints (nirāmisa), and is not a ground for defilements. Those foods, however, are resorted to by worldlings (puthujjanas), are accompanied by worldly taints (sāmisa), and are grounds for defilements. Those foods do not equal even a fraction, a part, or a sixteenth part of this bliss of Nibbāna.

Now, wishing to teach the Dhamma referred to as “yaṃ mayajja paributtaṃ,” he said, “The Dhamma has been well-taught by the Buddha, the descendant of Gotama, who sees the limitless (ñeyyadhamma).” The meaning is: He saw with his self-enlightened knowledge (sayambhū-ñāṇa) the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu), which is peaceful and limitless because it has no arising or passing away. He is called “Aparimitadassī” because he is one who habitually sees the infinite and limitless objects of knowledge (ñeyyadhamma). That descendant of Gotama who sees the limitless...
243:
Having attained the fruit of Arahatship, wishing to declare his attainment (aññā), he recited the verse: "Whose taints are exhausted" (Yassāsavā parikkhīṇā).

In that verse, "Whose taints are exhausted" means for that supreme person, the four taints such as the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava) are completely exhausted, destroyed by the Noble Path. "Unattached to nutriment" (āhāre ca anissito) means that person is not dependent on, does not cling to, and does not enter into nutriment through the supports of craving and views. This statement is merely an illustration. In this verse, by taking nutriment as the head, the four requisites should also be understood as included. Alternatively, the word "nutriment" here should be known as a synonym for requisites. In the phrase "Void and signless" (suññato animitto ca), the undirected liberation (appaṇihita-vimokkha) is also included. These three are names for Nibbāna itself. Nibbāna is called "void" (suñña) because of the absence of greed and so on; being liberated from them, it is called "void liberation" (suññata-vimokkha). Likewise, it is called "signless" (animitta) because of the absence of signs of greed and so on, and the absence of signs of formations (saṅkhāra-nimitta); being liberated from them, it is called "signless liberation" (animitta-vimokkha). It is called "undirected" (appaṇihita) because of the absence of longings for greed and so on; being liberated from those longings, it is called "undirected liberation" (appaṇihita-vimokkha). For one who dwells making that Nibbāna his object through the power of the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti), these three kinds of liberation are his range (gocara). "Like the track of birds in the sky, his path is hard to follow" (ākāseva sakuṇtānaṃ, padaṃ tassa durannayaṃ) means: just as it is impossible to know of birds flying in the sky that "they went treading with their feet in this place, they went striking with their breasts in this place, with their heads in this place, or with their wings in this place," even so, it is impossible to make known of such a monk that "he went by such a path to the state of hell and so on."

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Vijaya is finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Eraka

"Sensual pleasures are suffering, Eraka" (dukkhā kāmā eraka) is the verse of the Venerable Elder Eraka. How did it arise? This Elder Eraka had also made a resolution under previous Buddhas and accumulated merits in various births. In the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha, he was reborn in a respectable family. Upon reaching the age of discretion, one day he saw the Teacher and, with a confident mind, not finding anything suitable to give to the Teacher, he thought, "Indeed, I will perform merit which is the essence of the body." He cleared the path where the Teacher would travel and made it level. The Teacher [traveled] on the path thus prepared by him...
244:
...proceeded. Seeing the Blessed One there, with a confident mind, he paid homage and, raising his hands in salutation with a faithful heart, he stood without letting go of the joy (pīti) having the Buddha as its object until the Blessed One had passed beyond the range of sight.

Due to that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the celestial world. Performing merits repeatedly and wandering only in happy destinies (sugati), in this Buddha-dispensation, he was reborn in Sāvatthī as the son of a distinguished householder. He was named Eraka. He was handsome, beautiful, pleasing, and endowed with supreme skill in various duties. His parents brought a maiden suitable in terms of family, appearance, conduct, age, and skill, and performed the marriage ceremony.

Living in the house cohabiting with that woman, because he was in his final existence, his mind became agitated (saṃvigga) concerning saṃsāra due to some cause of spiritual urgency (saṃvega-vatthu). He went to the Teacher, heard the Dhamma, gained faith, and went forth. The Teacher gave him a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). Having taken the meditation subject, after a few days had passed, he lived overcome by dissatisfaction (ukkaṇṭhā). Then the Teacher, knowing the movement of his mind, spoke the verse "Sensual pleasures are suffering, Eraka" by way of advice.

When Eraka heard that verse, he thought, "I have done what is improper. Having taken a meditation subject from such a Teacher, I have lived letting go of that meditation subject and being full of wrong thoughts (micchā-vitakka)." Feeling spiritual urgency (saṃvega), he applied himself to insight (vipassanā) and before long attained Arahatship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

'Having crossed a small river, the Visionary One was going to the forest; I saw that Fully Enlightened One, Siddhattha, endowed with noble marks.
Taking a hoe and a basket, I made that path level; having paid homage to the Teacher, I gladdened my own heart.
In the ninety-four aeons since I performed that deed, I do not know of any unhappy destiny; this is the fruit of giving a path.
In the fifty-seventh aeon, I was a ruler of people, a leader of men named Suppabuddha.
My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha's bidding has been done.'

Having become an Arahat, wishing to declare his attainment, he repeated the very verse spoken by the Blessed One:
'Eraka, sensual pleasures are suffering. Eraka, sensual pleasures are not happiness. Eraka, he who desires sensual pleasures desires suffering. Eraka, he who does not desire sensual pleasures does not desire suffering.'

In that verse, 'Sensual pleasures are suffering' (dukkhā kāmā) means both the objects of sensual pleasure (vatthu-kāma) and the defilement of sensual pleasure (kilesa-kāma) are suffering because they are the cause of suffering, and because they are suffering due to change (vipariṇāma-dukkha) and suffering of saṃsāra. They are unbearable and produce suffering. Indeed, the Blessed One has said: 'Sensual pleasures provide little gratification, much suffering, and much despair; the danger in them is great,' and so forth.
245:
"Eraka, sensual pleasures are suffering; Eraka, sensual pleasures are not happiness. Eraka, whoever desires sensual pleasures, desires suffering. Eraka, whoever does not desire sensual pleasures, does not desire suffering." The Elder repeated this very verse spoken by the Blessed One.

In that verse, "dukkhā kāmā" means that these objective sensual pleasures (vatthukāma) and defiled sensual desires (kilesakāma) are suffering because they are the basis of suffering, and because they have the nature of the suffering of change (vipariṇāma-dukkha) and the suffering of the round of rebirths (saṃsāra-dukkha); they are difficult to endure and produce suffering. Thus, it was said: "Sensual pleasures provide little enjoyment, much suffering, and much despair; the danger in them is even greater," and so on. With the word "Eraka," the Blessed One first addressed him, and later the Elder spoke of himself by name. "Na sukhā kāmā" means that these sensual pleasures are not happiness to one who knows (their faults), but to one who does not know, they appear as happiness. As it was said: "He who sees happiness as suffering, and sees suffering as a thorn," and so on. "Yo kāme kāmayati, dukkhaṃ so kāmayati" means that whatever being desires objective sensual pleasures with defiled sensual desire, that desiring is suffering for him because it is accompanied by burning in the present, and because it is the cause of suffering in the lower realms and the cause of suffering in the round of rebirths in the future. Objective sensual pleasures are the basis of suffering. Thus, it means that he desires the nature of suffering, the cause of suffering, and the basis of suffering. The other (following) verse-line is spoken to make that same meaning known by way of the opposite; therefore, the meaning of that verse should be understood by the reversal of the meaning previously stated.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Eraka is finished.
246:
## 4. Mettajittheragāthāvaṇṇanā
"Namo hi tassa bhagavato" and so on—this is the verse of the Venerable Mettaji Thera. What is its origin? It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Anomadassī, he was born in a good family, and upon reaching maturity, he became very devoted to the Dispensation. He built a railing (vedikā) with bricks around the Bodhi tree and performed the task of plastering it with lime. The Blessed One gave him a blessing (anumodanā). Due to that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the deva world, and after performing merits repeatedly and wandering through the worlds of devas and humans, he was born as the son of a certain Brahmin in the Magadha country during the time of our Buddha's arising; he was named Mettaji.

When he reached maturity, he saw the danger in sensual pleasures and went forth as an ascetic. While living in the forest, he heard of the Buddha's arising and, prompted by past causes, went to the Blessed One and asked questions concerning the process of existence (pavattinivatti) and its cessation. When the Blessed One answered the questions, he gained faith, ordained, developed insight (vipassanā), and attained Arahantship. This matter is stated in the Apadāna as follows:

"I once built a railing for the Bodhi tree of the Sage Anomadassī; having offered a mass of lime, I performed the work with my own hands.
Seeing that well-performed deed, Anomadassī, the Best of Men, the Teacher, standing in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks, spoke these verses:
'By this deed of plastering with lime, and by his volition and aspiration, after enjoying prosperity, he will make an end of suffering.
I have a bright complexion, and with a one-pointed and well-concentrated mind, I bear my final body in the Dispensation of the Perfectly Enlightened One.
One hundred aeons ago from this Bhadda-kappa, there was a Wheel-turning King named Sabbaghana, possessed of great power.
My defilements have been burnt away... pe... the Buddha's Dispensation has been fulfilled.'"

Having attained Arahantship, wishing to praise the Blessed One, he spoke this verse:
"Homage to that Blessed One, the glorious son of the Sakyans; by Him, the Supreme One, this supreme Dhamma has been well taught."

In that verse, "namo" means let there be homage. The word "hi" is a mere particle. "Tassa" refers to that Blessed One who, having fulfilled the thirty perfections, destroyed all defilements and penetrated the peerless Perfect Enlightenment (sammāsambodhi). He is called "Sakyaputta" because he is the son of the great King Suddhodana, a Sakyan king. He is called "Sirīmato" (glorious) because he is endowed with the glory of the attainment of merit (puñña-sampatti) which is not shared with others, or with the glory of the noble physical body (rūpakāya) surrounded by all beings, or with the glory of the Dhamma-body (dhammakāya) consisting of the supramundane states such as the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) and right efforts (sammappadhāna).
247:
In that verse, 'Namo' means homage. 'Hi' is merely a particle. 'Tassa' refers to that Blessed One who, having fulfilled the thirty perfections and destroyed all defilements, realized the incomparable Supreme Enlightenment; He is called 'Sakyaputta' because He is the son of the Sakyan King (King Suddhodana). He is called 'Sirīmā' (the Glorious One) because He is endowed with unique merit and possessed of the supreme splendor of the physical body (rūpakāya) and the splendor of the Dhamma body (dhammakāya). The meaning is: 'May there be homage to that Blessed One, the Sakyan son, the Glorious One; I pay homage to that Blessed One.' 'Tena' means 'by that Blessed One.' The word 'ayaṃ' refers to the Dhamma being manifest to oneself. 'Aggappattena' means (the Blessed One) who has reached the highest omniscience, or the state of being the most noble and supreme through all virtues. 'Aggadhammo' means the supreme ninefold supramundane Dhamma (navavidhalokuttaradhamma) which is well-expounded and unerringly shown.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Venerable Mettaji is Finished.

## 5. Commentary on the Verses of Venerable Cakkhupāla

'Andhohaṃ hatanettosmi' and so forth is the verse of the Venerable Cakkhupāla. What is its origin? This Elder, too, having made an earnest aspiration (adhikāra) under previous Buddhas and performing meritorious deeds in various births, was born into a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha. Upon reaching the age of discretion, when the great festival of honoring the stupa was being held after the Blessed One's Parinibbāna, he took an umā flower and offered it to the stupa. Due to that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the celestial realm and, after performing repeated merits, wandered through the realms of devas and humans. In this present Buddha's era, he was born in Sāvatthī as the son of a householder named Mahāsuvaṇṇa. They named the boy 'Pāla'. While his mother was running and wandering here and there, she obtained another son. The parents named that son 'Cūḷapāla' and called the elder one 'Mahāpāla'. When they reached maturity, they were bound by the ties of household life. At that time, the Teacher was residing at the Jetavana monastery in Sāvatthī. Then, Mahāpāla went to the monastery along with lay devotees who were going to Jetavana. Having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he gained faith. Entrusting the burden of the household business to his younger brother, he himself entered the monkhood. Having received full ordination (upasampadā), he lived for five years in the presence of his teachers and preceptors. After completing the rains retreat and performing the Pavāraṇā ceremony, he took a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) from the Teacher and...
248:
(Venerable Cakkhupāla), having obtained about sixty companion monks of similar practice, sought a suitable place for meditation with them. Depending on a certain border village, he resided in a forest leaf-hut built and offered by the lay devotees of that village, and practiced the Dhamma of a recluse. An eye disease arose in that Elder. A physician prepared and gave him medicine. The Elder did not follow the instructions given by the physician. Therefore, his eye disease worsened. The Elder, reflecting that "The stilling of the disease of defilements is more noble for me than the stilling of the eye disease," ignored the eye disease and became intensely devoted only to insight meditation (vipassanā). While he was striving in meditation, his eyes failed and his defilements were destroyed simultaneously. He became a dry-insight Arahant (sukkhavipassaka). Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

"When the Blessed One Siddhattha, honored by the world and worthy of receiving offerings, had attained Parinibbāna, there was a great festival for the stupa.

While the festival for the Great Sage Siddhattha was proceeding, I took an umā flower and offered it upon the stupa.

In the ninety-four aeons since I offered that flower, I have not known a woeful state; this is the fruit of honoring the stupa.

In the ninth aeon from this, there were eighty-five powerful wheel-turning monarchs (cakkavatti) named Somadeva.

My defilements are burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out."

Later, while the Elder remained at the monastery due to his eye disease, the lay devotees saw the monks who had gone to the village for alms and asked, "Why has the Elder not come?" Having heard the reason, they were overcome with grief. Bringing alms-food, they said, "Venerable Sir, do not worry about anything; now we ourselves will bring alms-food and attend to you," and they did so. The monks, too, established in the Elder's advice, attained Arahantship before long. After completing the rains retreat and performing the Pavāraṇā ceremony, they said, "Venerable Sir, we will go to Sāvatthī to pay homage to the Teacher."

The Elder said, "I am weak and blind, and the road is full of danger. There will be peril for you who travel with me. You go first. Having gone, pay homage to the Teacher and the Great Elders on my behalf. To Cūḷapāla..."
249:
“Please send a man after telling him of my condition,” he said. Those monks, though they repeatedly entreated him, did not get permission to go [with him]. Saying “Very well,” they accepted, put away their lodgings, took leave of the lay devotees, and in due course went to Jetavana. They paid homage to the Teacher and the Great Elders on behalf of that Elder. On the second day, while wandering for alms in Sāvatthī, they told Cūḷapāla of that matter. Cūḷapāla said, “Venerable sirs, this is my nephew named Pālita; I will send him.” They said, “The road is dangerous; it is not suitable for a layman to go alone. Therefore, he must be ordained.” So they ordained him and sent him forth.

That novice (sāmaṇera) in due course went to the Elder, announced himself, and while leading the Elder back, heard the voice of a woman gathering wood and singing in a forest area near a certain village. His mind became infatuated; he let go of the end of the staff and said, “Venerable sir, please stay here for a moment until I return.” He went to that woman and there fell into a breach of virtue (sīla). The Elder thought, “Just now I heard the sound of a woman’s song, and the novice is taking a long time; surely he must have fallen into a breach of virtue.” The novice returned and said, “Venerable sir, let us go.” The Elder asked, “What is it, have you become a wicked person?” The novice remained silent, and even when asked repeatedly, he did not speak.

The Elder said, “I have no need for my staff to be held by a wicked person like you. You may go.” Again, the novice said, “Venerable sir, the road is very dangerous, and you are blind. How will you go?” The Elder, wishing to show this meaning, said, “O fool, even if I must lie here and die, or roll back and forth, there is no such thing as traveling with a wicked person like you,” and he recited this verse:

“I am blind, with destroyed eyes, having entered a difficult journey.
Even lying down, I will go, but not with a wicked companion.”

In that verse, ‘Andho’ means one whose eyes are defective. ‘Hatanetto’ means one with destroyed eyes. By this, he distinguishes the state of blindness already mentioned, saying, ‘I am blind because my eyes were destroyed through the failure of effort (payoga-vipatti), not because I was born blind.’ Alternatively, this word ‘Andho’...”
250:
...as in the words of the Majjhima Nikāya, ‘He supports his aged, blind parents,’ it shows the deficiency of the physical eye (maṃsa-cakkhu). It is not like the words in the Udāna, ‘All these wanderers are blind and sightless,’ or in the Aṅguttara Nikāya, ‘The blind, the one-eyed, and the two-eyed,’ which show the deficiency of the eye of wisdom (paññā-cakkhu). To show this, he said, ‘I am one with destroyed eyes.’ By this, he shows blindness in the literal sense (mukhya). ‘Entered a difficult journey’ (kantāraddhāna-pakkhando) means having entered a long road in a desolate forest; it does not mean having entered the journey of saṃsāra, the thicket of the wilderness of rebirth (jāti-kantāra), etc. For this Elder stood having transcended such a difficult journey. ‘Even lying down’ (sayamānopi) means even while lying; even if he had to crawl and roll on the ground with his chest and knees when his feet could no longer carry him, he would go. ‘Not with a wicked companion’ (na sahāyena pāpena) should be understood as: he will not go together with such a wicked person as a companion.

Hearing this, the other (Pālita) was struck with spiritual urgency (saṃvega). Thinking, ‘Indeed, I have committed a grave and rash deed,’ he wept with arms outstretched and fled into the forest thicket. Then, due to the power of the Elder’s virtue, the Sakka’s Paṇḍukambala stone throne showed signs of heat. Knowing the reason, Sakka went to the Elder, making himself known as if he were a man going to Sāvatthī. Taking the end of the staff, he shortened the path and brought the Elder to Sāvatthī that very evening. In the Jetavana monastery at Sāvatthī, he seated the Elder on a wooden bench in the leaf-hut built by Cūḷapālita. Then, making it known in the guise of a friend that the Elder had arrived, he departed. Cūḷapālita also attended upon the Elder with great respect for the rest of his life.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Cakkhupāla Thera is finished.

## 6. The Commentary on the Verses of Khaṇḍasumana Thera

“Having given a single flower” is the verse of the Venerable Khaṇḍasumana Thera. What is its origin? It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was born into a good family. When he reached the age of discretion and the Teacher had attained Parinibbāna, he performed a great offering by surrounding the stupa with sandalwood railings. Due to that meritorious deed, he enjoyed grand prosperity among devas and humans. In the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, he was born into a householder’s family. When the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna, while the King was making offerings of flowers to the golden stupa, he could not find any flowers. Seeing a single jasmine flower of a certain kind, with a great price...
251:
He made known his arrival in the guise of a friend of Elder Cakkhupāla and departed. Cūḷapālita also served that Elder for the rest of his life. Thus, the conclusion should be noted. The commentary (vaṇṇanā) on the verses of Elder Cakkhupāla is finished.

## 6. Khaṇḍasumanattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

The verse beginning with "Ekapupphaṃ cajitvāna" is that of the Venerable Elder Khaṇḍasumana. The account of his life is as follows: This Elder was born into a wealthy family during the time of Kassapa Buddha. When the Buddha attained Parinibbāna, the King organized a flower offering for the golden stupa. Unable to find flowers, he saw a single jasmine flower (khaṇḍasumana), bought it at a high price, and offered it at the stupa. In doing so, he experienced great joy and satisfaction (pīti-somanassa). Due to that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the deva realm and enjoyed heavenly bliss for eighty koṭis (800 million) of years. In this Buddha's era, he was born into the Malla royal family in the city of Pāvā.

At the time of his birth, sugar crystals (khaṇḍasakkharā) and jasmine flowers (sumanapuppha) appeared in the house; therefore, they named him "Khaṇḍasumana". When he reached maturity, while the Blessed One was staying in Cunda's mango grove in Pāvā, he approached Him, heard the Dhamma, gained faith, and ordained. Practicing insight meditation (vipassanā), he soon became an Arahat endowed with the six supernormal knowledges (abhiññā). This is stated in the Apadāna:

"The Victor named Padumuttara, the Foremost of the World, the Bull among Men, the Fully Enlightened One, attained Parinibbāna like a great mass of fire being extinguished.

After the Great Hero attained Parinibbāna, a magnificent stupa was built; people from afar came to pay homage at the noble and supreme house of relics.

With a clear mind and joyful heart, I made a sandalwood pedestal; at that time, the structure of the stupa appeared clearly, befitting a stupa.

Whether being reborn in the state of a deva or a human, I have never seen a lowly state; this is the fruit of my past deed.

One thousand five hundred aeons ago from this Bhadda-kappa, there were eight powerful Wheel-turning Kings named Samatta.

My defilements have been burnt away... (omission) ...the Buddha's teaching has been carried out."

Having attained Arahatship, while reflecting on his past lives, he saw that his meritorious deed of offering the jasmine flower in that life was the cause of his heavenly attainments and a strong support for Nibbāna. Desiring to express this through an inspired utterance (udāna), he recited this verse:

"Having offered a single flower, I enjoyed bliss in the heavens for eighty koṭis of years; by the remainder, I am now extinguished (attained Nibbāna)."
252:
In that verse, "ekapupphaṃ" means a single flower; here, it refers to a jasmine flower (sumanapuppha). "Cajitvāna" means having given away or offered as an act of worship to the Buddha's stupa. "Asīti vassakoṭiyo" means eighty koṭis (800 million) of years by human reckoning. This phrase is in the accusative case (dutiyā vibhatti) in the sense of continuous duration (accanta-saṃyoga). It should be understood as referring to repeated births in Tāvatiṃsa, the second of the six sensual heavens. Therefore, the plural "saggesu" (in the heavens) is used because of the repeated births in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. "Paricāretvā" means having enjoyed pleasure by engaging the five senses in objects such as visible forms, or having oneself served and attended to by celestial nymphs. "Sesakenamhi nibbuto" refers to the volition (cetanā) which was the remainder from the merit of offering the flower—merit that gives rise to worldly attainments—and which served as a support for the cessation of the round of rebirth (vivaṭṭūpanissaya). This is said because the volitions that arose before and after the flower offering were numerous. Alternatively, "sesakena" means that while the result of that meritorious deed was not yet exhausted, he attained Nibbāna through the extinction of defilements (kilesa-parinibbāna). By this, he shows that the very existence (attabhāva) in which he realized Arahatship, being his final existence, is also a result of that merit. In other places too, it is stated with this meaning: "by the remainder of the result of that deed".

## Khaṇḍasumanattheragāthāvaṇṇanā is finished.

## 7. Tissattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

The verse beginning with "Hitvā satapalaṃ kaṃsaṃ" is that of the Venerable Elder Tissa. What is the background story? This Elder also had performed meritorious services (adhikāra) under previous Buddhas. In the time of Vipassī Buddha, he was born into a family of cart-makers. When he reached maturity, one day he saw the Buddha and, with a clear and faithful mind, made a plank out of a piece of sandalwood and offered it to the Buddha. The Buddha made use of that plank. Due to that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the deva realm and wandered between the deva and human worlds. In this Buddha's era, he was born into the royal family of the city of Roruva. When he reached maturity and his father passed away, he was established in the kingship. He became "unseen friends" with King Bimbisāra and sent him gifts such as rubies, pearls, and garments. To him, King Bimbisāra...
253:
At the time of this Buddha's appearance, he was born into the royal family in the city of Roruva. When the prince came of age and his father passed away, he ascended to the kingship and became an unseen friend of King Bimbisāra, sending him gifts such as rubies, pearls, and garments. King Bimbisāra, wishing to return the favor, had the life and conduct of the Buddha painted on an exquisite cloth and the Law of Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda) inscribed on a golden plate, and sent them to him.

When the king saw these gifts, due to his past merits (adhikāra) performed under previous Buddhas and because this was his final existence, he gazed upon the Buddha’s conduct on the cloth and the sequence of Dependent Origination on the golden plate. Contemplating the processes of arising and ceasing in Saṃsāra and taking the sequence of the Dispensation (Sāsana) to heart, spiritual urgency (saṃvega) arose within him. Thinking, "I have seen the likeness of the Blessed One, and I have understood a portion of the sequence of the Dispensation; sense pleasures are full of suffering and full of tribulation; what is the use of living in a household now?", he renounced the kingdom, shaved off his hair and beard, donned saffron-dyed robes, and ordained for the sake of the Blessed One. Taking an earthen bowl, just like King Pukkusāti, he departed from the city while the great multitude wept. He traveled by stages to the city of Rājagaha, approached the Blessed One who was staying at the Sappasoṇḍikapabbhāra, paid homage, and sat in a suitable place.

The Blessed One taught the Dhamma. Having heard the Dhamma teaching, he took up a subject of meditation for insight (Vipassanā) and, living with diligent effort, he developed insight and attained Arahatship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

"In the past, I was a vehicle maker, well-trained in woodwork. Having made a sandalwood plank, I offered it to the Friend of the World (Lokabandhu).

This celestial mansion of mine, well-fashioned of gold, shines brightly. Elephant-vehicles, horse-vehicles, and divine vehicles stand ready.

Palaces and palanquins arise according to my wish. My wealth is inexhaustible; this is the fruit of the offering of the plank.

In the ninety-one aeons since I gave that plank, I have known no miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of the offering of the plank.

In the fifty-seventh aeon, there were four wheel-turning kings (Cakkavatti) named Nimmitā, endowed with the seven treasures and possessed of great power.

My defilements are burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out."

Having attained Arahatship, wishing to express his practice through a verse of inspiration (Udāna), he recited this verse:

"Having abandoned the golden bowl weighing a hundred palas and adorned with a hundred streaks, I have taken an earthen bowl; this is my second consecration."

In that verse, 'hitvā' means having abandoned. 'Satapalaṃ' refers to that golden bowl which weighs a hundred palas; thus, it means a golden bowl of a hundred palas in measure. 'Kaṃsaṃ' means a dish or bowl. 'Sovaṇṇaṃ' means made of gold. 'Satarājikaṃ' means being exquisite due to the decorations around the rim and being adorned with various streaks and many markings...
254:
“Having abandoned the golden bowl weighing a hundred palas and adorned with many streaks of color, I have taken an earthen bowl; this is my second consecration.” Thus he recited the verse.

In that verse, 'hitvā' means having renounced. 'Satapalaṃ' means that which weighs a hundred palas; it refers to the golden bowl of a hundred palas in measure. 'Kaṃsaṃ' means a bowl (dish). 'Sovaṇṇaṃ' means made of gold. 'Satarājikaṃ' means being full of various markings, both because of the exquisite decorations on the rim and the beauty of various colored streaks. 'Aggahiṃ mattikāpattaṃ' means that after previously eating from such a precious golden vessel, he now follows the advice of the Buddhas, saying: “Now I have discarded that and taken a bowl made of clay; oh, how good! I have well-practiced the conduct of the Noble Ones (Ariyas).” By praising the bowl, he expresses his joy in renouncing the kingdom and entering the monkhood. Therefore, he said, “This is my second consecration.” Taking into account the first royal consecration, this entering into monkhood is my second consecration. Indeed, that royal consecration was defiled by lust and so on, accompanied by danger and anxiety, associated with harm, linked with suffering, and low; whereas this [ordination] is the opposite of that—it is supreme and sublime. This is the meaning.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Tissa is finished.

## 8. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Abhaya

The verse beginning with “Rūpaṃ disvā sati muṭṭhāti” is the verse of the Venerable Abhaya Thera. What is its origin? This Venerable Abhaya also had performed merits (adhikāra) under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit that is a supporting condition for liberation (vivaṭṭa) in various births. In the time of Sumedha Buddha, he was born into a good family, and when he came of age, he saw Sumedha Buddha one day and, with a devout heart, made an offering of Salala flowers. Due to that meritorious deed, he was reborn among the devas and, performing merits repeatedly, he wandered only in the happy realms (sugati). In this Buddha's appearance, he was born into a Brahmin family in Sāvatthī and received the name Abhaya. When he came of age, being urged by his past merits, he went to the monastery one day, heard the Dhamma teaching of the Teacher, gained faith, and ordained. Having performed the preliminary duties, he lived practicing the work of insight (Vipassanā). Then, one day...
255:
When entering the village for alms, he saw a woman who was adorned and decorated. Due to improper attention (ayoniso manasikāra), intense lust arose in him based on her appearance. That monk returned to the monastery and, rebuking his own mind, thought: "Defilements have arisen in me who looked at a visible object with a lapse of mindfulness; I have done what is improper." At that very moment, he developed insight (vipassanā) and attained the fruit of Arahantship. This matter is stated in the Apadāna as follows:

"The Buddha named Sumedha, the Unconquered, the Self-Become, desiring to cultivate seclusion, entered the great forest.
Seeing a salala tree in bloom, I wove a wreath and offered it to the Buddha Sumedha, the Leader of the World, in his very presence.
Because I offered that flower thirty thousand aeons ago, I have never known a woeful rebirth; this is the fruit of offering to the Buddha.
Nineteen aeons ago, there were sixteen Cakkavatti kings named Sunimmita, endowed with the seven treasures and great power.
My defilements are burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled."

Upon attaining Arahantship, by illustrating the arising of defilements in himself, he wished to show: "For one who follows the way of defilements, there is no opportunity to raise one's head from the suffering of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa-dukkha). I, however, no longer follow them." Thus, he spoke this verse:

"Seeing a form, mindfulness is lost, for one who attends to a pleasant sign;
With a lustful mind, one feels, and remains clinging to it;
His taints (āsavas) increase, leading to the root of existence."

In that verse, "rūpaṃ" means a desirable visible object, which in this context refers to a woman's appearance. "Disvā" means seeing with the eye and grasping that visible object by noting the major and minor features through the eye-door. "Sati muṭṭhā" means the disappearance of mindfulness that was occurring as "foulness" (asubha) regarding the body which is of a foul nature. To show how mindfulness is lost upon seeing a visible object, he said: "piyaṃ nimittaṃ manasikaroto" (for one who attends to a pleasant sign). Making a pleasant sign of the object that has appeared, such as "it is beautiful, it is pleasant"...
256:
The construction is: for one who attends with improper attention, mindfulness is lost. Being in such a state, "with a lustful mind, one feels," meaning that with a mind thoroughly stained by lust, one experiences and delights in that visible object. While delighting, "one remains clinging to it," meaning that by clinging, one swallows that object, becomes bound by it, and continues to exist in it. For such a person, "his taints increase, leading to the root of existence," meaning the four taints such as the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava), which have the nature of leading to the state of being the root or cause of existence in saṃsāra, increase more and more for that person; they do not decrease. "In my case, however, by standing in reflection (paṭisaṅkhāna), developing insight, and penetrating the Truths, those four taints have been abandoned without remainder and exhausted through the sequence of the Paths"—this is the meaning.

## The Commentary on the Verse of Venerable Abhaya is finished.

## 9. Commentary on the Verse of Venerable Uttiya

The verse beginning with "Saddaṃ sutvā sati muṭṭhā" is that of the Venerable Uttiya. As for the background story: This monk had also performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit that serves as a powerful support for liberation (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) in various lives. In the time of Sumedha Buddha, he was born into a good family and, upon reaching maturity, saw the Teacher one day. With a mind full of faith, he prepared and offered a throne worthy of a Buddha in the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭī), spread with coverings and gonaka carpets.

Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, and in this Buddha-dispensation, he was born into the Sakyan royal family in Kapilavatthu and was named Uttiya. When he came of age, he saw the Buddha's majesty at the assembly of the Buddha's kinsmen, gained faith, and ordained. While practicing the duties of a recluse, he entered the city for alms one day. On the way, he heard the sound of a woman singing, and due to improper attention, desire and lust (chandarāga) arose for that sound. However, by the power of reflection, he suppressed that lust, returned to the monastery, and being moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega), sat in his daytime quarters. At that very moment, he developed insight and attained Arahantship. This matter is stated in the Apadāna as follows:

"To the Sumedha Buddha, the Great One of the world, endowed with virtues,
I offered a throne together with a covering.
At that time, that throne became endowed with the seven treasures.
Knowing my intention, it appeared for me at all times.
Because I offered that throne thirty thousand aeons ago,
I have never reached a woeful rebirth; this is the fruit of offering a throne.
Twenty thousand aeons ago, there were three Cakkavatti kings
named Suvaṇṇābha, endowed with the seven treasures and great power.
My defilements are burnt away...
I have followed the teaching of the Buddha."

Thus it is said (in the Apadāna). That Elder, having reached Arahantship, by illustrating the arising of defilements in himself...
257:
“I offered a throne, complete with upper and lower coverings, to the Blessed One Sumedha, the Foremost of the World, the Such-like One. At that time, that throne was endowed with the seven jewels. Knowing my intention, it appeared for me at all times. Thirty thousand aeons ago, I gave that throne. Due to this fruit of offering the throne, I have never known a woeful state. Twenty thousand aeons ago, there were three powerful Universal Monarchs endowed with the seven jewels, named Suvaṇṇābha. My defilements are burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.”

Upon reaching the fruit of Arahantship, by showing the arising of his own defilements, he wished to show: “For one who does not loathe defilements, there is no lifting of the head (liberation) from the suffering of the round of rebirths; but I indeed loathe those defilements.” Thus, he spoke this verse:

“Having heard a sound, one who is muddled in mindfulness and attends to a pleasant sign, experiences it with a lustful mind and remains clinging to it. For him, the taints (āsavas) that lead to the round of rebirths (saṃsāra) increase.”

In that verse, “saddaṃ” means a pleasant sound-object (saddārammaṇa). “Saṃsāraupagāmino” means:

“The continuous and uninterrupted succession of the aggregates (khandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense bases (āyatanas) is called saṃsāra.”

Because they are the cause of and lead to this round of rebirths, they are called “saṃsāraupagāmi.” There is also a variant reading “saṃsārūpagāmino.” The rest is as explained in the preceding verse.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Uttiya Thera is finished.
258:
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Uttiya, the ninth section of the Tenth Chapter of the Book of Ones, is finished.

## 10. (Second) Commentary on the Verses of Devasabha Thera

“Endowed with the Right Efforts” (Sammapadhānasampanno) is the verse of the Venerable Devasabha Thera. What is its origin? This elder also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulated wholesome roots that were powerful conditions for the fruit of Arahantship in various lives. In the time of the Blessed One Sikhī, he was born into a good family. Upon reaching maturity, one day he saw the Blessed One Sikhī and, with a confident mind, made an offering of Bandhujīvaka flowers. Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans. When our Buddha appeared, he was born into the Sakyan royal family in Kapilavatthu and was named Devasabha.

When he reached maturity, he saw the Buddha's power when the Teacher came to settle the dispute concerning the Rohiṇī River. With a confident mind, he established himself in the refuges. Later, while the Teacher was staying at the Nigrodhārāma monastery, he approached the Teacher, gained faith, and went forth. Having performed the preliminary duties and practicing insight meditation (vipassanā), he soon attained Arahantship. This is stated in the Apadāna:

“Like the moon, stainless and pure, exceptionally clear and untroubled,
With craving for the three types of existence destroyed, having crossed over the entanglement in the world.
To the Sage who brings peace to the people, the best of those who help others cross,
Meditating in the forest, one-pointed and well-concentrated, (I saw him).
Having strung Bandhujīvaka flowers with a thread, I offered them to the Buddha Sikhī, the Kinsman of the World.
Thirty-one aeons ago from this Bhadda-kappa, I performed that act of offering flowers. Because of that merit, I have never known a woeful state; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.
Seven aeons ago from this, there was a powerful Universal Monarch named Samantacakkhu, who had a great following.
My defilements are burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.”

Upon reaching Arahantship, based on the bliss of liberation he had attained, with a sense of joy and gladness, he uttered this inspired verse (udāna):

“Endowed with the Right Efforts, having the Foundations of Mindfulness as his range,
Covered with the flowers of liberation, the one without taints will attain Parinibbāna.”

(The meaning is: The monk who possesses the four Right Efforts, who has the four Foundations of Mindfulness as his object of focus, and who is adorned with the flower of the fruit of Arahantship, being free from taints, will attain Parinibbāna.)

In that verse, “sammapadhānasampanno” means possessing the four Right Efforts, having completed the necessary tasks through those four Right Efforts. “Satipaṭṭhānagocaro” means that the four Foundations of Mindfulness, such as contemplation of the body, are the range of objects for that person; it means having a mind well-established in the four Foundations of Mindfulness. The fruit of Arahantship, which has a supreme fragrance due to the beauty of supramundane qualities, is called “flowers.” Because he is well-adorned in every way with those flowers of the fruit of Arahantship, he is called “vimuttikusumasañchanno.” “Parinibbissatyanāsavo” means that such a well-practiced monk will soon become one free from taints and will attain Parinibbāna.
259:
Venerable Devasabha Thera, having attained the fruit of Arahantship and being filled with joy and satisfaction based on the bliss of Arahantship he had attained, uttered this inspired utterance (udāna):

“Endowed with the right efforts, having the foundations of mindfulness as his domain,
Covered with the flowers of liberation, the taintless one will attain final Nibbāna.”

In that verse, ‘sammappadhānasampanno’ means one who is endowed with the fourfold right efforts, having completed the tasks to be done through those four right efforts. ‘Satipaṭṭhānagocaro’ means one for whom the four foundations of mindfulness, such as mindfulness of the body, are the domain or the place of occurrence; it means one whose mind is well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness. Because of the beauty of supramundane qualities, the fruit of Arahantship itself, which is supremely fragrant, is called ‘flowers’; being thoroughly and well-adorned and decorated with those flowers of the fruit of Arahantship, he is called ‘vimuttikusumasañchanno’. ‘Parinibbisatyanāsavo’ means that a bhikkhu who practices well in this way will soon become free from taints and will attain Parinibbāna through the Nibbāna element with residue and the Nibbāna element without residue. This indeed was the Elder’s declaration of final knowledge (aññābyākaraṇa).

## The Commentary on the (Second) Devasabha Thera’s Verses is finished.

## The Commentary on the Tenth Group (Dasama Vagga) is finished.

## 11. Ekādasama Vagga

## 1. Commentary on the Verses of Venerable Belaṭṭhānika Thera

The verse beginning with “Hitvā gihittaṃ anavositatto” is that of the Venerable Belaṭṭhānika Thera. What is its origin? This Elder was also one who had performed meritorious deeds (adhikāra) under previous Buddhas. Thirty-one aeons ago from this present Bhadda Kappa, during the time of the Blessed One Vessabhū, he was born into a Brahmin family. Upon reaching maturity, he became proficient in the Brahmin arts, renounced the household life to become an ascetic, and wandered about surrounded by a group of ascetics. One day, upon seeing the Blessed One Vessabhū, he was filled with joy and satisfaction. With a mind of devotion based on the perfection of the Teacher’s wisdom, he offered flowers dedicated to that wisdom.

Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans. In this Buddha’s era, he was born into a Brahmin family in Sāvatthī and received the name Belaṭṭhānika. When he reached the age of discretion, he heard the Dhamma of the Blessed One, gained faith, and ordained. Taking a subject of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna), he lived in the Kosala country. However, he became lazy, was prone to physical grooming, and possessed harsh speech. He did not apply his mind to the recluse’s duties. At that time, the Blessed One, seeing the maturity of Venerable Belaṭṭhānika’s knowledge, stirred him with this verse of instruction:

“Having abandoned the lay life but with unfinished business,
Plough-mouthed, gluttonous, and lazy,
Like a great hog fed on fodder,
The dullard enters the womb again and again.”

Upon seeing the Blessed One and hearing this verse, the Elder was struck with spiritual urgency (saṃvega). Because his knowledge had reached maturity, he developed insight (vipassanā) and soon attained Arahantship.
260:
When that young man reached the age of discretion, he heard the Dhamma teaching of the Blessed One, gained faith, and ordained. Taking a subject of meditation, he lived in a forest monastery in the Kosala country. However, he was lazy, fond of physical grooming, and had harsh speech; he did not apply his mind to the recluse’s duties. At that time, the Blessed One, seeing the maturity of his knowledge, stirred him with this verse of radiance:

“Having abandoned the lay life but with unfinished business, plough-mouthed, gluttonous, and lazy,
Like a great hog fed on fodder, that person of little wisdom undergoes rebirth again and again.”

Through this verse of radiance, the Buddha stirred him. Seeing the Blessed One as if he were sitting right in front of him and hearing that verse, he was struck with spiritual urgency (saṃvega). Because his knowledge had reached maturity, he practiced insight meditation and soon attained the fruit of Arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

“I saw the Blessed One Vessabhū, shining like a Kaṇikāra flower, sitting in a mountain cleft, illuminating all directions like the morning star.
Three young men, well-trained in their own arts, followed behind me carrying shoulder-poles.
The ascetic took seven flowers placed in a basket and offered them to the wisdom of the Blessed One Vessabhū.
Because I offered those flowers thirty-one aeons ago from this Bhadda Kappa, I have never known a woeful state; this is the fruit of honoring [the Buddha’s] wisdom.
Twenty-nine aeons ago, I was a powerful Cakkavatti king named Vipulābha, endowed with the seven treasures.
My defilements have been burnt away... the Buddha’s teaching has been completed.”

Upon attaining Arahantship, both to honor the Blessed One’s instruction and to declare his attainment of Arahantship by way of contrast, he recited that very same verse.
261:
In this verse, 'hitvā gihittaṃ' means renouncing the state of a householder and ordaining as a monk. 'Anavositatto' means having a task that is not appropriately completed; it refers to the state of being unfinished for one who ordains in the Dispensation (Sāsana) because the appropriate full understanding (pariññā) and so forth have not been finalized, meaning one whose duties are not yet done. Alternatively, 'anavositatto' means one who has not lived according to the sequence; one who has not practiced the life to be lived through the sequence of the seven purifications (visuddhi) and the four paths (magga), meaning one who has not lived in the ten noble dwellings (ariyavāsa). He is called 'mukhanangalī' (mouth-plough) because he possesses a plough called the mouth. It means one who digs himself up by using harsh speech toward others, just as one digs the earth with a plough. 'Odariko' means one who is devoted to the belly, intent on nourishing the stomach. 'Kusīto' means lazy, one who does not apply himself to meditation (bhāvanā).

To show the disadvantage of such a person, he said: "Like a great hog fed on fodder, the fool enters the womb again and again." The meaning of that verse has already been stated below. In this verse, just as the fool, due to the nature of having unfinished tasks despite being ordained, enters the womb again and again, a wise one like me does not. Being of the opposite nature to that fool, having reached the summit through right practice, I attain Parinibbāna. Thus, it should be understood that he declared his Arahatship through the method of contrast (vyatireka).

## The Commentary on the Verse of Belatthānika Thera is finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Verse of Setuccha Thera

The verse beginning with 'Mānena vañcitāse' is that of the Venerable Setuccha Thera. What is its origin? This Thera also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit that is a powerful support for liberation (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) in various births, was reborn in a respectable family during the time of Tissa Buddha. Upon reaching maturity, one day he saw the Blessed One Tissa and, with a heart full of faith, offered a very sweet jackfruit and a well-prepared coconut dish (nāḷikerasaḷava). Due to that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the deva world and, wandering between the worlds of devas and humans, was reborn as the son of a provincial king during the time of our Buddha's appearance. He was named Setuccha. When his father passed away, he was established in the kingship, but due to a lack of effort and energy (ussāhasatti), he failed in his royal duties. Consequently, the kingdom fell into the hands of others. Reaching a state of suffering, he felt spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and, while wandering through the countryside...
262:
...seeing the Blessed One, he approached Him, heard the Dhamma, gained faith, and ordained. While performing the preliminary practices (parikamma), he attained Arahatship on that very day. This is stated in the Apadāna:

"In the past, I gave fruit to the Blessed One Tissa; I also gave a coconut and a well-regarded snack. Having given that to the Buddha, to Tissa the Great Sage, I rejoice, being one who obtains desires, and I was reborn wherever I wished. Ninety-two aeons ago, I gave that gift; since then, I have not known a miserable rebirth. This is the fruit of the gift of fruit. Thirteen aeons ago, there was a king equal to Sakka (Inda), a Cakkavatti of great power, endowed with the seven treasures. My defilements are burnt away... (and so forth) ...I have followed the Buddha's teaching."

Upon reaching Arahatship, wishing to censure the defilements, he spoke this verse:

"People are deceived by conceit, they are being defiled among conditioned things; oppressed by gain and loss, they do not attain concentration."

In that verse, "mānena vañcitāse" means being deceived by the destruction of the treasure of merit through the power of self-exaltation and disparaging others, which arises from conceit such as "I am better." "Saṅkhāresu saṅkilissamānāse" means being defiled among conditioned things (saṅkhata-dhamma), both internal and external, such as the eye and so forth, and forms and so forth; it means falling into defilement through the power of craving and grasping, based on those objects, thinking "This is mine, this I am, this is my self." "Lābhālābhena mathitā" means being oppressed, crushed, and overcome by the attraction and repulsion (anunaya-paṭigha) that arise due to the gain and loss of requisites such as bowls and robes, or clothes and so forth. This is just an illustration; it should be understood that the remaining worldly conditions (lokadhamma) are also included here. "Samādhiṃ nādhigacchanti" means that such persons never find, obtain, or reach one-pointedness of mind (citt'ekaggatā) through the power of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā), because of the absence of qualities conducive to concentration and the presence of the opposite qualities. In this verse, just as the ignorant who are overcome by conceit and so forth do not attain concentration, the wise like me, who are not oppressed by worldly conditions, do attain concentration. Thus, it should be understood that he declared his Arahatship through the method of contrast (vyatireka).

## The Commentary on the Verse of Setuccha Thera is finished.

The verse beginning with "Na taṃ daḷhaṃ bandhanamāhu dhīrā" is that of the Venerable Bandhana Thera. This Thera also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, was a court official in the palace of a certain king during the time of Siddhattha Buddha. One day, seeing the Blessed One walking in the palace courtyard with his retinue, he felt faith and took Kaṇikāra flowers and offered them to the Sangha...
263:
Those without wisdom cannot attain concentration in this way. But those like me, who are not overwhelmed by the worldly conditions, do indeed attain concentration. Thus, it should be understood as a declaration of Arahantship (aññābyākaraṇa) by way of exclusion (vyatireka).

## The Commentary on the Verse of Elder Setuccha is finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Verse of Elder Bandhura

"I have no need for this" is the verse of the Venerable Elder Bandhura. What is its origin? This Elder, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, was a palace official in the inner court of a certain king during the time of Buddha Siddhattha. One day, seeing the Blessed One walking in the royal courtyard with his followers, he felt inspired and, taking Kaṇavera flowers, offered them to the Leader of the World and the Saṅgha. Due to that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the deva world and wandered only through happy states. In this Buddha's era, he was reborn as the son of a wealthy merchant in the city of Sīlavatī and was named Bandhura. When he reached maturity, he went to Sāvatthī on some business. There, he went to the monastery with some lay devotees, heard the Buddha's teaching, gained faith, and ordained. As his knowledge matured, he practiced insight meditation and soon attained Arahantship. This is stated in the Apadāna:

"The Blessed One named Siddhattha, the Chief of the World, the Best of Men, entered the city, surrounded by his disciples.
I was a recognized palace official in the king's inner court; sitting in the palace, I saw the Leader of the World.
Taking Kaṇavera flowers, I scattered them over the community of monks; having made a special offering to the Buddha, I scattered even more.
In the ninety-four aeons since I honored him with those flowers, I have not known a woeful state; this is the fruit of honoring the Buddha."
264:
"Eighty-seven aeons ago, there were four powerful Wheel-turning Monarchs, endowed with the seven treasures and great strength.
My defilements are burnt away... [as before]... the Buddha's bidding has been done."

Having attained Arahantship and remaining grateful, he went to the city of Sīlavatī to repay the kindness of the king who had been helpful to him. While preaching to the king, he revealed the Four Noble Truths. At the conclusion of the truths, the king became a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna) and, having built a great monastery named Sudassana in his city, offered it to the Elder. Great gains and honor arose. The Elder handed over the monastery and all the gains and honor to the Saṅgha. He himself lived by wandering for alms as before. After staying there for a few days, he wished to go to Sāvatthī.
