The monks said, "Venerable sir, please stay here. If there is any lack of the four requisites, we will provide them for you." The Elder, wishing to show, "Friends, I have no need for grand requisites; I can subsist on whatever requisites I receive; I am satisfied only with the taste of Dhamma," spoke this verse:

"I have no need for this [material gain]; I am happy, being satisfied with the taste of Dhamma. Having drunk the supreme and best of tastes, I will no longer associate with the poison [of sensual pleasures]."

In that verse, "I have no need for this" means: "I have no need for this gain of material things, this taste of material requisites, with which you wish to satisfy me by saying 'we will provide.' I have no use for it. Contentment is the highest happiness; I subsist only on whatever requisites I receive." Now, showing the primary reason for having no need for those material things, he said, "Happy, being satisfied with the taste of Dhamma." This means he is satisfied and delighted with the taste of the thirty-seven qualities contributing to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma) and the nine supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma); he is endowed with the highest happiness. "Having drunk the supreme and best of tastes" means he remains having drunk the aforementioned taste of Dhamma, which is the chief and best among all tastes. Therefore, it was said: "The taste of Dhamma excels all tastes." "I will no longer associate with the poison" means: "I, who remain having drunk such a taste of Dhamma, will no longer associate with the taste of sensual objects, which is like poison."

The explanation of the verse of the third Elder, Bandhura, is finished.
265:
I, who stand having drunk the essence of the Dhamma, which is supreme among all tastes, will not form an association or connection with the taste of sense objects, which is like poison; the meaning is that there is no reason to do so.

## The Commentary on the Verse of Bandhura Thera is finished.

## 4. Commentary on the Verse of Khitaka Thera

“My body is light indeed” is the verse of the Venerable Khitaka Thera. What is its origin? This elder also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, accumulating merit in various existences. In the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was reborn as a Yakkha general. One day, while sitting in an assembly of Yakkhas, he saw the Teacher sitting at the foot of a certain tree. He approached, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat in a suitable place. The Teacher preached the Dhamma to him. Having heard the Dhamma, expressing great rapture and joy, he clapped his hands, stood up, paid homage to the Teacher, circumambulated Him, and departed.

Through that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans. In this Buddha-era, he was reborn in a Brahmin family in Sāvatthī and was named Khitaka. When he reached the age of discretion and became wise, he heard about the great psychic powers of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. Prompted by his past wholesome roots, thinking, “I too shall become one possessed of psychic power,” he went forth as a monk. Taking a meditation subject from the Blessed One and striving in tranquility and insight (samatha-vipassanā), he soon became an Arahant endowed with the six supernormal knowledges (chaḷabhiññā). This is stated in the Apadāna:

“The Buddha named Paduma, the supreme among bipeds, the leader of men, having emerged from the forest, was preaching the Dhamma, the One with Vision.

There was an assembly of Yakkhas near the Great Sage; those Yakkhas who had arrived for some purpose beheld the Buddha at that moment.

Knowing the voice of the Buddha and the teaching of the Deathless, with a clear and happy mind, I clapped his hands and attended upon Him.

See the fruit of a well-performed service to the Teacher; for thirty thousand aeons, I have not been reborn in the four states of misery.”
266:
“In the past thirty aeons, there were Wheel-turning Kings named Sumangala, endowed with the seven treasures and great power. My defilements have been burnt away... the Buddha’s teaching has been carried out.”

Having attained Arahantship, and particularly through his mastery over psychic powers, he lived experiencing various kinds of psychic power, benefiting beings through the miracle of psychic power (iddhi-pāṭihāriya) and the miracle of instruction (anusāsanī-pāṭihāriya). When asked by monks, “Friend, how do you exercise psychic power?”, he spoke this verse to explain that matter:

“My body is light indeed,
And touched by great rapture and bliss;
Like cotton-wool moved by the wind,
My body seems to float.”

It is also said that he spoke this by way of an inspired utterance (udāna).

In that verse, “lahuko vata me kāyo” (my body is light indeed) means: through the suppression of hindrances (nīvaraṇa) and so forth, through the fourteen ways of training the mind, through the development of the four bases of power (iddhipāda), and through well-practiced mastery (vasībhāva), my physical body (rūpakāya) is very light indeed. The intention is that because of such suppression of hindrances, I can transform this physical body (karajakāya), which is supported by the slow-moving great elements, according to the power of the mind. “phuṭṭho ca pီtisukhena vipulena” (and touched by great rapture and bliss) is connected as: my body is touched by bliss accompanied by great and sublime rapture pervading everywhere. This was said to show how the body became light. For, along with the entry into the perception of bliss (sukha-saññā), there is the entry into the perception of lightness (lahu-saññā). Here, the pervading of bliss should be understood by way of the matter produced by that mind. If it is asked: “How can there be the pervading of rapture and bliss for one who possesses the fourth jhāna? Is it not that the fourth jhāna has transcended rapture and bliss?”—This is true. However, this statement about being touched by rapture and bliss is not made according to the characteristics of the fourth jhāna, but rather according to the preliminary stage (pubbabhāga). “pītisukhena” means bliss similar to that accompanied by rapture; for here, equanimity (upekkhā) is intended as “bliss” because of its peaceful nature and its association with special knowledge. Thus it is said: “He enters the perception of bliss and the perception of lightness” (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.101). Whether having the jhāna used as a basis (pādakajjhāna) as the object, or the physical body as the object, he enters, goes into, and touches the perception of bliss and the perception of lightness that arise together with the psychic mind.
267:
"He reaches [it]"—this is also the meaning there. Thus it is said in the Commentary: "What is called 'perception of happiness' (sukhasaññā) is the perception associated with equanimity. For equanimity is called 'happiness' because it is peaceful. That very perception should also be known as 'perception of lightness' (lahusaññā) because it is liberated from the hindrances and from opposing states such as applied thought (vitakka). For one who has entered into that [perception], even the physical body (karajakāya) becomes extremely light, like a tuft of cotton. With a body appearing as light as a tuft of cotton blown by the wind, he goes to the Brahmā realm."

Therefore, he said: "Like cotton blown by the wind, my body seems to float." The meaning of that verse is: Whenever I wish to go to the Brahmā realm or elsewhere by psychic power, then my body becomes just like a tuft of cotton blown by the wind, leaping into the sky.

## The commentary on the verses of the Elder Khitaka is finished.

## 5. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Malitavambha

The verse beginning with "Ukkaṇṭhito" is that of the Venerable Elder Malitavambha. What is its origin? It is said that during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was reborn as a bird in a lake not far from the Himālaya mountains. The Blessed One Padumuttara, wishing to favor him, went there and walked back and forth on the shore of the lake. The bird, seeing the Blessed One and having a clear mind, took kumuda lilies from the lake and offered them to the Blessed One.

Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans, and during the appearance of this Buddha, he was reborn as the son of a Brahmin in the city of Kurukaccha and was named Malitavambha. When he reached maturity and became wise, he approached the Great Elder Pacchābhūma, and having heard the Dhamma from him, he gained faith and went forth. He lived practicing the work of insight (vipassanā). The nature of that Elder was such that: in a place where suitable food was difficult to obtain but other requisites were easy to get, he would not depart. However, in a place where suitable food was easy to obtain but other requisites were difficult to get, he would not stay but would depart. While living thus, due to the perfection of his causes and his nature as a Great Man, he soon developed insight and reached Arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

"Near the Himālaya mountains, there was a large lake covered with paduma and red lotuses, and spread with white puṇḍarīka lotuses. At that time, I was a bird named Kukuttha in that lake, virtuous, wise, and skilled in what is wholesome and unwholesome. The Blessed One Padumuttara, the Knower of the World, Worthy of Offerings, came near that lake. I cut a kumuda lily born in the water and offered it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, knowing my intention, accepted that offering. Due to the power of that merit from giving, I did not go to a state of misery for a hundred thousand aeons. In the sixteen-hundredth aeon, there were eight universal monarchs of great strength named Varuṇa. Now, my defilements are burnt away; the Buddha's teaching has been carried out."

Attaining Arahantship and reflecting on his own practice, he uttered this inspired utterance: "A wise person, even if not delighted in mind, should not leave if [the place is] suitable; even if delighted in mind, one should depart [if it is harmful]; one should not stay in a place associated with harm."
268:
Near the Himavanta mountains, there was a great natural lake covered with Paduma and Uppala lotuses, and spread with white Puṇḍarīka lotuses.

At that time, there was a bird named Kukuttha in that lake, who was virtuous, endowed with wisdom, and skilled in discerning merit and demerit.

The Great Sage Padumuttara, the Knower of the World and the Recipient of Offerings, wandered near that natural lake.

Having cut a water-born Kumuda lily, I offered it to the Great Sage. Knowing my intention, the Great Sage accepted it.

Having given that gift, and being urged by that root of merit, I did not fall into a state of misery for a hundred thousand aeons.

In the sixteen-hundredth aeon, there were eight powerful wheel-turning monarchs named Varuṇa.

My defilements are burnt away... (pe) ... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.

Having reached the fruit of Arahantship and reflecting on his own practice, he uttered this inspired utterance:
"Even if weary, one should not stay; even if delighted, one should depart. A wise person should not live a life that is not connected with benefit."

In that verse, "Even if weary, one should not stay" means: In whichever dwelling I reside, if weariness and dissatisfaction with the higher wholesome states arise due to not obtaining suitable food (bhojana-sappāya), yet I stay there because other suitable conditions are obtained, I should not depart. In the phrase "na vase" (should not stay), the word "na" (not) should also be connected with the word "pakkame" (should depart). "Even if delighted, one should depart" means: In whichever dwelling I reside, if there is no weariness because there is no lack of requisites and I am greatly delighted, yet if other suitable conditions (sappāya) are not obtained, I should depart from that dwelling and not stay. It should be understood that by practicing in this way, I attained my goal before long. This interpretation (yojanā) is for reflecting on one's own practice. However, in giving advice to others, it should be applied with the meaning: "one should stay, one should not depart."

"A wise person should not live a life that is not connected with benefit" means: In a dwelling where requisites are easy to obtain, but the practice of a recluse (samaṇa-dhamma) does not reach fulfillment; or in a dwelling where requisites are hard to obtain, and the practice of a recluse also does not reach fulfillment—such a dwelling is called "not connected with benefit" in this Sasana. Therefore, a wise person who desires his own benefit should not live in such a way. It should be understood that one should stay in a place where one finds a dwelling endowed with the five factors and obtains the seven kinds of suitable conditions (sappāya).

The commentary on the verses of Malitavambha Thera is finished.

## 6. Suhemantattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

This verse beginning with "Sataṃ raṃsisahassāni" belongs to the long-lived Suhemanta Thera.
269:
It should be applied by way of considering one's own practice and instructing others, in terms of the meaning of staying or departing. "A wise person should not dwell in a residence that is not conducive to the goal" means a residence where the four requisites are easily obtained but the practice of a monk (samaṇadhamma) does not reach fulfillment, or a residence where the four requisites are difficult to obtain and the practice of a monk also does not reach fulfillment; such a residence is called 'not conducive to the goal' (not associated with progress) in this Dispensation. Therefore, a wise person who desires his own benefit should not dwell in such a place. The meaning is that one should only dwell in a place where a residence endowed with the five factors is obtained, and where the seven suitable things (sappāya) are also obtained.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Malitavambha is finished.

## 6. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Suhemanta

The verse beginning with "Sataliṅgassa atthassa" is the verse of the Venerable Suhemanta Thera. As for its origin: This noble one had also performed meritorious service (adhikāra) under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit that is a powerful support for the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa) in various births. Ninety-two aeons ago, during the time of Tissa Buddha, he was a hunter wandering in the forest. To show him favor, the Blessed One entered the forest and sat at the foot of a tree near him.

Seeing the Blessed One, he felt a clear and confident mind; he picked fragrant Punnāga flowers and offered them to the Blessed One. Due to that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the celestial realm and, performing merits repeatedly, he wandered through the worlds of gods and humans. In the time of our current Buddha, he was reborn as the son of a wealthy Brahmin in the region of Pāriyanta and was named Suhemanta. When he reached the age of wisdom and maturity, he approached the Blessed One who was staying in the Migadāya (Deer Park) of Saṅkassanagara. Upon hearing the Dhamma, he gained faith and was ordained. He became a master of the Tipitaka, developed insight (vipassanā), and before long became an Arahant endowed with the six supernormal powers (chaḷabhiññā) and the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). Thus it is said in the Apadāna:

"Having entered the deep forest, I lived as a hunter;
Seeing a blooming Punnāga tree, I recollected the Best of Buddhas."
270:
"Having picked those beautiful and fragrant Punnāga flowers, I made a stupa of sand and offered them to Tissa Buddha.

"Because of the merit of offering those flowers ninety-two aeons ago, I have not known a woeful state. This is the fruit of Buddha-pūjā.

"Ninety-one aeons ago, I was once a powerful Cakkavatti (Universal Monarch) endowed with the seven treasures, a dispeller of darkness.

"My defilements have been burnt away... the Dispensation of the Buddha has been fulfilled."

Upon attaining Arahantship, he thought: "I have reached the path and fruit that a disciple ought to reach; it would be good if I now provide support to the monks." Having thought thus, being one who had attained the analytical insights and being untiring, he dwelt instructing, repeatedly advising, cutting off doubts, and preaching the Dhamma to the monks who approached him, explaining the subjects of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna) clearly, without entanglement or complexity. Furthermore, one day, desiring to show the distinction of the higher Dhamma to the monks and wise persons who approached him, he spoke this verse:

"Of a meaning that has a hundred signs,
And bears a hundred characteristics,
The fool sees only a single factor,
But the wise man is a seer of a hundred."

In that verse, 'sataliṅgassa' means 'liṅga' (signs/genders) because they make known the hidden meaning; they are the bases for the application (pavatti-nimitta) of words to meanings. Because there are many—not just a hundred—such bases, it is called 'sataliṅga'. Here, the word 'sata' (hundred) does not mean a specific number as in 'a hundred, a thousand', but means 'many'. 'Atthassa' refers to the meaning of what is to be known. What is to be known is called 'attha' because it is to be reached (araṇīya) by knowledge. Even though a meaning is single, it has many signs (liṅga), such as the names 'Sakka, Purindada, Maghavā', or 'Paññā, Vijjā, Medhā, Ñāṇa'. The reason (pavatti-nimitta) the word 'Inda' is applied to the lord of Tāvatiṃsa is not the same reason the words 'Sakka' and so on are applied; rather, they are applied for other reasons. Likewise, the reason the word 'Paññā' is applied to Right View is not the same reason the words 'Vijjā' and so on are applied. Therefore, it is said, 'sataliṅgassa atthassa'.
271:
"Satalakkhaṇadhārino" means one who possesses many characteristics. It is called a characteristic (lakkhaṇa) because it is marked by a certain cause. The nature of a cause reaches the state of being a cause by depending on its own effect. Because of that cause, it is marked as "this is the cause of this effect." That cause is found in many varieties even within a single meaning. Therefore, it is said, "Satalakkhaṇadhārino." Alternatively, they are called characteristics (lakkhaṇā) because they are marked. It refers to the specific modes such as the conditioned nature (saṅkhatatā) of various meanings. These specific modes should be understood as specific states in terms of essence. These modes are also called "signs" (liṅga) because they make known the general characteristics such as impermanence (anicca) of those phenomena. These modes are the aspects of that meaning, as many are found even in a single meaning. Thus it is said, "Satalingaassa atthassa, satalakkhaṇadhārino." For this reason, the Venerable Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma (Dhammasenāpati), said: "All phenomena in all their aspects come into the range of the Buddha's knowledge-door."

"Ekagadassī dummedho" refers to a foolish person of weak wisdom who, in a meaning that has many signs and many characteristics, sees only one part due to lack of broad wisdom. Seeing only a single sign or a single characteristic, they cling to what they have seen as "this alone is the truth" and reject the views of others as "the other is empty." Like a blind man feeling an elephant, they grasp only one part. Such a person is called foolish because of not knowing the specific modes that exist and because of distorted clinging. "Satadassī ca paṇḍito" means a wise person can see all the many aspects existing in that meaning with their eye of wisdom. Or, a wise person is one who, having seen the many aspects available in that meaning with their own eye of wisdom, also shows and clarifies them to others; such a person is called discerning and skilled in meanings. In this way, the Elder clarified to the monks his own attainment of the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) which had reached the highest point.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Suhemanta is finished.
272:
## 7. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Dhammasava

The verse beginning with "Pabbajiṃ tulayitvāna" is the verse of the Venerable Elder Dhammasava. Its origin (uppatti) is as follows: In the time of Padumuttara Buddha, this Dhammasava was a brahmin named Suvaccha, who had reached the further shore of the three Vedas. Seeing the faults in the household life, he went forth as an ascetic and, having built a hermitage in a mountain valley in a forest area, lived with many other ascetics. Then, Padumuttara Buddha, wishing to plant the seed of merit for that ascetic, stood in the air near the hermitage and displayed a miracle of psychic power (iddhipāṭihāriya). Seeing that miracle, the ascetic, with a devoted mind and wishing to make an offering, had nāgapuppha flowers gathered. The Teacher, thinking "This much seed of merit is enough for this ascetic," departed. The ascetic took the flowers, scattered them on the path where the Teacher had traveled, and stood with palms joined in reverence, purifying his mind. Due to that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the celestial world and wandered only through the happy destinations (sugati). When our Buddha appeared, he was reborn in a brahmin family in the Magadha kingdom and received the name Dhammasava. When he reached maturity, being urged by his sufficiency of conditions (hetusampatti), he saw the danger of household life and the benefits of renunciation. He approached the Blessed One who was residing at Dakkhiṇāgiri, and upon hearing the Dhamma, he gained faith and went forth. While practicing insight meditation (vipassanā), he attained Arahantship before long. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

'A brahmin named Suvaccha, a master of the mantras, lived in a mountain valley, surrounded by his disciples.

The Conqueror named Padumuttara, the recipient of offerings, came to me, wishing to deliver me.

He walked in the air, emitted smoke, and likewise displayed a flaming power. Knowing my joyful mind, he departed facing the east.

Seeing that wonderful, marvelous, and hair-raising event, I took nāgapuppha flowers and scattered them on the path he had gone.

In the hundred thousandth aeon from this one, I scattered those flowers. Because of that devotion of mind, I have never been reborn in a miserable destination (duggati).'
273:
Thirty-one aeons ago, there was a king named Mahāraha, endowed with the seven treasures, a Wheel-Turning Monarch (Cakkavatti) of great power.

My defilements have been burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.

Having reached the fruit of Arahantship and reflecting on his own practice, the Elder, filled with joy, uttered this inspired utterance (udāna):

"Having weighed and reflected on the transition from the household life to the homeless life, I have gone forth; I have attained the three knowledges and fulfilled the Buddha's teaching." Thus he spoke this verse.

In that verse, "pabbajiṃ tulayitvāna" means having reflected and investigated with wisdom, which is like a scale, the disadvantages in the household life—starting with "the household life is crowded, a path of dust"—and the disadvantages in sensual pleasures—starting with "sensual pleasures provide little satisfaction, much suffering, and much despair"—and the benefits in renunciation (nekkhamma), which is the opposite of those. The remaining words are as explained previously. This verse itself was the Elder's declaration of final knowledge (aññābyākaraṇa).

## The Commentary on the Verse of Elder Dhammasava is finished.

## 8. Commentary on the Verse of Elder Dhammasavapitu

The verse beginning with "Sa vīsavassasatiko" is that of the Venerable Elder Dhammasavapitu. As for the background: This Elder had also made special aspirations under previous Buddhas. He was born into a family in a world empty of Buddhas. Upon reaching maturity, he saw a Paccekabuddha residing on a mountain named Bhūtagana and, with a devoted heart, made an offering of grass-spike flowers (tiṇasūla). Due to that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the celestial realm and wandered only through happy destinies (sugati). In this Buddha-era, he was born into a Brahmin family in the Magadha country. Upon reaching maturity, he married and had a son named Dhammasava. When that son went forth, he himself was one hundred and twenty years old and thought, "My son is still so young..."
274:
"...and has gone forth. Why then should I not go forth?" With such a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega), he went to the Teacher, heard the Dhamma, and went forth. Practicing insight meditation (vipassanā), he soon realized the fruit of Arahantship. This matter is stated in the Apadāna:

"Not far from the Himālaya mountains, there is a mountain named Bhūtagana. There, a Jina, a self-enlightened one (Sayambhū) who had transcended the world, resided."
"Taking a grass-spike flower, I offered it to the Buddha. Because of that merit, for a hundred thousand aeons, I did not go to the four woeful states."
"Counting back from now, eleven aeons ago, there was a Wheel-Turning Monarch of great power named Dharaṇīruha, endowed with the seven treasures."
"My defilements have been burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled."

Upon reaching the fruit of Arahantship, reflecting on his own practice and wishing to utter an inspired utterance out of joy:
"At the age of one hundred and twenty, I entered the homeless life. I have attained the three knowledges in succession and fulfilled the Buddha's teaching." Thus he spoke this verse.

In that verse, "sa vīsavassasatiko" means that I, being one hundred and twenty years old; I, being over one hundred and twenty years of age from birth. "Pabbajiṃ" means I have reached the state of a monk. The remaining words are as explained previously. This verse itself was the Elder's declaration of final knowledge.

## The Commentary on the Verse of Elder Dhammasavapitu is finished.

## 9. Commentary on the Verse of Elder Saṅgharakkhita

The verse beginning with "Na nūnāyaṃ paramahitānukampino" is that of the Venerable Elder Saṅgharakkhita. As for the background: This Elder also had made aspirations in the presence of previous Buddhas and accumulated merits in various lives. Ninety-four aeons ago, he was born into a family. Upon reaching maturity, one day he saw seven Paccekabuddhas residing at the foot of a mountain. With a devoted heart, he plucked forest flowers and offered them. Due to that meritorious deed, that noble son was reborn in the celestial realm. Performing merits repeatedly, he wandered only through happy destinies. When our Buddha appeared, he was born into a wealthy merchant family in the city of Sāvatthī. He was named Saṅgharakkhita. Upon reaching maturity, he gained faith and went forth. Taking a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), he lived in a certain place with another monk as a companion. Not far from where the Elder resided, at an anthill, a doe gave birth and was protecting her young fawn...
275:
Having seen the Paccekabuddhas and with a mind full of faith, he picked Kadamba flowers and offered them. Due to that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the deva world and, repeatedly performing meritorious deeds, wandered only through the happy realms (sugati). During the time of the current Buddha's appearance, he was reborn in a wealthy (ibbha) family in the city of Sāvatthī, and his name was Saṅgharakkhita. When he reached the age of discretion, he gained faith and went forth as a monk. Taking a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) and accompanied by another monk, he lived in the forest.

In a thicket not far from the Elder's dwelling, a mother deer had given birth and was guarding her young fawn. Out of love for her offspring, she did not go far to find food, and because she could not find grass or water nearby, she was exhausted and suffering. Seeing that deer, the Elder was moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega), thinking: "How amazing indeed is this world! It is bound by the bond of craving and experiences great suffering, yet it is unable to cut that bond of craving." Using that very deer as a goad (spur for insight), he developed insight (vipassanā) and attained the fruit of Arahantship. This is stated in the Apadāna:

"Not far from the Himavantā, there is a mountain named Kukkuṭa;
At the foot of that mountain, seven Buddhas were dwelling.
Seeing a Kadamba tree in bloom, shining like a king of lamps,
I held up Kadamba flowers with both hands and scattered them over the seven Buddhas.
In the ninety-fourth aeon (kappa) ago, I offered those flowers;
Due to that merit, I have never known a miserable rebirth (duggati). This is the fruit of offering to the Buddha.
In the ninety-second aeon from now, there were seven kings named Puppha,
Endowed with the seven treasures, universal monarchs (cakkavatti) of great power.
My defilements have been burnt away... (and so on) ...the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled."

After attaining Arahantship, knowing that his companion monk was living with many wrong thoughts (micchā-vitakka), he wished to admonish him by using that same deer as a metaphor, and recited this verse:

"Surely this monk, though gone into seclusion, does not reflect upon the Teaching of the One who is compassionate for the supreme welfare.
For he lives with unrestrained faculties, just like the mother deer with her young fawn in the forest."
276:
In that verse, in the phrase "Na nūnāyaṃ", "na" is a particle of negation, and "nūna" is used in the sense of reflection. It should be analyzed as "nūna ayaṃ". "Paramahitānukampino" refers to the Blessed One who is habitually compassionate for the supreme or peerless welfare of beings. "Rahogato" means gone into a secret place, gone to an empty dwelling, or endowed with physical seclusion (kāya-viveka). In the word "anuvigaṇeti", the two words "na nūna" should be brought forward and connected as "na nūna anuvigaṇeti", meaning "I think he does not reflect" or "I speculate that he does not apply himself". "Sāsanaṃ" refers to the teaching of practice (paṭipatti-sāsana), specifically the development of meditation on the Four Truths. "Tathā hi" means for that very reason, precisely because of not applying himself to the Teacher's instruction. "Ayaṃ" refers to this monk. "Pākatindriyo" means having faculties in their natural (unrestrained) state because the six faculties, with the mind as the sixth, are released toward their respective objects; it means having unrestrained eye-doors and so on. To show the metaphor for that monk who lives with unrestrained faculties because the attachment of craving has not been cut, he said: "Just like the mother deer with her young fawn in the forest."

Just as this mother deer, being of a youthful nature, experiences suffering in the forest because the love for her offspring is not cut, and cannot transcend that suffering; in the same way, this monk, living with unrestrained faculties because attachment is not cut, cannot transcend the suffering of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa-dukkha). There is also a reading "taruṇavijātikā", meaning one who has a newly born young offspring. Hearing these words, that monk was moved by spiritual urgency, developed insight, and before long attained Arahantship.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Saṅgharakkhita Thera is finished.

## 10. Usabhattheragāthāvaṇṇanā (Commentary on the Verses of Usabha Thera)

"On the mountain peaks, the trees are well-flourished"—this is the verse of the Venerable Usabha Thera. What was its origin? This monk also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and, performing merits that were strong supports for liberation (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) in various births, was reborn as a deva in the time of the Blessed Buddha Sikhī, thirty-one aeons ago. One day, having seen the Teacher and with a mind full of faith, he made an offering with divine flowers. That floral offering remained in the form of a flower pavilion for seven days. There was a great assembly of devas and humans.
277:
Through that meritorious deed, he wandered among devas and humans. In this Buddha’s era, he was reborn into a wealthy family in the kingdom of Kosala, and his name was Usabha. Upon reaching maturity, he gained faith in the Teacher during the acceptance of the Jetavana monastery. Having ordained and performed the preliminary duties, he resided in a forest at the foot of a mountain. At that time, as the early rains of the monsoon fell heavily, the mountain peaks were covered with dense foliage of trees, shrubs, and creepers. One day, the Elder emerged from his cave and, seeing the beauty of the forest and the mountain, reflected with wise attention: 'Even these inanimate things like trees reach growth through the suitability of the season. Why then, having obtained a suitable season, should I not reach growth in spiritual virtues?' Thus reflecting, he recited this verse:

'Trees on the mountain peaks are well-grown,
Sprinkled by the fresh, lofty clouds;
To Usabha, who desires seclusion and is mindful of the forest,
They bring about exceeding well-being.'

In that verse, 'nagā' means trees. Some say 'nāgā,' but it also means trees. 'Nagaggesu' means on the mountain peaks. 'Susaṃvirūḷhā' means having roots well-grown all around, with branches, sprouts, and twigs flourishing well around and above. 'Udaggameghena navena sittā' means heavily rained upon by the first, noble, and great monsoon clouds. 'Vivekakāmassa' means for one who desires mental seclusion (citta-viveka) which is secluded from defilements. Having already attained physical seclusion (kāya-viveka) by living in the forest, he now seeks mental seclusion, which is the basis for attaining the seclusion from the substrata of existence (upadhi-viveka); it refers to one who is striving with wakefulness. Therefore, it says 'araññasaññino' (mindful of the forest). Forest-dwelling is praised and extolled by the Teacher. And that forest-dwelling is for the sake of fulfilling serenity and insight meditation (samatha-vipassanā-bhāvanā). Thus, thinking 'I shall take that fulfillment into my own hands,' he is one who is mindful of the forest and abounds in the thought of renunciation (nekkhamma-saṅkappa). 'Janeti' means they produce (uppādenti).
278:
Because he desires mental seclusion (citta-viveka), he has attained physical seclusion (kāya-viveka) by living in the forest. Now, mental seclusion, which leads to the cessation of defilements, should be attained; thus, it refers to one who is constantly striving with wakefulness, longing for that seclusion. Therefore, the Blessed One praised living in the forest. As long as living in the forest is beneficial for the fulfillment of serenity and insight meditation, he thinks, 'I must make it my own,' and thus, going to the forest, he is one who abounds in the thought of renunciation.

The word 'janeti' is a singular form used in a plural sense. Some teachers read it as 'janenti.' 'Bhiyyo' means further and further (exceedingly). In saying 'to Usabha,' he refers to himself as if he were another. 'Kalyataṃ' means the health of the mind, its fitness for work (kammaññatā), and its suitability for meditation. This meaning has already been stated below. Thus, while the Elder Usabha was reciting this verse, he intensified his insight and attained Arahatship.

Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:
'When I was a son of the devas, I worshipped Sikhi, the Leader,
With Mandārava flowers, I offered them to the Buddha.
For seven days, there was a canopy of divine flowers over the Tathāgata,
All the people gathered and paid homage to the Tathāgata.
In the thirty-first aeon from now, the flowers I worshipped with,
Due to that fruit of Buddha-worship, I have not known a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.
In the tenth aeon from now, I was a king named Jutindhara,
Endowed with the seven treasures, a Wheel-turning Monarch of great power.
My defilements have been burned away... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.'

This very verse became the Elder's declaration of final knowledge (aññā-byākaraṇa).

## The Commentary on the Verse of Usabha Thera is finished.
## The Commentary on the Eleventh Group is finished.
## 12. The Twelfth Group
## 1. Commentary on the Verse of Jenta Thera

The verse beginning with 'Duppabbajjaṃ ve duradhivāsā gehā' is that of the Venerable Jenta Thera. What is the background? This Elder also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit as a support for liberation in various births. In the time of Sikhi Buddha, he was reborn as a son of the devas. One day, seeing the Teacher, he worshipped him with Kiṃkirāta flowers with a devoted heart. Through that merit, he wandered among devas and humans. In this Buddha's era, he was born into a merchant family in the kingdom of Kosala. They named him Jenta. When he reached the age of wisdom, he gained faith in the Teacher while the Jetavana monastery was being accepted and ordained. Having performed the preliminary duties, he lived at the foot of a mountain in the forest. He reflected: 'Ordination is indeed difficult to do; living in a house is difficult; the Dhamma is also difficult to understand.'
279: This Elder also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, accumulated wholesome roots in various births as a support for Nibbāna. In the time of the Buddha Sikhī, he was a deva. One day, upon seeing the Blessed One, he was filled with devotion and offered kakkaru flowers (kiṃkirāta flowers). Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans. When this Buddha appeared, he was reborn in the village of Jenta in the kingdom of Magadha as the son of a provincial king (maṇḍalika rāja) and was named Jentatissa (Jenta). When he reached the age of discretion, being urged by the momentum of his past merits even from a young age, his mind inclined toward renunciation. However, he thought: 'Renunciation is indeed difficult to perform; living in a home is also hard to endure; the Dhamma is profound; and wealth is hard to acquire. What then should I do?' Thus, he wandered about with many such thoughts. One day, he went to the presence of the Teacher and listened to the Dhamma. From the time he heard the Dhamma, he delighted in renunciation. He ordained in the presence of the Teacher, took up a subject of meditation, developed insight, and through the easy practice and swift intuition (sukhāya paṭipadāya khippābhiññāya), he realized Arahatship. This is stated in the Apadāna: 'When I was a deva, I worshipped Sikhī, the Leader. Holding up a kakkaru flower, I offered it to the Buddha. In the thirty-first aeon from now, I offered that flower; because of that offering to the Buddha, I have not known a miserable rebirth. In the ninth aeon from now, I was a king, supreme among beings, endowed with the seven treasures, a wheel-turning monarch of great power. My defilements have been burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.' Having reached Arahatship, while reviewing his own practice, he was filled with joy, thinking, 'I have indeed been able to cut off the thoughts that arose in me at the beginning.' Desiring to show the manner in which those thoughts arose and how they were perfectly cut off, he uttered this verse: 'Hard is renunciation, indeed, and hard to endure is the home; the Dhamma is profound, and wealth is hard to acquire. Difficult is our livelihood with whatever is obtained; it is fitting to constantly contemplate impermanence.' In that verse, 'duppabbajjaṃ' means that renouncing the mass of wealth, whether small or great, and the circle of relatives, and giving one's heart to this Dispensation to ordain is difficult to do; thus it is 'difficult renunciation.' The word 've' is a mere particle, or it expresses emphasis, meaning 'renunciation is indeed painful.'
280:
Regarding the phrase "It is suffering": If one were to dwell in and govern a house, houses are difficult to dwell in. This is because a king dwelling in a house must perform royal duties, a ruler must perform the duties of a ruler, and a householder must perform the duties of a householder. One must also support and look after attendants, friends, recluses, and brahmins. Even while performing these various duties, the household life is hard to satisfy, like a broken pot or the great ocean. Therefore, considering that dwelling in and governing houses is painful and difficult to do, it is said to be "difficult to dwell in" and "a difficult dwelling."

If one were to follow the life of renunciation (pabbajjā), the Dhamma is profound. The goal for which one renounces, the Dhamma of penetration (paṭivedha-saddhamma), is a state to be attained by the renunciant and is very deep. Because it is the domain of profound wisdom, it is hard to see and hard to penetrate due to the profundity of the Dhamma.

If one were to dwell in a house, the wealth and possessions that are indispensable for living in a house are difficult to acquire. Those possessions are difficult to acquire because they must be obtained with pain and hardship. This being so, if one abandons the household life and follows only the life of renunciation, even then, our livelihood in this Buddha's Sasana with whatever requisites are obtained is difficult and painful. Because of the difficulty of dwelling for householders, the difficulty of acquiring wealth, and the need to subsist on whatever is obtained in the house, our livelihood is arduous and exhausting.

In that case, what should be done? It is proper to constantly contemplate impermanence (aniccatā) throughout the entire day and during the early and late watches of the night, regarding the entire collection of phenomena belonging to the three planes. It is fitting to contemplate and develop insight (vipassanā) as "impermanent" because they have arising and passing away, because they have a beginning and an end, and because they are only temporary. Since other contemplations are easily accomplished once the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā) is perfected, only the contemplation of impermanence is mentioned here. This is because what is impermanent does not deviate from being suffering and non-self, and because it is easy for one staying in the Sasana to grasp happiness [through this].

Therefore, He taught: "What is impermanent, that is suffering; what is suffering, that is non-self," and "Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease," and "Conditioned things are of the nature to decay." In this way, having suppressed the thoughts (vitakka) that arose one after another through their respective opposites, and having begun insight through the door of impermanence, he now shows that his task is completed. Thus, he said "attanō paṭipattiṃ" and so forth. This indeed was the Thera's declaration of final knowledge (aññā-byākaraṇa).

## The commentary on the verses of Jenta Thera is finished.
281:
## 2. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Vacchagotta

“Tevijjohaṃ mahājhāyī” and so forth is the verse of the Venerable Elder Vacchagotta. How did it come to be? This elder also had performed special meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, planting the seeds of merit that serve as a strong support for liberation (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) in various existences. During the time of the Buddha Vipassī, he was born into a good family in the city of Bandhumatī. Upon reaching maturity, one day, together with the king and the citizens, he performed a Buddha-pūjā. Thereafter, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans, and in this Buddha’s era, he was born as the son of a wealthy Brahmin in the city of Rājagaha. Because he belonged to the Vacchagotta clan, he was known by the name Vacchagotta.

When he reached maturity, he became proficient in the Brahmin sciences. While searching for liberation, which is the fruition of Arahantship, he found no essence in those sciences. Consequently, he went forth as a wandering ascetic (paribbājaka). Approaching the Blessed One, he asked a question, and upon hearing the Blessed One’s answer, he was filled with devotion and went forth as a monk in the presence of the Blessed One. While striving in the practice of insight (vipassanā), he soon became an Arahant endowed with the six supernormal powers (chaḷabhiññā). This account is stated in the Apadāna:

“Like the rising sun with a hundred rays, like the golden-rayed sun, like the moon on the fifteenth day of the full moon, the Leader of the World was proceeding.

Sixty-eight thousand Arahants, all with taints destroyed, surrounded the Sambuddha, the Lord of bipeds, the Bull among men.

Having swept that path where the Leader of the World was proceeding, I planted a banner there with a heart full of devotion.

In the ninety-one aeons since I planted that banner, I have not known a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of the gift of a banner.

Four aeons ago, I was a king of great power, endowed with all excellent qualities, known as Sudhaja.

My defilements have been burned away... the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

Being endowed with the six supernormal powers, he reflected on his own practice and, filled with joy, uttered this inspired verse (udāna):
282:
“I am one with the triple knowledge, a great meditator, skilled in the tranquility of the mind. My own goal (Arahantship) has been attained; the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

In that verse, “tevijjohaṃ” means: although in the past, because I had reached the further shore of the three Vedas, Brahmins recognized me as a “triple-knowledge Brahmin” (brāhmaṇo tevijjo), that recognition was merely a name, as there is no actual function of true knowledge (vijjā) in the Vedas. But now, because I have attained the three knowledges such as the knowledge of recollecting past lives, I am a “triple-knowledge one” (tevijja) in the ultimate sense. He is a “great meditator” (mahājhāyī) because he burns away the entire mass of defilements belonging to the side of origin (samudaya) without remainder, and because he contemplates the great, noble, and sublime Nibbāna through the great meditation of the Path and Fruition. “Cetosamathakovido” means he is skilled in steadying the mind by stilling the defiling states that cause mental agitation. By this, he states the cause for being one with the triple knowledge. Indeed, one is a “triple-knowledge one” through the knowledge of the destruction of taints (āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa) accompanied by skill in concentration, not by mere knowledge alone. “Sadattho” is the same as “sakattho”; the letter ‘k’ has been changed to ‘d’, as in the Pali passages such as “anuppattasadattho.” By the word “sadattho,” the fruition of Arahantship should be understood. It is called “sakattho” (one’s own goal) because it is connected to oneself, because it does not abandon oneself, because it is one’s own ultimate meaning, and because it is one’s own benefit. I have reached, or attained, that aforementioned goal (sadattho). By saying this, he demonstrates that his state as a great meditator has reached its pinnacle. The rest is as previously explained.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Vacchagotta is finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Vanavaccha

“Acchodikā puthusilā” and so forth is the verse of the Venerable Elder Vanavaccha. How did it come to be? This elder also had performed special services (adhikāra) under previous Buddhas, planting the seeds of merit that are the cause for Nibbāna in various existences. During the time of the Buddha Vipassī, he was born into a good family. Upon reaching wisdom, while earning a living by working for others, he committed an offense against someone. Threatened by the fear of death, while fleeing, midway on his journey...
283:
Seeing the Bodhi tree and having a mind full of faith, he swept the area around the base of that Bodhi tree, made an offering with Asoka flowers along with their stalks, and while bowing and facing the Bodhi tree, he sat in the cross-legged posture. Even upon seeing enemies who had come to kill him, he did not allow his mind to be corrupted against them; contemplating only the Bodhi tree, he fell into a precipice as deep as the height of a hundred men. Due to that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the celestial realm. After performing various merits repeatedly and wandering through the worlds of gods and humans, he was reborn in Rājagaha as the son of a wealthy Brahmin during the time of this Buddha's appearance and was named "Vaccha." When he came of age, he attained faith at the assembly of King Bimbisāra, went forth as a monk, and attained Arahantship. Therefore, it is stated in the Apadāna:

"Engaged in the service of another, I committed a fault. Seized by fear and danger, I fled into the forest."

"Seeing a blossoming tree, I took well-prepared red Asoka flowers with their stalks and scattered them over the Bodhi tree as an offering."

"Having swept that Pāṭali tree, the best of trees, I sat down at the foot of the Bodhi tree in the cross-legged posture."

"Searching for the path I had taken, the enemies came towards me. Even upon seeing them, I remained there contemplating the supreme Bodhi tree."

"Having bowed to the Bodhi tree with a clear mind, I fell into a terrifying mountain abyss many palm-trees deep."

"Ninety-one aeons ago, I offered those flowers. Due to the fruit of that worship of the Bodhi tree, I know of no rebirth in the four woeful states."

"In the third aeon from now, I was a powerful Cakkavatti king named Susaññata, endowed with the seven treasures."

"My defilements have been burned away... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled."

After attaining Arahantship, because he took great delight in solitude, he lived only in the forest. Thus, the name "Vanavaccha" became well-known. On another occasion, the Elder went to Rājagaha to favor his relatives. At that time, his relatives pleaded, "Venerable Sir, please stay in a nearby monastery for our benefit; we will attend to you." The Elder, wishing to make known his delight in seclusion by praising the beauty of the mountains, recited this verse: "Those mountains with clear waters, broad stone slabs, frequented by monkeys and deer, and covered with moss—they delight me." In that verse, "acchodikā" refers to mountains having clear, pure, non-turbid, and subtle waters.
284:
(That Elder Vanavaccha) went to Rājagaha. Having stayed there for a few days receiving the ministrations of his relatives, he showed signs of wanting to depart. At that time, his relatives pleaded, "Venerable Sir, please stay in a nearby monastery for our benefit; we will attend to you." The Elder, wishing to make known to those relatives his delight in seclusion by praising the beauty of the mountains, recited this verse:

"Those mountains with clear waters and broad stone slabs,
Frequented by monkeys and deer,
Covered with water-moss—
They delight me."

In that verse, "acchodikā" means that because those mountains have clear, non-turbid, and subtle waters, where it should be said as "acchodaka," it is stated as "acchodikā" by way of gender transformation (liṅgavipallāsa). By this word, he shows the abundance of water in those mountains. "Puthusilā" means they are called so because those mountains have broad, wide stone slabs that are soft and pleasant to the touch. By this expression, he shows the excellence of the dwelling place. They are called "gonaṅgula" (black or brown monkeys) because they have tails like those of cows. Because they are mixed with those monkeys and deer such as the pasada wandering here and there, they are called "gonaṅgulamigāyutā." By this word, he shows that those mountains are not frequented by humans and are endowed with the characteristics of the forest. "Ambu-sevāla-sañchannā" means being covered with water-moss in various places due to the water constantly trickling from the springs. "Te selā ramayanti maṃ" means that such great mountains where I dwell delight me through my delight in seclusion; the meaning is that for that reason, I shall go only to that place. This very verse was the Elder's declaration of final knowledge (aññābyākaraṇa).

## The Commentary on the Verses of Vanavaccha Thera is finished.

## 4. Commentary on the Verses of Adhimutta Thera

The verse beginning with "Kāyaduṭṭhullagaruno" is that of the Venerable Adhimutta Thera. What is its origin (uppatti)? It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was reborn in a Brahmin family, and upon reaching maturity, he achieved mastery in the Brahmin sciences. Regarding sense pleasures...
285:
Seeing the danger in sensual pleasures, he renounced the household life. While living in the forest as an ascetic, he heard that a Buddha had appeared in the world and approached human habitation. Seeing the Blessed One walking, surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks, he felt a heart full of faith and spread his bark-cloth robe at the feet of the Teacher. The Teacher, knowing his intention, stood upon that bark-cloth robe. He worshipped the Blessed One who stood there with kāḷānusārī fragrance and praised Him with ten verses beginning with 'You deliver this world.' The Teacher gave him a prophecy, saying, 'In the future, one hundred thousand aeons from now, you will become a monk in the dispensation of the Sammasambuddha named Gotama and will be endowed with the six supernormal powers (chaḷabhiññā),' and then He departed.

Due to that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the celestial realm. From then until this Buddha appeared, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans. In this Buddha's dispensation, he was reborn into a Brahmin family in Sāvatthī and was named Adhimutta. When he reached maturity, he completed his studies in the Brahmin arts, but seeing no essence in those arts and being in his final existence, he sought Nibbāna, the way of escape. Seeing the majesty of the Buddha during the acceptance of the Jetavana monastery, he gained faith and was ordained in the presence of the Teacher. Practicing insight meditation (vipassanā), he soon attained Arahatship. This is stated in the Apadāna:

Like a flaming Kaṇikāra tree, like a blazing lamp-stand, like the shining healing star (Osadhī), or like lightning in the sky.

Without trembling, without fear, like a lion, the king of beasts, illuminating the light of knowledge and crushing the hosts of heretics.

I saw the Lord of the World (Lokanātha), who delivers this world, who cuts off all doubts, and who roars like a lion.

I was then an ascetic with matted hair, wearing a black antelope skin, noble, upright, and powerful. Taking my bark-cloth robe, I spread it at His feet.

Taking kāḷānusārī fragrance, I anointed the Tathāgata. Having anointed the Sammasambuddha, I praised the Lord of the World.

'O Great Sage (Mahāmuni) who has crossed the flood, You deliver this world. You illuminate it with the light of knowledge; Your supreme knowledge is unobstructed.'
286:
'You have set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakka) and crushed the opposing heretics. Like a victorious bull, You have made the earth tremble.

Just as waves in the great ocean break upon the shore, even so, all wrong views break against Your knowledge.

Just as when a fine-mesh net is spread in a pond, the creatures that enter the net are immediately oppressed,

Even so, O Lord, the heretics in the world who rely on various sectarian views only revolve within Your noble knowledge.

You are the foundation for those drifting in the four floods (ogha). You are the protector of the friendless, the refuge for those stricken by fear, and the ultimate resort for those desiring liberation.

You are the Unique Hero (Ekavīra), peerless, a treasury of loving-kindness and compassion. You are incomparable, perfectly tranquil, peaceful, self-controlled, such a one (tādī), and a conqueror of enemies.

You are the Wise One (Dhīra), free from delusion, free from craving, and without doubt. You are the delightful one, one who has vomited out all faults, stainless, restrained, and pure.

You have transcended attachments, destroyed pride, attained the three knowledges (tevijja), and reached the end of the three worlds. You have transcended all boundaries, honor the Dhamma, attained Your goal, and bring about welfare.

You are a savior like a boat, a bringer of comfort like a treasure. You are like a fearless lion and like a noble, majestic elephant.'

Having praised Padumuttara, the Greatly Renowned, with these ten verses and having worshipped the feet of the Teacher, I then stood in silence.

Padumuttara, the Knower of the Worlds, the Recipient of Offerings, standing in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks, spoke these verses:

'He who has praised My virtue, My knowledge, and the True Dhamma—I shall proclaim his future; listen to my words.

For sixty thousand aeons, he will rejoice in the celestial realm. Surpassing other devas, he will exercise sovereignty.'
287:
Later, having gone forth, urged by the root of wholesome merit, he will go forth in the dispensation of the Blessed One Gotama.

Having gone forth, avoiding evil deeds with the body, and fully understanding all taints (āsavas), he will attain Nibbāna, free from taints.

Just as a thundering cloud refreshes this earth, so too, O Great Hero, you have refreshed me with the Dhamma.

Having praised the virtue, wisdom, and Dhamma of the Lord of the World, I have reached the supreme peace, the deathless state of Nibbāna.

May that Blessed One, the Visionary One, remain for a long time; may those who do not yet know, come to know; may they reach the deathless state of Nibbāna.

This is my final birth; all existences have been uprooted. Having fully understanding all taints, I dwell free from taints.

A hundred thousand aeons ago, I praised the Buddha; as a result of that praise, I have never known a woeful state (apāya).

My defilements (kilesas) are burnt up ... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.

After reaching Arahantship, wishing to admonish the monks living with him who were habituated to bodily grooming—
"While life is diminishing, for one who prioritizes bodily grooming and is greedy for physical comfort, where can there be the goodness of a recluse (samaṇa)?" — he spoke this verse.

In that verse, 'kāyaduṭṭhullagaruno' means: 'duṭṭhulla' is the state of being associated with the foul (asubha); one who prioritizes the association with the foulness of one's own body is called 'kāyaduṭṭhullagaru'. It means one who, lacking the wisdom to escape [Saṃsāra], is habituated only to nourishing and grooming the body; [it refers] to such a person. 'Hiyyamānamhi jīvite' means while the formation of life is rapidly ending, like the water of small rivers. 'Sarīrasukhagiddhassāti' means greed for the comfort of one's own body through fine food and so forth...
288:
...to such a person who has fallen into [greed]. 'Kuto samaṇasādhutā' means for a person of such a nature, for what reason or cause could there be the goodness of a recluse or the state of being a good recluse? The meaning is that the goodness of a recluse exists only for one who is absolutely indifferent to the body and life, who is content with whatever is available, and who has aroused energy.

## The explanation of the verses of Adhimutta Thera is finished.

## 5. The explanation of the verses of Mahānāma Thera

The verse beginning with 'Esāvahiyyase pabbatenā' is that of the Venerable Mahānāma Thera. What is its origin? This [Mahānāma Thera] also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and, accumulating merit in various births, was born into a Brahmin family during the time of the Blessed One Sumedha. Having mastered the Brahmin sciences, he abandoned the household life, built a hermitage on the bank of a certain river, and lived there teaching mantras to many Brahmins. Then one day, the Blessed One, to favor him, went to his hermitage. Seeing the Blessed One, the Brahmin was inspired with faith, prepared a seat, and offered it. While the Blessed One was seated, he offered very sweet honey. The Blessed One consumed it, gave a prophecy about the future in the manner mentioned below in the story of Adhimutta Thera, and departed. Due to that meritorious deed, he was born in the celestial realm and, after wandering only through happy realms (sugati), was born into a Brahmin family in Sāvatthī during the time of our Buddha Gotama. He received the name Mahānāma and, upon reaching maturity, approached the Blessed One, heard the Dhamma, gained faith, and went forth. Having taken a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), while living on Mount Nesādaka, he was unable to suppress the uprising of defilements. Feeling weary of his own life, thinking, "What is the use of this life of mine with a defiled mind?", he climbed a high mountain peak and, pointing to himself as if to another, saying, "I will throw you from this mountain and kill you," he spoke this verse:

"Full of many Kuṭaja and Sallaki trees,
From this Mount Nesādaka, famous and well-covered,
O Mahānāma, you are falling away from this [spiritual] level."
289:
In that verse, 'esāvahiyyase' means 'Mahānāma, you are falling away (from the higher Dhamma); parihāyasi—you are declining.' 'Pabbatena' means by this mountain which is the place of residence. 'Bahukuṭajasallakikena' means endowed with many Kuṭaja trees (Indasāla trees) and Sallakī trees (or Indasāla trees). 'Nesādakena' means by the mountain of this name. 'Girinā' means by the rocky mountain. Indeed, a mountain is called 'pabbata' because it stands with sections known as joints (pabba). It is called 'giri' because it swallows (giraṇa) water and essential substances such as medicines through the power of oozing and so forth. Since both meanings are possible here, after saying 'pabbatena', 'girinā' is said again. 'Yasassinā' means famous and renowned for all virtues. 'Paricchadena' is called 'paricchada' either because it is covered all around by various trees, bushes, and creepers, or because it is your shelter for living.

The meaning here is: Mahānāma, if you abandon your meditation subject and are full of discursive thoughts, you will fall away from this Nesādaka mountain, which is a suitable place of residence endowed with shade and water. Now I will throw you down from this mountain and kill you. Therefore, one should not live under the influence of discursive thoughts. In this way, while threatening himself, the Elder applied himself to insight meditation and attained the fruit of Arahantship. This matter is stated in the Apadāna as follows:

'On the bank of the river Sindhu, my hermitage was well-prepared. There, I taught my disciples the Itihāsa (history) along with the Lakkhana (science of marks).'
'Those disciples, who were lovers of Dhamma, well-trained, and eager to hear the good instruction, having reached the further shore of the six auxiliary sciences (saḷaṅga), lived on the bank of the Sindhu.'
'Skilled in omens and marks, seeking the supreme goal, they lived in the forest at that time.'
'At that time, the Buddha named Sumedha arose in the world. Out of compassion for us, that Leader approached.'
'To the Great Hero Sumedha, the Leader of the World, who had arrived, I made a grass mat and offered it to the Chief of the World.'
'Taking honey from the forest, I offered it to the Best of Buddhas. Having consumed it, the Buddha spoke these words:'
290:
“I will praise the one who, with a confident mind, gave this honey to me with his own hands; listen to my words as I speak.

Due to this gift of honey and this grass mat, he will rejoice in the celestial world for thirty thousand aeons.

Thirty thousand aeons from now, a Buddha named Gotama by clan, born in the Okkāka family, will arise in the world.

An heir to his Dhamma, his breast-born son, created by the Dhamma, having fully understood all taints (āsavas), he will attain Nibbāna, free from taints.

When he comes from the celestial world to this human world and enters his mother's womb, a rain of honey will fall, covering the earth with honey.

Just as I emerge from the mother's womb, which is difficult to cross, even then a rain of honey will fall for me at all times.

Having gone forth from the home life into homelessness, I am a recipient of food and drink; this is the fruit of the gift of honey.

I have been perfected in all sensual pleasures among gods and humans, and by that very gift of honey, I have reached the destruction of the taints.

When it rains and the grass is four finger-breadths high, when the trees are in full bloom, I live always happy and free from taints in a secluded house or at the foot of a tree like a pavilion.

I have transcended all existences—middle, high, and low. Today my taints are exhausted; now there is no more rebirth.

Because of that gift I gave thirty thousand aeons ago, I do not know of any miserable rebirth (duggati); this is the fruit of the gift of honey.

My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.”

This very verse was the Elder's declaration of final knowledge (aññābyākaraṇa).

## The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Mahānāma is Finished.
291:
## 6. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Pārapariya

The verse beginning with 'Chaphassāyatane hitvā' is that of the Venerable Elder Pārapariya. What is its origin? This Pārapariya also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and had been accumulating merit in various existences. In the time of the Blessed One Piyadassī, he was reborn in a hunter's family. When he reached the age of discretion, while wandering in a certain forest thicket, the Blessed One Piyadassī, wishing to favor him, entered the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) and sat there.

While searching for game, the man reached that place and, seeing the Teacher, his heart was filled with devotion. Placing the Blessed One within, he constructed a pavilion of branches and covered it with lotus flowers (paduma) in the shape of a gabled house (kūṭāgāra). Experiencing sublime rapture and joy, he remained there for seven days, paying homage. Day by day, he removed the withered flowers and covered the structure with fresh ones.

At the end of the seven days, the Teacher emerged from the attainment of cessation and turned his thoughts to the Saṅgha of monks. At that very moment, about eighty thousand monks surrounded the Teacher. Deities gathered, thinking, 'We shall hear the sweet discourse on the Dhamma,' and a great assembly took place. The Teacher, while performing the act of appreciation (anumodanā), prophesied his future prosperity among gods and humans, and his attainment of disciple-enlightenment (sāvaka-bodhi) during the time of this present Buddha, and then departed.

Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, and in this Buddha's era, he was reborn in a Brahmin family in Rājagaha. Having reached the age of discretion, he became a master of the three Vedas. He was known by the name Pārapariya because he belonged to the Pārapariya clan. While he was teaching the Vedas to many Brahmins, he saw the power and majesty of the Buddha when the Teacher entered Rājagaha. Gaining faith, he ordained and, practicing the work of insight (vipassanā), he soon attained Arahatship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:

"The Blessed One named Piyadassī was the Self-Enlightened One, the Leader of the World;
That Buddha, desiring seclusion, was a Sage skilled in concentration (samādhi).

Having entered a forest thicket, the Great Sage Piyadassī,
Spreading out his rag-robe, that Supreme Man sat down.

In the past, I was a hunter in the wild forest;
At that time, I was wandering about, searching for a small deer (pasada)."
292:
"In that forest, I saw the Fully Enlightened One, who had crossed the flood and was free from taints (anāsava),
Appearing like a Sāla tree king in full bloom, or like the sun risen with a thousand rays.

Having seen Piyadassī of great fame, the God of gods,
I then entered a lake and brought back lotus flowers (paduma).

Having brought the delightful lotuses with a hundred petals,
I constructed a gabled structure and covered it with those lotuses.

Compassionate and merciful, the Great Sage Piyadassī,
The Buddha, the Conqueror, dwelt in that gabled structure for seven days and nights.

Discarding the old, withered lotuses, I covered it again with fresh ones;
At that moment, I stood there with hands raised in salutation (añjali).

Emerging from concentration (samādhi), the Great Sage Piyadassī,
The Leader of the World, sat looking towards the quarters.

At that time, an attendant named Sudassana, of great psychic power,
Knowing the mind of the Teacher, the Buddha Piyadassī,

Surrounded by eighty thousand monks,
Approached the Leader of the World who was sitting peacefully in the forest.

All the deities dwelling in that forest thicket,
Knowing the mind of the Buddha, also gathered at that time.

When the Yakkhas, Kumbhaṇḍas, and Rakkhasas had assembled,
And the Saṅgha of monks had arrived, the Conqueror spoke these verses:

'This man has praised and honored me for seven days,
And has made a dwelling place for me; I shall proclaim his story, listen to my words.'

'With wisdom, I shall proclaim the Dhamma that is very difficult to see, very subtle,
Deep, and well-expounded; listen to my words.'

'For fourteen aeons, he will exercise the sovereignty of the gods;
A great gabled mansion covered with lotus flowers will be his.'"
293:
"'It will be carried in the sky; this is the fruit of the offering of flowers.
For one hundred and twenty-four aeons, he will wander through (god and human realms) in succession.

There, a celestial mansion made of flowers will be carried in the sky for him;
Just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf,

Even so, defilements will not cling to his knowledge.
This man, having discarded the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa) with his mind,

Generating a mind for renunciation (nekkhamma), will go forth from the home life to homelessness.
At that time, while the flower-mansion is being carried, he will depart (for the forest).

For the wise and mindful one dwelling at the foot of a tree,
That flower-mansion will be carried over his head at the foot of that tree.

Having offered robes, alms-food, medicinal requisites, and lodgings
To the Saṅgha of monks, he will attain Nibbāna, free from taints.'

Traveling with a gabled mansion, I went forth into the monkhood;
Even while living at the foot of a tree, the gabled mansion is maintained for me.

In me, there is no craving (intention) for robes or alms-food;
Being endowed with meritorious deeds, I receive completed requisites.

By my count, many billions of aeons have passed in vain;
World-Leaders (Buddhas) have passed away (without appearing).

One thousand eight hundred aeons ago, the Guide named Piyadassī appeared;
Having served that Buddha, I have come to this present birth.

In this life, I have seen the Fully Enlightened One named Anoma, the One with Vision;
Having approached that Buddha, I went forth into the homeless life.

Making an end of suffering, the Buddha, the Conqueror, taught me the Path;
Having heard the Dhamma of that Buddha, I have reached the Unshakable State (Nibbāna).

Having pleased the Buddha Gotama, the Bull of the Sakyans,
And having fully understood all taints, I dwell free from taints."
294:
"One thousand eight hundred aeons ago, I worshipped the Buddha; because of that act of worshipping the Buddha, I have not known a miserable rebirth. This is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.

'My defilements have been burnt away ... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.'

Having attained Arahantship and reflecting on his own practice, with a heart full of joy, he uttered this verse as an inspired utterance:

'Having abandoned the six sense bases, with guarded doors and well-restrained, having vomited the root of suffering, I have reached the destruction of the taints.'

In that verse, 'chaphassāyatanē hitvā' means having abandoned the six internal sense bases, such as the eye, which are called 'sense bases' (phassāyatana) because they are the places where the six contacts, such as eye-contact, arise; this abandonment is through the relinquishing of the defilements associated with those bases. 'Guttadvāro susaṃvuto' means that because of such abandonment, the eye-door and others are guarded; they are well-restrained because they are firmly closed by the door-panel of mindfulness, which prevents the entry of evil states such as covetousness (abhijjhā) that tend to arise at those doors. Alternatively, it means having guarded doors because the six doors, with the mind as the sixth, are protected in the manner mentioned, and being well-restrained because of being well-disciplined in body and so forth; thus should the meaning be understood here. 'Aghamūlaṃ vamitvāna' means having vomited the fault known as ignorance (avijjā) and craving for existence (bhava-taṇhā), which are the roots of the suffering of the round of rebirths, or all the faults of defilements, by drinking the emetic medicine known as the Noble Path (ariya-magga), thereby ejecting them and casting them out from one's internal continuity. 'Patto mē āsavakkhayo' means that the taints such as the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava) are exhausted in this Nibbāna; or, because it is reached through the exhaustion of those taints, it is called the destruction of taints (āsavakkhaya), referring to Nibbāna and Arahantship. He made known his attainment of Arahantship through this inspired utterance, saying 'I have reached, I have attained that destruction of taints.'

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Pārāpariya is finished."
295:
## 7. Yasa-theragāthā-vaṇṇanā

The verse beginning with 'Suvilitto suvasano' is that of the Venerable Elder Yasa. What is its origin? This Elder Yasa had also performed extraordinary merit (adhikāra) under previous Buddhas and had accumulated wholesome deeds that serve as a support for liberation from the round of rebirths (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) in various existences. In the time of Buddha Sumedha, he was a Naga King of great power; he invited the community of monks headed by the Buddha to his abode and offered a great alms-giving. He offered the Buddha three very costly robes, and to each monk, he offered a pair of very costly cloths along with all the requisites of a recluse. Due to that meritorious deed, wandering through the worlds of devas and humans, he became the son of a wealthy merchant in the time of Buddha Siddhattha and worshipped the Great Bodhi-tree (Mahābodhi) with the seven gems. In the time of Buddha Kassapa, he went forth in the Dispensation and practiced the Dhamma of a recluse. Thus wandering only in the happy realms, in the time of our Buddha, he was reborn in the city of Bārāṇasī as the son of a merchant of great wealth; he was named Yasa and was extremely delicate. 'He had three palaces'—all such details should be understood as they appear in the Khandhaka of the Vinaya Mahāvagga.

Urged by his past wholesome causes, during the night, seeing the unseemly state of his sleeping attendants, he was moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega). Wearing his golden slippers, he left the house. He exited through the city gate opened by devas and, reaching the vicinity of the Isipatana Deer Park, he cried out, 'Friends, I am indeed distressed! Friends, I am indeed oppressed!' At that time, the Buddha was staying in Isipatana and, in order to favor Yasa, was walking to and fro in the open air. The Buddha said, 'Come, Yasa, this is not distressed, this is not oppressed.' Hearing that there is indeed a place that is not distressed and not oppressed, he became joyful, took off his golden slippers, approached the Buddha, and sat down to one side. The Buddha taught him the progressive discourse (anupubbīkathā) and then the teaching of the Four Noble Truths; at the conclusion of the truths, he became a Stream-enterer (sotāpanna). Later, while the Buddha was teaching the Four Noble Truths to his father who had come searching for him, Yasa realized Arahantship. This is stated in the Apadāna:

'My well-created mansion is submerged in the great ocean;
Goodly created is the pond, resounding with the cries of ruddy geese.'
296: Rivers flow there with beautiful banks and delightful scenery, covered with Mandālaka flowers, as well as Paduma and Uppala lotuses. They are teeming with fish and turtles, crowded with various birds, echoing with the cries of peacocks and cranes, and the sweet songs of cuckoos and other birds. Pigeons, ducks, geese, and Cakkavāka birds that frequent the rivers; partridges, Sāḷikā birds, Pammaka birds, and Jīvajīvaka birds are found in this river. Geese and cranes cry out; many owls and Pingala birds are present. There are sands of rubies and pearls, endowed with the seven gems. Trees made entirely of gold, wafting various fragrances, illuminate my mansion day and night at all times. Sixty thousand musical instruments play evening and morning; sixteen thousand women always surround me. Leaving the mansion, with a clear and joyful mind, I paid homage to the Great Famed One, Sumedha, the Leader of the World. Having prostrated before the Fully Enlightened One, I invited him along with the Saṅgha. That Wise One, Sumedha, the Leader of the World, accepted. The Great Sage Sumedha, having given me a Dhamma talk, dismissed me. Having prostrated before the Fully Enlightened One, I returned to my mansion. I addressed my attendants: 'All of you, assemble! In the morning, the Buddha will come to our mansion.' The attendants said: 'It is a gain for us, a great gain for us who live near you. We too shall make an offering to the Teacher, the Best of Buddhas.' Having prepared food, drink, and refreshments, I announced the time. The Leader of the World arrived with a hundred thousand Arahants who had stilled their defilements. I welcomed him with five-fold musical instruments. The Supreme Man sat upon a throne made entirely of gold.
297: At that time, there was a ceiling made entirely of gold; fans were waved amidst the Saṅgha of monks. I satisfied the Saṅgha of monks with abundant food and drink; I offered a pair of robes to each member of the Saṅgha. He whom they call Sumedha, the recipient of the world's offerings, sitting amidst the Saṅgha of monks, spoke these verses: 'He who has satisfied me and all these monks with food and drink—I shall praise him; listen to my words. For eighteen hundred aeons, he will delight in the deva world; a thousand times he will be a Cakkavatti king. Whatever birth he attains, whether as a deva or a human, he will always carry a canopy made entirely of gold. In thirty thousand aeons, a Teacher named Gotama by clan, born of the Okkāka family, will arise in the world. He will be an heir to that Buddha's Dhamma, a legitimate son born of the Dhamma. Having fully understood all taints (āsavas), he will attain Nibbāna, free from taints. Sitting amidst the Saṅgha of monks, he will roar a lion's roar. They will hold a parasol over his funeral pyre; he is burnt beneath the parasol. I have attained the state of a recluse; my defilements have been burnt away. Whether in a pavilion or at the foot of a tree, I have no distress. The gift I gave thirty thousand aeons ago—I know no miserable destination (duggati). This is the fruit of that entire gift. My defilements have been burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out,' he said. Then the Blessed One stretched out his right arm to the venerable Yasa and said, 'Come, monk (Ehi Bhikkhu).' Immediately upon these words, he appeared with hair and beard two finger-breadths long, carrying the eight requisites, like a senior elder of a hundred years' standing.
