The venerable Yasa, reflecting on his own practice and filled with inspiration, by the power of his previous practice through the 'Ehi Bhikkhu' ordination, being well-anointed, well-dressed, and adorned with all ornaments, recited this verse: 'I, who previously had a body well-anointed with perfume, was well-dressed, and adorned with all ornaments, have now attained the Three Knowledges; the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.' In that verse, 'suvilitto' means being anointed with good, fragrant sandalwood. 'suvasano' means wearing good, costly garments from the Kāsī kingdom. 'sabbābharaṇabhūsito' means being adorned with all types of ornaments.
298:
He became like an elder of sixty years of rains. That Venerable Yasa, reflecting on his own practice and uttering a verse of solemn utterance, by the power of his previous habit from the time he attained the status of an 'Ehi Bhikkhu' monk, said:

"Well-anointed, well-dressed,
Adorned with all ornaments,
I have attained the three knowledges;
The Buddha's teaching has been done."

In that verse, "Suvilitto" means having a body anointed with excellent saffron and sandalwood. "Suvasano" means being well-dressed in very expensive cloth from the Kāsika kingdom. "Sabbābharaṇabhūsito" means being adorned with all ornaments, such as head-dresses and so forth. "Ajjhagamiṃ" means I have attained or I have reached. The remaining words are as previously explained.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Yasa is Finished.

## 8. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Kimila

"Abhisattova nipatati" is the verse of the Venerable Elder Kimila. What is its origin (uppatti)? This Elder Kimila had also performed meritorious deeds of service (adhikāra) in the presence of previous Buddhas and performed merits in various existences. In the time of the Blessed One Kakusandha, having been born in a good family and reached the age of discretion, after the Teacher had attained Parinibbāna, he made an offering in the form of a pavilion with salala flowers dedicated to the relics. By the power of that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, and after wandering between the worlds of gods and humans, in this Buddha-era, he was born into the Sakyan royal family in the city of Kapilavatthu and was named Kimila. When he reached maturity, he lived endowed with great wealth and possessions. The Teacher, seeing the maturity of his knowledge, while staying at Anupiyā to induce spiritual urgency (saṃvega), created an illusion of a beautiful woman in her first youth and showed her before him. Then, he gradually made her appear as if overcome by old age, disease, and ruin. Seeing that state, Prince Kimila, wishing to express his extreme spiritual urgency, said:
299:
“Age falls away as if cursed; the form, though remaining the same, seems like another. I remember myself, though not departed for long, as if I were someone else.”

In that verse, “Abhisattova” means as if ordered and commanded by the gods, saying, “Go quickly, do not stay.” There is also a variant reading “Abhisaṭṭho vā,” which means as if urged by someone saying, “Go swiftly.” “Nipatati” means it passes by, it runs on, it does not stay; it means it reaches destruction and decay moment by moment. “Vayo” refers to the specific stages of the body, such as childhood and youth. Here, however, youth is intended; for that stage appeared to him as if running away and being exhausted. “Rūpaṃ” refers to the perfection of form. Alternatively, it refers to the body, as in the passages: “Depending on bones, depending on sinews, and depending on flesh, the space enclosed is designated as form (rūpa).” “Aññamiva tatheva santaṃ” means that although this form exists in that very same manner, it appears to me as if it were another. Some teachers read “Tadeva santaṃ.” “Tasseva sato” means of me, who is no other. “Avippavasato” means not being away for a long time. Indeed, because of a long absence, even one who is not another appears as if another; the meaning here is that such a long absence is not present. “Aññasseva sarāmi attānaṃ” means I remember, perceive, and recognize this self-identity of mine as if it were the body of another being.

Thus, as the elder reflected on the nature of impermanence (anicca), a very strong spiritual urgency (saṃvega) arose. Having been moved by that urgency, he approached the Teacher, heard the Dhamma, gained faith, and ordained. Having established insight meditation (vipassanā), he attained Arahatship before long. Regarding this, it is said in the Apadāna:

“When the Buddha Kakusandha, the Brahmin, the one who had lived the life, had attained Parinibbāna, I took salala flowers and made a pavilion.”

“Having gone to Tāvatiṃsa, I obtained a magnificent celestial mansion. I outshone other gods; this is the fruit of that meritorious deed.”
301:
“Ninety-four aeons ago, I gave that fruit; because of that gift of fruit, I have never known a state of woe. This is the fruit of offering fruit. My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.” Thus he spoke.

Having become one with the six supernormal powers, later, not long after the Buddha had passed into Parinibbāna, an agreement was made to chant the Dhamma (the First Council). While the Great Elders were residing in various places, one day he saw the Venerable Ānanda—who was still a trainee (sekha)—preaching the Dhamma surrounded by a large assembly. Wishing to arouse in Ānanda the effort to attain the higher paths, he recited this verse:

“Having gone to the forest thicket at the foot of a tree,
Setting Nibbāna in your heart,
Meditate, Gotama, and do not be negligent.
What will the meaningless chatter (biḷibiḷikā) of the people do for you?”

In that verse, 'rukkhamūlagahanaṃ' means a forest thicket that is at the foot of a tree. There are forest thickets that are not at the foot of a tree, and there are feet of trees that are not forest thickets. Among these, by taking 'the foot of a tree', it shows the place is endowed with shade and is free from the dangers of wind and sun. By taking 'forest thicket', it shows the absence of wind danger due to being sheltered, and the absence of crowding by people. By both together, it shows the suitability for meditation. 'Pasakkiya' means having approached near. 'Setting Nibbāna in your heart' means placing Nibbāna in the heart and mind, thinking, “By practicing in this way, I must attain Nibbāna.” 'Jhāya' means meditate through the contemplation of characteristics (lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna); it means to develop the meditation on the Path along with the meditation on insight (vipassanā). 'Gotama' is addressing the Treasurer of the Dhamma by his clan name. 'Do not be negligent' means do not fall into negligence regarding the three trainings, which are the most noble wholesome states. Now, to show the Elder's negligence as it then existed and to reject it, he said, “What will the meaningless chatter of the people do for you?” In that verse, 'biḷibiḷikā' means the act of making the sound 'wi-li-wi-li'. Just as the occurrence of the sound 'bi-li-bi-li' is useless, what benefit will such 'biḷibiḷikā'-like fame among people do for you? What kind of goal will it achieve for you? Therefore, he gave the advice: “Give up fame among people and be one who strives for your own true goal.”

Upon hearing this advice, other monks also became stirred by the words that smelled of seclusion. Spending the time by walking in meditation for many parts of the night and developing insight, just as he was about to lie down on his couch after entering the monastery, he attained the fruit of Arahantship.

The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Vajjiputta is finished.

The verse beginning with 'Pañcakkhandhā pariññātā' is that of the Venerable Elder Isidatta. This Elder Isidatta had performed special meritorious deeds in the presence of previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit that is the cause for liberation from the round of rebirths in various existences. In the time of Vipassī Buddha, he was born into a householder's family.
302:
Hearing that instruction, he was stirred by the words of the other monks regarding the "scent of rot." Spending much of the night in walking meditation and intensifying his insight, he entered his dwelling; just as he lay down on the couch, he attained Arahantship.

## The Commentary on the Verse of Vajjiputta Thera is finished.

## 10. Commentary on the Verse of Isidatta Thera

"The five aggregates are fully understood" is the verse of the Venerable Isidatta Thera. What is its origin? This Isidatta Thera had also performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit that serves as a support for liberation from the round of rebirths in various existences. In the time of Vipassī Buddha, he was born into a good family, and upon reaching the age of discretion, he saw the Blessed One walking along the road one day. With a heart full of faith, he offered a sweet āmoda fruit. Due to that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the celestial realm and, after performing merits repeatedly and wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was born in this Buddha's era as the son of a caravan leader in Vaḍḍha village in the country of Avanti. He was given the name Isidatta.

When he reached adulthood, he became an unseen friend of Citta the householder in Macchikāsaṇḍa. Having received a message sent by Citta the householder describing the qualities of the Buddha, he gained faith in the Dispensation. He ordained under the Elder Mahākaccāna and, having undertaken the practice of insight, he soon attained the six supernormal powers (abhiññā). This matter is stated in the Apadāna as follows:

"To the Golden-hued Buddha, the Recipient of Offerings,
Who was walking along the road, I offered an āmoda fruit.

In the ninety-one aeons since I offered that fruit,
I have not known a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of the gift of fruit.

My defilements have been burnt away... [pe]... the Buddha's Dispensation has been fulfilled."

After attaining the six supernormal powers, he asked permission from the Elder, saying, "I will go to serve the Buddha." Gradually traveling to the Middle Country (Majjhima Desa), he approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat in a suitable place.
303:
While sitting near the Buddha, the Teacher greeted him with words of welcome, such as "Monk, are you well? Are you keeping fit?" In response, the monk declared his Arahantship by saying, "Venerable Sir, since the time I entered Your Majesty's Dispensation, all my sufferings have vanished, and all dangers have been stilled." He then recited this verse:

"The five aggregates are fully understood;
They remain with their roots cut.
The end of suffering (Nirvana) has been reached;
I have attained the destruction of the taints (Arahantship)."

In that verse, 'pañcakkhandhā pariññātā' means: "My five aggregates of clinging have been fully understood and known through the Path-knowledge (maggapaññā) accompanied by insight-knowledge (vipassanā-paññā), realizing 'This is suffering, this much is suffering, there is no suffering beyond this.' There is nothing more to be understood regarding these aggregates." 'Tiṭṭhanti chinnumūlakā' means: because they have been fully understood, and because their roots such as ignorance (avijjā) and craving (taṇhā) have been completely cut and abandoned by the Noble Path, these aggregates remain until the cessation of the final consciousness. 'Dukkhakkhayo anuppatto' means: because the roots are cut, the end of the suffering of the round of rebirths, which is Nirvana, has been reached and attained. 'Patto me āsavakkhayo' means: because the end of all taints such as the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava) has been reached, the state called the destruction of taints, which is Arahantship, has been reached and attained. Some teachers read 'antimoyaṃ samussayo'. This means: because Nirvana has been attained, this body of mine is the last and final one; there is now no further rebirth. Whatever has not been explained in various places is clear according to the method already mentioned below.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Isidatta is finished.

## The Commentary on the Twelfth Vagga is finished.

## The Commentary on the Verses of the Elders in the Paramatthadīpanī is finished.

## adorned with the verses of one hundred and twenty Elders.
304:
## 2. Dukanipāta
## 1. Paṭhamavagga
## 1. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Uttara

In the Dukanipāta, the verse beginning with "Natthi koci bhavo nicco" is the verse of the Venerable Elder Uttara. What is the account of this Elder's origin? This Elder also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit that serves as a support for the attainment of Nibbāna in various existences. During the time of Sumedha Buddha, he was a Vijjādhara (a knowledge-holder) and traveled through the sky. At that time, the Teacher, in order to favor that Vijjādhara, sat at the foot of a certain tree in the forest, emitting the six-colored Buddha rays. While traveling through the sky, the Vijjādhara saw the Blessed One and, with a heart full of faith, descended from the sky and worshipped the Blessed One with very pure and abundant Kaṇikāra flowers. By the power of the Buddha's majesty, those flowers remained above the Teacher in the form of an umbrella. Due to that merit, he had an exceedingly faithful heart and, after passing away in a later life, was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Enjoying grand divine splendor, he remained there for the full lifespan, and after passing away from there, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans. In the time of our Buddha's appearance, he was born in Rājagaha as the son of a wealthy Brahmin (Brāhmaṇamahāsāla) and was named Uttara. When he reached the age of discretion and became wise, he attained mastery in the Brahminical sciences and became highly esteemed by the people for his birth, appearance, knowledge, age, and virtuous conduct. Seeing Uttara's abundant prosperity, the great minister of Magadha, Vassakāra, wishing to give him his daughter, expressed his desire. Uttara, having a desire for liberation from Saṃsāra, rejected the minister's proposal. From time to time, he attended upon the General of the Dhamma, and after hearing the Dhamma from the Venerable Sāriputta, he gained faith and ordained. Being one who fulfilled his duties, he attended upon and served the Elder.

At that time, an illness arose in the Venerable Sāriputta. To find medicine for the Elder, the novice Uttara took his bowl and robes early in the morning and left the monastery. On the way, he placed his bowl on the bank of a pond and went near the water to wash his face. At that moment, a thief who had tunneled into a house...
305:
The thief, pursued by guards, fled through the main city gate and, while running, dropped the bundle of jewels he had taken into the novice's bowl and escaped. The novice returned to the side of his bowl. The king's men, pursuing the thief, saw the bundle in the novice's bowl and, saying, "This is the thief; this person committed the theft," they tied the novice's hands behind his back and brought him to the Brahmin Vassakāra. At that time, Vassakāra was appointed to the king's judicial office and was administering punishments. Thinking, "This person previously did not heed my words and ordained among the mere shaven-headed ascetics," and harboring a grudge, he ordered the novice to be impaled alive on a stake without properly investigating the case.

Then, the Blessed One, seeing the maturity of the novice's knowledge, went to that place. He placed his hand—which had soft, long fingers like a net, and palms like a stream of liquid cinnabar and gold, with white radiance mixed with the gem-like light of his flickering fingernails—upon Uttara's head and said, "Uttara, this suffering has arisen as the result of your past karma. In the ripening of that karma, you must practice endurance through the power of reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa)." Having said this, he taught the Dhamma suitable to his disposition. Due to the touch of the Teacher's hand, which was like an infusion of the Deathless, and because of the faith and joy that arose, the novice Uttara attained grand rapture and joy. By ascending the path of insight (vipassanā-magga) he had practiced and because his knowledge had reached maturity, and through the Teacher's graceful teaching, he exhausted all defilements through the sequence of the paths at that very moment and became one endowed with the six supernormal powers (abhiññā). This is stated in the Apadāna:

"The Fully Enlightened One named Sumedha, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man,
The Blessed One, desiring seclusion, went to the Himālaya forest.

Having entered the Himālaya, the supreme, compassionate Sage,
The most excellent of beings, sat down cross-legged.

I was then a Vijjādhara, a traveler in the sky,
Holding a well-made trident, I was traveling through the air.

Like a fire burning on a mountain peak, like the full moon,
Like a kingly Sāla tree in full bloom, the Buddha illuminated the forest."
306:
When I came out of the forest, the Buddha's rays, resembling the light of a reed fire, raced forth; seeing those rays, I inspired faith in my heart.

While searching, I saw a Kaṇikāra flower with a divine fragrance; taking three flowers, I worshipped the Buddha, the Best of Beings.

By the power of the Buddha, those three flowers of mine then stood with stems upward and faces downward, providing shade for the Teacher.

Through that well-performed deed and the aspiration of my will, I left the human body and reached the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

There, my well-created mansion is known as 'Kaṇikārī'; it is sixty leagues in height and thirty leagues in width.

One hundred thousand gables made of pure gold, adorned with a thousand pillars and a hundred pinnacles, and decorated with banners, appeared in my mansion.

Thrones made of gold, made of gems, made of rubies, and made of crystal appeared according to my wishes and desires.

And a costly bed was equipped with woolen carpets and coverlets; a rug with hair on one side was indeed provided with a pillow.

Leaving the mansion and wandering through the celestial realm, I traveled as I wished, escorted by a host of gods.

Standing beneath the flowers, my upper canopy was covered with Kaṇikāra flowers for a hundred leagues all around.

Sixty thousand musical instruments attended upon me evening and morning; they always surrounded me day and night with unwearied effort.

There, I delighted in dancing, singing, and the playing of instruments; possessing the desired sensual pleasures, I rejoiced in play and delight.

Then, eating and drinking in that celestial realm, I rejoiced in Tāvatiṃsa; together with a host of nymphs, I rejoiced in that supreme mansion.
307:
For five hundred times, I exercised the kingship of the gods.
For three hundred times, I was a Universal Monarch.
As for the vast regional kingships, they are beyond counting.

Wandering through various lives, I obtained great wealth.
There is no deficiency in my possessions; this is the fruit of offering to the Buddha.

I wandered only in two states of existence: the celestial realm and the human realm.
I know no other destination; this is the fruit of offering to the Buddha.

I was born only in two families: the Khattiya and the Brāhmaṇa.
I know not of being born in a low family; this is the fruit of offering to the Buddha.

Elephant-vehicles, horse-vehicles, palanquins, and litters—
All these I obtained; this is the fruit of offering to the Buddha.

Hosts of female slaves, hosts of male slaves, and well-adorned women—
All these I obtained; this is the fruit of offering to the Buddha.

Silk garments, woolen garments, linen garments, and cotton garments—
All these I obtained; this is the fruit of offering to the Buddha.

Fresh new clothes, fresh new fruits, and fresh new food of excellent flavor—
All these I obtained; this is the fruit of offering to the Buddha.

"Eat this hard food, eat this soft food, sleep in this place"—
All these I obtained; this is the fruit of offering to the Buddha.

I am one who is worshipped in all places; my fame has risen very high.
I always have a large following; I always have an inseparable assembly.
I am the most excellent among my kinsmen; this is the fruit of offering to the Buddha.

I know neither cold nor heat; there is no burning fever.
Furthermore, there is no mental suffering in my heart.

I wandered through various lives having a complexion like the color of gold.
I know not of ugliness; this is the fruit of offering to the Buddha.
308:
"Passing away from the world of gods, urged by the root of merit, I was born in the city of Sāvatthī in a very wealthy Mahāsāla family.

Renouncing the five strands of sensual pleasure, I entered the homeless life. At the age of seven from birth, I attained Arahantship.

The Buddha, the One with Vision, knowing my virtues, granted me higher ordination. Though young, I am worthy of offerings; this is the fruit of offering to the Buddha.

My divine eye is purified; I am skilled in concentration; I have reached the pinnacle of the supernormal powers; this is the fruit of offering to the Buddha.

I have attained the four analytical insights in due order; I am proficient in the bases of psychic power; I have reached the pinnacle of all dhammas; this is the fruit of offering to the Buddha.

Because of the merit of worshipping the Buddha thirty thousand aeons ago, I have not known a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of offering to the Buddha.

My defilements are burnt away... I have followed the Buddha's teaching."

Having become one with the six supernormal powers, he rose from the stake and, out of compassion for others, stood in the air and performed a miracle. The great multitude was filled with wonder and amazement. At that very moment, his wound was healed. Then, when asked by the monks, "Friend, while experiencing such suffering, how were you able to apply yourself to insight meditation?", he replied, "Friends, I had already seen the danger of saṃsāra and the nature of conditioned things long ago. Thus, even while experiencing such suffering, I was able to develop insight and attain the special distinction," and he spoke these two verses:

"There is no state of existence that is permanent, nor are conditioned things eternal. These aggregates arise and then pass away again and again.

Knowing this danger, I have no desire for existence; having escaped from all sensual pleasures, I have reached the destruction of the taints."
309:
In that verse, "there is no existence that is permanent" refers to the various types of existence such as kammabhava (existence as action), upapattibhava (existence as rebirth), kāmabhava (sensual existence), rūpabhava (fine-material existence), arūpabhava (immaterial existence), saññībhava (percipient existence), asaññībhava (non-percipient existence), nevasaññīnāsaññībhava (neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient existence), ekavokārabhava (one-constituent existence), catuvokārabhava (four-constituent existence), and pañcavokārabhava (five-constituent existence). Among these, whether it be a lowly existence, a middling existence, a noble existence, a long-lived existence, an existence mostly of happiness, or an existence of mixed happiness and suffering—there is no such thing as a permanent, stable, lasting, or undecaying phenomenon. This is because they arise dependent on their respective causes. Since this is so, the connection is made: "There are also no permanent formations (saṅkhāra)."

The five aggregates, which are called "formations" (saṅkhāra) because they are conditioned by causes, arise under the name of "existence" (bhava). Being subject to change through aging and death, they are impermanent phenomena of a changing nature. Because this is true, they are called "formations." Therefore, He said: "Those aggregates arise and pass away again and again." These five aggregates, spoken of by the names of "existence" and "formations," arise repeatedly according to their causes; and having arisen, they are oppressed by aging and then pass away and break up. By this, He shows that the five aggregates, known by the terms "existence" and "formations," have the nature of arising and passing away.

Because for one who contemplates formations by applying the three marks, the three types of existence appear like a burning house, having known beforehand through the wisdom of insight the danger and fault in the conditioned, the formations seen through the mark of impermanence appear more clearly as suffering and non-self. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "What is impermanent is suffering; what is suffering is non-self."

Because for one who contemplates formations by applying the three marks, the three types of existence appear as fearful like a burning house, he said: "I have no desire for existence." Thus, for one whose mind has turned away from all forms of existence, not even a trace of longing for sensual pleasures remains. Therefore, he said: "I have escaped from all sensual pleasures." The word "amhi" should be connected as "I am." It means that just as one is free from human sensual pleasures, his mind has also turned away from divine sensual pleasures.

"I have reached the destruction of the taints" means that because he has thus well-contemplated formations, has clearly seen the danger in existences, and has a mind unattached to sensual pleasures, even if he were sitting on the point of a stake, I have... reached.
310:
I have reached the destruction of the taints, Nibbāna, and the fruit of Arahantship. Other fellow practitioners who have not yet reached the fruit of Arahantship should also strive to attain that fruit of Arahantship—thus he gave advice to the monks.

## The commentary on the verses of the Elder Uttara is finished.

## 2. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Piṇḍolabhāradvāja

The verse beginning with "Nayidaṃ anayena" is the verse of the Venerable Piṇḍolabhāradvāja. What is the background story? It is said that during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, this venerable one was reborn in the lion species and lived in a mountain cave. To show favor to that lion, the Blessed One entered the lion's dwelling cave while it was out searching for food and sat there, having entered the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti). When the lion returned after finding food, it saw the Blessed One at the cave entrance and was filled with joy. It made an offering with flowers born of water and land, and with a clear and confident mind, it stood with mindfulness directed toward the Buddha, roaring the lion's roar at the three times of the day to ward off wild beasts in the forest and protect the Blessed One. Just as on the first day, it made offerings for seven days. After seven days, the Blessed One emerged from the attainment of cessation and, thinking, "This will be a strong supporting condition (upanissaya) for his attainment of the fruit of Arahantship," He flew into the sky and went to the monastery while the lion was still watching.

The lion, like the Pālileyyaka elephant, unable to bear the suffering of separation from the Buddha, passed away and was reborn in a wealthy family in the city of Haṃsavatī. When he came of age, he went to the monastery with the city dwellers, heard the Dhamma, and performed a great almsgiving for seven days. Having performed meritorious deeds throughout his life, he wandered repeatedly through the worlds of devas and humans. In the time of our Blessed One, he was reborn in the city of Kosambī as the son of King Udena's chaplain, named Bhāradvāja.

When he came of age, he learned the three Vedas and taught them to five hundred young brahmins. Due to his nature as a heavy eater and having unsuitable behavior, he was abandoned by his students and went to the city of Rājagaha. There, seeing the gains and honor of the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks, he ordained in the Dispensation. However, he wandered about without knowing moderation in food, so the Teacher established him in knowing moderation in food by means of a skillful device. Thereafter, he practiced insight and soon became an Arahant endowed with the six supernormal powers (abhiññā). Therefore, it is stated in the Apadāna: "In the past, I was a hunter wandering in the forest. At that time, I saw the Blessed One, who was stainless and had reached the end of all phenomena, and having taken a piyāla fruit, I offered it to the Blessed One."
311:
The Blessed One, having established him in the state of knowing the measure through skillful means, he practiced insight meditation (vipassanā) and before long became one possessed of the six supernormal knowledges (chalabhiññā). Regarding this, it is said in the Apadāna:

"In the past, I was a hunter wandering in the forest. At that time, I saw the stainless Buddha, the one who has reached the end of all phenomena (dhamma).
Taking a piyāla fruit, I offered it with a clear mind and with my own hands to the supreme Buddha, the heroic one, the field of merit.
In the thirty-first aeon from this present one, I gave that fruit. Due to that meritorious deed, I have not known a miserable rebirth (duggati). This is the fruit of the offering of fruit.
My defilements have been burnt away... (pe)... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled."

Having become one possessed of the six supernormal knowledges, he uttered a lion's roar (sīhanāda) saying, "That which is to be attained by disciples in the presence of the Blessed One, I have attained," and also among the Saṅgha of monks, "If anyone has doubt regarding the Path or the Fruit, let him ask me." Therefore, the Blessed One placed him in the foremost position, saying, "Monks, among my monk disciples who are roarers of the lion's roar, this Piṇḍolabhāradvāja is the foremost."

One day, out of compassion for a stingy Brahmin of wrong view who had been his friend during his time as a layman and who had come to him, the Elder spoke words related to giving and generosity. That Brahmin, thinking, "This Elder wishes to destroy my wealth," even while frowning, said, "I give you one meal." The Elder replied, "Give that meal to the Saṅgha, do not give it to me," and directed it to the Saṅgha. Again, when the Brahmin showed dissatisfaction, thinking, "This Elder wants me to give to many people," on the second day, the Venerable Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, inspired the Brahmin by explaining the great fruitfulness of offerings made to the Saṅgha. At that time, the Elder thought, "This Brahmin thinks that I am urging him to give out of greed for food. He does not know that I have fully understood nutriment in every aspect. Come, I shall let him know," and he uttered:

"This life of mine is not by wrong means,
Nutriment is not close to my heart,
This physical body is sustained by nutriment,
Seeing thus, I wander for alms."
312:
"The Buddhas and the virtuous have known that homage and offerings in families are mud;
It is a subtle thorn, difficult to extract; honor is hard for a base person to give up."

He spoke these two verses. Therein, 'Nayidaṃ anayena jီvitaṃ' means: this life of mine is not through wrong livelihood (anesanā) such as giving bamboo or giving flowers, because of the absence of attachment to life. 'Nāhāro hadayassa santiko' means: nutriment, when consumed, does not bring peace to the heart (the mind) like the knowledge of the Path and Fruit; rather, it merely destroys immediate hunger. Alternatively, 'Nāhāro hadayassa santiko' means that because of the absence of craving for tastes (rasataṇhā), nutriment does not stick near my heart, which is the base of craving for tastes. Some also read it as 'santike'. For one who wanders greedy for food and occupied with gain and honor, nutriment is said to be 'near the heart' because it must be frequently reflected upon. However, for one who has fully understood nutriment and has abandoned desire and lust (chandarāga) therein, nutriment is not 'near the heart' because there is no reflection such as 'How might I obtain it?'. If there is no attachment to life and no craving for the taste of food, then why do you wander for alms? Anticipating this question, he said: 'This physical body is sustained by nutriment; seeing thus, I wander for alms.' Nutriment means food; it is the cause for the persistence of this body; therefore, it is 'sustained by nutriment'. 'This body has a persistence dependent on nutriment'—seeing thus, knowing thus, and keeping this meaning in his wisdom, he wanders for alms, meaning he seeks alms-food.

Wishing to show that one like himself should not be thought of as being bound by homage, offerings, gain, and honor when approaching families for the sake of requisites, he spoke the verse beginning with 'Paṅko'. Its meaning is: that praise of virtues and offerings that will occur among families and householders for monks who have approached for the sake of requisites—because it causes those with undeveloped minds to sink and makes them soiled—the Buddhas and others have known, fully understood, or declared it as 'mud' (paṅka). Therefore, that...
313:
For the virtuous, honor and offerings do not lead to bondage because they have already abandoned the defilements. But for the unvirtuous (asappurisa), honor and offerings are like a subtle and hard-to-extract thorn, because they are difficult to perceive, cause affliction, pierce within, and are impossible to pull out. For this very reason, a base person finds it difficult to abandon or extract such honor and offerings. Because he does not practice the path to abandon honor and offerings, he cannot abandon them and thus becomes bound by defilements. Hearing these words, the brahmin became greatly inspired by the Elder.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Piṇḍolabhāradvāja is finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Valliya

The verse beginning with "Makkaṭo pañcadvārāya" is that of the Venerable Valliya. What is its origin? This Elder, too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit in various lives, was reborn in a family home thirty-one aeons ago from this Bhadda-kappa. When he reached the age of discretion, one day he went into the forest for some business. There, he saw the Paccekabuddha named Nārada living at the foot of a tree. With a heart full of faith, he built a hut with reeds, thatched it with grass, and offered it. He also cleared the Paccekabuddha's walking path, scattered sand, and offered it.

Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans. In this Buddha-era, he was reborn in Sāvatthī as the son of a wealthy brahmin (brāhmaṇa-mahāsāla) and was named Valliya. When he reached maturity and youth, he wandered about following the dictates of his senses. Through association with a good friend (kalyāṇamitta), he approached the Blessed One, heard the Dhamma, and gained faith. He ordained and, practicing insight meditation (vipassanā), soon attained Arahantship. That Elder spoke thus in the Apadāna:

"Not far from the Himālaya, there is a mountain named Hārita. At that time, the Paccekabuddha named Nārada lived at the foot of a tree.

"I made a hut of reeds and thatched it with grass. Having cleared the walking path, I offered it to the Paccekabuddha."
314:
“Due to that well-performed deed and my volitional aspirations, I left the human body and reached the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

“In that heaven, my well-constructed celestial mansion, created from the reed-hut, was sixty leagues high and thirty leagues wide.

“For fourteen aeons, I delighted in the heavenly realm. Seventy-one times, I exercised the rule of the gods.

“Thirty-four times, I was a Wheel-turning Monarch. The number of times I was a regional king is beyond counting.

“Having ascended the palace of Dhamma, endowed with all excellent qualities, I live as I wish in the Dispensation of the Sakyan Son.

“Thirty-one aeons ago from this era, I performed that deed. Because of that deed, I know no miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of offering a reed-hut.

“My defilements have been burned away... [pe]... the Buddha's bidding has been done.”

Having attained Arahantship, wishing to declare his attainment (aññā-byākaraṇa) by illustrating how his mind used to wander at will among sense objects like forms during his time as a worldling, and how it is now restrained by the Noble Path, he spoke these two verses:

“The monkey-like mind enters the reed-hut of the body with its five doors, and wanders through the doors, repeatedly shaking them.

“Stop, O monkey-mind! Do not run. This running of yours is not as it was before. You are now restrained by wisdom; you shall not go far.”

In those verses, "shaking" (ghaṭṭayanto) means: just as a monkey consuming fruit shakes the tree many times by letting go of one branch and grabbing another due to its restless nature, so too, through the various doors such as the eye, the mind lets go of one object and takes another among sense objects like forms. Thus, by the power of establishing the mental continuum, it remains steady and unmoving...
316:
When the woman who was offering milk moved her hands and feet and poured it, he uttered the words, "Sister, enough." In the third year, during the rains retreat, while striving and exerting, he reached Arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna: "With a confident and joyful mind, I filled the water-pot for the unsurpassed Saṅgha of monks of the Buddha Padumuttara." "Whether on a mountain top, a tree top, in the sky, or on the ground, whenever I desire drinking water, it quickly appears for me." "In the hundred thousandth aeon from this one, I gave that gift then. Because of that gift of water, I do not know of any woeful rebirth." "My defilements are burnt... the Buddha's Dispensation has been fulfilled."

Having become an Arahant, by way of explaining his preliminary practice, he spoke these two verses to declare his attainment: "On the bank of the Ganges, a hut was made of three palm leaves; my bowl is like a corpse-vessel, and my robe is of rags." "Within two rains retreats, only one word was spoken by me; in the third rains retreat, the mass of darkness was shattered."

In those verses, "Tiṇṇam me tālapattānaṃ, gaṅgātīre kuṭī katā" means making a small hut on the bank of the Ganges river to protect from the rain using three palm leaves that had fallen from a palm tree. By this, he shows his contentment with his lodging (senāsana-santosa). Indeed, it was said by the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta: "For one sitting cross-legged, if the rain does not wet the knees, it is enough for the comfortable living of a monk who has directed his mind (to Nibbāna)."

There is also a variant reading "tālapattīnaṃ," but the meaning is the same. "Chavasittova me patto" means my bowl is like a vessel for pouring milk for a corpse; it means it is like a vessel used for pouring milk for those who have died.
317:
The meaning is: "Paṃsukūlañca cīvaraṃ" means my robe is a rag-robe made from discarded rags found on roadsides, cemeteries, and so forth. With these two words, he shows contentment with requisites.

"Dvinnṃ antaravassānaṃ" means within the two years from the time of ordination until the attainment of Arahantship. "Ekā vācā me bhāsitā" means "Enough, sister"—I spoke only this single sentence refusing the milk; there was no other utterance. By this, he shows supreme restraint of body and speech. "Tatiye antaravassāmhi" means within the third year, even before that year was complete. "Tamokhandho padālito" means the mass of darkness, which is ignorance (avijjā), has been destroyed by the Path of Arahantship; the underlying tendency of ignorance (avijjānusaya) has been utterly cut off. By this, he speaks of the total abandonment of all defilements.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Gaṅgātīriya is finished.

## 5. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Ajina

The verses beginning with "Api ce hoti tevijjo" are those of the Venerable Elder Ajina. As for the background: This elder also performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas. Accumulating merit in various existences, he was born into a family home in a world empty of Buddhas. Upon reaching maturity, he went to the forest for some business and saw a Paccekabuddha named Sucintita, who was afflicted by illness. With a confident mind, he offered clarified butter (ghee) for the purpose of medicine.

Due to that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the heavenly world and wandered only through happy destinations. In this Buddha's era, he took rebirth in the home of a poor Brahmin in Sāvatthī. At the time of his birth, he was received with an antelope skin (ajina); therefore, they named him Ajina. Because he had not performed deeds conducive to wealth, he was born into a poor family and, even after reaching maturity, wandered about with little food and drink. Seeing the Buddha's power at the acceptance of the Jetavana monastery, he gained faith and ordained. Practicing insight meditation (vipassanā), he soon became an Arahant with the six supernormal powers. However, due to past karma, he had few gains and remained obscure. The food he received was only of poor quality. Due to the power of his karma, worldling monks and novices looked down on him as an "obscure person." Then, the elder, to stir those monks, spoke these two verses beginning with "Api ce hoti tevijjo."
318:
To the Blessed One, Sucintita, the Foremost in the world, the Bull among men, who was dwelling in the great forest, afflicted by a wind-ailment.

Having seen him and having inspired my mind with confidence, I offered clarified butter. Due to that deed performed and accumulated, this Bhāgīrathī Gaṅgā river,

And the four great oceans, become clarified butter for me. This fearsome earth, immeasurable and incalculable,

Knowing my intention, becomes honey-sugar. These trees on the four continents, the plants and the earth-born,

Knowing my intention, they become wish-fulfilling trees. Fifty times I exercised the sovereignty of the gods as Sakka, the lord of gods.

Fifty-one times I was a wheel-turning monarch. I also held vast regional kingship beyond counting.

Ninety-four aeons ago, I gave that gift. Because of the merit of offering that clarified butter, I have not known a woeful state. This is the fruit of offering clarified butter.

My defilements are burnt... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out (he said).

Even after reaching the fruit of Arahantship, due to the residual effect of past karma, he was one of few gains and remained obscure. Even the food designated for the community (uddesabhatta) or distributed by tickets (salākabhatta) that he received was of poor quality. Due to the result of karma, worldling monks and novices despised the Elder Ajina, saying, "He is an obscure person." The Great Elder, wishing to stir those monks—

Even if one is a possessor of the three knowledges (tevijja), a conqueror of death, and taintless (anāsava),

Fools, out of ignorance, despise him as "one who is unknown."
319:
“But the person who is a receiver of food and drink here in this world, even if he is of evil nature, he is honored by them.” He spoke these two verses.

In those verses, the word 'api' is a particle in the sense of conjecture (sambhavana). 'Ce' is in the sense of supposition (parikappana). 'Hoti' means it happens or is. Because he is endowed with the three knowledges, he is called 'tevijjo'. Because he abandons death, he is called 'maccuhayi'. Because of the absence of the taints of sensual desire etc., he is called 'anasavo'. This is what is meant—Because of the attainment of these three knowledges: the knowledge of the divine eye (dibbacakkhu-nana), the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivasa-nana), and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (asavakkhaya-nana), he is called 'tevijjo'. For that very reason, because the taints of sensual desire etc. are completely exhausted in every way, he is 'anasavo'. Because he does not take up a new existence in the future, there is no death, thus he is 'maccuhayi'.

Even if he is a person of such extraordinary qualities, fools despise him as an unknown person. Noble sons rightly go forth from the home life to the homeless life for the sake of the fruit of Arahatship and Nibbana. Even such a supreme man who stands having reached his own goal, fools and unwise persons despise him as 'not well-known, not famous' because of the absence of gains and honors that would make them say 'he is a practitioner of dhutanga, he is very learned, he is a preacher of Dhamma'. Why? Because of not knowing. He shows that the very cause there is the ignorance of virtues.

Just as fools, due to not knowing virtues and being heavy with gain, despise even one who is worthy of praise, so also, due to not knowing virtues and being heavy with gain, they praise even one who should be despised. To show this, he spoke the second verse. In that verse, 'yo' is an indefinite term. The word 'ca' is in the sense of distinction (vyatireka); by that, it creates the distinction of this person from the aforementioned person. 'Kho' is in the sense of emphasis (avadharaṇa). 'Annapanassa' is a mere illustration. 'Labhi' means one who has gains. 'Idha' means in this world. He is called 'puggala' because he fills and flows into various abodes of beings through aging and death. 'Papadhammo' means one of low nature.

This is the meaning here—But the person who is a receiver of only material requisites like robes etc., and not of jhanas etc., even though he is of low nature due to evil desires and immorality, he is honored and respected by fools in this world because they value material gains.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Ajina is finished.
320: ## 6. Commentary on the Verses of Meḷajina Thera "Yadāhaṃ dhammamassosiṃ" and so forth is the verse of the Venerable Meḷajina Thera. What is its origin? This Meḷajina Thera also had performed meritorious services under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit in various existences. In the time of Sumedha Buddha, he was born in a good family home. When he reached the age of discretion, one day, seeing the Blessed One going for alms, with a confident mind, he offered a delicious and fragrant Āmoda fruit. Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the worlds of gods and humans. In the time of our Buddha, he was born into a Khattiya family in the city of Vārāṇasī and received the name Meḷajina. Having mastered various arts and sciences, he became a wise and competent person, famous in all directions. While the Blessed One was staying at Isipatana in Vārāṇasī, Meḷajina went to the monastery, approached the Teacher, and upon hearing the Dhamma, gained faith and ordained. Practicing insight meditation (vipassanā), he attained Arahantship on that very day. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna— "The Blessed One, the Self-Awakened One, the Unconquered, possessing a thousand rays, having emerged from seclusion, came out for the sake of alms-resort. Seeing the Bull among Men, I approached with fruit in hand. With a confident and joyful heart, I offered the Āmoda fruit. In the ninety-fourth aeon from now, I gave that fruit then; because of that gift of fruit, I do not know of any miserable rebirth. My defilements have been burnt away... etc... the teaching of the Buddha has been carried out." Later, after attaining Arahantship, when asked by the monks, "Friend, have you attained any superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma) such as jhāna, path, or fruition beyond the ten wholesome courses of action of humans?" he wished to roar a lion's roar and spoke these two verses— "When I heard the Dhamma of the Teacher as he was speaking, from that time on, I have known no doubt in the Omniscient One, the Unconquered. In the Caravan Leader, the Great Hero, the Best of Charioteers, and in the Path or the Practice, no doubt exists for me."
321:
In those verses, 'yadā' means 'at which time'. 'Ahaṃ' is a reference to oneself. 'Dhammaṃ' refers to the Four Noble Truths. 'Assosiṃ' means 'I have heard'. 'Satthuno' means 'of the Teacher'; he is called the Teacher because he disciplines venayyas (beings to be tamed) through benefits in the present life and so forth. 'Kaṅkhaṃ' means 'doubt'. 'Sabbaññū' means 'the Omniscient One'; he is so called because he knows the conditioned and the unconditioned without remainder. 'Aparājite' means 'in the Unconquered One'; he is so called because he is not defeated by any danger. 'Satthavāhe' means 'in the Caravan Leader'; he is so called because he leads venayyas from the difficult journey of saṃsāra to Nibbāna.

The meaning is this: From the time I heard the Four Noble Truths from the Teacher as he was preaching the Dhamma, I reflected upon and attained it through the ear-door. From that hearing onwards, I have no doubt in the Omniscient Buddha who knows the conditioned, unconditioned, and conventional truths without remainder through his self-evolved knowledge, and who sees without obstruction. I have no doubt in the 'Unconquered One' (Aparājita) because he overcame the five Maras and thus cannot be defeated by them, and because he possesses the irresistible Wheel of Dhamma (appaṭihata dhammacakka) in the world including the devas. I have no doubt in the 'Caravan Leader' (Satthavāha) because he leads venayyas out of the wilderness of greed and so forth. I have no doubt in the 'Great Hero' (Mahāvīra) because of his great prowess. I have no doubt in the 'Supreme Buddha' (Sammāsambuddha), the most excellent of charioteers, because he tames those who are difficult to tame (purisadamma) with ultimate discipline. I no longer know doubt, such as 'Is the Buddha really the Buddha or not?', because I no longer need to rely on others. Likewise, I have no doubt or uncertainty (vicikicchā) regarding the Noble Path thus preached, or the practice of virtue (sīla) and so forth which are its foundation, wondering 'Is this the way out of saṃsāra or not?'. Here, by stating the absence of doubt in the Noble Dhamma, it should be understood that the absence of doubt in the Noble Saṅgha is also stated, because one established in that Dhamma does not change otherwise.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Meḷajina Thera is finished.

## 7. Commentary on the Verses of Rādha Thera

'Yathā agāraṃ ducchannaṃ' and the following verses are those of the Venerable Rādha Thera. What is the background story? It is said that in the time of the Buddha Padumuttara, he was born into a good family in the city of Haṃsavatī. When he reached the age of discretion, he went to the monastery, approached the Teacher, paid homage, and sat in a suitable place. Seeing the Teacher appoint a certain monk to the foremost position among those who possess quick-wittedness (paṭibhāneyyakānaṃ), he himself desired that position, made a wish, and performed a great donation and grand offerings to the Teacher. Having made this aspiration, he passed away from that life and accumulated merits in various existences. In the time of the Buddha Vipassī, he was born into a good family. When he reached the age of discretion, one day he saw the Teacher going for alms and, with a devout mind, offered sweet mangoes. Due to that meritorious deed, he was born in the deva world and, after performing merits repeatedly and wandering between the worlds of devas and humans, he was born into a Brahmin family in Rājagaha in the time of our Buddha. He was named Rādha. When he reached old age...
322:
(He) performed a great donation. He also performed a grand offering to the Teacher. Having made this aspiration, he passed away from that life and accumulated merits in various existences. In the time of the Buddha Vipassī, he was born into a good family. When he reached the age of discretion, one day he saw the Teacher going for alms and, with a devout mind, offered sweet mangoes. Due to that meritorious deed, he was born in the deva world and, after performing merits repeatedly and wandering between the worlds of devas and humans, he was born into a Brahmin family in Rājagaha in the time of our Buddha. He was named Rādha. When he reached old age while living the householder life, he was mistreated by his wife and children. Thinking, 'What is the use of living the householder life? I will go forth,' he went to the monastery, approached the elder monks, and requested ordination. The monks rejected him, saying, 'This Brahmin is old and will not be able to fulfill the major and minor duties.' He then went to the Buddha and informed him of his intention. The Buddha, seeing his possession of the supporting conditions (upanissaya), ordered the General of the Dhamma (Venerable Sāriputta) to ordain him. By developing insight (vipassanā), he attained Arahatship before long.

This is stated in the Apadāna:
'To the Buddha of golden hue, who is worthy of receiving offerings, as he was walking on the road, I offered a mango fruit.'
'Ninety-one aeons ago, I gave that fruit; since then, I have not known a miserable rebirth. This is the result of offering fruit.'
'My defilements have been burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.'

After attaining Arahatship, while living in the presence of the Teacher, he became the foremost among those who recognize the quick-wittedness (paṭibhāna) that serves as the basis for the Buddha's Dhamma teachings. Indeed, based on the Elder's view and conduct, new and diverse Dhamma teachings occurred to the Buddha. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'Monks, among my monk disciples who are quick-witted, Rādha is the foremost.' One day, wishing to praise meditation (bhāvanā) by saying, 'These beings are overcome by lust due to lack of meditation; if there is meditation, that lust does not exist,' he spoke these two verses beginning with 'Yathā agāraṃ'.

133-4. In those verses, 'agāraṃ' means any house whatsoever. 'Ducchannaṃ' means poorly thatched, full of holes and gaps. 'Samativijjhati' means the rain-shower penetrates through. 'Abhāvitaṃ' means just as the rain penetrates that house, [so lust penetrates the mind] that is not developed with meditation (samatha and vipassanā)...
323:
Because it is devoid of development (bhāvanā), the mind that is undeveloped is pierced by lust. This means not only lust, but all defilements such as hatred, delusion, and conceit also pierce a mind of such a nature. 'Well-developed' (subhāvitam) means a mind well-developed through the development of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā). Just as rain cannot penetrate a well-roofed house, defilements such as lust cannot penetrate such a mind.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Rādha is Finished.

## 8. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Surādha

The verses beginning with 'My birth is indeed exhausted' (khīṇā hi mayhaṃ jāti) are those of the Venerable Elder Surādha. What is the story of their origin? This elder also had performed special merit under previous Buddhas. Having accumulated merits in various lives, he was born in a respectable family during the time of the Buddha Sikhī. Upon reaching maturity, one day he saw the Teacher and, with a heart full of faith, offered a citron (mātuluṅga) fruit. Due to that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the deva world. After performing further merits and wandering only through the happy realms (sugati), he was born as the younger brother of the aforementioned Elder Rādha during the time of this Buddha's appearance. He was named Surādha. When his elder brother Rādha went forth, he himself also went forth. While practicing the work of insight (vipassanā), he attained Arahatship before long. Regarding this, it is said in the Apadāna:

'Like a blossoming Kaṇikāra flower, like the full moon,
Like a shining lamp-tree, I saw the Leader of the World.
Taking a citron fruit, I offered it to the Teacher,
The Hero worthy of offerings, with my own hands and a faithful heart.
In the thirty-first aeon from now, I gave that fruit;
Due to the merit of that gift of fruit, I have not known a miserable rebirth.
My defilements are burned away... (and so on)... I have followed the Buddha's teaching.'

After reaching Arahatship, in order to show how the Dispensation leads out of suffering, he declared his attainment of Arahatship through the two verses beginning with 'My birth is indeed exhausted.' My birth is exhausted; the process of becoming has reached its end. I have followed the instruction of the Buddha, the Conqueror of the five Maras, and have fully practiced the noble conduct of the Path. I have completely uprooted the combination of craving and ignorance called the 'lead to becoming' (bhavanetti), which overwhelms the continuity of beings and does not allow escape from Saṃsāra. For the sake of that Nibbāna, the fruit of Arahatship, for which I entered the homeless life from the household life, I [have attained] the lower fetters...
324:
135-6. In those verses, 'khīṇā' means exhausted, come to an end. 'Jāti' means becoming or the arising of becoming. 'The teaching of the Victor has been lived' means the holy life of the Path (maggabrahmacariya), the instruction of the Perfectly Enlightened One, the Victor (jina), has been fully lived and completed. 'The net called craving has been abandoned' means that because it overwhelms the continuity of beings and allows no opportunity to escape, wrong view (diṭṭhi) and ignorance (avijjā), which are called 'the net,' have been uprooted by the Path. 'The lead to becoming has been uprooted' means that craving, known as the 'lead to becoming' (bhavanetti) because it leads to and continues existence such as the sensual realm, has been completely pulled out. 'For the sake of which I went forth' means for the purpose of which I entered the homeless life from the household life. That purpose, which is the end of all fetters (saṃyojana)—both the lower and higher ones—the ultimate goal called Nibbāna, the personal goal called Arahatship, has been attained by me.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Surādha is Finished.

## 9. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Gotama

The verses beginning with 'They sleep happily' (sukhaṃ supanti) are those of the Venerable Elder Gotama. The story of their origin is as follows: This elder also had performed special merit under previous Buddhas. Having accumulated merits that serve as a support for liberation (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) in various lives, he was born in a respectable family during the time of the Buddha Vipassī. Upon reaching maturity, one day he saw the Buddha and, with a heart full of faith, offered an āmoda fruit. Due to that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the deva world. After performing merits repeatedly and wandering only through the happy realms, he was born in a Brahmin family in Rājagaha during the time of this Buddha's appearance and was named Gotama. At the age of seven, he underwent the initiation ceremony (upanayana), wandered for alms of gold and silver, and received a thousand coins. While keeping that wealth in a suitable place and practicing his observances, at the age of sixteen or seventeen, he was led astray into sensual pleasures by bad friends. He gave that thousand coins to a prostitute and reached the destruction of his holy life (brahmacariya). When that prostitute, seeing Gotama's appearance as a practitioner of the holy life, showed signs of disdain, he became disenchanted in a single night. Remembering his life of holiness and his loss of wealth, he felt remorse, thinking, 'I have done what is improper.' The Teacher, knowing his wealth of supporting conditions (hetusampatti) and the movement of his mind...
325:
(The Blessed One) showed himself nearby. Having seen the Blessed One and with a heart full of faith, he approached him; the Blessed One taught him the Dhamma. Having heard the Dhamma and gained faith, while being ordained, he attained Arahantship even at the end of the hair-cutting ceremony. This matter is stated in the Apadāna:

“I gave an āmoda fruit to the Sambuddha of golden hue, worthy of offerings, as he was walking along the street.

In the ninety-one aeons since I gave that fruit, I have not known a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of giving fruit.

My defilements are burnt up... I have followed the Buddha's teaching.”

Having attained Arahantship and spending time in the bliss of absorption and fruition, a former lay friend approached and asked, “Friend, having received alms like a treasure, what did you do upon ordaining?” Hearing this, the Elder did not say, “I did such and such,” but instead, showing the faults of women and declaring his own state of being free from lust (wishing to declare his attainment), he spoke these two verses beginning with “Sukhaṃ supanti.”

In that verse, “Sukhaṃ supanti munayo, ye itthīsu na bajjhare” means those monks (sages) who are not bound by the bond of lust to women who are objects or causes [of lust], being practitioners of austerity and having restrained senses, sleep happily and live happily; the meaning is that there is no suffering for them. “Supanti” (they sleep) is just an illustration.

“Sadā ve rakkhitabbāsu” means those who must certainly be guarded at all times. Even if women are kept on the upper floor of a seven-storied palace where no men are present, or even if they were kept inside one's belly, it is impossible to guard them; therefore, they must be guarded at all times like cows that eat crops. Or, because of their many-sided minds, they must be guarded at all times because their minds change even when the husband provides clothes and ornaments. Or, they must be guarded because their minds need to be guarded by covering the nature of the body with flowers, scents, etc.

“Yāsu saccaṃ sudullabhaṃ” means it is impossible to find truthful speech in those women. Women would even enter fire, eat poison, take up weapons, or kill themselves by hanging, but they are unable to stand in truth. Therefore, he shows: “How happy indeed are the sages who live having avoided such women.”
327:
With a joyful and delighted mind, he created a golden sand stupa through psychic power and performed daily offerings with about three thousand flowers made of gold and other materials, performing meritorious deeds throughout his life. Having maintained his meditative absorptions (jhāna) without decline, he was reborn in the Brahma realm upon passing away. After staying there for the full lifespan and passing away, he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, wandering repeatedly between the celestial and human realms. During the time of this Buddha's appearance, he was reborn into a Licchavī royal family in the city of Vesālī and was named Vasabha. Upon reaching maturity, he saw the Buddha's majesty during the Lord's visit to Vesālī; having gained faith, he ordained, practiced insight meditation (vipassanā), and soon attained the fruit of Arahantship. This account is stated in the Apadāna (Ap. Thera 2.50.57-92):

“Not far from the Himavanta, there is a mountain named Samagga;
My hermitage was well-constructed, and my leaf-hut was well-fashioned.

I was an ascetic named Nārada, practicing fierce austerities,
And fourteen thousand disciples attended upon me.

While staying in seclusion and peace, I then thought thus:
‘All these people worship me, but I do not worship anyone.

I have no one to admonish me, nor is there anyone to speak [corrective] words to me;
I am living in the forest without a teacher or preceptor.

That person whom I should attend upon and toward whom I should show respect—
Such a teacher I do not have; living in the forest is [thus] useless.

I shall search for an object of worship, and likewise a teacher who is venerable and worthy of esteem;
I shall live with a support, and then no one will be able to blame me.’

Not far from my hermitage, there was a small river with shallow banks,
With good landing places, delightful, and filled with pure sand.

Approaching that river named Amarika at that time,
I gathered the sand and made a sand stupa (cetiya).

Those who were the Fully Enlightened Ones, the Sages who brought an end to existence—
Their stupa is of such a nature; I made it as a symbol of them.”
328:
“Having made the sand stupa, I fashioned it to have a golden appearance; I worshipped it with three thousand golden bell-flowers.

Every evening and morning, with inspired joy and hands joined in reverence, I paid homage to that sand stupa as if the Fully Enlightened One were present before me.

Whenever defiled thoughts related to the household life arose, I would remember the well-constructed stupa and reflect upon it immediately.

‘While living in dependence on the Buddha, the Caravan Leader and Guide who leads beings to Nibbāna, O friend, it is not proper for you to live with defilements,’ (thus I admonished myself).

As soon as I reflected on the stupa, a sense of reverence (garava) arose in me; I was able to dispel the evil thoughts, like a great elephant struck by a goad.

While living in this manner, the King of Death oppressed me; passing away there in peace, I went to the Brahma realm.

After living there for the full lifespan, I was reborn in the celestial realm; eighty times, I exercised the sovereignty of the gods as the Lord of Devas (Sakka).

Three hundred times, I was a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti); as for the vast regional kingships, they are beyond counting.

I enjoy the results of those golden bell-flowers; in every birth, a hundred thousand nurses surround me.

Because of my devotion to the stupa, no dust or dirt clings to my body; sweat does not pour from my limbs, and I am always one of great radiance.

Oh, how well-constructed was my stupa! How auspicious was the sight of the Amarika River! By having made the sand stupa, I have now reached the unshakable state (Nibbāna).

For a person who desires to perform merit and seeks the essence, whether the field (of merit) is good or not is not the main thing; only one's own practice is the achiever of the goal.

Just as a strong man, desiring to cross the ocean, might take hold of a small piece of wood and leap into the great lake...”
329:
“...Thinking, ‘Depending on this wood, I shall cross the great ocean,’ a man might cross the sea through exertion and energy.

In the same way, I performed that deed, which was small and slight; depending on that deed, I have crossed over the cycle of rebirth (saṃsāra).

When my final birth arrived, urged by my root of merit, I was born in a very wealthy family of high status in the city of Sāvatthī.

My parents, who possessed faith, had gone to the Buddha for refuge; both of them, having seen the state (attained the path), followed the Dispensation.

Taking the bark that had fallen from the Bodhi tree, they made a golden stupa; they worshipped it evening and morning as if in the presence of the Son of the Sakyans.

On Uposatha days, they would bring out the golden stupa, and spend the three watches of the night praising the virtues of the Buddha.

As soon as I saw that stupa, I remembered my sand stupa; while sitting in a single seat, I attained Arahantship.

While searching for that Hero, I saw the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta); leaving the household, I ordained in his presence.

At the age of seven from birth, I attained Arahantship; the Buddha, the One with Vision, knowing my virtues, granted me full ordination (upasampadā).

While still a child, the task to be done was completed by me; I have now done what was to be done in the Dispensation of the Son of the Sakyans.

This sage, who has transcended all enmity and fear, and surpassed all attachments—O Great Hero, he is your disciple; this is the fruit of the golden stupa.

My defilements have been burnt away... the Buddha's Dispensation has been fulfilled.”

However, after reaching Arahantship, wishing to favor his lay supporters, he did not refuse the requisites they offered and consumed them just as they were received. Worldlings (puthujjanas), thinking, “This person is very much devoted to the comfort of his body and has an unguarded mind,” looked down on him. The Elder...
330:
The Elder lived ignoring that matter. Not far from that Elder, a certain deceitful monk of evil desires lived deceiving the people, presenting himself as if he were of few desires and contented. The multitude honored him as if he were an Arahant. Then Sakka, the king of devas, knowing that matter, approached the Elder and asked, "Venerable Sir, what does a deceitful person do?" The Elder, censuring the one with evil desires, spoke these two verses:

"First he kills himself, then he kills others. Like a bird-hunter with a decoy bird, he kills himself by making himself well-slain."

"One is not a Brahmin by outward appearance alone; one is a Brahmin by inner virtue. In whom there are evil deeds, O Sakka, know that he is indeed a dark person."

In those verses, 'First he kills himself' means that a deceitful person, while deceiving the world with his deceitful behavior, kills himself first through evil states such as evil desires, and destroys his own portion of merit. 'Then he kills others' means that the deceitful person, having first killed himself in the manner described, later kills others—those who honor him, thinking, "This monk is virtuous and noble." He destroys them by making the offerings they made to him yield little fruit and by wasting their requisites.

To show the distinction in the killing of oneself, even though a deceitful person destroys both, it is said: 'He kills himself by making himself well-slain.' When that deceitful person kills himself, he does so by making himself 'well-slain' (thoroughly destroyed).

To illustrate this: 'Like a bird-hunter with a decoy bird'—here, 'vītaṃsa' refers to a decoy bird (a trap bird), and 'pakkhiyā' refers to a bird-hunter. Just as a bird-hunter, while deceiving and killing other birds with that decoy bird, kills himself in this world through the blame of the wise and his sinful nature, and in the next world through rebirth in states of misery and defilement; yet he cannot kill those birds in the next world. Similarly, a deceitful person, by deceiving the world through hypocrisy, kills himself in this life through remorse and the blame of the wise, and in the next world through the defilements of states of misery; however, he cannot cause those donors of requisites to reach the suffering of the four lower realms. Indeed, it is said that a deceitful person kills (destroys) the donor only by making the gift yield no great fruit. He kills only by making it fruitless. Truly, the Blessed One...
331:
...it is said that he kills the donor only by making the gift yield little fruit, not by making it entirely fruitless. For it was said by the Blessed One: 'By giving a gift to a human being who is immoral, a thousandfold reward is to be expected.' (M. Ni. 3.379). Therefore, it is said, 'He kills himself by making himself well-slain.'

In this way, to show that individuals who remain merely at the level of outward cleansing are not truly pure, but are pure only through internal purity, he spoke the second verse beginning with 'Na brāhmaṇo'. Its meaning is: one does not become a Brahmin merely by outward perfection, such as the refinement of postures. Here, the word 'vaṇṇa' (color/appearance) denotes perfection. Internally, however, one becomes a Brahmin through perfection in virtue and other qualities. It should be understood that 'one who has barred out evil is called a Brahmin.' Therefore, 'O Sakka, king of devas, know that in whom evil and low deeds exist, he is certainly a dark person, a base individual.' Hearing this, Sakka rebuked the deceitful monk, admonished him saying, 'Practice the Dhamma,' and returned to his own place.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Vasabha Thera is finished.
## The Commentary on the First Chapter of the Book of Twos is finished.
## 2. The Second Chapter
## 1. Commentary on the Verses of Mahācunda Thera

'Su ssūsā' and so forth are the verses of the Venerable Mahācunda Thera. What is the background? This Elder also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit in various lives. In the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, he was born into a potter's family and, upon reaching maturity, earned his living through the potter's trade. One day, seeing the Teacher and having a heart full of faith, he made a well-fashioned clay alms-bowl and offered it to the Blessed One. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans, and in this Buddha-era, he was born in Nālaka village in the kingdom of Magadha as the son of the Brahmin lady Rūpasārī, becoming the younger brother of the Venerable Sāriputta Thera. His name was Cunda. When he came of age, he was ordained under the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta) and, relying on him, practiced insight meditation, soon becoming an Arahant endowed with the six supernormal powers. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

I was a potter in the city of Haṃsavatī.
I saw the Blessed One Vipassī, who was free from the stains of defilement, who had crossed the flood of Saṃsāra, and was free from taints.
I offered a well-fashioned clay bowl to the Blessed One.
Because I offered a bowl to the Blessed One who was endowed with the quality of uprightness, I received a golden vessel in every life I was born.
I also enjoyed bowls and drinking vessels made of silver, gold, and rubies.
This is the fruit of the merit of offering a bowl.
I became the most supreme among attendants and in wealth.
In a good field...
332:
Having initiated insight meditation (vipassanā) and through diligent effort, Venerable Cunda soon became an Arahant possessing the six higher powers (chalabhiññā). Regarding this, it is stated in the Apadāna:

“In the city of Haṃsavatī, I was once a potter. I saw the Buddha Vipassī, who was free from the dust of defilements, who had crossed over the flood of saṃsāra, and who was free from taints (āsavas).

I offered a well-made clay bowl to the Buddha, the Most Excellent One. By offering that bowl to the Blessed One, who was upright and possessed the quality of steadfastness (tādi):

In whatever life I was reborn, I obtained a golden vessel. I also enjoyed bowls and drinking cups made of silver, gold, and gems. This is the fruit of my meritorious deed. I became supreme among those with retinues and wealth.

Just as a seed, even if small, when sown in a good field, delights the farmer when there is a good flow of rain—

In the same way, this gift of a bowl sown in the Buddha-field will delight me when the flow of rain that is joy (pīti) falls.

As many as there are groups of the Saṅgha and other assemblies, there is no field equal to the Buddha-field, which bestows happiness upon all beings.

Homage to you, O Noble Man! Homage to you, O Supreme Man! By having offered a single bowl, I have reached the Unshakable State (Nibbāna).

Ninety-one aeons ago, because I offered a bowl then, I have not known a woeful state (duggati) since that time. This is the fruit of offering a bowl.

My defilements have been burnt away... (pe) ... I have fulfilled the Buddha’s teaching.”

After becoming an Arahant with the six higher powers, wishing to praise the reliance on a teacher (garūpanissaya) and living in seclusion (vivekavāsa), which were the causes of his attainment (sampatti), he said:

“The desire to listen (willingness to learn) increases knowledge. Knowledge increases wisdom. Through wisdom, one knows the meaning (the cause and effect). The known meaning brings happiness.”
333:
“One should resort to remote lodgings and practice for liberation from the fetters. If one does not find delight there, one should live in the Saṅgha, being mindful and having a guarded self.” He spoke these two verses.

In those passages, 'sussūsā' means the desire to listen to all knowledge that is worthy of being heard; it also means living in attendance upon a teacher. One who wishes to hear about the benefits (attha) should approach noble friends (kalyāṇamitta), perform duties, and attend to them. When the teachers are pleased by such attendance and wish for one to sit nearby, one sits near them and listens with attentive ears to what should be heard; thus, living with a teacher is also called 'sussūsā' because it is the cause of listening. This 'sussūsā' increases and expands the knowledge related to the Truths (Sacca) and Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda) for the person endowed with it; thus it is called 'sutavaddhanī' (that which increases knowledge). It means it makes one very learned (bahusacca).

'Sutaṃ paññāya vaddhanaṃ' means that the state of being very learned (bahusacca), which is described in such ways as 'one who remembers what he has heard, a storehouse of what he has heard' and 'here, a certain person has much knowledge of the Sutta, Geyya, and Veyyākaraṇa,' increases wisdom, which is the cause for abandoning unwholesome states and attaining wholesome states. Thus it is said, 'knowledge increases wisdom.' Regarding this, the Blessed One said: 'Bhikkhus, the noble disciple who is armed with the weapon of knowledge abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome; he abandons what is blameworthy and develops what is blameless; he maintains himself in purity.'

'Paññāya atthaṃ jānāti' means that a person of great learning, established in knowledge consisting in what is heard (sutamayā-ñāṇa), while practicing that noble practice, investigates the meaning according to what he has heard, contemplates the Dhamma, and through meditation (bhāvanā), understands and penetrates the meaning as it really is—distinguishing between the mundane and supramundane, the present life and so forth, and suffering and so forth. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'Having known the meaning and having known the Dhamma in accordance with the scriptures as they were learned, he becomes one who practices the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma.'”
334:
“One examines the meaning of the teachings one has memorized; for one who examines the meaning, the teachings become receptive to contemplation. When there is receptivity to contemplation of the Dhamma, desire arises. When desire has arisen, one makes an effort. Having made an effort, one compares. Having compared, one strives. Being resolute (with a mind directed towards Nibbāna), one realizes the supreme truth with the body and sees it penetratingly with wisdom” (M. Ni. 2.432), and so forth.

“The known meaning brings happiness” means that when the aforementioned benefits of the present life and the meaning of suffering, etc., are known and attained as they truly are, it brings about and accomplishes happiness, categorized as mundane and supramundane.

Since stable meditative wisdom (bhāvanā-paññā) cannot be accomplished by mere hearing, he said, “One should associate... (pe) ...liberation,” to show the method of practice for that wisdom. In that verse, by the words “One should associate with secluded dwellings,” he speaks of physical seclusion (kāyaviveka). By mentioning physical seclusion, since the abandonment of fetters will also be mentioned, it should be understood that things like restraint through virtue (sīla-saṃvara), which are the secluded living of one worthy of seclusion, are accomplished here even if not directly stated. “One should practice for liberation from the fetters” means that one should practice and develop insight meditation (vipassanā-bhāvanā) and the meditation on the path (magga-bhāvanā) in such a way that the mind is liberated from the fetters.
