If one does not find delight in those secluded dwellings as they are obtained, or in the superior wholesome states, due to not attaining any distinction between before and after, then one should dwell mindfully, having a mind guarded by maintaining the meditation subject within the community of monks (Sangha), and establishing the guard of mindfulness at the six sense doors. For one who dwells in this way, liberation from the fetters might indeed occur; this is the meaning.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Mahācunda is finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Jotidāsa

“Ye kho te,” etc., are the verses of the Venerable Elder Jotidāsa. What is the background (uppatti)? This elder also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and, accumulating merit in various lives, was born into a good family during the time of Sikhī Buddha. Upon reaching the age of discretion, one day, seeing the Teacher going for alms, he offered a kāsumārika fruit with a confident mind. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans.
335:
In this Buddha-era, he was born as the son of a wealthy Brahmin in the Pādiyattha (Pāveyyaka) district; his name was Jotidāsa. When he reached maturity and was living as a householder, one day he saw the Venerable Mahākassapa Thera wandering for alms in his village. With a confident mind, he offered a meal and, after hearing the Dhamma from the elder, built a large monastery on a mountain near his village. He had the elder reside there and attended to him with the four requisites. Due to the elder's Dhamma teaching, he gained a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega), ordained, and while practicing insight meditation, soon became an Arahant with the six supernormal powers (chaḷabhiññā). Therefore, it is stated in the Apadāna:

“I saw the Buddha, the stainless one, the foremost in the world, the bull among men, sitting in the midst of the mountains, shining like a kaṇikāra flower.
With a confident mind and a joyful heart, I raised my joined palms to my head, took a kāsumārika fruit, and offered it to the Best of Buddhas.
In the thirty-first kappa from this one, because of the intention with which I offered that fruit then, I have not known an unhappy rebirth; this is the fruit of the offering of fruit.
My defilements have been burned away... (pe) ...the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.”

After attaining the six supernormal powers, he studied the Tipitaka and became especially proficient in the Vinaya Piṭaka. When he had reached ten rains (vassa) and was capable of attending to a following, he went to Sāvatthī with many monks to pay homage to the Blessed One. On the way, to relieve the fatigue of the journey, he entered a park of the ascetics (titthiyas) and sat down in a suitable place. Seeing a Brahmin practicing the “five-fold heat” (pañcatapa) penance (with four fires and the sun), he asked, “Brahmin, while there are other things that should be burned (tapanīya), why do you burn something else?” Hearing this, the Brahmin became angry and said, “O shaveling monk, what are the other things that should be burned?” The elder taught him the Dhamma with this verse:

“Anger (kopa), envy (issā), and harming others (paraheṭhanā), conceit (māna), arrogance (sārambha), intoxication (mada), and negligence (pamāda), craving (taṇhā), ignorance (avijjā), and attachment to existence (bhava-saṅgatī)—these are the things to be burned, not the form-aggregate (rūpakkhandha).”

Upon hearing this Dhamma, that Brahmin and all the other ascetics in that park ordained under the elder. The elder...
336: Having gone to Sāvatthī with them, paid homage to the Blessed One, and stayed there for a few days, he went to his own birthplace. Desiring to exhort his relatives of various views who believed in purification through sacrifice and who had come to see him, he spoke these two verses: 'Those people who, through binding (with leather straps and so forth) and various acts (of oppression and killing), being of cruel effort, oppress humans; they too are cast into those very same (acts of oppression), for kamma indeed does not disappear. Whatever kamma a person performs, whether good or evil, of that very kamma they are the heir, whatever kamma they do.' He spoke these two verses. In those verses, 'ye' is an indefinite designation. 'Te' is the correlative of that same indefinite. Both words are connected with the word 'janā' (people). 'Kho' is a mere particle. 'Veṭhamissena' means by binding the head and so forth with pieces of leather straps and so on. There is also a reading 'vedhamissena,' which has the same meaning. 'Nānattena ca kammunā' means by various types of deeds that harm others, such as beating, killing, cutting off hands and feet, and administering small doses of poison. 'Manusse' (humans) is just an illustration; therefore, it means any living beings. 'Uparundhanti' means they oppress or harass. 'Pharusūpakkamā' means those with cruel efforts or cruel actions. 'Janā' means beings. 'Te pi tatth'eva kīranti' means those aforementioned persons, by whatever kamma (oppression) they harassed others, they themselves are cast into those very same causes; the meaning is that they experience that very same kind of suffering. There is also a variant reading 'tath'eva kīranti,' meaning just as they themselves caused suffering to others, in the same way they are treated by others and come to suffering. Why? 'Na hi kammaṃ panassati'—kamma indeed does not disappear; kamma that has been accumulated certainly does not vanish without giving its fruit (vipāka); the intention is that it definitely ripens when the remaining conditions coincide. Now, in order to analyze the meaning briefly stated as 'kamma indeed does not disappear' and to clarify the fact that beings have kamma as their own property, he spoke the verse beginning with 'Yaṃ karoti.' The meaning of that verse is: whether that kamma is wholesome or unwholesome...
337: ...a being performs it, and while performing it, in whatever way that kamma is capable of giving fruit, in that way they accumulate it. 'Tassa tass'eva dāyādo' means because they take only the fruit of that specific kamma, they are the partaker of the result to be given by that specific kamma. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'Young man, beings are owners of their kamma, heirs to their kamma,' and so forth (M. Ni. 3.289). Upon hearing these verses, the Elder's relatives established themselves in the knowledge of kamma-ownership. ## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Jotidāsa is finished. ## 3. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Heraññakāni. The verse beginning with 'Accayanti ahorattā' is that of the Venerable Elder Heraññakāni. What is its origin (uppatti)? It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was born into a good family in the city of Haṃsavatī. When he reached maturity, he lived as a servant (bhataka) of others. One day, while a disciple of the Teacher named Sujāta was seeking rag-robes (paṃsukūla), that man gave half of his lower garment. By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Wandering repeatedly among devas and humans, in this Buddha-dispensation, he was born as the son of a village headman (gāmabhojaka) who suppressed thieves under King Kosala. His name was Heraññakāni. When he reached maturity and his father passed away, the King appointed him to that very position of village headman. Seeing the power of the Buddha at the time of the acceptance of Jetavana Monastery, he gained faith, handed over that position to his younger brother, asked the King's permission, and ordained. By developing insight (vipassanā), he attained Arahantship before long. Concerning this, it is said in the Apadāna: 'A disciple of the Blessed One Padumuttara, named Sujāta, was then wandering among rubbish heaps seeking rag-robes. I, a servant of others in the city of Haṃsavatī, gave half a cloth and paid homage with my head. By that well-performed deed and by my intention and aspiration, I abandoned the human body and went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.'
338:
I have exercised the kingship of the gods as the Lord of Devas (Sakka) thirty-three times; I have been a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) seventy-seven times.

Due to the merit of giving half a cloth, I obtained vast regional kingship (padesarājja) beyond counting, and I enjoy it free from fear. If I so desire today, I could cover this region, including its forests and mountains, with linen cloths (khomadussa); this is the fruit of giving half a cloth.

In the hundred thousandth aeon from now, I gave that gift then; due to the fruit of giving half a cloth, I have not known a miserable rebirth (duggati). My defilements are burnt... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.

Having attained Arahatship, wishing to turn his younger brother away from that work (worldly affairs), and seeing him still delighting in it, he admonished him, saying:

'Days and nights pass by, life is cut short; the life of mortals is exhausted like the water in small streams. Yet the fool does not realize while committing evil deeds; later it becomes bitter for him, for the ripening of his evil is painful.'

In those verses, 'accayanti' means they pass away, they depart very quickly. 'Ahorattā' means nights and days. 'Jīvitaṃ uparujjhati' means the life faculty ceases by way of momentary cessation. For it is said: 'Moment by moment, O bhikkhu, you are born, you age, you die, you pass away, and you are reborn.' 'Āyu khīyati maccānaṃ' means the life of these beings called 'mortals' (maccā) because of their nature to die; their life, which is limited to a maximum of 'a hundred years or a little more for one who lives long,' is exhausted, reaching destruction and dissolution. How? 'Kunnadīnaṃva odakaṃ'—just as the water of small mountain streams (kunnadī) does not last long but is exhausted very quickly, disappearing as soon as it arrives, so too the life of beings is exhausted very quickly. Here, 'odaka' is used for 'udaka' (water), just as 'mānasa' is used for 'mana' (mind).
339:
Then, 'the fool does not realize while committing evil deeds' means that although this saṃsāra is impermanent, the fool commits evil deeds through the power of greed or anger. Even while committing them, he does not realize (the result of suffering). It is not that there is no one who, while doing evil, does not know 'I am doing evil,' but it is said 'he does not realize' because he does not know 'the ripening of this kamma will be such suffering.'

'Later it becomes bitter for him' means that although he does not realize 'the ripening of this kamma will be such' at the moment of accumulating the evil deed, later, for that fool reborn in hell and so forth, there is only bitter, undesirable suffering. For the ripening of that evil kamma is indeed evil, base, and undesirable. Having heard this advice, the Elder's younger brother asked the King for permission, ordained, and before long achieved his own goal (sadattha), Arahatship.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Heraññakāni is finished.

## 4. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Somamitta

The verse beginning with 'Parittaṃ dāruṃ' belongs to the Venerable Elder Somamitta. What is its origin? This one also had performed meritorious services under previous Buddhas and was accumulating merit in various births. In the time of the Blessed One Sikhi, he was born in a respectable family. Upon reaching maturity, he heard of the Buddha's virtues and, with a heart full of faith, one day saw a Kimsuka tree in bloom. He took the flowers and, intending them for the Teacher, threw them into the air as an offering. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered among devas and humans. In this Buddha-era, he was born into a Brahmin family in Bārāṇasī and received the name Somamitta. Having mastered the three Vedas, and because of his familiarity with the Elder named Vimala, he went to him frequently. Hearing the Dhamma, he gained faith in the Dispensation, ordained, and received higher ordination. He lived fulfilling the major and minor duties. However, the Elder Vimala was lazy and full of sloth, spending his days and nights in that manner. Somamitta thought, 'What benefit is there in relying on a lazy person?' He left him and approached the Elder Mahākassapa. Abiding by his advice, he established insight (vipassanā) and before long attained Arahatship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:

'Seeing the blossoming Kimsuka flowers, I raised my hands in homage and, recollecting the Blessed One, threw them into the air as an offering. Due to that well-performed deed and the intention of my prayer, I abandoned the human body and reached the Tāvatiṃsa realm. In the thirty-first aeon from now, because of the flower offering I made then, I have not known a miserable rebirth. This is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha with flowers. My defilements are burnt... (etc.) ...the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.'

So it was said. Furthermore, after reaching Arahatship, wishing to urge the Elder Vimala with an admonition:
340:
“Seeing a kimsuka flower in bloom, I raised my hands in reverential salutation (añjali) and, remembering the Most Excellent Buddha, I made an offering in the sky.

Through that well-performed deed and through my intentions and aspirations, I left the human body and reached the Tāvatiṃsa realm.

Thirty-one aeons ago from now, I performed that deed (of offering flowers); because of the merit of that worship of the Buddha, I have never known a woeful rebirth.

My defilements (kilesas) have been burnt away; all existences have been uprooted. Like an elephant that has broken its bonds, I live without cankers (anāsava).

Indeed, my coming into the presence of the Buddha was a good coming; the three knowledges (tevijjā) have been attained, and the teaching of the Buddha has been fulfilled.”

Upon reaching Arahantship, he spoke these two verses, rebuking the Elder Vimala with an exhortation—

“Just as one might sink in the great ocean by clinging to a small piece of wood, so too, even one who lives a good life sinks by relying on a lazy person. Therefore, one should avoid that lazy person of inferior energy.

One should dwell together with the wise who are secluded, who are noble (ariyas), whose minds are resolute (pahitatta), who are ever meditative, and who are always of stirred-up energy.”

In those verses, the phrase “Just as one might sink in the great ocean by clinging to a small piece of wood” means that even a clansman who loves virtue (sīla) sinks in Saṃsāra by relying on a lazy and shameless person; he cannot reach Nibbāna, the other shore of Saṃsāra. Because this is so, one should avoid in every way that person of inferior energy who is called ‘lazy’ (kusīta) because they cause one to sink loathsomely, unable to lift their head through the power of superior wholesome states, and because of their lack of stirred-up energy. One should not follow the example of such a person’s conduct.

Thus, having shown the danger of laziness through the verse based on the individual, the verse beginning with “pavittehi” is now spoken to show the benefits of stirred-up energy.
341:
The meaning of that verse is: Those who are secluded (pavitta) by way of physical seclusion (kāya-viveka) are called ‘Noble’ (ariyas) because they are far from defilements for that very reason. They are called ‘Resolute’ (pahitatta) because their minds are sent towards Nibbāna. They are ‘Meditators’ (jhāyino) by way of concentration on an object (ārammaṇūpajñāna) and concentration on characteristics (lakkhaṇūpajñāna). They are of ‘Stirred-up Energy’ (āraddhavīriya) because their energy is exerted at all times. They are ‘Wise’ (paṇḍitā) because they are endowed with wisdom, both mundane and supramundane. One who desires to accomplish their own goal (the fruit of Arahantship) should dwell and live together with such wise persons. Hearing those words, the Elder Vimala, with a mind full of spiritual urgency (saṃvega), developed insight (vipassanā) and attained his goal (the fruit of Arahantship). This meaning will be further clarified later.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Somamitta is Finished.

## 5. The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Sabbamitta

‘Jano janamhi sambaddho’—this is the verse of the Venerable Sabbamitta Thera. How did it arise? He too was one who had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas. While accumulating merits in various births, ninety-two aeons ago from this Bhadda-kappa, during the time of the Buddha Tissa, he was born into a family of hunters. Wandering in the forest, he lived by killing wild animals and eating their meat. Later, the Blessed One, in order to show him favor, displayed three footprints near his dwelling and departed. Because that hunter had practiced under previous Buddhas in the past, upon seeing the footprints marked with the wheel-sign, his mind was filled with devotion, and he made an offering with koraṇḍa flowers. Due to that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and wandered only through the happy realms (sugati). When this Buddha appeared, he was born into a Brahmin family in the city of Sāvatthī and was named Sabbamitta. When he reached the age of discretion, he saw the power of the Buddha on the day the Jetavana monastery was accepted, gained faith, and ordained. Taking a meditation subject, he lived in the forest. After spending the rainy season retreat, while traveling to Sāvatthī to pay homage to the Blessed One, he saw a young fawn caught in a snare set by hunters along the way. Although the mother deer had not entered the snare, she would not go far due to her love for her offspring, yet she could not approach the snare for fear of death. The young fawn, terrified and struggling, was crying out piteously. Seeing this, the Elder reflected, ‘Alas, how suffering is rooted in the affection of beings!’ As he continued his journey, he saw many thieves who had captured a man alive (jīvagāha), wrapped him in bundles of straw, and were burning him, causing him to scream and wail intensely. Based on these two incidents, spiritual urgency (saṃvega) arose in him, and while the thieves were listening, he recited these two verses beginning with ‘Jano janamhi sambaddho’:

‘A person is bound to another person (by the bond of craving).
A person relies on and clings to another person (through greed).
A person [is troubled by] a person...’
342:
Seeing a man captured alive, his body wrapped in straw and set on fire, and hearing him crying out with a very loud voice, the Elder was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) on account of both (the young deer and that man). While those thieves were listening, he recited these two verses:

"People are bound to people; people rely only on people;
People are oppressed by people, and people also oppress people.
What benefit is there for him from people (relied upon through craving), or what benefit from people born (as parents)?
Abandoning people, go forth, having left behind (craving and anger) that oppress many people."

In those verses, "jano" (people) refers to the foolish worldling. "Janamhi" (in people) means in other persons. "Sambaddho" (bound) means being bound by the fetters of craving, being attached in such ways as, "This is my son, this is my mother," and so on. Alternatively, it means having a mind attached in the sense of, "These people support me, I live depending on them."

"Janamevassito jano" (people rely only on people) means that one person relies on another, clinging to and possessing them through craving, thinking, "This is my son, my daughter," and so on. "Jano janena heṭhīyati, heṭheti ca jano janaṃ" (people are oppressed by people, and people also oppress people) means that because of the absence of the knowledge of ownership of deeds (kammassakatā-ñāṇa) and the lack of penetration into the truth of reality, one is unable to remain equanimous. Just as a person clings to another through the power of greed, so too, through the power of anger, one person is oppressed and afflicted by another. Not knowing that "this oppression will return to me as the fruit of oppression," a person oppresses another.

"Ko hi tassa janenattho" (what benefit is there for him from people) means what benefit is there for that other person from someone relied upon through the power of craving or oppressed through the power of anger? "Janena janitena vā" (or from people born) means what benefit is there even from another person born of one as a parent? "Janaṃ ohāya gacchaṃ taṃ, heṭhayitvā bahuṃ janaṃ" (abandoning people, go forth, having left behind that which oppresses many people) means that since this is the only suitable course for a person wandering in saṃsāra, those who go forth having completely abandoned that person, the craving that afflicts them, and the anger that stands oppressing many people, (reach Nibbāna, the place of safety).
343:
The meaning is: if one goes forth having abandoned (craving and anger), one would reach the place of safety where they do not oppress. Indeed, due to ignorance, beings are as if clinging to one another through the power of greed, and as if oppressing one another through the power of anger. Not knowing that such oppression will result in ill effects only upon themselves, they tend to oppress others. What benefit is there in clinging through craving or oppressing through anger? Even if it be a person born of one as a parent, what benefit is there? For beings wandering in saṃsāra, this is the only suitable process. Therefore, those who go forth having completely abandoned that person, as well as the craving and anger that oppress many people, reach Nibbāna, the place of safety.

Having spoken thus, the Elder immediately applied himself to insight meditation (vipassanā) and attained Arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

"In a former life, after my parents had died, I was a forest worker.
I lived by killing animals; I had no merit.

Near my dwelling, the Buddha Tissa, the Supreme Leader of the World,
Out of compassion, the Visionary One showed three footprints.

Seeing the footprints trodden by the Teacher named Tissa,
With a joyful heart, I gained confidence in the footprints.

Seeing a blooming Koraṇḍa tree growing from the earth,
Taking the flowers along with the buds, I worshipped the most excellent footprints.

By that well-performed deed and by my intentions and aspirations,
Having abandoned the human body, I went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

In whatever rebirth I arose, whether as a deity or a human,
I had a complexion like the Koraṇḍa flower; I was possessed of great radiance.

Ninety-two aeons ago from now, because of the deed I performed then,
I do not know a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of worshipping the footprints.

My defilements are burnt away... (etc.)... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out."

Those thieves, having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Elder, were moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega), ordained, and practiced the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma (lokuttara-dhamma).

## The Commentary on the Verses of Sabba-mitta Thera is finished.
344:
## 6. Commentary on the Verses of Mahākāḷa Thera

"Kāḷī itthī" and so forth is the verse of the Venerable Mahākāḷa Thera. What is its origin? This Mahākāḷa Thera also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit in various lives. Ninety-two aeons ago from this auspicious aeon, he was born into a respectable family. When he reached the age of discretion, he went to the forest for some business. There, seeing a discarded robe (paṃsukūla-cīvara) hanging from a branch of a tree, he felt a mind of devotion, thinking, "The banner of the Noble Ones is hanging there!" He then took Kinkani flowers and worshipped the discarded robe.

Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered among devas and humans. In this Buddha's era, he was born into a family of caravan leaders in the city of Setavya and received the name Mahākāḷa. Having reached the age of discretion and living the household life, he took goods with five hundred carts and went to Sāvatthī for trade. Having parked the caravan in a certain place and dispelled the fatigue of the journey, he was sitting with his attendants. In the evening, seeing lay devotees going to the Jetavana monastery with perfumes, garlands, and so on in their hands, he himself went to the monastery with them. Having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he gained faith and ordained. He then undertook the cemetery-dweller's practice (sosānikaṅga) and lived in a cemetery.

Then one day, a woman named Kāḷī, a corpse-burner, for the sake of the Elder's meditation subject, took a recently deceased body, cut both thighs, cut both arms, and split the head like a bowl of curd. Having made all the limbs and parts appear as if they were still connected, she placed it in a suitable spot for the Elder to observe and sat down to one side. The Elder, seeing that corpse and wishing to admonish himself, said:

"Kāḷī, the woman of large build and crow-like complexion,
Having broken one thigh and then the other thigh,
Having broken one arm and then the other arm,
And having split the head like a bowl of curd,
This woman sits having joined (the corpse) together."
345:
"Whoever, being unwise, creates the substrate (upadhi) of defilements, that person of little wisdom undergoes suffering again and again. Therefore, one who knows the cause of suffering should not create the substrate; may I not lie down again with a split head," he uttered these two verses.

In those verses, 'Kāḷī' is the name of that woman, or she is called so because of her dark complexion. 'Brahatī' means one with a large body, endowed with height and girth. 'Dhaṅkarūpā' means one who has an appearance like a crow, being dark-colored. 'Satthiñca bhetvā' means having broken the thigh bone of the corpse along with the knee. 'Aparañca satthiṃ' means having broken the other thigh bone as well. 'Bāhañca bhetvā' means having broken the arm bone specifically at the upper arm. 'Sīsañca bhetvā dadhithālakaṃ vā' means having split the head of the corpse; it means that because it was split, the brain oozed out like a bowl of curds struck by a stick or staff. 'Esā nisinnā abhisandahitvā' means this woman sits as if spreading out a meat stall, having joined together the severed and broken parts of the corpse by placing those parts back in their original positions.

'Yo ve avidvā upadhiṃ karoti' means even seeing the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) brought near by this woman, one who is unwise and unskilled abandons the meditation subject and, through improper attention (ayoniso manasikāra), produces the substrate of defilements (kilesūpadhi). Such a person of little wisdom, not transcending saṃsāra, undergoes suffering in hell and so forth again and again. 'Tasmā pajānaṃ upadhiṃ na kayirā' means because it is so, therefore, one who knows specifically "this is how suffering arises in this world," practicing proper attention, should not produce the substrate of defilements. Why? 'Māhaṃ puna bhinnasiro sayissaṃ' means just as this corpse lies with a broken body, so too, by being one who increases the cemetery (kaṭasivaḍḍhaka) through repeated births in saṃsāra due to the substrates of defilements, may I not lie down with a split head. While saying this, Elder Mahākāḷa developed insight and attained Arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:

Not far from the Himavantā mountains is a mountain named Udaṅgaṇa. There I saw a rag-robe (paṃsukūla) hanging from the top of a tree. Then, I plucked three kiṅkaṇi flowers and with a joyful heart, I honored the rag-robe. Due to that well-performed meritorious deed and the volition and aspiration, I left the human body and went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Ninety-one aeons ago from this auspicious aeon...
347:
At the time of this Buddha's appearance, he was born into a Brahmin family in Rājagaha and received the name Tissa. Upon reaching maturity, he became a master of the three Vedas and taught the mantras to five hundred young students, reaching the pinnacle of fame and following. While the Blessed One was traveling to Rājagaha, Tissa saw the Buddha's spiritual power and gained faith. He then ordained as a monk, practiced insight meditation (vipassanā), and before long attained Arahatship. This account is stated in the Apadāna (Ap. Thera 2.49.190-220) as follows:

"Having entered the Sal forest, I well-prepared my hermitage. At that time, it was well-covered with Sal flowers, and I lived in that secluded forest.

"The Blessed One Piyadassī, the Self-Enlightened, the Supreme Person, the Buddha who desired seclusion, approached that Sal forest.

"Leaving my hermitage, I went into the deep forest. At that time, I was wandering in the forest searching for roots and fruits.

"There I saw the Buddha Piyadassī, of great fame, sitting well-composed in meditative attainment, shining brilliantly in the great forest.

"Having erected four pillars, I well-constructed a pavilion over the Buddha and covered it with Sal flowers.

"Having maintained that Sal-covered pavilion for seven days, I gladdened my mind there and paid homage to the Buddha, the Best of Beings.

"At that time, the Blessed One, the Supreme Man, having emerged from concentration, sat looking ahead a distance of a yoke.

"A disciple of the Teacher Piyadassī named Varuṇa, together with one hundred thousand masters of the senses (Arahats), approached the Leader.

"The Blessed One Piyadassī, the Senior of the World, the Bull among Men, the Conqueror, sitting in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks, manifested a smile.

"The Elder Anuruddha, the attendant of the Teacher Piyadassī, having arranged his robe over one shoulder, questioned the Great Sage:

'Blessed One, what is the cause for the Teacher's smile? The Teacher manifests a smile only when there is a reason.'"
348:
"Remembering the deed of that young man who held a Sal-flower roof over me for seven days, I have manifested this smile.

"I do not see any place where this merit will not bear fruit; whether in the deva world or the human world, the opportunity for this merit to ripen is never exhausted.

"For that person endowed with meritorious deeds living in the deva world, as far as his retinue extends, it will be covered by a roof of Sal flowers.

"There, being peaceful and possessed of meritorious deeds, he will always delight in divine dances, songs, and instrumental music.

"As far as his retinue extends, there will be a fragrant scent. At that very moment, a rain of Sal flowers will also fall.

"When this man passes away from the deva world, he will come to the human world. In this human world too, he will always be provided with a Sal-flower roof.

"In this human world, dance and song, accompanied by well-played instruments, will always surround me; this is the fruit of Buddha-pūjā.

"When the sun rises, a rain of Sal flowers falls; because of being joined with meritorious deeds, it rains at all times.

"One thousand eight hundred aeons from now, a Teacher named Gotama, born of the Okkāka lineage, will appear in the world.

"His heir in the Dhamma, his breast-born son, created by the Dhamma, having fully understood all taints (āsavas), will attain Nibbāna, being taintless.

"For him who penetrates the Dhamma, there will be a Sal-flower roof; even while he is being cremated on the funeral pyre, there will be a roof in that place."

Having praised the ripening of the result, the Great Sage Piyadassī preached the Dhamma to the assembly, satisfying them with the rain of Dhamma.

"I exercised divine sovereignty in the deva worlds for thirty aeons, and I have been a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) sixty-seven times."
349:
"Coming from the deva world to this human world, I obtain abundant happiness. In this human world too, I obtain a Sal-flower roof; this is the fruit of the pavilion offering.

"This is my final existence, my last birth. In this human world too, there will be a Sal-flower roof at all times.

"Having pleased the Great Sage Gotama, the Bull of the Sakyans, I have reached the unshakable state (Nibbāna), having abandoned victory and defeat.

"Because I honored the Buddha eighteen hundred aeons ago, I do not know any miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of Buddha-pūjā.

"My defilements are burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled."

That Elder Tissa, having reached Arahatship, became especially preeminent in receiving gains and honors. At that time, some worldling (puthujjana) monks, seeing the Elder's gains and honors, showed signs of envy and intolerance due to their foolishness. The Elder, knowing this, and wishing to reveal the danger in gains and honors as well as his own lack of attachment to them, recited these two verses:

"A shaven-headed one, clad in the outer robe (saṅghāṭi), who receives food, drink, clothing, and bedding, gains many enemies.

"Knowing this danger, this great fear in honors, a monk should wander mindful, with few gains and untainted by craving."

The meaning of the verses is: He is 'muṇḍa' (shaven) because his hair is shaved off without leaving even a topknot. He is 'saṅghāṭipāruta' (clad in the outer robe) because he wears the patched-together saṅghāṭi robe. If a monk who has thus undergone a change in appearance and lives dependent on others receives food, snacks, and so on, many envious people will arise, and thus he gains many enemies. Therefore, knowing this great fear, this vast danger and fault in gains and honors, and keeping fewness of wishes and contentment in his heart, he becomes one of 'few gains' by avoiding even gains that arise through blameless means. Because of having few gains, he is 'untainted' (anavassuta) by the absence of the moisture of craving. A monk should wander mindful, through the power of mindfulness and wisdom which are the causes of contentment, either because he sees the danger in saṃsāra or because he has destroyed the defilements.
350:
By the power of mindfulness and clear comprehension, being mindful, one should practice, wander, and dwell. Upon hearing these words, those monks immediately asked the Elder for forgiveness.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Tissa is finished.

## 8. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Kimila

"Pācīnavaṃsadāyamhi" and so forth is the verse of the Venerable Elder Kimila. How did it arise? His previous efforts, his sense of urgency (saṃvega), and his ordination were already stated in the commentary on the verse "Abhisatto" in the Ekakanipāta. Through that verse, the Elder showed the cause of his own attainment of distinction. Here, however, it should be understood that he shows his harmonious living together with the Venerable Anuruddha and the Venerable Nandiya after having attained distinction. To show how they lived while dwelling in harmony, he spoke these two verses:

"In the Eastern Bamboo Grove (Pācīnavaṃsadāya), the companions who are sons of the Sakyans,
Having abandoned no small amount of wealth, delight in the alms received in their bowls.
With aroused energy and resolute intent, always of firm effort,
They delight in the joy of the Dhamma, having abandoned worldly delight."

In those verses, "Pācīnavaṃsadāyamhi" means in the forest named Pācīnavaṃsa, which is protected, guarded, and well-defined. That forest is called "Pācīnavaṃsadāya" because it is situated in the eastern direction of the village and is surrounded by bamboo thickets, or because it is a bamboo forest. "Sakyaputtā" refers to the Sakyan princes such as the Venerable Anuruddha and others. "Sahāyakā" means companions, so called because they proceed together through the arising of saṃvega, ordination, the practice of recluse-dharma, and living together. "Pahāya anappake bhoge" means having discarded great masses of wealth inherited through family lineage and obtained through the great power of merit. There is also a Pali reading "sahāyā nappake". "Uñche pattāgate ratā" means by the practice of gathering alms...
352:
Through that meritorious deed, wandering only in the happy realms, he was born in Kapilavatthu during the time of this Buddha's appearance as the son of King Suddhodana, conceived in the womb of Mahāpajāpati Gotamī. On the day of his naming, they named him 'Nanda' because he was born bringing joy to the assembly of relatives. When Nanda reached maturity, the Teacher, having set in motion the noble Wheel of Dhamma and working for the benefit of the world, went to Kapilavatthu. In the assembly of relatives, he preached the Vessantara Jātaka, taking the falling of the Pokkharavassa rain as the occasion. On the second day, while entering for alms, he established his father in the fruit of Stream-entry with the verse 'Uttiṭṭhe nappamajjeyya'. Having gone to the palace, he established Mahāpajāpati Gotamī in the fruit of Stream-entry and the King in the fruit of Once-returning with the verse 'Dhammaṃ care sucaritaṃ'.

On the third day, while the ceremonies for Prince Nanda's consecration, house-warming, and marriage were taking place, the Buddha entered for alms, placed the bowl in Prince Nanda's hand, and after speaking words of blessing, went to the monastery without taking the bowl back. He had the prince, who arrived at the monastery holding the bowl, ordained even though he was unwilling. Knowing that he was oppressed by dissatisfaction (anabhirati) due to being ordained in such a way, the Buddha removed his dissatisfaction through a skillful means. Prince Nanda, reflecting wisely and undertaking insight meditation, soon attained the fruit of Arahantship. Regarding this, it is said in the Apadāna:

'The Blessed One Atthadassī, the Self-awakened One, the Leader of the World, the Tathāgata, approached the bank of the Vinatā River.

Coming out of the water, I, a turtle dwelling in the water, approached the Leader of the World, wishing to carry the Buddha across.

"O Buddha, Great Sage Atthadassī, please climb upon my back. I shall carry you across. You are the one who makes an end of suffering."

Knowing my intention, the famous Atthadassī, the Leader of the World, climbed upon my back and stood there.

From the time I became self-aware, from the time I reached the age of discretion, I have never had such happiness as when I was touched by the soles of his feet.

Having crossed over, the famous Buddha Atthadassī stood on the riverbank and spoke these verses:'
353:
'As long as the thought (of merit) lasted, I crossed the current of the Ganges; and this wise king of turtles carried me across.

Because of this merit of carrying the Buddha and because of his heart of loving-kindness, he will rejoice in the deva realm for eighteen hundred aeons.

Coming from the deva realm to this human world, urged by the root of his wholesome merit, he will cross the flood of doubt while sitting in a single seat.

Just as even a small seed planted in a good field delights the farmer with its fruit when there is proper rainfall,

Even so, in this Buddha-field taught by the Fully Enlightened One, when the rain of Dhamma falls properly, the fruit shall delight me.

I am one whose mind is directed toward striving, peaceful, and free from acquisitions. Having fully understood all taints, I dwell without taints.

In the eighteen hundred aeons since I performed that deed, I have not known a miserable rebirth. This is the fruit of carrying (the Buddha) across.

My defilements are burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.'

Upon reaching Arahantship and experiencing the bliss of liberation (vimutti-sukha), he reflected on the defilements he had abandoned and the happiness he had gained, thinking, 'Oh, how skillful is the Teacher in means, by which I have been pulled out from the mire of existence and established on the dry land of Nibbāna!' With a heart full of joy, he uttered these verses of inspiration (udāna):

'Due to improper attention, I was devoted to external adornment. I was conceited, fickle, and oppressed by sensual lust.

Through the Buddha, the kinsman of the Sun, who is skillful in means, I practiced wisely and pulled my mind out of existence.'

In these verses, 'ayoniso manasikāra' refers to one who has the perception of beauty (subha-saññā) by attending to this foul body as beautiful due to improper attention.
354:
It means because of perceiving this foul body as beautiful. 'Maṇḍanaṃ' refers to the decoration of one's body with ornaments such as jewelry, and with flowers, perfumes, and so on. 'Anuyuñjisaṃ' means I have practiced repeatedly; the meaning is that I was one devoted to the decoration of the body. 'Uddhata' means one with an unsettled mind due to intoxication with birth, lineage, appearance, youth, and so forth. 'Capala' means fickle because of having an unsteady mind like a forest monkey, or fickle because of being engaged in the frivolity of decorating the body and clothes. 'Āsiṃ' means I was. 'Kāmarāgena' should be understood in connection as: I was oppressed, tormented, and obstructed by strong passion for sensual objects.

'Upāyakusaleṇa' means by the Blessed One, the Buddha, who is the cause and who is skilled and proficient in the means of taming those to be disciplined. Here, the third case (instrumental) is used in the sense of cause (hetu). He speaks referring to the removal of his own sensual passion by showing him the nymphs who were like singed monkeys and by urging him with reproachful words. The Blessed One, first taking the princess Janapadakalyāṇī as a reference, said: "Just as this monkey is, so is Janapadakalyāṇī in comparison to these pink-footed nymphs." Like one extracting a large splinter with a small one, or like a physician who, after moistening the body with an oily drink, removes the defect through vomiting and purging, He caused Nanda's mind to become detached from Janapadakalyāṇī by showing him the pink-footed nymphs. Then, through reproachful words, He made his mind detached even from those nymphs and established him in the Noble Path through the proper practice of tranquility and insight (samatha-vipassanā). Therefore, it is said: "Having practiced properly, I have pulled out the mind that was stuck in the existence of saṃsāra." The meaning is: having properly practiced the path of purification, namely tranquility and insight, through skillful means, I have lifted my mind, which was submerged in the mire of saṃsāra, with the hand of the Noble Path and established it on the dry land of Nibbāna.

After uttering this inspired utterance (udāna), the Elder approached the Blessed One the next day and said: "Venerable Sir, I release the Blessed One from that promise which the Blessed One made to me for the sake of obtaining five hundred pink-footed nymphs." The Blessed One also said: "Nanda, when your mind was liberated from the taints (āsavas) without clinging, only then was I released from that promise." At that time, the Blessed One [regarding] the Elder Nanda...
355:
The Blessed One, knowing that he had particularly guarded doors in his sense faculties, and manifesting that quality, placed him in the foremost position among those who guard the sense doors, saying: "Monks, among my monk disciples who guard the doors of the senses, Nanda is the foremost." Indeed, that Elder, thinking, "I reached such a state of perversion because of my lack of restraint over the senses; I shall thoroughly subdue that very lack of restraint," became energetic and possessed strong moral shame and dread (hiri-ottappa). Because of his previous meritorious deeds (adhikāra) in that regard, he reached the pinnacle of perfection in the restraint of the sense faculties (indriya-saṃvara).

## The Commentary on the Verses of Nanda Thera is finished.

## 10. Commentary on the Verses of Sirimatta Thera

The verse beginning with "Pare ca naṃ pasaṃsanti" is the verse of the Venerable Sirimatta. How did it originate? This [Elder] also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and, accumulating merit in various lives, fulfilled the perfections of the Blessed One Padumuttara. While staying in the Tusita heaven, he was reborn in a Brahmin family. Upon reaching maturity, he mastered the three Vedas, and became an expert in the Nighaṇḍu, Keṭubha, the science of phonology, and the Itihāsas as the fifth. He was a grammarian, proficient in the Lokāyata and the marks of a Great Man (Mahāpurisalakkhaṇa). Due to his inclination for renunciation, he abandoned sensual pleasures, became an ascetic, and lived in the Himalayan region surrounded by eighty-four thousand ascetics in a hermitage created by deities. Having attained the jhānas and supernormal knowledges (abhiññā), and because of his past meritorious deeds and the signs mentioned in the texts of marks, he recollected the qualities of the Buddha. Intending to honor the past Buddhas, he built a sand stupa (pulinacetiya) at a bend in a river and delighted in making offerings. Seeing that sand stupa, the ascetics asked, "In whose honor is this offering being made?" The teacher-ascetic, citing the texts of marks and explaining the marks of a Great Man found therein, praised the qualities of the Buddha according to his own ability. Hearing those words, the ascetics also became clear-minded and, from then on, lived making offerings to the stupa in honor of the Perfectly Enlightened One.

At that time, the Bodhisatta Padumuttara passed away from the Tusita heaven and descended into his mother's womb. In his final existence, the thirty-two omens...
357:
“Venerable sir, you worship this stupa made of sand; we also wish to know about it. Being asked, please tell us.

Are the Buddhas, the ones with five kinds of eyes and great fame, pointed out in the Mantas? I worship those Excellent Buddhas of great fame.

What are those Great Heroes like, the All-knowing ones, the Leaders of the World? What is their appearance, what is their conduct, and what is the nature of those of great fame?

Buddhas are endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, and also with forty teeth. Their eyes are like those of a young calf, and their color is like the jiñjuka fruit.

When those Buddhas walk, they look only a yoke's length ahead. Their knees do not creak, and the sound of joints is not heard.

When the Sugatas walk, they walk lifting their feet; they lift the right foot first. This is the nature of the Buddhas.

Like the maned lion king, those Buddhas are fearless. They do not exalt themselves, nor do they disparage other beings.

They are free from conceit and humiliation, and have an equal mind towards all beings. Buddhas do not exalt themselves; such a nature of not exalting oneself is the nature of the Buddhas.

When the Buddhas are born, they manifest light. They cause this entire earth to shake in six ways.

They also see the hells; at the time of the Buddha's birth, hell is cooled. A great cloud rains heavily; such a nature is the nature of the Buddhas.

Such are those Great Beings, incomparable and of great fame. In appearance, there is none who surpasses them; the Tathāgatas are immeasurable.

All the disciples, being respectful, rejoiced at my words. They practiced accordingly to the best of their ability and strength.

Those who desired their own merit, believing my words and having a mind wishing to honor the Buddha, worshipped the sand stupa.”
358:
Then the deity of great fame passed away from the Tusita heaven and took rebirth in the mother's womb. At that time, the ten-thousandfold world system shook violently.

While I was standing on the walking path not far from the hermitage, all the disciples assembled together and came to me.

“The earth roars like a bull, howls like a lion king, and bellows like a crocodile. What kind of result will there be?” (the disciples asked).

“I have praised that Buddha near the sand stupa; that Blessed One, the Teacher, has now entered the mother's womb.”

Having spoken a Dhamma talk to those disciples and praised the Great Sage, I dismissed my disciples and sat down cross-legged.

My strength was indeed exhausted, and a severe illness oppressed me. Remembering the Excellent Buddha, I passed away right there.

Then all the disciples assembled together and prepared a funeral pyre. Taking my body, they placed it upon the pyre.

Those disciples, overcome by the dart of grief, came together and surrounded the pyre, weeping with their hands raised in salutation to their heads.

While those disciples were lamenting, I then came near the pyre and said, “O wise disciples, I am your teacher; do not grieve.”

“Strive for your own welfare day and night without laziness. Do not be negligent; the opportune moment of a Buddha's arising has been attained by you,” (I advised).

Having admonished my disciples, I returned to the heavenly world. I enjoyed myself in the heavenly world for eighteen aeons.

Five hundred times I was a Universal Monarch, and many hundreds of times I exercised the sovereignty of the devas.

In the remaining aeons, I wandered through various existences. I do not know of any woeful state; this is the fruit of that worship (of the sand stupa).
359:
Just as many trees bloom in the month of Kattika, even so, I was made to bloom by the Great Sage (through the Fruition of Arahatship).

My energy is like a draft ox, carrying me to Nibbāna, the security from the four bonds. Like a great elephant breaking its bonds, I live free from taints, having severed the bond of craving.

In the hundred thousandth aeon [ago], I praised a Buddha; because of the merit of that praise, I do not know of any rebirth in the four woeful states. This is the fruit of that praise.

My defilements are burnt... (pe)... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.

Worldling monks and novices, not knowing the Venerable Sirimatta—who was endowed with the six supernormal powers—to be an Ariya, criticized him with various words, considering him unworthy of praise because he had few gains and was not sought after by the people. However, they praised the Elder Siriwaḍḍha, considering him worthy because he received many gains of the four requisites and was respected and honored by the people. Then, the Venerable Sirimatta, wishing to blame the state of worldlings, thinking, "Praising the unworthy and blaming the worthy is indeed the fault of these worldlings," spoke these two verses:

"If one is not concentrated in oneself, yet others praise him; that praise from others is in vain, for he himself is not concentrated.

If one is well-concentrated in oneself, yet others blame him; that blame from others is in vain, for he himself is well-concentrated."

In those verses, "pare" means others besides oneself; here, however, it refers to fools other than the wise. Because they speak without knowing and without investigating the facts, their praise, like their blame, is of no account. "Naṃ" refers to that person. "Pasaṃsanti" means they praise and extol a person even falsely, either through ignorance or because of being overwhelmed by craving, attributing non-existent qualities such as, "This monk is an attainer of jhāna, he is an Ariya." The word "ca" used here...
360:
...has the sense of comparison to oneself. By this, it shows that others praise that person, but that is merely their praise; in reality, there is no ground for praise in that person.

"Attā ce asamāhito" means: if the person whom others praise is not himself concentrated by way of Path-concentration, Fruition-concentration, or even just Access or Absorption concentration; or if he has a distracted and wandering mind because the defilements, which are the opposites of concentration, have not yet been abandoned. By the word "asamāhito," he shows the absence of qualities that have concentration as their cause. "Moghaṃ" is a neuter derivative used as an adverb, as in "visamaṃ candimasūriyā parivattanti" (the moon and sun revolve unevenly). "Pare pasaṃsanti" means: those who praise that unconcentrated person praise him in vain, uselessly, and without basis. Why? Because that person's mind is not concentrated, meaning he himself is not concentrated.

In the second verse, "garahanti" means: they blame, disparage, or revile an Ariya who is an attainer of jhāna, either due to their own lack of wisdom or due to a mind of anger, by pointing out a supposed lack of practice, saying, "This monk does not apply himself to wakefulness, not even for the duration of milking a cow; he lives mostly for the sake of strengthening his body, delighting in sleep, delighting in talk, and delighting in company," or by destroying his reputation. The rest is to be understood in the same manner as explained for the first verse.

Thus, when the Elder revealed his own state of being free from defilements and Siriwaḍḍha's state of having defilements through these verses, Siriwaḍḍha, having heard them, was moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega). He developed insight and before long fulfilled his own goal, the Fruition of Arahatship. Those who had criticized also apologized to the Elder.

## The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Sirimatta is finished.

## The Commentary on the Second Chapter is finished.
361:
## 3. Tatiya Vagga
## 1. Uttara Thera Gāthā Vaṇṇanā

The verse beginning with "Khandhā mayā pariññātā" is that of the Venerable Uttara Thera. What is its origin? This Venerable Uttara had also performed meritorious deeds of high aspiration (adhikāra) under previous Buddhas and had accumulated wholesome deeds serving as a support for the cessation of the cycle (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) in various existences. Ninety-four aeons ago, during the time of Siddhattha Buddha, he was reborn in a family home. Upon reaching the age of discretion, he gained faith in the Dispensation and declared himself a lay devotee (upāsaka). When the Buddha attained Parinibbāna, he gathered his relatives, collected many offerings, and performed the worship of the relics.

Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans. In this present Buddha-era, he was reborn in a Brahmin family in the city of Sāketa and received the name Uttara. When he came of age, he went to Sāvatthī on some business and, seeing the Twin Miracle (yamaka-pāṭihāriya) performed at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba mango tree, he gained faith. Later, due to the discourse of the Kāḷakārāma Sutta, his faith increased greatly; he ordained, went to Rājagaha with the Teacher, and attained higher ordination (upasampadā). While residing there in Rājagaha, he practiced insight meditation (vipassanā) and before long became an Arahant endowed with the six supernormal knowledges (chaḷabhiññā). Regarding this, it is stated in the Apadāna:

"When the Lord of the World, Siddhattha, the Leader of the World, had attained Parinibbāna,
Having gathered my relatives, I performed the worship of the relics.
In the ninety-fourth aeon ago, I worshiped those relics;
Due to the merit of that relic-worship, I have not known a woeful state.
My defilements have been burnt away... (etc.) ...the Buddha's Dispensation has been fulfilled."

After becoming an Arahant with the six supernormal knowledges, while the Teacher was residing in Sāvatthī, he came from Rājagaha to Sāvatthī to attend upon the Buddha. When asked by the monks, "Friend, have you brought the task of monkhood to its consummation?", he recited these verses, wishing to declare his attainment of the fruit of Arahantship:

"The aggregates are fully understood by me, craving is well uprooted by me,
The factors of enlightenment are developed by me, I have reached the destruction of the taints."
362:
"That 'I', having fully understood the aggregates, having uprooted the net of craving,
Having developed the factors of enlightenment, shall attain Parinibbāna, free from taints."
He recited these two verses.

In those verses, 'aggregates' (khandhā) refers to the five aggregates of clinging. 'Fully understood' (pariññātā) means they are known and defined as "This is suffering; there is nothing beyond this." By this term, he speaks of the realization through full understanding (pariññābhisamaya) of the Noble Truth of Suffering. 'Craving' (taṇhā) is so called because it lusts (thirsts). 'Well uprooted' (susumūhatā) means they are eradicated at the root. By this term, he speaks of the realization through abandoning (pahānābhisamaya) of the Truth of Origin. 'The factors of enlightenment are developed by me' means they are called factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) either because of the harmony of the dhammas such as mindfulness, which is called enlightenment (bodhi), or because they are the factors of the noble person (ariya-puggala) who possesses that enlightenment. I have developed, produced, and increased the dhammas included in the Path, known as mindfulness, investigation of states, energy, joy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity. By the inclusion of the factors of enlightenment alone, it should be understood that all path factors and all requisites of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma) that arise together with them are also included. Thus, he shows the realization through development (bhāvanābhisamaya) of the Truth of the Path. 'I have reached the destruction of the taints' means I have reached and realized the Unconditioned Dhamma (Asaṅkhata Dhamma) named 'destruction of taints' because the taints such as the taint of sensual desire are destroyed therein. By this term, he speaks of the realization through witnessing (sacchikiriyābhisamaya) of the Truth of Cessation. By this much, he shows his attainment of Nibbāna with residue (sa-upādisesa-nibbāna).

Now, however, wishing to show the attainment of Nibbāna without residue (anupādisesa-nibbāna), he spoke the second verse beginning with "Sohaṃ". Its meaning is: That 'I', having fully understood the aggregates in the manner stated, and while thus understanding, having uprooted from my mental continuum the craving named 'the ensnarer' (jālinī)—which has the nature of weaving together repeatedly what is called the occurrence of internal and external bases, divided into past and so on, in one's own continuity and the continuity of others—and while thus uprooting it, having developed the aforementioned various factors of enlightenment and brought them to the fulfillment of development, and having remained free from taints because of that very fulfillment, I shall now, with the cessation of the final consciousness, attain Parinibbāna like a fire without fuel (upādāna).

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Uttara is finished.
363:
## 2. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Bhaddaji

The verse beginning with "Panādo nāma so rājā" is that of the Venerable Bhaddaji Thera. How did it originate? It is said that during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was born into a Brahmin family. Upon reaching the age of discretion, he mastered the sciences and arts of the Brahmins. Renouncing sensual pleasures, he went forth as an ascetic and lived in a hermitage he built in a forest. One day, seeing the Teacher traveling through the air, his heart was filled with faith, and he stood with palms joined in reverence. The Teacher, knowing his inclination, descended from the sky. To the Blessed One who had descended, he offered honey, lotus roots, ghee, and milk. Out of compassion for him, the Blessed One accepted them, spoke words of appreciation (anumodanā), and departed. Due to that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the Tusita heaven, where he stayed for the full lifespan. Thereafter, wandering only through the happy realms (sugati), he became a wealthy merchant during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī. He provided food for sixty-eight thousand monks and offered them sets of triple robes.

Having performed many such meritorious deeds, he was reborn in the deva realm and stayed there for the full lifespan. Passing away from there, he was reborn in the human world during a period void of Buddhas. He served five hundred Paccekabuddhas with the four requisites. Passing away from there, he was reborn in a royal family. While ruling the kingdom, he served his son who had attained Paccekabodhi. When that son attained Parinibbāna, he took the relics, built a stupa, and made offerings. Thus, having performed various meritorious deeds in those various lives, in the time of our Buddha, he was reborn in the city of Bhaddiya as the only son of the merchant Bhaddiya, who possessed wealth of eighty crores. He was given the name Bhaddaji. His prosperity in terms of power, wealth, and retinue in his final birth was like that of a Bodhisatta.

At that time, the Teacher, after spending the rainy season in Sāvatthī, traveled to the city of Bhaddiya with a large community of monks to favor the young Bhaddaji. He stayed in the Jātiyāvana forest, awaiting the maturation of the youth's knowledge. The youth, sitting in his palace, opened a window and looked out. Seeing a great crowd of people going to hear the Dhamma from the Blessed One, he asked, "Where is this crowd going?" Upon hearing the reason, he himself went to the Teacher with a large retinue to [hear] the Dhamma...
364:
While listening to the Dhamma, even while adorned with all his ornaments, he exhausted all defilements and attained Arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

"At that time, I descended into a pond frequented by various elephants. For the sake of food, I was pulling up lotus roots in that pond.

At that time, the Buddha named Padumuttara, the Blessed One wearing crimson robes, was traveling through the air.

I then heard the sound of him shaking his rag-robes. Looking upwards, I saw the Leader of the World.

Standing right there, I requested the Leader of the World (to accept) honey along with lotus roots, milk, ghee, and lotus stalks.

'May the Buddha, the One with Five Eyes, accept this out of compassion for me.' Then the Teacher, the Compassionate One of great fame, descended (from the sky).

The Buddha, the One with Five Eyes, accepted my first alms out of compassion. Having accepted it, the Fully Enlightened One gave me words of appreciation.

'O man of great merit, may you be happy; may your destination (gati) be fulfilled. Through this gift of lotus roots, may you obtain abundant happiness.'

Having said this, the Fully Enlightened One named Padumuttara, the Conqueror, took the alms and departed through the air.

Thereafter, taking the lotus roots, I returned to my hermitage. Having hung the lotus roots on a tree, I reflected repeatedly on my gift.

Then a great wind arose and shook the forest. In the sky, there was a roar, and lightning struck.

Then a lightning bolt fell upon my head. While I was sitting there, I passed away.

Being endowed with meritorious deeds, I was reborn in Tusita. Though my physical body fell (to the ground), I rejoiced in the deva realm."
365:
"Eighty-six thousand women, well-adorned, serve me evening and morning; this is the fruit of the offering of lotus stalks. Having come to a human birth, I was then happy; I had no lack of wealth; this is the fruit of the offering of lotus stalks. Compassionately treated by that God of gods, the Such-like One, all taints are exhausted; now there is no more rebirth. In the hundred-thousandth aeon from now, when I gave lotus stalks, I have not known a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of the offering of lotus stalks. My defilements are burnt... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out."

When Elder Bhaddaji attained the fruit of Arahantship, the Teacher addressed the merchant Bhaddiya: "Your son, while listening to the Dhamma even while fully adorned, has attained Arahantship. Therefore, it is proper for him to ordain right now; if he does not ordain, he will pass away (attain Parinibbāna)." The merchant said, "There is no need for my son to pass away while he is still young; please let him ordain." The Teacher ordained him, and after staying there for seven days, he traveled to the village of Koṭigāma on the banks of the Ganges. The villagers of Koṭigāma offered a great gift to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha. While the Teacher was about to give the blessing (anumodanā), Elder Bhaddaji went outside the village and sat down, entering a meditative attainment (samāpatti), thinking, "I will rise only when the Teacher arrives near the road by the bank of the Ganges." Even when the senior elders arrived, he did not rise, but rose only when the Teacher arrived. The worldling monks criticized him, saying, "This newly ordained monk is stiff with pride and did not rise even when the senior elders arrived."

The villagers of Koṭigāma constructed many rafts for the Teacher and the Saṅgha. The Teacher, wishing to reveal the psychic power of Bhaddaji, stood on a raft and asked, "Where is Bhaddaji?" Elder Bhaddaji approached the Teacher, saying, "I am here, Bhante," and stood with palms joined. The Teacher said, "Come, Bhaddaji, board the same boat with us." He then flew up and landed on the boat where the Teacher was standing. When they reached the middle of the Ganges, the Teacher asked, "Bhaddaji, where is the jeweled palace you occupied when you were King Mahāpanāda?" "It is submerged right here," he replied. "If that is so, Bhaddaji, dispel the doubts of your fellow practitioners," the Teacher commanded. At that moment, relying on the Teacher's power, Elder Bhaddaji used his psychic power to grip the twenty-five yojana palace with his big toe and lifted it into the air. As it rose, the twenty-five yojana palace emerged from the water. Then, five thousand fish about the size of small frogs, who were his relatives in a previous life and were attached to the house through greed, came up with the palace and tumbled back into the water. Seeing those fish, the Teacher said, "Bhaddaji, your little fish relatives are suffering." At the Teacher's word, the Elder released the palace, and it settled back in its original place. When the Teacher reached the other bank, the monks said, "Bhante, Bhaddaji..."
366:
The Elder, having paid homage to the Teacher, went by psychic power and, gripping the pinnacle of the palace between his toes, took the palace of twenty-five yojanas and rose into the air. As he rose, he lifted the palace of twenty-five yojanas out of the water. Then his relatives from a previous life, who had become fish, turtles, and frogs due to their greed for the palace, tumbled and fell into the water as the palace rose. Seeing them falling, the Teacher said, "Dear Bhaddaji, your relatives are suffering." At the Teacher's word, the Elder released the palace. The palace settled back in its original place.

When the Teacher reached the other bank, the monks asked, "Venerable Sir, when did Elder Bhaddaji live in this palace?" The Teacher then told the Mahāpanāda Jātaka and gave the ambrosia of the Dhamma to the multitude. The Elder also showed the golden palace he had previously occupied and, praising it with these two verses, declared his attainment of Arahantship:

"There was a king named Panāda, whose sacrificial pillar (palace) was made of gold;
It was sixteen sections wide and rose a thousandfold in height.

With a thousand sections and a hundred knobs, it was adorned with golden banners;
There, six thousand Gandharvas (dancers) danced in seven ways."

In these verses, "Panāda named that king" means that in the past, there was a king by the name of Panāda; because that existence has passed away, he refers to himself as if he were another person. From the time he attained kingship, he was known as "King Mahāpanāda" because he was endowed with great royal power, such as constant energy, and great fame. "Whose pillar was made of gold" means that this palace-pillar of the king was made of gold. "Sixteen sections wide" means it was sixteen sections in width. That measurement is about half a yojana. "Rose a thousandfold in height" means they say the height of this palace was a thousand sections. That height is twenty-five yojanas in measurement. Some teachers lengthen the sound of "āhu" to "āhū" for the sake of the meter, meaning "it was." "A thousand sections" means it had a thousand stories. "A hundred knobs" (satageṇḍu) means it had a hundred courtyards or terraces. "Adorned with banners" (dhajālu) means it was equipped with banner-staffs and flags erected on the pinnacles of various terraces. "Made of gold" (haritāmaya) means it was made of pure Jāmbūnada gold. Some say it was like pure green emeralds. "Gandharvas" refers to the dancers. "Six thousand in seven ways" means six thousand dancers in seven locations of that palace...
367:
In height, it was twenty-five yojanas in extent. Some teachers say that in these verses, the word 'āhū' has been lengthened to 'āhū' for the sake of metrical ease; they say 'āhu' has the meaning of 'ahosi' (it was).

'Sahassakaṇḍo' means having more than a thousand stories. 'Satageṇḍu' means having more than a hundred palace courtyards. 'Dhajālu' means being endowed with banners and flags, such as staff-banners and cloth-banners, which were hoisted on the pinnacles of those various palace courtyards. 'Haritāmaya' means made of cāmīkara gold. Some teachers, however, say it is like genuine green emeralds. 'Gandhabbā' refers to dancers. 'Cha sahasāni sattadhā' means that six thousand dancers danced in seven ways in seven places of that palace to delight the king. Although they danced in this way, they were unable to make the king laugh. Then, Sakka, the king of devas, sent celestial dancers to perform a festival, and only then did the king laugh.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Bhaddaji Thera is finished.

## 3. The Commentary on the Verses of Sobhita Thera

'Satimā paññavā' and so forth are the verses of the Venerable Sobhita Thera. As for the background story: he too was one who had performed meritorious services under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit in various births. In the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was reborn in a family home in the city of Haṃsavatī. When he came of age, while listening to the Teacher’s Dhamma desanā, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the foremost position among those who possess the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa). He himself aspired to that position and performed meritorious deeds. Wandering only through the happy realms (sugati), he was reborn in a brahmin family in the time of the Blessed One Sumedha. When he reached the age of discretion, he achieved mastery in the arts and sciences of the brahmins. Inclined toward renunciation, he abandoned the household life and went forth as an ascetic. Having built a hermitage in a forest region near the Himavanta mountains, he lived subsisting on forest roots and fruits. Hearing of the arising of a Buddha, he traveled toward the city of Bhaddavatī where the Teacher resided, staying only one night at each place along the way. With a mind full of faith, he worshipped the Teacher with six verses beginning with 'Tuvaṃ satthā ca ketu ca'.
368:
When he praised the Buddha in this way, the Teacher also revealed the future prosperity that would come to this noble son. Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans, and in this present Buddha-arising, he was reborn in a brahmin family in Sāvatthī. They gave him the name Sobhita. Later, having heard the Teacher’s Dhamma desanā, he gained faith and went forth. Developing insight (vipassanā), he became an possessor of the six supernormal powers (chaḷabhiññā). He also became one who attained mastery (vasībhāva) in the knowledge of recollecting past lives. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

'To the south of the Himavanta, my hermitage was well-constructed;
Seeking the supreme goal, I lived in the great forest then.

Content with gain or loss, and with roots and fruits,
Seeking a teacher, I lived alone.

The Fully Enlightened One named Sumedha then appeared in the world;
Revealing the Four Truths, he was lifting up the great multitude.

I did not hear of the Fully Enlightened One, nor did anyone tell me;
Only after eight years had passed did I hear of the Leader of the World.

Removing the fireplace and sweeping the hermitage,
Taking up my carrying pole, I departed from the great forest.

Staying for one night in villages and market towns,
In due course, I then approached the city of Candavatī.

At that time, the Blessed One Sumedha, the Leader of the World,
Lifting up many beings, was preaching the state of the Deathless.

Passing through the crowd and worshipping the Ocean of Conquest (Jina-sāgara),
Placing the antelope skin on one shoulder, I praised the Leader of the World.

You are the Teacher, the Pinnacle, the Banner, and the Sacrificial Post for living beings;
You are the Refuge, the Support, and the Island, O Supreme among bipeds.

O Hero, subtle in vision, you deliver the people;
There is no other deliverer in the world superior to you, O Sage.'
369:
'It might be possible to measure the great ocean with the tip of a blade of kusa grass;
But, O All-Knowing One, it is not possible to measure your knowledge.

It might be possible to carry the earth by placing it on a balance scale;
But, O Visionary One, there is no measure for your wisdom.

It might be possible to measure the sky with a rope or a finger;
But, O All-Knowing One, it is not possible to measure your virtue.

The water in the great ocean, the sky, and the earth—
These things are measurable; but you, O Visionary One, are immeasurable.'

Having praised the All-Knowing One of great fame with six verses,
I then stood silently with my hands raised in salutation.

That Buddha named Sumedha, of vast wisdom and excellent intelligence,
Sitting in the midst of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, spoke these verses:

'He who has praised my knowledge with a clear and confident mind,
I shall praise him; listen to my words as I speak.

For seventy-seven aeons, he will delight in the deva world;
A thousand times, he will be the King of Devas and exercise celestial rule.

And many hundreds of times, he will be a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti);
The instances of being a regional king (padesarāja) will be vast and beyond counting.

Whether as a deva or a human, being endowed with meritorious deeds,
With undiminished intentions, he will be one of sharp wisdom.

Thirty thousand aeons from now, born in the Okkāka clan,
The Teacher named Gotama by clan will appear in the world.

Departing from the home, he will go forth without worldly attachments;
At the age of seven from birth, he will touch the fruit of Arahantship.'

From the time I can remember myself, from the time I reached the Dispensation,
In this interval, I have never known an unwholesome intention.
370:
“Wandering through all existences, I have experienced prosperity and happiness. That I have no lack of wealth and possessions is the fruit of having praised the [Omniscient] Knowledge.

My three fires [of lust, hatred, and delusion] are extinguished; all existences are uprooted; all taints are exhausted; now there is no more rebirth.

Thirty thousand aeons ago, I praised that [Omniscient] Knowledge. Because of that merit, I have never known [never reached] a woeful state. This is the fruit of having praised the Knowledge.

My defilements are burned away [destroyed] ... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.”

That Elder Sobhita, having reached the fruit of Arahatship, while recollecting the sequence of his past aggregates in order, saw as far back as his rebirth without consciousness in the realm of unconscious beings (Asaññasatta). Beyond that, for five hundred aeons, he did not see the occurrence of consciousness (mental phenomena), seeing it only at the end [of that period]. Reflecting, “What is this?”, he came to the conclusion through logical deduction: “It must be the existence in the realm of unconscious beings.” Therefore, the Blessed One said: “Monks, there are long-lived devas named unconscious beings (Asaññasatta). Passing away from there, Sobhita was reborn here. That Sobhita knows that existence; Sobhita recollects it” (similar in meaning to the words in the Pārājika Commentary). Seeing his skill in recollecting through such logical deduction, the Teacher placed the Elder in the foremost position among those who can recollect past existences. For that very reason, this Venerable Sobhita, reflecting on his extraordinary knowledge of recollecting past lives and the practice that was its cause, became joyful and, wishing to utter an inspired utterance (udāna) explaining that meaning, spoke these two verses:

“Being mindful, wise, and possessed of exerted strength and energy, I, a monk, have recollected five hundred aeons as if in a single night.

Developing the four foundations of mindfulness, the seven [factors of enlightenment], and the eight [path factors], I have recollected five hundred aeons in just a single night,” he spoke these two verses.

In those verses, “satimā” (mindful) means one who is mindful due to the fulfillment of the development of the foundations of mindfulness, which is endowed with personal attainment, and due to reaching the abundance of mindfulness. “Paññavā” (wise) means one who is wise due to the fulfillment of the six higher powers (abhiññā) and due to reaching the abundance of wisdom. He is called “bhikkhu” (monk) because he has broken the defilements.
371:
He is called “āraddhabalavīriyo” (one with exerted strength and energy) because of the completion and fulfillment of the five powers such as faith, and the fourfold right exertion. Here, by the mention of “powers” (bala), faith and the others are taken, even though mindfulness and the rest also exist as powers, just as it is said, “cattle and bulls,” or “the accumulation of merit and the accumulation of knowledge.” “I recollected five hundred aeons in a single night” means recollecting as if in a single night. The word “viya” (like/as if) is elided here. By stating it this way, he demonstrates his mastery (vasībhāva) of knowledge in the recollection of past lives.

Now, to show the practice by which his state of being mindful, etc., and his extraordinary knowledge of past lives were accomplished, he spoke the second verse beginning with “cattāro” (four). In that verse, “cattāro satipaṭṭhāne” refers to the four foundations of mindfulness, such as mindfulness of the body, categorized by their respective objects, which are a mixture of mundane and supramundane. “Satta” refers to the seven factors of enlightenment. “Aṭṭha” refers to the eight path factors. For one whose mind is well-established in the foundations of mindfulness, the seven factors of enlightenment indeed reach fulfillment in development; likewise, the Noble Eightfold Path reaches fulfillment. Therefore, the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, said: “With the mind well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness, having developed the seven factors of enlightenment as they really are,” and so on. Among the thirty-seven qualities contributing to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma) divided into seven groups, when fulfillment in development is reached in one group, there is no such thing as not reaching it in the remaining groups. “Bhāvayaṃ” means because of developing. The remaining terms are as previously explained.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Sobhita is finished.

## 4. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Valliya

“Yaṃ kiccaṃ daḷhavīriyena” and the following verses are those of the Venerable Elder Valliya. What is the background story? This Elder also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and, accumulating merit in various existences, was born into a Brahmin family during the time of Sumedha Buddha. Reaching the age of discretion and achieving mastery in the Vedic sciences, he renounced eighty crores of wealth and became an ascetic. While living in a hermitage he built on the bank of a river in a forest at the foot of a mountain, he saw the Teacher who had come to favor him.
