With a devoted heart, he spread out a black antelope skin and...
372:
(He) offered (the black antelope skin). Having worshipped the Blessed One, who was seated there, with flowers and sandalwood, and having offered mango fruits, he paid homage with the five-point prostration. To him, the Blessed One, manifesting the perfection of the seat where He sat, spoke words of appreciation and departed. Due to that meritorious deed, wandering through the realms of devas and humans, he was reborn in a Brahmin family in Vesālī during the time of this Buddha's appearance and was named "Kaṇhamitta." Upon reaching maturity, seeing the Buddha's majesty during the Blessed One's visit to Vesālī, he gained faith and was ordained in the presence of the Elder Mahākaccāyana. Being of dull wisdom and slow effort, he lived for a long time depending only on a wise fellow practitioner. The monks said, "Just as a creeper cannot grow without depending on something like a tree, so this monk cannot grow without depending on some wise person," and thus they addressed him only as "Valliya." Later, however, he approached the Elder Veṇudatta, and established in his advice, living mindfully and clearly comprehending, as his knowledge matured, he wished to ask the Elder about the sequence of practice:

"What task should be done by one of firm energy, what task should be done by one desiring to know (the Four Noble Truths), that task I shall do; I shall not fail. Behold my energy and exertion.

And you, tell me the path, the straight way plunging into the Deathless; I shall know through silence (wisdom), as the current of the Ganges flows to the ocean." Thus he spoke these two verses.

In those verses, "Yaṃ kiccaṃ daḷhavīriyena" means the task to be performed or practiced with firm energy and steady exertion, or by a person of great responsibility with firm energy. "Yaṃ kiccaṃ boddhumicchatā" means the task to be done by one desiring to know, to realize the Four Noble Truths or Nibbāna itself. "Karissaṃ nāvarajjhissaṃ" means I shall now do that task, I shall not fail, I shall practice according to the instruction. "Passa vīriyaṃ parakkamaṃ" means behold the Right Effort, called "vīriya" because of its proper instigation in the dhammas to be practiced, and called "parakkama" because of its stepping forward to higher and higher stages; it shows his desire to act, saying it is not just hearsay.
373:
"Tvañca" is an address to the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitta) who gives the meditation subject. "Me" means "to me." "Maggamakkhāhi" means "tell me the Noble Path" or "tell me the meditation subject of the Four Truths that leads to the Supramundane Path." "Añjasaṃ" means the "straight path" because it does not lean towards the two extremes, being the Middle Way. It is called "Amatogadhaṃ" (plunging into the Deathless) because it is established as that which leads to Nibbāna. "Monena" means through knowledge, the wisdom of the Path. "Monissaṃ" means I shall know, I shall penetrate, I shall reach Nibbāna. "Gaṅgā-sotova sāgaraṃ" means just as the current of the Ganges flows into the great ocean without fail, even so, "If I strive in the meditation subject, I shall attain Nibbāna through Path-knowledge; therefore, tell me that meditation subject." Thus he requested the meditation subject from the Elder.

Hearing those words, the Elder Veṇudatta gave him the meditation subject. He, too, striving in the meditation subject, soon developed insight and reached Arahantship. This is stated in the Apadāna:

"Having abandoned the five strands of sensual pleasure, which are pleasant and delightful to the mind, and having abandoned eighty crores of wealth, I went forth into the homeless life.

Having gone forth, I avoided evil deeds of the body; having abandoned verbal misconduct, I lived on the riverbank.

While I was living alone, the Greatest of Buddhas approached me; not knowing He was the Buddha, I only performed the duties of welcome.

Having performed the welcome, I asked His name and lineage: 'Are you a deva, a Gandhabba, or Sakka, the giver of gifts (Purindada)?'

'Who are you, or whose son? Are you Mahābrahmā come here? You illuminate all directions like the rising sun.'

'O Great One, the marks of wheels with a thousand spokes are seen on your feet; who are you, or whose son? How may we know you?'

'Please declare your name and lineage, and remove my doubt.' 'I am not a deva, nor a Gandhabba, nor am I Sakka, the giver of gifts.'

'I have no state of Brahma; I am superior and more excellent than those. I have transcended their domain and have destroyed the bonds of craving.'"
374:
Having burned away all defilements and attained the supreme Enlightenment (Sambodhi), I heard the words of that Buddha and spoke these words:

"Great Sage (Mahāmuni), if you are the All-knowing Buddha, the one who brings an end to suffering, please reside here; I shall honor you."

I spread out a rug of antelope skin (ajina) and offered it to the Teacher. The Blessed One sat there like a lion in a mountain cave.

Quickly climbing the mountain, I took a mango fruit, a Sālakalyāṇika flower, and precious sandalwood.

Quickly lifting them all up, I approached the Leader of the World (Lokanāyaka). Having given the fruit to the Buddha, I honored him with the Sāla flower.

Anointing him with sandalwood, I paid homage to the Teacher. With a confident mind and great joy, I paid homage with vast rapture.

Sitting on the antelope skin, Sumedha, the Leader of the World, gladdening me then, proclaimed my meritorious deed:

"Because of this gift of fruit and both the scent and the flower, he will rejoice in the deva realm for twenty-five hundred aeons.

With undiminished intentions, he will be a ruler who wields power (Vasavatti). In the twenty-six hundredth aeon, he will attain human status.

He will be a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) of great psychic power, ruling over the four continents. There will be a city named Vebhāra, created by Vissakamma.

That city will be made entirely of gold and adorned with various jewels. In this way, he will wander through the cycle of births (saṃsāra).

Being honored everywhere among devas and humans, when he reaches his final birth, he will be born into a brahmin family (Brahmabandhu).

Departing from the household life, he will become a homeless monk. Having reached the further shore of higher knowledges (Abhiññā), he will attain Nibbāna, free from taints (āsavas)."
375:
Having spoken these words, the Buddha Sumedha, Leader of the World, departed through the air even as I was watching.

Due to that well-performed meritorious deed and my volitional aspirations, I left the human body and reached the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

Passing away from the Tusita heaven, I was born in a mother's womb. In that womb where I resided, there was no lack of wealth.

While I was in the mother's womb, through my wish, food, drinks, and nourishment appeared for my mother as desired.

Five years after birth, I entered the homeless life of a monk. Upon the shaving of my hair, I attained Arahantship.

Searching for my past deeds, I did not see them nearby, but I recollected my merit from thirty thousand aeons ago.

Homage to you, O Noble Man! Homage to you, O Supreme Man! By depending on your teaching, I have reached the unshakable state (Nibbāna).

Thirty thousand aeons ago, I honored the Buddha. Since then, I have never known an unhappy rebirth (duggati). This is the fruit of honoring the Buddha.

My defilements are burned away... [etc.] ... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.

Having reached Arahantship and wishing to declare his attainment, the Elder Valliya recited these verses.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Valliya Thera is Finished.

## 5. Commentary on the Verses of Vītāsoka Thera

The verse beginning with "Kese me olikhissanti" is that of the Venerable Vītāsoka Thera. What is its origin? This Elder also had made aspirations under previous Buddhas and accumulated merits in various lives. In the time of Buddha Siddhattha, he was born into a brahmin family. Having mastered the sciences and arts of the brahmins, [he renounced] sensual pleasures...
376:
...renouncing sensual pleasures, he ordained as an ascetic. While living in the forest surrounded by a large group of ascetics, he heard that a Buddha had arisen. Filled with joy, he thought, "Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are rare to see, like the flowering of an udumbara tree; I must approach him now." While traveling with a large retinue to see the Buddha, when only one and a half leagues (yojanas) remained, he was afflicted by disease. Passing away with a perception focused on the Buddha, he was reborn in the deva realm. After wandering repeatedly through the realms of devas and humans, he was born as the younger brother of King Dhammāsoka, 218 years after the Buddha's Parinibbāna. He was named Vītāsoka.

When Vītāsoka reached maturity, he mastered the arts and sciences that princes must learn. Relying on the Elder Giridatta, even as a layman, he became proficient and confident in the Suttanta Piṭaka and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka. One day, while having his beard trimmed, he took a mirror from the barber's hand and looked at his body. Seeing wrinkles and grey hair, he was struck by spiritual urgency (saṃvega). Directing his mind toward insight (vipassanā) and exerting himself in meditation, he became a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna) right there in his seat. Then, he ordained in the presence of the Elder Giridatta and soon attained Arahantship. This matter is stated in the Apadāna:

"I was a reciter of the mantras, a bearer of the mantras, one who had reached the end of the three Vedas. I was also proficient in the knowledge of marks (lakkhana), history (itihāsa), the lexicon (nighaṇḍu), and the ritual (keṭubha).

At that time, students came to me like the flow of a river. I taught the mantras to those students day and night without weariness.

At that time, the Buddha named Siddhattha arose in the world. Having destroyed the darkness, he set in motion the light of knowledge.

One of my students spoke to the other students, and having heard that matter, they then came and informed me.

'The All-knowing Buddha, the Leader of the World, has arisen in the world. The people follow that Buddha; we no longer have any gain.'

'Buddhas, the Visionary Ones of great fame, arise according to causes. It would be good if I could see the Supreme Buddha, the Leader of the World.'"
377: I took the antelope skin, the bark garment, and the water pot, and having departed from the hermitage, I addressed my disciples: "Like the flower of the Udumbara, like the rabbit-mark on the moon, like milk for crows, a Leader of the World is very difficult to find. A Buddha has arisen in the world; human birth is also difficult to obtain. Even when both are present, hearing the Dhamma is extremely rare. A Buddha has arisen in the world; we shall obtain the eye (of Dhamma). Come, let us all go to the presence of the Fully Enlightened One." Then, all those carrying water pots, wearing antelope skins, and bearing the weight of matted hair, departed from the forest. Looking only a yoke's length ahead, seeking the supreme goal, free from the fault of attachment, they came like fearless lions. With few duties, not restless, prudent and of peaceful conduct, living by gathering fruits and roots, they approached the Best of Buddhas. When only one and a half leagues remained, a disease arose in me. Remembering the Best of Buddhas, I passed away there. In the ninety-four aeons since I obtained that perception (of the Buddha), I have not known a miserable rebirth. This is the fruit of perceiving the Buddha. My defilements are burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out. Having attained Arahantship, wishing to declare his attainment, he spoke these two verses: "A barber approached to shave my hair. Then, taking a mirror, I reflected upon my body. The body appeared empty; the darkness within the mass of gloom vanished. All bonds (defilements) are severed; now there is no more rebirth."
378:
In that verse, 'The barber approached, saying "I will shave my hair"' means that during his time as a layman, at the time of grooming his beard, the barber (nhāpita) approached him, being called 'kappaka' because he prepares (kappeti) the hair and the like by way of cutting and so on, thinking 'I will prepare my hair.' 'From that' means from that barber. 'Reflected on the body' means that by seeing the signs of the face such as graying hair and wrinkles in a mirror that shows the whole body, he reflected on his own body overcome by old age, thinking 'Alas, my body is overcome by old age!'

To me who was reflecting thus, the body appeared as hollow. My body was seen by wisdom as being empty of the nature of permanence, stability, and happiness. Why? Because the darkness in the gloom had disappeared. Because of the darkness called unwise reflection (ayoniso manasikāra), people are like the blind regarding their own bodies; they do not see the existing nature of foulness (asubha) and the like, but grasp the non-existing aspect of beauty (subha) and the like. In that body which causes blindness, the darkness of ignorance (avijjā) has disappeared through the light of knowledge called wise reflection (yoniso manasikāra). For that very reason, the defilements called 'cola' (rags) have been completely cut off, because like thieves they plunder and destroy the treasure of merit, because they are not to be taken or kept by the virtuous, and because they are to be loathed by the noble and powerful like a piece of rag discarded on a rubbish heap. Because they have been well uprooted by the topmost path, there is no more rebirth for these defilements now or in the future.

## The commentary on the verses of the Elder Vītasoka is finished.

## 6. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Puṇṇamāsa

The verses beginning with 'Having abandoned the five hindrances' are those of the Venerable Elder Puṇṇamāsa. As for the origin—this venerable one also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit in various lives. He was born into a respectable family in the time of the Blessed One Tissa. Having reached the age of discretion, one day, while the Teacher was dwelling in the forest, the Teacher hung his rag-robe (paṃsukūla) on a tree branch and entered the perfumed chamber (gandhakuṭī). At that time, this man, entering the thicket with a bow in hand, saw the Teacher's rag-robe and, with a heart full of faith, put down his bow and [recollected] the qualities of the Buddha...
379:
(He) remembered the rag-robe and paid homage to it. Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, and in this Buddha-era, he was reborn in a householder's family in Sāvatthī. It is said that on the day of his birth, all the vessels in that house were filled with gold coins. Therefore, they named the boy Punnamāsa. When he reached adulthood, he married, and after a son was born, he abandoned the household life and ordained. Living in a village monastery, through striving and effort, he became an Arahant endowed with the six higher powers. This is stated in the Apadāna:

"There was a Blessed One named Tissa, the Self-become, the Supreme Person. Having placed a rag-robe (on a tree), the Victor entered the monastery.
I was wandering in search of food, carrying a bent bow. Taking a sword, I entered the forest.
There I saw a rag-robe hanging on the top of a tree. Right there, I laid down my bow and, raising my joined palms to my head,
With a confident mind, a joyful heart, and with abundant rapture, I remembered the Buddha, the Best, and paid homage to the rag-robe.
Ninety-two aeons ago, I paid homage to that rag-robe; since then, I have not known a miserable rebirth. This is the fruit of that homage.
My defilements are burned away... (etc.) ... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out."

Having become an Arahant with the six higher powers, he went to Sāvatthī, paid homage to the Teacher, and lived in a cemetery. Not long after his arrival, his son passed away. Hearing of the Elder's arrival, the child's mother thought, "The kings will take away this heirless property," and wishing for the Elder to disrobe, she went to him with a large retinue, exchanged greetings, and began to entice him. To make known his state of being free from passion, the Elder stood in the air and, by way of praising his own practice, preached the Dhamma to her:

"Having abandoned the five hindrances, for the attainment of security from bondage, taking the mirror of Dhamma, one's own knowledge and vision..."
380:
"I reflected on this body, all of it, inside and out; both internally and externally, this body was seen to be empty." He spoke these two verses.

In those verses, "having abandoned the five hindrances" means having given up the five hindrances such as sensual desire and destroying them through the attainment of jhāna. "For the attainment of security from bondage" means for the attainment of Nibbāna, which is secure and unassailed by the four bondages such as the bondage of sensuality. "Mirror of Dhamma" means the mirror that is the Dhamma. Just as a mirror shows the presence or absence of flaws in the physical body of the one looking, so too the mirror of Dhamma, which is the knowledge and vision of insight (vipassanā) because it enables the understanding of the common and specific characteristics of phenomena, shows the qualities especially in the mental body (nāmakāya) to the one practicing insight by revealing pure and defiled states and by being the means to abandon those defilements. Therefore, he said:

"Taking the mirror of Dhamma, one's own knowledge and vision,
I reflected on this body, all of it, inside and out."

"This body" means my own individual existence (attabhāva), which is a collection of phenomena. Because of its nature as internal and external bases, I reflected on the entire body, inside and out, without exception, taking the mirror of Dhamma, and saw it with the eye of wisdom as "impermanent," "suffering," and "non-self." To me seeing thus, "both internally and externally," in my own continuity and in the continuity of others, the body was seen to be empty—the individual body consisting of the five aggregates was seen as it really is with the eye of wisdom to be empty, devoid of any permanent essence. Indeed, the entire five aggregates are called "body" (kāya) in such passages from the Saṃyutta Nikāya as: "Bhikkhus, for the fool obstructed by ignorance and fettered by craving, this body has thus been produced." By the word "was seen" (adissatha), he declared his attainment of Arahantship, showing that he has completed his task, saying, "What was to be seen in the body has been seen; there is nothing further for me to see now." Thus, the Elder preached the Dhamma to his former wife with these verses, established her in the refuges and the precepts, and sent her away.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Punnamāsa is finished.
381:
## 7. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Nandaka

"Just as a noble thoroughbred" is the verse of the Venerable Elder Nandaka. What is the origin of this verse? This elder, too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit in various existences, was born in a border region during the time of the Buddha Sikhī. Upon reaching maturity, he lived as a hunter wandering in the forest. One day, seeing the walking path (caṅkama) of the Blessed One, he felt a heart of devotion and scattered sand as an offering. Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, and in this Buddha-dispensation, he was reborn into a householder's family in the city of Campā. They gave him the name Nandaka. His elder brother was named Bharata. His brother's previous deeds (pubbayoga) will be made clear in the subsequent story.

When the two brothers reached maturity and became wise, they heard that the Venerable Soṇa Koḷivisa had ordained. They thought, "If even the youth Soṇa, who is so delicate and tender, has ordained, what then of us?" and so they both ordained. Among the two brothers, Bharata soon developed insight (vipassanā) and became an Arahant endowed with the six supernormal powers (chaḷabhiññā). Nandaka, however, due to the strength of his defilements, was not yet able to exert himself in insight, but merely continued the practice of insight meditation. Then, Elder Bharata, knowing his younger brother's inclination and wishing to be a support to him, took him as his attendant monk (pacchāsamaṇa), left the monastery, and sat down near a road to give him a discourse on insight.

At that time, while a caravan of carts was passing by, an ox yoked to a cart fell down in a muddy place, unable to pull the cart out. Then the caravan leader unyoked the ox from the cart, gave it grass and water, and after its fatigue had subsided, yoked it to the front of the cart again. Then the ox, its fatigue having ceased and its strength regained, pulled the cart out of the mud and placed it on firm ground. Then Elder Bharata pointed this out to Nandaka, saying, "Friend Nandaka, do you see the action of this ox?" When Nandaka replied, "I see it," the Elder said, "Reflect well on this meaning."

Nandaka thought, "Just as this ox, having recovered from fatigue, pulled the load out of the mud, so too should I pull myself out of the mud of saṃsāra." Taking that very object as his basis and practicing insight, he attained Arahantship before long. This is stated in the Apadāna:

In a previous life, I was a hunter seeking deer in the forest.
I saw the walking path of the Buddha Sikhī in the forest.
Taking sand in my garment-fold, I scattered it on the walking path of the glorious Buddha Sikhī with a heart of devotion and joy.
Thirty-one aeons ago, I scattered that sand; because of that deed, I have never known a woeful state. This is the fruit of offering sand.
My defilements are burnt away; I have followed the teaching of the Buddha.
382:
In a previous life, I was a hunter seeking the 'wind-deer' (vātamiḡa) in the forest; while searching, I saw the walking path (caṅkama).

With a heart of devotion and joy, I took sand in my garment-fold and scattered it as an offering on the walking path of the glorious Buddha Sikhī.

Thirty-one aeons ago, I scattered that sand; by the fruit of that meritorious deed, I have never known (never reached) a woeful state. This is the fruit of offering sand.

My defilements are burnt away... (pe)... I have followed and practiced the instruction of the Buddha.

After attaining Arahantship, wishing to declare his attainment in the presence of his elder brother, Elder Bharata, he recited these two verses:

"Just as a noble thoroughbred, having stumbled, stands firm again, and gaining further urgency (saṃvega), bears the burden without shrinking.

So do you regard me as a thoroughbred, a disciple of the Fully Enlightened One, a true-born son of the Buddha, endowed with vision."

In those verses, "bhijjo laddhāna saṃvegaṃ adīno vahate dhuraṃ" means: Gaining urgency by thinking, "It is not suitable for my birth, strength, and energy to not bear the burden that has come upon me," he bears or carries his burden repeatedly and excessively with an undepressed mind (adīnamānasa, alīnacitta). There is also a reading "alīno," which has the same meaning. The remaining words are just as explained in the commentary on the verses of Elder Ramaṇီyavihārī below.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Nandaka is finished.

The verses of the Venerable Elder Bharata begin with "Come, Nandaka" (Ehi Nandaka). This elder, too, was born into a family during the time of the Buddha Sikhī, and upon reaching maturity and becoming wise, one day, having a pleasing appearance...
383:
## 8. Bharatattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

"Come, Nandaka, let us go"—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Bharata. What is the occasion for its arising? It is said that this elder was born into a respectable family during the time of the Blessed One Anomadassī. Having reached the age of discretion, one day, while carrying a pair of sandals that were pleasing to the sight and soft to the touch, he saw the Teacher walking on the ambulatory. With a mind full of faith, he offered the sandals and said, "Venerable Sir, please wear these sandals. May wearing them lead to my welfare and happiness for a long time." To show favor to that young man, the Blessed One wore the sandals. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered among devas and humans, and in the time of our Buddha's arising, he was born into a householder's family in the city of Campā and was named Bharata. When he reached maturity, he heard that the Venerable Elder Soṇa had gone forth and, moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega), thinking, "Even that Soṇa has gone forth," he himself went forth. Having performed the preliminary duties and practicing insight meditation (vipassanā), he soon became an Arahant endowed with the six supernormal knowledges. This is stated in the Apadāna:

"The Blessed One Anomadassī, the Eldest in the World, the Bull among Men, having emerged from the day-rest, the One with Vision ascended the ambulatory.

Taking well-made sandals, as I was traveling on a long journey, I saw the Fully Enlightened One, the Anomadassī Buddha, walking on foot, beautiful to behold.

Having inspired faith in my own mind, I took out the sandals, placed them at his feet, and spoke these words:

'O Great Hero, O One of Happy Destination, O Leader, please wear them. Through this gift of sandals, I wish to obtain a good result; may that purpose of mine be fulfilled.'

The Blessed One Anomadassī, the Eldest in the World, the Bull among Men, having put on the sandals, spoke these words:

'He who, with a faithful heart, gave me these sandals with his own hands—I shall praise him; listen to my words.

Having understood the voice of the Buddha, all the devas assembled, with uplifted minds, joyful, filled with rapture, and with hands joined in reverence.'"
384:
"Through the gift of sandals, this person will reach happiness; he will rule as the king of devas for fifty-five times.

He will be a Cakkavatti (Universal Monarch) a thousand times, and as for the position of a regional king, it will be vast and beyond counting.

In an incalculable aeon from now, a Teacher named Gotama by clan, born of the Okkāka dynasty, will arise in the world.

He will be an heir to the Dhamma of that Blessed One, a legitimate son created by the Dhamma; having fully understood all taints (āsavas), he will attain Nibbāna, free from taints.

That meritorious person will be born in the deva realm or the human realm; he will obtain a vehicle comparable to the vehicles of the devas.

Palaces, palanquins, vehicles, well-adorned elephants, and chariots yoked with noble horses always appear for me.

Even when I left the household life for the forest, I departed by chariot; while my hair was being shaved, I attained Arahantship.

Gains have been well-obtained by me; my commerce has been well-applied. By giving a single pair of sandals, I have reached the unshakable state (Nibbāna).

In an incalculable aeon from now, I gave those sandals; because of that merit, I have never known a miserable rebirth (duggati). This is the fruit of the gift of sandals.

My defilements are burnt away... the instruction of the Buddha has been carried out."

Then, the elder, endowed with the six supernormal knowledges, after his younger brother, the Elder Nandaka, had declared his attainment of Arahantship as mentioned below, thought: "Now Nandaka too has become an Arahant. Come, let us both go to the presence of the Teacher and report our completion of the holy life." While speaking to the Elder Nandaka, he said:

"Come, Nandaka, let us go to the presence of the Preceptor; let us roar the lion's roar in the presence of the Excellent Buddha."
385:
"Out of compassion for us, the Sage made us go forth; that goal of ours has been attained, the destruction of all fetters." He recited these two verses.

In those verses, "Nandaka" is an address. "Ehi" (Come) means bringing him to his presence. "Gacchāma" (Let us go) is a word expressing the action of going together by the two of them. "Upajjhāyassa" means to the presence of the Fully Enlightened One. Indeed, the Fully Enlightened One, with his All-seeing Eye and Buddha-eye, sees the inclinations, underlying tendencies, and conduct of beings as they truly are. Because he closely observes the faults and merits of the world including the devas, he especially deserves to be called "Upajjhāya" (Preceptor). To show the purpose of going, he said, "We will roar the lion's roar in the presence of the Best of Buddhas." Because it is a fearless sound made by declaring true qualities, it is called a "lion's roar" (sīhanāda). It means we will roar in the presence of the Buddha, who is the best among all beings because he is the Fully Enlightened One, or the best among the Buddhas such as the Disciple-Buddhas (Sāvaka-buddhas).

To show the manner in which he wished to roar the lion's roar, he spoke the verse beginning with "Yāya." In that verse, "Yāya" means for the sake of that goal, by the attainment of the goal of the fruit of Arahantship and Nibbāna. "No" means our (or us). "Anukampāya" means having favored us, he made us two brothers go forth. "Muni" is the Blessed One. "So no attho anuppatto" means that goal, which is the fruit of Arahantship—the destruction of all fetters—has been attained and realized by us.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Bharata Thera is finished.

## 9. The Commentary on the Verses of Bhāradvāja Thera

"Thus do the wise roar," and so on. This is the verse of the Venerable Bhāradvāja Thera. What is its origin? This elder also had made an aspiration under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merits in various existences. Thirty-one aeons ago, he was born in a family home. When he reached the age of discretion, one day he saw a Paccekabuddha named Sumana wandering for alms.
386:
With a clear mind, he offered a well-ripened vallikāra fruit. Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans. In this Buddha's era, he was born into a Brahmin family in the city of Rājagaha and became known by his clan name, Bhāradvāja. When he reached adulthood and was living the household life, he had a son. He named the son "Kaṇhadinna." When the son reached the age of discretion and became wise, he sent him to the city of Takkasilā, saying, "Dear son, go and learn the arts in the presence of such-and-such a teacher and then return."

While traveling on the way, Kaṇhadinna met a certain Great Elder who was a disciple of the Buddha and a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitta). Having heard the Dhamma from him, he gained faith and went forth. Having performed the preliminary duties and practicing the work of insight (vipassanā), he attained Arahantship before long. This is stated in the Apadāna:

"A Buddha named Sumana lived then in the city of Takkarā.
Taking a vallikāra fruit, I offered it to the Self-Existent One.
Thirty-one aeons ago, I gave that fruit.
Since then, I have not known a bad rebirth; this is the result of the gift of fruit.
My defilements are burnt away... (etc.) ... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out."

Later, his father Bhāradvāja approached the Blessed One who was staying at the Veḷuvana monastery. After hearing the Dhamma, he went forth and soon realized the fruit of Arahantship. Then the son, coming to Rājagaha to pay homage to the Buddha, saw his father sitting in the presence of the Buddha. With a joyful heart, he thought, "My father too has gone forth. Has he reached the pinnacle of the monk's task?" Wishing to investigate and knowing his father's state as one whose taints are destroyed, he wanted to make him roar the lion's roar. So he asked, "Venerable sir, it is good that you have gone forth. Have you reached the pinnacle of the monk's task?" Bhāradvāja Thera, wishing to show his son the attainment of the Path and Fruit he had achieved, recited these two verses:

"The wise roar thus, like lions in a mountain cave;
The heroes who have won the battle, having conquered Māra and his host.
The Teacher has been served by me, the Dhamma and Saṅgha have been honored.
I am joyful and happy, seeing my son free from taints."

In those verses, "Nadanti" means they utter a fearless sound by declaring true qualities. The word "Evaṃ" (thus) shows the manner of the words spoken now. "Sappaññā" (the wise) refers to those who have reached the fullness of wisdom by attaining the wisdom of the Path of Arahantship. "Vīrā" (heroes) are so called because they are endowed with the four right efforts (sammappadhāna). For that very reason, they are those who possess the wisdom of the Path of Arahantship, having won the battle by conquering Kilesa-māra, Abhisaṅkhāra-māra, and Devaputta-māra, known as "savāhana" (with his host), because they have crushed the entire army of defilements.
387:
In that verse, 'nadanti' means they utter a fearless sound, they roar, by virtue of proclaiming qualities as they truly are. 'Evaṃ' is used here to show the manner of speaking. 'Sappaññā' refers to those who have reached the fullness of all wisdom through the attainment of the wisdom of the highest path (Arahatta-magga). 'Vīrā' means they are called heroes because they are endowed with the fourfold right effort (sammappadhāna). Because of that very energy, by crushing the entire mass of defilements and conquering the Mara of defilements (Kilesamāra) together with his army, the Mara of conditioned formations (Abhisaṅkhāramāra), and the Mara as a deity (Devaputtamāra), the wise who have completely conquered the battle roar—this is how it is connected.

Having thus shown the lion's roar (sīhanāda) through the victory over what should be conquered, he now spoke the second verse beginning with 'Satthā ca pariciṇṇo me' to show that through the proper service to the teacher who should be served and the fulfillment of the desired benefit. In that verse, 'Satthā ca pariciṇṇo me' means "My teacher, the Fully Enlightened One, has been served and attended to by me through following his advice (ovāda) and instructions (anusāsanī) as taught; I have not acted contrary to the Dhamma"—this is the meaning. 'Dhammo saṅgho ca pူjito' means "I have honored and revered the ninefold supramundane Dhamma, and the Noble Saṅgha who have reached the path in due order according to the practice and who have attained equality in virtue (sīla) and view (diṭṭhi)." "And I am glad and happy to see my son free from taints (anāsava)" means "Seeing my son as one who is taintless, whose taints are entirely exhausted, I am glad and satisfied with unworldly joy (nirāmisa pīti) because of that sight; for that very reason, I have become happy with unworldly pleasantness (nirāmisa somanassa)."

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Bharadvāja is finished.

## 10. Kaṇhadinnattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

The verses beginning with 'Upāsitā sappurisā' are those of the Venerable Kaṇhadinna Thera. What is the background story? This elder also had made an aspiration under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merits in various births. Ninety-four aeons ago, he was born into a good family. Upon reaching maturity, one day he saw a Paccekabuddha named Sobhita and, with a clear mind, made an offering of Punnāga flowers. Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans. In this Buddha's era, he was born into a Brahmin family in Rājagaha and received the name Kaṇhadinna. When he came of age, being urged by the perfection of his supporting conditions (upanissaya-sampatti), he approached the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, and having heard the Dhamma, he gained faith. That Kaṇhadinna approached the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, and the Dhamma...
388:
...approached (Venerable Sāriputta), heard the Dhamma, gained faith, ordained, developed insight (vipassanā), and attained Arahatship. This is stated in the Apadāna:
"The Buddha named Sobhita was then living at Cittakūṭa. Taking a mountain Punnāga flower, I specially honored the Self-Enlightened One. In the ninety-fourth aeon ago, the Buddha I honored—due to that fruit of honoring the Buddha, I do not know of any miserable rebirth (duggati). This is the fruit of honoring the Buddha. My defilements have been burnt away... (and so on) ...the Buddha's teaching has been carried out."
After attaining Arahatship, while declaring his attainment, he spoke these two verses:
"Good men have been served, the Dhamma has been heard repeatedly. Having heard it, I have entered the path that plunges into the Deathless. For me who was smitten by lust for existence, lust for existence no longer exists for me. It was not in the past, it will not be for me in the future, and it does not exist for me now."

In that verse, 'upāsitā' means served or attended to through the service of practice. 'Sappurisā' refers to the noble persons (ariya-puggala) such as the Elder Sāriputta and others who are endowed with good qualities like virtue (sīla). By this, he shows his own fulfillment of the first two wheels (cakka). Indeed, without living in a suitable locality (patirūpadesavāsa), reliance on good men (sappurisūpanissaya) is not possible. 'Sutā dhammā' means the teachings connected with the Truths (sacca), dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), etc., which were grasped through the sense of hearing. By this, showing his own great learning (bāhusacca), he shows the fulfillment of the latter two wheels. 'Abhiṇhaso' means frequently, not just from time to time. This word should also be connected with 'upāsitā sappurisā'. 'Sutvāna paṭipajjissaṃ, aññasaṃ amatogadhaṃ' means having heard those teachings, having grasped the mental and physical phenomena (nāmarūpa-dhamma) mentioned therein by way of their characteristics etc., and gradually developing insight, I have entered or reached the Noble Eightfold Path, which is the straight way leading to and established in Nibbāna, the Deathless. 'Bhavarāgahatassa me sato' means for me who was smitten by the craving for existence (bhavataṇhā) in the beginningless saṃsāra. Or it means for me who has destroyed the lust for existence with the path of Arahatship. 'Bhavarāgo puna me na vijjati' means therefore, lust for existence no longer exists for me now. 'Na cāhu na ca me bhavissati na ca me etarahi vijjati' means although lust for existence occurred to me in the past as a worldling (puthujjana) and as a trainee (sekha), since the time I attained the path of Arahatship, it has not occurred, it will not occur in the future, and it does not exist or is not found now. Why is it not found? Because...
389:
"Bhavarāgahatassa me sato" means when I was being oppressed by the craving for existence in the beginningless saṃsāra; or it means when I was one whose lust for existence had been destroyed by the Path of Arahantship. "Bhavarāgo puna me na vijjati" means for that very reason, lust for existence no longer exists for me now. "Na cāhu na me bhavissati, na ca me etarahi vijjati" means although lust for existence had occurred to me in the past during the stages of a worldling (puthujjana) and a trainee (sekha), since reaching the Path of Arahantship, it has not occurred, nor will it occur to me in the future, nor does it exist or can it be found now; the meaning is that it has been abandoned. In this verse, by the words "lust for existence" alone, the absence of conceit and so forth is also stated because they share the same basis, thus showing the state of having all fetters of existence completely exhausted.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Kaṇhadinna is Finished.

## The Commentary on the Third Group is Finished.

## 4. The Fourth Group

## 1. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Migasira

"Yato ahaṃ pabbajito" and so forth is the verse of the Venerable Migasira. What is its origin? This Elder also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and was accumulating merit in various lives. During the time of Kassapa Buddha, he was born into a Brahmin family. Upon reaching maturity, one day he saw the Blessed One and, with a devoted mind, offered eight handfuls of grass. Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans. In this Buddha-era, he took rebirth in a Brahmin family in the Kingdom of Kosala and was named Migasira because he was born under the Migasira constellation.

When he reached maturity, he attained mastery in the sciences and arts of the Brahmins and learned the mantra called Chavasīsamanta (the skull-spell). By reciting this mantra, he could tap the skull of those who had been dead for even three years with his fingernail and know, "This being is reborn in such and such a place." Not desiring the household life, he went forth as a wandering ascetic (paribbājaka). Relying on that skill, he was honored and respected by the world, and traveling with abundant gains and offerings, he arrived at Sāvatthī...
390:
That Migasira went to the presence of the Blessed One and, wishing to demonstrate his own power, said, "O Gotama, I know the place of rebirth of those who have died." When asked, "How do you know?" he replied, "By having the skulls of the dead brought to me, reciting a mantra, and tapping the skull with my fingernail, I know their place of rebirth, such as hell and so forth." Then the Blessed One had the skull of a monk who had attained Parinibbāna brought and said, "First, tell the destination (gati) of the owner of this skull." That wanderer recited the mantra and tapped the skull with his fingernail, but he could see neither the beginning nor the end.

Then the Blessed One said, "O wanderer, are you unable?" He replied, "I will investigate further first," and although he turned it over and over, he still could not see. How could he know the destination of an Arahant through an external mantra? Then sweat poured from his forehead and armpits. Feeling ashamed, he stood in silence. The Blessed One asked, "Wanderer, are you weary?" He replied, "Yes, Bhante, I am weary. I do not know the destination of this person. Do you know it?" "I know his destination, and I know even far beyond this," the Blessed One said, and added, "This person has reached Nibbāna."

The wanderer said, "Please grant this knowledge to me." The Blessed One said, "In that case, go forth (ordain)," and after ordaining him, He first directed him in the meditation subject of tranquillity (samatha). When he was established in the jhānas and direct knowledges (abhiññā), the Buddha instructed him in the practice of insight (vipassanā). While performing the work of insight, that Elder Migasira attained the fruit of Arahantship before long. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

"To the Blessed Kassapa, the Brahmin who had reached the end of his task, with a devoted and joyful mind, I offered eight handfuls of grass.

In this very eon, because of that meritorious deed of offering eight handfuls of grass, I have not known a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of offering eight handfuls of grass.

My defilements are burned away... etc... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out."

Having reached the fruit of Arahantship, and wishing to declare his attainment:

"Since I went forth in the teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened One, being liberated (through the power of tranquillity and insight), I have ascended and transcended the realm of sensuality (kāmadhātu)."
391:
"While the Great One was looking on, then my mind was liberated. My liberation is unshakable due to the destruction of all fetters." — He spoke these two verses.

In those verses, "Yato ahaṃ pabbajito sammāsambuddhasāsane" means from the time I went forth in the teaching of the Buddha, the Blessed One; starting from the time of going forth. "Vimuccamāno uggacchiṃ" means first being liberated from the side of defilements through tranquillity and insight, I arose by hearing the pure Dhamma. Thus ascending, "kāmadhātuṃ upaccagaṃ" means I completely transcended the realm of sensuality through the Path of Non-returning (anāgāmimagga).

"Brahmuno pekkhamānassa, tato cittaṃ vimucci me" means while the Buddha, the Blessed One—who is called 'Brahma' in the sense of being the most excellent as the head of the world including the devas—was looking on with great compassion, thinking, "How does this son of good family practice after going forth in my teaching?", after the attainment of the Path of Non-returning, my mind was completely liberated from all defilements through the attainment of the Highest Path (Arahantship). "Akuppā me vimuttīti, sabbasaṃyojanakkhayā" means because of having such a liberated mind and due to the destruction and complete exhaustion of all fetters, he declared his attainment of Arahantship, saying, "My liberation is unshakable."

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Migasira is Finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Sivaka

"Aniccāni gahakānīti" and so forth is the verse of the Venerable Sivaka. As for the origin: This Elder also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and was accumulating merit in various lives. During the time of Vipassī Buddha, he was born into a noble family. Upon reaching the age of discretion, one day he saw the Blessed One wandering for alms and, with a devoted mind, took the bowl, filled it with barley cakes, and offered them. Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans. In this Buddha-era, he was born into a Brahmin family in the city of Rājagaha and was named Sivaka. When that youth Sivaka reached maturity, in the arts and sciences...
392:
When that youth Sivaka reached maturity, he attained mastery in the arts. Having an inclination toward renunciation, he abandoned sensual pleasures and wandered as a paribbājaka (wandering ascetic). While wandering, he approached the Teacher, heard the Dhamma, and having gained faith, he ordained. While practicing Vipassanā meditation, he attained Arahatship before long. Regarding this, it is stated in the Apadāna: 'While the Great Sage Vipassī was wandering for alms, seeing his empty bowl, I filled it with a lump of cake and offered it. Because of that alms-offering ninety-one aeons ago, I have not known a woeful state; this is the fruit of the offering of a lump of cake. My defilements have been burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.'

Upon reaching Arahatship, wishing to declare his attainment, he recited these two verses: 'Unstable are the houses [built] again and again in various births; as long as I was searching for the house-builder, birth again and again was painful. O house-builder, you are seen! You shall not build the house again. All your rafters are broken, and the ridge-pole is shattered. My mind has reached the unconditioned; in this very life, defilements will be extinguished.'

In those verses, 'Unstable are the houses again and again in various births' means that the houses of individual existence (attabhāva), which arise repeatedly in various lives, are not permanent, not stable, and exist only for a brief and short duration. 'Searching for the house-builder' means wandering through Saṃsāra for this long a time seeking the carpenter of craving (taṇhā) who builds this house of individual existence. The phrase 'Birth again and again is painful' states the reason for searching for the house-builder. Because birth is mixed with aging, sickness, and death, reaching it again and again is truly painful; and as long as that house-builder is not seen, birth does not cease. Therefore, it means he wandered searching for that craving.
393:
'O house-builder, you are seen' means that now he has been seen with the eye of the Knowledge of the Noble Path (ariya-magga-ñāṇa), by which that craving can be seen. 'You shall not build the house again' means that you shall not and cannot again build my house, which is called individual existence (attabhāva), in this round of rebirths (saṃsāra-vaṭṭa). 'All your rafters are broken' means that all your rafters, which are the defilements (kilesa) without exception, have been broken by me. 'The ridge-pole of the house is also shattered' means that now the ridge-pole of the house of individual existence built by you, which is ignorance (avijjā), has also been destroyed. 'The mind has reached the unconditioned' means that my mind has been made to reach the state beyond boundaries, and has been made to attain the nature of non-arising in the future. Therefore, 'it will be destroyed in this very life' means it will be demolished in this very existence; it will cease with the cessation of the final consciousness.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Sivaka Thera is finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Verses of Upavāṇa Thera

The verse beginning with 'Arahaṃ sugato' is that of the Venerable Upavāṇa Thera. What is its origin? This Venerable Upavāṇa was born into a poor family during the time of Buddha Padumuttara and became wise upon reaching maturity. When the Buddha passed into Parinibbāna, taking the relics of that Buddha, humans, devas, nāgas, garuḍas, kumbhaṇḍas, yakkhas, and gandhabbas built a seven-yojana-high stupa made of the seven kinds of jewels. At that stupa, he tied his well-washed upper robe to the tip of a bamboo pole, made it a banner, and offered it in worship. A Yakkha general named Abhisammata, who was appointed by the devas to worship and protect the stupa, held that banner invisibly in the sky and circumambulated the stupa three times to the right in worship. Seeing that event, he felt exceedingly great devotion. Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans, and in this Buddha-era, he was born into a Brahmin family in Sāvatthī and was named Upavāṇa. When he reached maturity, on the day the Jetavana Monastery was accepted, he saw the Buddha's power, gained faith, and ordained. While practicing Vipassanā, he attained Arahatship and became one possessed of the six supernormal powers (chaḷabhiññā). Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

The Conqueror named Padumuttara, who reached the end of all Dhammas,
Shining like a great mass of fire, the Fully Enlightened One passed into Parinibbāna.
394:
The great multitude gathered and, having honored the Tathāgata, prepared a well-fashioned funeral pyre and placed the body upon it.

After performing the funeral rites, they brought the relics to that shrine. All those devas and humans built a Buddha-stupa.

The first terrace was made of gold. The second terrace was also made of rubies. The third terrace was made of silver. The fourth terrace was made of crystal.

Furthermore, the fifth terrace was made of lohitaṅka gems. The sixth terrace was made of masāragalla stone. The entire upper portion was made of the seven kinds of gems.

The base was made of rubies, and the railing was made of gems. The stupa, entirely made of gold, rose one league high into the sky.

Then the devas gathered at that shrine and consulted together: "We too shall build a stupa for the Lord of the World, the Steadfast One."

"The relics are not divided; the body is a single mass. We shall build a casing over this Buddha-stupa built by humans," they consulted.

With the seven kinds of gems, the devas increased it by another league. The stupa became two leagues in height and dispelled the darkness.

Then the nāgas gathered at the site of the stupa and consulted together: "Humans and devas have already built a stupa for the Buddha."

"May we not be heedless; the devas and humans are heedful. We too shall build a stupa for the Lord of the World, the Steadfast One," they consulted.

Collecting indanīla, mahānīla, and the rubies called jotirasa together, they covered the Buddha-stupa.

The Buddha-shrine became entirely made of gems; at that time, it was three leagues in height and produced light.

The garuḍas also gathered and consulted together: "Humans, devas, and nāgas have performed offerings to the Buddha."
395:
"May we not be heedless; the devas and humans are heedful. We too shall build a stupa for the Lord of the World, the Steadfast One."

Those garuḍas made a stupa entirely of gems and also a casing. They also increased the tall Buddha-shrine by one league.

The Buddha-stupa shone, being four leagues in height. Like the newly risen sun, it illuminated all directions.

Then the kumbhaṇḍas gathered and consulted together. Humans, devas, nāgas, and likewise garuḍas (had already consulted).

They each built an excellent stupa for the Most Excellent Buddha. "May we not be heedless; the devas and humans are heedful."

"We too shall build a stupa for the Lord of the World, the Steadfast One. We shall cover the tall Buddha-shrine with gems."

They also increased the tall Buddha-shrine by one league. At that time, the stupa shone, being five leagues in height.

Then the yakkhas gathered at that stupa and consulted together. Humans, devas, nāgas, garuḍas, and kumbhaṇḍas (had already consulted).

They each built an excellent stupa for the Most Excellent Buddha. "May we not be heedless; the devas and humans are heedful."

"We too shall build a stupa for the Lord of the World, the Steadfast One. We shall cover the tall Buddha-shrine with crystal."

They also increased the tall Buddha-shrine by one league. At that time, the stupa shone, being six leagues in height.

Then the gandhabbas gathered and consulted together. Humans, devas, nāgas, kumbhaṇḍas, and likewise garuḍas (had already consulted).

"All have built a Buddha-stupa; we are the only ones here who have not yet done so. We too shall build a stupa for the Lord of the World, the Steadfast One."
396:
The gandhabbas made seven levels of railings and offered banners and umbrellas. At that time, the gandhabbas built a stupa entirely of gold.

Then the stupa, seven leagues in height, shone brilliantly. Day and night were no longer distinguished; there was light at all times.

The light of the moon, sun, and stars could not overcome its radiance. Within a hundred leagues around, there was no need even to light a lamp.

At that time, all the people honored the stupa. Those people did not climb the stupa but threw their offerings into the air to honor it.

A yakkha named Abhisammata, appointed by the devas, placed the banners or flower garlands on top of the stupa.

Those people did not see the yakkha; they only saw the flower garlands and wreaths moving. All those who went along seeing this went to a happy destination.

Both those who were opposed to the Dhamma taught by the Buddha and those who were devoted to the Dispensation honored the stupa, wishing to see the miracles.

At that time, I was a laborer in the city of Haṃsavatī. Seeing the people rejoicing, I then thought:

"This Blessed One is indeed noble; in the relic-house of this Blessed One, these people, though rejoicing and performing meritorious deeds, are never satisfied."

"I too will perform a meritorious deed for the stupa of the Lord of the World, the Steadfast One. In the future, may I be an heir to the teachings of that Blessed One," I thought.

I made a banner out of my upper robe, which had been well-washed by a laundryman, attached it to the tip of a bamboo pole, and raised it into the air.

The yakkha named Abhisammata took my banner and carried it through the air. Seeing the banner fluttering in the wind, I became exceedingly joyful.

Having gained faith in that offering of a banner, I approached a monk. Having paid homage to that bhikkhu, I asked about the result of offering a banner.
397:
That monk preached a Dhamma talk to me that caused joy and delight. "You shall enjoy the fruit of that banner-offering at all times," (he said).

"The fourfold army of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry shall always surround you. This is the fruit of the banner-offering."

"Sixty thousand musical instruments and well-decorated drums shall always surround you. This is the fruit of the banner-offering."

"Eighty-six thousand women, well-adorned, wearing exquisite clothes and ornaments, wearing jeweled earrings,"

"With wide eyelashes, smiling faces, good perception, and slender waists, shall always surround you. This is the fruit of the banner-offering."

"For thirty thousand aeons, you shall delight in the heavenly realm. Eighty times you shall be the King of Devas, ruling the divine kingdom."

"A thousand times you shall be a Cakkavatti (Universal Monarch). As for the status of a regional king, it is so vast it cannot be counted."

"In the hundred-thousandth aeon from now, a Teacher named Gotama by clan, born of the Okkāka family, shall arise in the world."

"Passing away from the heavenly realm, urged by the root of merit, you shall be born into a Brahmin family endowed with meritorious deeds."

"Renouncing eighty crores of wealth and many slaves and workers, you shall go forth in the Dispensation of the Blessed One Gotama."

"Having pleased the Fully Enlightened One Gotama, the Noble One of the Sakyans, you shall become a disciple of the Teacher by the name of Upavāṇa."

"The meritorious deed performed a hundred thousand aeons ago shows its fruit to me here. Like the speed of a well-shot arrow, it has burnt away my defilements."

"When I was a Cakkavatti ruling over the four great islands, banners were always hoisted for three leagues around me."
398:
In the hundred-thousandth aeon ago, whatever meritorious deed I performed, because of that deed, I have never known a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of the banner-offering.

My defilements are burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.

Thereafter, the Venerable Upavāṇa became the attendant of the Blessed One. At that time, a wind ailment arose in the Blessed One. A Brahmin named Devahita, who had been a friend of the Elder during his lay life, lived in Sāvatthī. That Brahmin had invited the Elder with the four requisites. Then, the Venerable Upavāṇa, having adjusted his lower robe and taking his bowl and robes, went to the house of that Brahmin. The Brahmin, realizing that "the Elder has come for some other purpose," said, "Venerable Sir, please speak, what do you require?" The Elder, wishing to tell the Brahmin the purpose of his coming, spoke these two verses:

"The Muni, who is honored by those worthy of honor in the world, who speaks well, and who practices seclusion, has a wind ailment. Brahmin, if there is hot water, please offer it to the Muni.

I wish to remove the illness of that Blessed One, who is honored by those worthy of honor, respected by those worthy of respect, and revered by those worthy of reverence." Thus he spoke these two verses.

The meaning of those verses is: In this world, he is honored by those worthy of honor such as Sakka and other devas, and Mahābrahmā and other Brahmās; respected by those worthy of respect such as King Bimbisāra and King Kosala; revered by those worthy of reverence such as the Great Consorts and the Arahants; called 'Arahaṃ' because of being far from defilements; called 'Sugato' because of his excellent going; the 'Muni' who knows all things; my Teacher, the God of gods, the Sakka above Sakkas, the Brahmā above Brahmās—that Blessed One now has an illness due to the disturbance of wind. Brahmin, if there is hot water, I wish to bring that hot water to appease the Blessed One's wind ailment. Hearing those words, the Brahmin offered hot water and medicine suitable for that wind ailment to the Blessed One. Through that medicine, the Blessed One's wind ailment was appeased. The Blessed One gave a talk of appreciation (anumodanā) to the Brahmin Devahita. Thus should the conclusion be noted.

The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Upavāṇa is finished.

## 4. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Isidatta

The verses beginning with "Diṭṭhā mayā" are the verses of the Venerable Elder Isidatta. This Elder also had made an aspiration under previous Buddhas and performed meritorious deeds in various lives. In the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, he was born in a good family, and when he reached the age of discretion, he took a fan and made an offering to the Bodhi tree. Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans, and when this Buddha appeared, he was born into a merchant family in the country of Sunāparanta and received the name Isidatta.
399:
He offered medicine suitable for the wind ailment to the Blessed One. Through that medicine, the Blessed One's illness was appeased. The Blessed One gave a talk of appreciation to that Brahmin.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Upavāṇa is finished.

## 4. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Isidatta

The verse beginning with "Diṭṭhā mayā" is the verse of the Venerable Elder Isidatta. What is the background? This Elder also had an aspiration made under previous Buddhas and performed meritorious deeds in various lives. In the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, he was born in a good family, and when he reached the age of discretion, he took a fan and made an offering to the Bodhi tree. Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans, and when this Buddha of ours appeared, he was born into a merchant family in the country of Sunāparanta and received the name Isidatta. When he reached maturity, he saw the miracle when the Blessed One accepted the Candanamāḷa monastery, and with a confident heart, he approached the Blessed One, heard the Dhamma, became a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna), and lived at home. A deity, out of compassion for Isidatta's welfare, wishing to urge him, recited these two verses:

"I have seen lay followers who bear the scriptures, who are in the habit of saying 'sensual pleasures are impermanent,' yet are intensely attached to jeweled earrings, and have longing for their children and wives.

Truly, because they do not know the Dhamma in this Dispensation, although they say 'sensual pleasures are impermanent,' they do not have the power to cut off their lust; therefore, they remain attached to children, wives, and wealth."

Thus the deity spoke these two verses.

In those verses, "Diṭṭhā mayā dhammadharā upāsakā, kāmā aniccā iti bhāsamānā" means: I have seen some lay followers in this world who bear the scriptures (Pariyatti Dhamma).
400:
Because they are bearers of the scriptural Dhamma (pariyatti-dhamma), they preach the Dhamma connected with the disadvantages of sensual pleasures, saying, "These sensual pleasures are indeed impermanent, suffering, and subject to change." However, they themselves are deeply infatuated with strong passion, having longing for gem-studded earrings, children, and wives. Being so infatuated and lustful with intense passion, they possess the "sap" of fetters regarding gems, earrings, or earrings adorned with gems, sons, daughters, and wives. It means: "I have seen those who say one thing but do another."

"Yato" means: because those lay followers (upāsakas) are extremely attached and have longing for gem-studded earrings, children, and wives, they therefore do not truly and certainly know the Dhamma in this Dispensation (Sāsana) as it really is. Even though they are like this, they also say, "Sensual pleasures are impermanent." It means that beings have a diverse nature by their own disposition. "Rāgañca tesaṃ na balatthi chettuṃ" means: because those lay followers do not have such power of wisdom (ñāṇabala) to completely cut off and eradicate passion, for that reason, being dependent through the power of craving (taṇhā), they cling to children, wives, and wealth, and cannot let go. The deity said all this by referring to that very lay follower under the pretext of another person. Upon hearing those words, the lay follower was moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega), ordained, and before long attained Arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

"At the foot of the noble Bodhi tree of the Blessed One Vipassī,
I took a fan with a joyful mind and fanned the supreme Bodhi tree.

Ninety-one aeons ago, because I fanned the supreme Bodhi tree,
I have not known a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of fanning.

My defilements have been burnt away... (and so on) ...the Buddha's bidding has been done."

When he attained Arahantship and was declaring his attainment (aññabyākaraṇa), he recited these very verses.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Isidinna Thera is finished.
401:
## 5. Commentary on the Verses of Sambula-Kaccāna Thera

The verse beginning with "Devo ca" is that of the Venerable Sambula-Kaccāna Thera. What is its origin? This elder also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and was performing merits in various births. Ninety-four aeons ago, he was born in a respectable family. When he reached the age of discretion, one day he saw the Paccekabuddha named Sataraṃsī, who had arisen from the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) and was wandering for alms. With a devoted mind, he offered a palmyra fruit.

Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered among devas and humans. In this Buddha-arising, he was born in a householder's family in the kingdom of Magadha and received the name "Sambula." Because he belonged to the Kaccāna clan, he was known as "Sambula-Kaccāna."

When he reached adulthood, he heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, gained faith, and ordained. He lived in a mountain cave named Bheravāya near the Himālaya, practicing the work of insight (vipassanā). Then one day, a great unseasonal cloud with thousands of layers arose and began to rain, thundering, roaring, emitting streaks of lightning, and crashing. Thunderbolts also struck. Hearing that sound, animals such as bears, leopards, forest buffaloes, and elephants, being terrified and trembling, let out fearful cries.

However, because the elder had well-initiated insight, he was without longing for his body or life. Without his hair standing on end (with no fear), and not thinking of that danger, he continued to practice the work of insight. Due to the departure of the heat and obtaining a suitable climate, he had a concentrated mind. At that very moment, he intensified his insight and attained Arahantship along with the supernormal knowledges (abhiññā). Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

"The Blessed One named Sataraṃsī, self-enlightened and unconquered,
Having arisen from seclusion, came forth for the sake of alms.

Seeing that Bull among Men, I, with a fruit in my hand, approached him.
With a devoted and joyful mind, I offered the palmyra fruit.

Ninety-four aeons ago, I gave that fruit then;
Because of that merit, I have not known a miserable rebirth. This is the fruit of the gift of fruit.

My defilements have been burnt away... (pe) ...the Buddha's bidding has been done."

Furthermore, having attained Arahantship, reflecting on his own practice with great joy, and wishing to manifest his attainment of Arahantship by way of an inspired utterance (udāna), he recited these two verses: "The rain falls, the rain thunders; and I dwell alone in a fearful cave. To me, dwelling alone in a fearful cave, there is no fear, no trembling, and no hair standing on end. This is the nature of me, who dwells alone in a fearful cave."
402:
Having attained the fruit of Arahantship and reflecting on his own practice, he was filled with joy. Desiring to declare his attainment of Arahantship by the power of an inspired utterance (udāna), he spoke these two verses:

“The rain falls, and the rain thunders,
And I dwell alone in a fearsome cave;
For me who dwells alone in a fearsome cave,
There is no fear, nor trembling, nor hair-standing-on-end.

For me who dwells alone in a fearsome cave,
That there is no fear, nor trembling, nor hair-standing-on-end,
This is my nature.”

In those verses, “Devo ca vassati, devo ca gaḷagaḷāyati” means the rain-cloud both pours down rain and thunders, making the sound “gaḷa-gaḷa.” Indeed, this is an imitation of the sound of thundering rain. “Ekako cāhaṃ bherave bile viharāmi” means I live alone without a companion in this fearsome mountain cave. “Tassa mayhaṃ evaṃbhūtassa me sato natthi bhayaṃ vā chambhitattaṃ vā lomahaṃso vā” means for me who exists in such a state, there is no fear known as mental terror, nor is there trembling of the body caused by that fear, nor even the mere standing of hair on end.

If asked why it is not there, he stated the reason with “Dhammatā mamesā.” For a person whose objects of experience are not fully understood, fear and so forth would occur because desire and lust (chandarāga) have not yet been abandoned. As for me, I have fully understood them in every way, and desire and lust have been completely eradicated. Therefore, the absence of fear and so forth is my nature; that the absence of fear and so forth is my Dhamma-nature, he thus declared his attainment of Arahantship.

## The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Sambulakaccāna is finished.
403:
...the absence of fear is my nature. That the absence of fear and so forth is my Dhamma-nature, he thus made manifest the fruit of Arahantship. The commentary on the verses of the Elder Sambulakaccāna is finished.

## 6. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nitaka
The verse beginning with “Kassa selūpamaṃ cittaṃ” is that of the Venerable Elder Nitaka. What is its origin? This elder had also performed meritorious deeds in the presence of previous Buddhas and had made an aspiration (adhikāra). While performing merits in various existences, during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, he lived as a park-keeper in the city of Bandhumatī. One day, seeing the Blessed One traveling through the air, he felt a heart full of faith and desired to offer a coconut. The Teacher, wishing to favor him, stood in the air and accepted the offering. Having offered the coconut, he experienced great rapture and joy.

Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans. In this Buddha’s era, he was born into a Brahmin family in the Kosala country and was named Nitaka. Upon reaching maturity, he heard the Dhamma from the Teacher, gained faith, and ordained. Taking a meditation subject and dwelling in the forest, he strove and attained Arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:

“In the city of Bandhumatī, I was then a park-keeper;
I saw the stainless Buddha, traveling through the path of the wind.

Taking a coconut, I offered it to the Best of Buddhas;
Standing in the air, the Greatly Renowned One accepted it.

Generating joy for me, bringing happiness in the present life,
Having offered the fruit to the Buddha with a very clear mind,

I then attained rapture and great, supreme happiness;
Just as a treasure arises, so did happiness arise in various births.

In the ninety-one aeons since I gave that fruit then,
I do not know of any miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of offering the fruit.

My divine eye is purified, I am skilled in concentration,
I have reached the perfection of supernormal knowledges;
This is the fruit of offering the fruit.

My defilements are burnt away... pe ... the Buddha’s teaching has been carried out.”

After attaining Arahantship, while the elder was dwelling in the bliss of fruition and the bliss of Nibbāna, the Elder Padhānapariggāhaka came to that forest retreat to examine the monks dwelling there and spoke the first verse beginning with “Kassa selūpamaṃ.”
404:
In that commentary, regarding the verse "Whose mind is like a rock, steady and unshakeable"—among the monks living in this forest, whose mind, through the attainment of the Fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala), is like a solid rock mountain, steady because of the absence of all trembling and the attainment of mastery (vasībhāva), and does not shake or waver due to any of the worldly conditions (lokadhamma)? Now, to show the manner of his unshakeability along with the reason, the Buddha spoke the words beginning with "Virattaṃ."

In that context, "virattaṃ rajanīyesu" means being detached from the things of the three realms which are the cause for the arising of lust, by means of the Noble Path (ariya magga) known as dispassion (virāga); it means that lust has been absolutely cut off in those things. "Kuppanīye" refers to all the grounds for resentment (āghātavatthu) which are the cause of anger. "Na kuppati" means he does not get angry or undergo any mental alteration. "Yassevaṃ bhāvitaṃ cittaṃ" means the mind of such a noble person (ariya) has been developed in the manner described to possess the quality of suchness (tādibhāva). "Kuto taṃ dukkhamessati" means from where will suffering, whether caused by beings or formations (saṅkhāra), come to that person? It means that for such a person, suffering no longer exists.

When the meaning of the question asked without specific reference was taken up by the Elder Nitaka as applying to himself, he explained another meaning with the second verse beginning with "My mind is like a rock." That verse has the same meaning as already stated.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Nitaka is finished.

## 7. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Soṇapoṭiriyaputta

"Na tāva supituṃ hoti" is the verse of the Venerable Soṇa, the son of Poṭiriya. What is its origin? This elder had also performed meritorious deeds (adhikāra) under previous Buddhas. In the time of the Blessed One Sikhi, he lived as a forest-dweller. One day, seeing the Teacher, he was inspired with faith and offered a kuruñjiya fruit to the Teacher. Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans, and in this Buddha's era, he was reborn in Kapilavatthu as the son of a village headman named Poṭiriya, and was named Soṇa. When he reached maturity, he became the general of the Sakyan King Bhaddiya. Then, when King Bhaddiya ordained in the manner mentioned above...
405:
The general thought, "Even the King has ordained; what is the use of me living the household life?" and he ordained. However, after ordaining, he lived delighting in sleep and did not devote himself to the practice of meditation (bhāvanā). While the Blessed One was staying in the mango grove named Anupiya, He radiated His aura to arouse mindfulness in that monk and, admonishing him with these verses, He spoke two verses:

"It is not yet time to sleep; the night is garlanded with stars. For those who understand, this night is only for being watchful (to practice)."

"If an elephant should trample one who has fallen from the elephant's back, death in battle would be better for me than living defeated by the defilements."

In those verses, "Na tāva supituṃ hoti, ratti nakkhattāmālinī" means: for a wise person who has obtained the ninth opportune moment (the appearance of a Buddha), having avoided the eight inopportune moments (akkhaṇa), as long as the Fruit of Arahantship has not been attained, it is not proper to sleep during this night garlanded with stars; it is not the time for sleeping. Rather, "Paṭizaggitumevesā, ratti hoti vijānatā" means: this night, being a time of special silence as humans, beasts, and birds have gone to sleep, is the time desired by the wise for being devoted to wakefulness (jāgariyānuyoga) and for guarding the practice (paṭipatti) within themselves.

Hearing these words, Elder Soṇa was struck with a sense of urgency (saṃvega). Establishing shame and fear of wrongdoing (hiri-ottappa), and undertaking the ascetic practice of living in the open air (abbhokāsikaṅga), he performed the work of insight (vipassanā) and spoke the second verse beginning with "Hatthikkhandhāva patitaṃ." In that verse, "avapatitaṃ" means falling headlong with feet upwards. "Kuñjaro ce anukkame" means if the elephant should trample. The meaning is: "When I mounted an elephant and entered the battlefield, if I fell from the elephant's back and were trampled to death by that elephant in the battle, that death would be better for me than living now while being defeated by the defilements."

While reciting this verse, he intensified his insight and reached Arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

"I was once a hunter in the forest. While wandering in the woods, I saw the Blessed One, who had reached the further shore of all things and had conquered the enemy of defilements. Taking a kuruñjiya fruit, I offered it with my own hands and a faithful heart to the Great Sage, who is like a field for sowing the seeds of merit."

"In the thirty-one aeons since I offered that fruit, I have not known the four lower realms. This is the fruit of offering the kuruñjiya fruit. My defilements are burned away... I have followed the instructions of the Buddha."

After he reached Arahantship, the Blessed One expressed appreciation (anumodanā) for the verses He had spoken. Thus, both verses are stated.
406:
In the past, I was a hunter wandering in the forest. I saw the Buddha, free from the dust of defilements, who had reached the further shore of all phenomena (dhammas).

With a heart full of faith, I took a kuruñjiya fruit with my own hands and offered it to that Supreme Buddha, the peerless field of merit, who possessed the quality of equanimity (tādi).

Thirty-one aeons ago from this present age, I gave that fruit at that time; because of that meritorious deed, I have not known a miserable rebirth. This is the fruit of offering fruit.

My defilements have been burned away... (and so forth) ... I have followed the Buddha's teaching.

Upon reaching Arahantship, the Elder recited both the verse spoken by the Teacher and the verse spoken by himself, beginning with "Falling from the elephant's back." By this recitation, he declared his attainment of Arahantship (aññābyākaraṇa).

## The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Soṇapoṭiriyaputta is finished.

## 8. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nisabha

"Having abandoned the five strands of sensual pleasure" is the verse of the Venerable Nisabha Thera. What is its origin? This Elder had also performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulated merit in various lives. In the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, he was born into a respectable family. Upon reaching maturity, one day he saw the Teacher wandering for alms and, with a heart full of faith, offered a kapittha fruit. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered only in happy realms. In this Buddha's era, he was born into a respectable family in the Koliyan country and was named Nisabha. When he came of age, he witnessed the Buddha's power during the war between the Sakyans and the Koliyans. Gaining faith, he ordained and attained Arahantship on that very day. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:

"I offered a kapittha fruit to the Buddha of golden hue, the recipient of offerings, as he was walking along the road.

Ninety-one aeons ago, I gave that fruit at that time; because of that meritorious deed, I have not known a miserable rebirth. This is the fruit of offering fruit.

My defilements have been burned away... (and so forth) ... I have followed the Buddha's teaching."
407: After reaching Arahantship, Elder Nisabha saw his fellow monks spending their time in negligence. Wishing to admonish them, he spoke the first verse: 'Having abandoned the five cords of sensual pleasure, which are dear in nature and delightful, having gone forth from the home life with faith, one should make an end of suffering.' The meaning of that verse is: Having abandoned—given up and relinquished—the five cords of sensual pleasure consisting of sights and so on, which are called 'dear in nature' (piyarūpa) because they are to be cherished by foolish worldlings, and 'delightful' (manorama) because they please the heart; having gone forth from the bond of the house by the power of faith in the fruit of kamma and faith in the Triple Gem; a wise person who has entered the monkhood and strives from the time of ordination should make an end of the suffering of the round of rebirths.
