After admonishing those monks in this way, he wished to reveal his own state of practice so they would not think, 'This elder only speaks to make others understand but does not practice himself.' Thus, he declared his attainment of Arahantship with the second verse: 'I do not delight in death, I do not delight in life; with mindfulness and clear comprehension, I only await the time (of parinibbāna).' In that verse, 'na-abhinandāmi maraṇaṃ' means not desiring death. 'na-abhinandāmi jīvitaṃ' is the reason for that statement; because I do not delight in life, I do not delight in death. For one who accumulates defilements and volitional formations (kilesa-abhisaṅkhāra) to bring about birth, aging, and death in the future, if they delight in the arising of a new life, they also delight in their own death by the law of necessity (nāntariya), because the cause has not been abandoned. An Arahant, however, has abandoned all states that lead to the accumulation of rebirth and stands in the states that lead to the cessation of rebirth. Having fully understood the basis of existence, just as they do not delight in life, they do not delight in death, because the cause has been well abandoned. Therefore, he said, 'I do not delight in death, I do not delight in life.' If such is the case, one might ask how an Arahant desires parinibbāna and how they remain until parinibbāna. He said, 'With mindfulness and clear comprehension, I only await the time.' After the parinibbāna of defilements is accomplished, having reached the fullness of mindfulness and wisdom, being mindful and clearly comprehending...
408:
I only await the time for the final passing away of the aggregates (khandha-parinibbāna), dwelling in expectation and anticipation of that time. I have no delight in death nor in life, for that delight has been uprooted by the path of Arahatship.

## The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nisabha is finished.

## 9. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Usabha

"Ambapallavasaṅkāsaṃ" and so forth is the verse of the Venerable Usabha. As for its origin: This Elder had also performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit in various existences. In the time of the Blessed One Sikhī, he was born in a respectable family. Upon reaching the age of discretion, he saw the Teacher wandering for alms one day and, with a heart full of faith, offered a kosamba fruit. Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, and in this Buddha-era, he was born into the Sakyan royal family in Kapilavatthu and was given the name Usabha. When he reached maturity, he saw the power of the Buddha at the assembly of the Teacher's relatives, gained faith, and ordained.

From the time of his ordination, he did not strive in the recluse's duties; instead, he delighted in company during the day and spent the entire night sleeping. One day, while sleeping heedlessly and without clear comprehension, he had a dream: he dreamt that he shaved his hair and beard, donned robes the color of mango shoots, and entered the city for alms while riding on the neck of an elephant. Seeing people there, he felt ashamed and descended from the elephant's back. Upon seeing himself, he woke up. "I, sleeping heedlessly and without clear comprehension, have seen such a dream," he thought. Gaining spiritual urgency (saṃvega), he developed insight (vipassanā) and soon attained Arahatship. Regarding this, it is stated in the Apadāna:

"Like a tree with drooping branches, having abandoned anger, the God of gods, the Bull among men, was proceeding along the road; at that time, I offered a kosamba fruit.

Thirty-one aeons ago from now, because of the fruit I offered then, I have not known a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of offering a fruit.

My defilements are burnt away... (pe)... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out."
409:
Then the Elder, making the dream he had seen like a goad (aṅkusa), and because he had attained Arahatship, wishing to declare his attainment by describing that very dream, spoke these two verses:

"Having placed on my shoulder the robe,
Which was like a mango shoot in color,
I entered the village for alms,
Seated upon the neck of an elephant.

Descending from the elephant's back,
I then gained spiritual urgency;
I, who was then conceited, became peaceful,
And reached the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya)."

In those verses, "ambapallavasaṅkāsaṃ aṃse katvāna cīvaraṃ" means placing the robe, which had the color of coral like a mango shoot, upon the shoulder as an upper garment. "Gāmaṃ" refers to entering his own royal city for alms while seated on the elephant's back. Just as he entered, while being watched by the great crowd, he descended from the elephant's back and, while standing, woke up. As soon as he woke, he gained spiritual urgency, thinking, "This happened because I fell asleep being heedless and without clear comprehension."

Other teachers, however, say: "While he was a king, he saw such a dream at night. At dawn, while wandering the city streets on an elephant, he remembered the dream, descended from the elephant, gained spiritual urgency, ordained in the presence of the Teacher, attained Arahatship, and then spoke these verses as an inspired utterance (udāna)." "Ditto" (conceited) means that although he was puffed up with pride of birth and wealth during his time as a king, he later gained spiritual urgency.

## The commentary on the verses of the Elder Usabha is finished.

## 10. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Kappaṭakura

"Ayami'ti kappaṭo" and so forth is the verse of the Venerable Kappaṭakura. As for its origin: This Venerable one also had merit performed under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit in various existences. In the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, he was born as a son of a good family. When he reached maturity, he saw the Blessed One one day sitting at the foot of a tree on the bank of the Vinatā River and, with a heart full of faith, worshipped Him with ketaka flowers. Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, and in this Buddha-era, he was born into a poor family in Sāvatthī. When he grew up, not knowing any other means of livelihood, he wore a piece of an old cloth (kappaṭa), held a bowl in his hand, and went from house to house begging for rice (kura) to eat. Therefore, he was known as "Kappaṭakura." When he reached adulthood, he made a living by reaping and selling grass. One day, while going to reap grass, he saw an Arahant, approached him, and paid homage.
410:
At the time of this Buddha's appearance, he was born into a poor family in Sāvatthī. Until he reached adulthood, he knew no other means of livelihood, so he wandered about seeking rice in various places, wearing a piece of old rag and holding a bowl in his hand. For this reason, he became known only as 'Kappaṭakura'. When he reached adulthood, while making a living by selling grass, he went to the forest one day to cut grass. There, he saw a certain Khīṇāsava (Arahant) Elder, approached him, paid homage, and sat down. The Elder preached the Dhamma to him. Having heard the Dhamma, he gained faith and, thinking, 'What is the use of this difficult livelihood for me?', he ordained as a monk and stored the old rag he had worn in a certain place.

Whenever discontent (anabhirati) with the Dispensation arose in him, he would look at that old rag, and his discontent would vanish as he regained spiritual urgency (saṃvega). Acting in this manner, he disrobed and re-ordained seven times. The monks informed the Blessed One of this matter. Then one day, the monk Kappaṭakura was sitting at the edge of the assembly in the Dhamma hall and fell asleep. The Blessed One, wishing to rebuke and admonish him, spoke these two verses:

'This is Kappaṭa, known as Kappaṭakura. While the jar of the Deathless is clear and overflowing, he has a mind that turns away from the Dhamma, [sleeping] on the path prepared for the cultivation of Jhanas.'

'Dear Kappaṭa, do not nod; let me, the Buddha, not strike you near the ear [with the hand of instruction]. Dear Kappaṭa, you truly do not know your measure, nodding in the midst of the Saṅgha.'

In those verses, 'Ayamiti kappaṭo kappaṭakuro' means that the monk Kappaṭakura had wrong thoughts (micchā-vitakka) such as, 'This is my old rag; I shall wear this and live however I can.' While I, the Buddha, am pouring out the jar of the Deathless, which is clear and overflowing, in various places, saying, 'I have attained the Deathless, I shall instruct, I shall preach the Dhamma,' and 'In this world shrouded in darkness, I shall beat the drum of the Deathless'...
411:
...While I am proclaiming and raining down the nectar of the Dhamma, in this Dispensation where the path of meditation (bhāvanā-magga) is prepared for the development of both mundane and supramundane Jhanas, the monk Kappaṭakura, despite such a path existing, turns away from the Dhamma of my Dispensation. With a dissatisfied mind, he wanders with the wrong thought, 'This rag is mine; I shall wear it and live.' Rebuking that Kappaṭakura, and wishing to show his negligent living—like catching a thief with the stolen goods—the Buddha spoke the verse beginning with 'Mā kho tvaṃ, kappaṭa, pacālesī'.

In that verse, 'Mā kho tvaṃ, kappaṭa, pacālesī' means, 'Dear Kappaṭakura, having sat down saying "I will listen to the Dhamma of the Buddha," do not fall into nodding or sleep; do not nod; do not fall asleep.' 'Let me not strike you near the ear with the hand of instruction while you are sleeping' means, 'Practice in such a way that I, the Buddha, do not have to admonish you further for the abandonment of defilements.' 'Na hi tvaṃ, kappaṭa, mattamaññāsī' means, 'Dear Kappaṭakura, while nodding in the midst of the Saṅgha, you do not know the proper measure. You do not even realize this much: "This extremely rare opportunity has been obtained; let it not pass me by." See how great your fault is!' Thus He rebuked him.

When the Blessed One had thus strongly restrained and rebuked him with these two verses, Kappaṭakura felt spiritual urgency (saṃvega), like a fierce elephant entering the right path after being pierced by a spear that can penetrate bone. He established insight (vipassanā) and before long attained Arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

'On the bank of the Vinatā River, the Supreme Man, the Buddha Vipassī, dwelt. I saw the stainless Buddha, one-pointed and well-concentrated.'
'At that time, with a mind of clear devotion and joy, I worshipped the Excellent Buddha with a Ketaka flower, which has a scent like honey.'
'Because of that meritorious deed of worshipping with a flower ninety-one aeons ago from this Bhadda-kappa, I have not known the four woeful states. This is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.'
'My defilements have been burnt away... the instruction of the Buddha has been carried out.'

After attaining Arahantship, he reflected that the two verses spoken by the Blessed One were the very cause of his attainment, and he recited them back. Therefore, those very verses became the instruction for the Elder Kappaṭakura.
412:
After reaching the fruit of Arahantship, he reflected that the two verses spoken by the Teacher were indeed the means (like a goad) for his attainment of Arahantship, and he recited them back. Therefore, those very verses became his declaration of supreme knowledge (aññābyākaraṇa).

## The commentary on the verses of Kappaṭakura Thera is finished.

## The commentary on the fourth chapter is finished.

## 5. The Fifth Chapter

## 1. Commentary on the verses of Kumārakassapa Thera

"Aho buddhā aho dhammā" (Oh, the Buddhas! Oh, the Dhamma!) and so forth is the verse of the Venerable Kumārakassapa Thera. How did it originate? This Elder also had performed meritorious services under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merits in various lives. In the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was born into a Brahmin family and became a wise man upon reaching maturity. However, in the Aṅguttara Commentary, it is said "in a noble family." He went to the Teacher and, while listening to the Dhamma, saw the Teacher appoint a monk to the foremost position (etadagga) among those of eloquent speech (cittakathika). Desiring that position himself, he made an aspiration and performed meritorious deeds corresponding to that aspiration. In the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, he practiced the Dhamma of a recluse and wandered only in the happy realms (sugati). When this Buddha appeared, he was conceived in the womb of a merchant's daughter in the city of Rājagaha.

That merchant's daughter had desired to ordain since she was a young girl, but although she pleaded with her parents, she did not receive permission and went to her husband's house. Without even knowing herself that she was pregnant, she served her husband and, with his permission, was ordained among the bhikkhunīs. When they saw her pregnancy, the bhikkhunīs questioned Devadatta. He said, "She is no longer a nun." They then reported it to the Buddha. The Teacher assigned the matter to the Venerable Upāli. The Elder summoned the families living in the city of Sāvatthī and the laywoman Visākhā, and while deciding the case in the midst of the assembly including the King, he said, "The pregnancy was obtained while she was still a layperson; therefore, her ordination is blameless." The Teacher gave his approval to the Elder, saying, "The case has been well decided."

That bhikkhunī gave birth to a son who was like a golden image. King Pasenadi of Kosala raised the young boy and named him "Kassapa."
413:
Later, the King adorned the boy and brought him to the presence of the Teacher to have him ordained. Because he was ordained while still a boy (kumāra), and because the Blessed One, when saying, "Call Kassapa" or "Give this fruit or food to Kassapa," was asked "To which Kassapa should it be given?" and replied "Give it to Kumārakassapa," he became known by the name given by the Teacher. Furthermore, because he was the King's foster son, he was known as Kumārakassapa even when he grew up.

From the time of his ordination, he practiced Vipassanā meditation and also studied the word of the Buddha. Meanwhile, a Great Brahmā who had been born in the Suddhāvāsa (Pure Abodes) realm—having previously practiced the Dhamma of a recluse with the Venerable Kumārakassapa on a mountain top and become an Anāgāmī (Non-returner)—thought, "I will provide the means for his attainment of the path and fruit by showing him the way of Vipassanā." He formulated fifteen questions and went to the Elder, who was living in the Andhavana forest, saying, "You should ask these questions to the Teacher." The Elder then asked those questions to the Blessed One. The Blessed One answered them for him. The Elder learned those questions exactly as the Teacher had explained them, and by developing the "womb" of Vipassanā, he attained Arahantship. This is stated in the Apadāna:

"One hundred thousand aeons ago, a Leader named Padumuttara, the hero who brought welfare to the whole world, arose.
At that time, I was a famous Brahmin, a master of the three Vedas. While wandering about for my daytime rest, I saw the Leader of the World.
I saw that Blessed One proclaiming the Four Truths, awakening the world together with the devas, and praising the foremost among eloquent speakers (vicitthakathika) in the midst of the great crowd.
Then, with a joyful heart, I invited the Tathāgata. Having decorated a pavilion with cloths of various colors and brightened it with various gems, I offered a meal there to the Saṅgha. Having offered food of various excellent flavors for seven days,
and having honored the Teacher together with his disciples with flowers of various colors, I prostrated at his feet and aspired for that position.
Then the Great Sage, who is the sole abode of compassion, with a face and eyes like a lotus..."
414:
(The Teacher said: "Behold this noble brahmin) who is full of joy and rapture, with hair standing on end, with eyes wide with a smile, who greatly desires my teaching, who is prostrate at my feet, wearing a single garment, and is of good heart." This man aspires to that position: to be foremost among those who speak eloquently (vicitrakathika).

One hundred thousand aeons from this Bhadda Kappa, a Teacher named Gotama, born of the Okkāka clan, will arise in the world.

His heir in the Dhamma, his breast-born son, created by the Dhamma, will be a disciple of the Teacher named Kumārakassapa.

By the power of his offering of varied flowers, cloths, and jewels, he will attain the foremost position among those who speak eloquently.

Due to that well-performed meritorious deed and his volitional aspirations, I abandoned the human body and reached the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

Wandering through various lives like an actor in the middle of a stage, I became the son of the deer-king Sākha and entered the womb of a doe.

While I was in my mother's womb, her turn to be slaughtered arrived. Abandoned by the deer-king Sākha, my mother went to the deer-king Nigrodha for refuge.

That deer-king Nigrodha, sacrificing his own life, freed my mother from death. At that time, my mother admonished me thus:

"One should associate only with Nigrodha; one should not live with Sākha. Death in the presence of Nigrodha is better than life in the presence of Sākha."

Admonished by that king of the deer-herd, I, my mother, and others, like people returning to their own homes from a foreign land, reached the delightful Tusita heaven.

Again, when the teaching of the Hero Buddha Kassapa was nearing its end, I climbed a mountain peak and strove in the Teacher's dispensation...
415:
In this present age, I was born into a wealthy merchant's family in Rājagaha. My mother, while pregnant, entered the homeless life of a renunciant.

When it was known that she was pregnant, she was taken to Devadatta, who said, "Destroy this wicked nun." But now, out of compassion from the Conqueror, the Lord of Sages, my mother gave birth to me safely in the nunnery.

Knowing this, the ruler of the land, King Kosala, raised me with the attendants of a prince. By name, I was Kassapa. Because of Mahā Kassapa, I became known as Kumāra Kassapa. After hearing the discourse on the body, which is like an ant-hill, taught by the Buddha,

from then on, my mind was liberated from all attachments. After taming King Pāyāsi, I attained the foremost position. My defilements are burnt... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.

Having attained Arahantship and being placed in the foremost position by the Teacher for being an eloquent speaker, he reflected on his own practice and, by way of illustrating the virtues of the Triple Gem, he declared his attainment of Arahantship:

"How wonderful are the Buddhas! How wonderful is the Dhamma! How wonderful is the perfection of our Teacher, in whose dispensation a disciple can realize such a Dhamma!

For incalculable aeons, I have possessed the view of self. Among those births, this is the last; this is the final physical aggregate. The wandering in the cycle of birth and death, and further becoming, no longer exist for me."

He uttered these two verses.

In those verses, 'Aho' is an exclamation expressing wonder. 'Buddhā' refers to the Omniscient Buddhas, used in the plural out of respect; it means "How wonderful are the Buddhas!" 'Dhammā' refers to the nine supramundane states along with the scriptural Dhamma. 'Aho no satthu sampadā' means "How wonderful are the perfections of our Teacher, the Possessor of Ten Powers!" 'Yattha' means "in which"...
417:
Having ordained and developed insight, he became a monk endowed with the six supernormal knowledges. This is stated in the Apadāna:

"In the forest, seeing the Buddha Atthadassī of great fame, with a clear and joyful mind, I offered a pilakkha fruit.

In the eighteen hundredth aeon ago, I offered that fruit. Due to the merit of offering that fruit, I have not known a miserable rebirth. This is the result of offering fruit.

My defilements are burned away... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled."

After becoming endowed with the six supernormal knowledges, while spending time in the bliss of meditative attainments, he saw one day two novices in that monastery picking flowers at the top of a tree; as the branch they had climbed broke, they were falling. The elder, through his psychic power, caught them with his hands and placed them safely on the ground. While preaching the Dhamma to those novices, he recited these two verses:

"The young monk who truly strives in the Buddha's teaching, he is awake among those who sleep; his life is not in vain.

Therefore, the wise person, remembering the teaching of the Buddhas, should devote himself to faith, virtue, confidence, and the vision of the Dhamma."

In those verses, "Yo" is an indefinite pronoun. "Have" is a particle used in the sense of firmness. "Daharo" means young or youthful. He is called a "bhikkhu" because he begs. "Yuñjati" means he exerts or strives. "Jāgaro" means one endowed with the quality of wakefulness. "Suttesu" means among those who are sleeping.

This is the meaning: A monk, even while being young and youthful, does not think, "I will only know [the Dhamma] later when I am old," but strives with the practice of diligence in the teaching of the Buddhas, exerting himself in the meditation of tranquillity and insight. He is "awake" by being endowed with the wakeful qualities such as faith, while others are "sleeping," being negligent and slumbering in the sleep of ignorance. Because he thus fulfills his own benefit and the benefit of others, his life is not in vain or empty. Since this is so, a monk who is wise and knows the taste of the supramundane Dhamma should strive, repeatedly remembering the advice and instruction of the Buddhas—striving in faith in kamma and its results (kamma-phala-saddhā) which proceeds in the manner of "there is kamma, there is the result of kamma"; in the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhi-sīla) which is supported by faith; in confidence in the Triple Gem, thinking "the Blessed One has well-proclaimed the Dhamma, the Saṅgha has practiced well"; and in the vision of the Four Noble Truths through the power of full understanding and so forth, by means of the Path-knowledge that arises together with insight-wisdom.
418:
The wise monk, endowed with the wisdom that tastes the essence of the supramundane Dhamma, who repeatedly reflects on the advice, exhortation, and instruction of the Buddhas—namely, the fourfold purification virtue (catupārisuddhisīla), the devotion to the Triple Gem expressed as 'The Blessed One is the Fully Enlightened One, the Dhamma is well-expounded, the Saṅgha has practiced well,' and the vision of the Four Noble Truths by means of full understanding (pariññā) and so forth through the Path-knowledge accompanied by insight-wisdom—should strive [in meditation], disregarding even his own head if it were on fire; he should exert effort and ardor in that [insight meditation]. This is the meaning.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Dhammapāla Thera is finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Verses of Brahmāli Thera

'Whose faculties have reached tranquility' is the verse of the Venerable Brahmāli Thera. What is its origin? This elder, too, having performed meritorious service under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit that serves as a support for liberation (vivaṭṭa) in various existences, was reborn in a respectable family during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī. Upon reaching the age of discretion, one day, seeing the Teacher wandering for alms, he was inspired with faith, paid homage, and offered a fruit called Pādaphala. The Teacher, having given a talk of appreciation, departed. Due to that meritorious deed, wandering through the realms of devas and humans, he was reborn in a Brahmin family in the Kosala kingdom during the time of the current Buddha's appearance and was named Brahmāli. When he reached the age of discretion, being urged by his fulfillment of conditions (hetusampatti), a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) arose regarding the round of rebirths. Relying on such a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitta), he ordained in the Buddha's Dispensation. Taking up a suitable meditation subject and dwelling in the forest, because his knowledge had matured, he soon developed insight and became an Arahant with the six higher powers. Thus, it is said in the Apadāna:

'To the Buddha of golden hue, worthy of receiving offerings, as he walked along the street, I offered a Pādaphala fruit.

Ninety-one aeons ago, when I offered that fruit, I have not known a miserable rebirth since then; this is the result of offering the fruit.

My defilements are burnt away... [etc.]... the Buddha's instruction has been carried out.'
420:
## 4. Commentary on the Verses of Venerable Mogharāja

'Chavipāpaka cittabhaddakā' and so forth is the verse of the Venerable Mogharāja. What is its origin? This Mogharāja Thera had also performed meritorious deeds of great merit (adhikāra) under previous Buddhas. In the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was born into a good family. When he reached the age of discretion, one day while listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain monk to the foremost position among those who wear coarse robes (lūkhacīvaradhara). Desiring that position, he made an aspiration and performed meritorious deeds throughout various births.

In the time of the Blessed One Atthadassī, he was born into a Brahmin family and reached the further shore of the arts and sciences of the Brahmins. While he was teaching the arts and sciences to young Brahmin students, one day he saw the Blessed One Atthadassī walking, surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks. With a heart full of faith, he prostrated with the fivefold touch (pañcapatiṭṭhita), and with hands joined in reverence (añjali) above his head, he praised the Teacher with six verses beginning with 'Yāvatā rūpino sattā'. He then filled a bowl with honey and offered it. The Teacher accepted the honey and gave a talk of appreciation (anumodanā).

Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans. In the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, he became a minister to the king named Kaṭṭhavāhana. He was sent by the king with a thousand men to invite the Teacher. Having gone to the presence of the Teacher and heard the Dhamma, he gained faith and ordained. He practiced the recluse's Dhamma (samaṇadhamma) for twenty thousand years. Passing away from that life, he wandered only in the happy destinations (sugati) for the interval between two Buddhas. In this current Buddha-arising, he was born into a Brahmin family and received the name Mogharāja. Having learned the arts under the Brahmin Bāvarī, he was moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and ordained as an ascetic. Surrounded by a thousand ascetics, he was sent to the presence of the Teacher along with Ajita and others. Being the fifteenth among them, he asked questions, and at the conclusion of the answers to the questions, he attained Arahatship. This is stated in the Apadāna:

'The Blessed One Atthadassī, the Self-Awakened, the Unconquered, walked along the main road surrounded by the community of monks.

Surrounded by my disciples, I came out from my house. Having come out, I saw the Leader of the World there.

Having paid homage to the Sambuddha, with hands joined in reverence above my head, and having inspired faith in my own heart, I praised the Leader of the World.'
421:
'As many beings as there are, whether with form, formless, or non-percipient, all of them are contained within Your knowledge.

Just as one might surround water with a fine-meshed net, whatever living beings are in the water, they are all within the net.

Those who possess volition, whether with form or formless, all of them are contained within Your knowledge.

You rescue this world which is entangled in darkness. Having heard Your Dhamma, they cross over the stream of doubt.

In the world covered by ignorance and overwhelmed by darkness, when Your knowledge shines forth, the darkness is destroyed.

You are the eye for all, the dispeller of great darkness. Having heard Your Dhamma, many people attain peace (nibbāna).

Having filled a small bowl with pure honey, I raised it with both hands and offered it to the Great Sage.

The Great Hero, the Great Seer, accepted it with His own hand. Having consumed that honey, the All-Knowing One rose into the sky.

Standing in the air, the Teacher Atthadassī, the Bull among Men, gladdening my heart, spoke these verses:

"He by whom this knowledge has been praised, and the Most Excellent Buddha has been lauded, through that clarity of heart, he shall not go to a woeful state.

He will exercise the sovereignty of the gods for fourteen times. He will rule the earth as a king for eight hundred times.

He will be a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) for five hundred times. He will exercise regional kingship on earth for countless times.

He will be a reciter of the Vedas, a master of mantras, and reach the further shore of the three Vedas. He will ordain in the dispensation of the Blessed One Gotama."'
422:
“That person named Mogharāja will investigate the deep and subtle meaning with the knowledge of insight and the path; he will become a disciple of the Teacher.

The Buddha Gotama, the supreme leader of men, will place that Mogharāja—who is endowed with the three knowledges, has completed his task, and is taintless—in the foremost position of those who wear coarse robes.

Having abandoned human sensual pleasures and the like, having cut the fetters of existence, and having fully understood all taints through the abandonment by eradication, I live taintless.

My defilements are burnt; the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.” Thus he spoke.

However, after reaching Arahantship, he wore rag-robes (paṃsukūla) endowed with three types of coarseness: coarseness of material, coarseness of stitching, and coarseness of dye. Because of this, the Teacher placed him in the foremost position of those who wear coarse robes. Later, due to past karma and the lack of physical care, skin diseases such as scabies and sores appeared and increased on the Elder's body. Thinking, “The monastery's bedding will become soiled,” he used to sleep even in the winter season in the fields of Magadha, spreading out mats of straw. One day, when the Elder approached to attend to the Teacher, paid homage, and sat in a suitable place, the Teacher, by way of friendly greeting, asked him with the first verse beginning with “Chavipāpakā.”

In that verse, “Chavipāpakā” means one with bad or inferior skin because the skin is broken by scabies, itch, and sores. “Cittabhaddakā” means one with a good or noble mind due to the abandonment of all defilements and the practice of the Brahma-vihāras. “Mogharāja” is the name used to address the Elder. “Satataṃ samāhito” means one whose mind is constantly and repeatedly concentrated through the concentration of the fruition of Arahantship. “Hemantikāsītakālarattiyo” means throughout the cold nights of the winter season. Here, the second case (accusative) is used in the sense of continuous duration (accantasaṃyoga). There is also a Pali reading “Hemantikā sītakālarattiyo.” There, “Hemantikā” means belonging to or included in the winter season. “Bhikkhu tvaṃ si” is asking, “Monk, who are you?” The Teacher asked, “In such a situation, when others do not offer you a monastery and you do not enter the communal monastery, what will you do? How do you maintain your physical existence during the aforementioned cold season?” Being thus questioned, the Elder Mogharāja, wishing to explain that matter to the Teacher, said—

“Venerable Sir, I have heard that all of Magadha is full of crops. Just as other monks who live happily [in good monasteries], I too sleep on a bed covered with straw.” In that verse—
423:
“Magadha is full of crops; I have heard that all of Magadha is [pleasant]. Just as other monks who live happily [in good monastery beds], I too shall sleep on a bed covered with straw.” Thus he spoke this verse.

In that verse, ‘sampannasassā’ means the successful growth of crops. ‘Magadhā’ refers to the Magadha country. Since ‘Magadhā’ refers to the princes living in the district, even a single district where they reside is spoken of in the plural as ‘Magadhā’ by way of conventional usage. ‘Kevalā’ means all, without exception. ‘Iti me sutaṃ’ means ‘thus I have heard.’ Here, ‘heard’ is said in reference to a place not yet seen. By those words, he shows that in such a time, he can live anywhere in all parts of Magadha. ‘Palālacchannako seyyaṃ, yathaññe sukhajīvino’ means just as other monks who live happily, having obtained suitable lodgings, sleep comfortably with good mats and blankets, so I too, having spread a mat of straw below and having my body covered with straw above and on the sides, shall sleep on a bed covered with straw; I shall make my bed. Thus he makes clear his contentment with whatever he receives (yathālābhasantosa).

## The Commentary on the Verses of Mogharāja Thera is Finished.

## 5. Commentary on the Verses of Visākhapañcālaputta Thera

“Na ukkhipe no ca parikkhipe pare” and so forth is the verse of the Venerable Visākha Pañcālaputta. As for the origin: This Elder also had performed meritorious service under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit that is a support for liberation from the cycle of rebirths in various existences. Fourteen aeons ago, he was born into a poor family in a border village. When he reached maturity, one day he went to the forest with the villagers who were wandering in search of fruits. In that forest, he saw a Paccekabuddha and, with a devoted mind, offered a creeper-fruit. Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans. In the time of this Buddha, he was born into a Maṇḍalika royal family in Magadha and was named Visākha. Because he was the son of a Pañcāla princess, he was later known as Pañcālaputta. When his father died, while he was ruling as king, the Teacher came near his village. He went to the Teacher and, having gained faith from hearing the Dhamma, he became a monk. When he went to Sāvatthī with the Teacher, he developed insight and soon became an Arahant with the six supernormal knowledges. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna: “The multitude of people came together; then they went to the forest to search for fruit. In that forest, I saw the Paccekabuddha, the self-enlightened one who is unconquered. With a devoted and joyful mind, I offered a creeper-fruit. Because of the merit of that offering of a creeper-fruit fourteen aeons ago, I have not known the four planes of misery; this is the result of offering a creeper-fruit. My defilements are burnt; I have followed the Buddha's teaching.” After that Pañcālaputta Thera, who possessed the six supernormal knowledges, went to his birthplace to support his relatives. In that place, the people [addressed] Pañcālaputta Thera...
424:
Having gone and heard the Dhamma, he gained faith and ordained. He then traveled to Sāvatthī with the Blessed One. While practicing insight meditation (vipassanā), he soon became an Arahant endowed with the six supernormal powers (chalabhiññā). This is stated in the Apadāna:

'At that time, all the people gathered and went into the forest seeking fruit. While searching, they found fruit at that time.'

'In that forest, I saw the Buddha (a Paccekabuddha), self-enlightened and undefeated. With a clear and joyful heart, I offered a creeper fruit.'

'Fourteen aeons ago from this Bhadda-kappa, because of that fruit offering, I have never known a woeful state; this is the result of offering fruit.'

'My defilements have been burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.'

Having become an Elder with the six supernormal powers, he went to his birthplace out of compassion for his relatives. There, people approached the Elder and heard the Dhamma from time to time. One day, they asked about the characteristics of a Dhamma preacher (Dhammakathika): 'Venerable Sir, with how many qualities is a person endowed to be called a Dhamma preacher?' Wishing to explain the characteristics of a Dhamma preacher, the Elder spoke these two verses:

'One should not exalt oneself, nor should one disparage others. One should not criticize others, nor should one disturb one who has reached the further shore.'

'One should not speak of one's own virtues in assemblies. One should be without restlessness, measured in speech, and well-conducted.'

'For one who sees the very subtle and profound meaning, who is skilled in wisdom, humble in demeanor, and who always follows the Buddha's conduct, Nibbāna is not difficult to attain.'

In those verses, 'na ukkhipe' means one should not exalt oneself; one should not praise oneself based on birth, great learning, and so on. 'no ca parikkhipe pare' means one should not disparage other persons by defining them by those same factors like birth or learning, or by destroying their reputation. 'na okkhipe pare' means one should not look down on others with a desire to criticize, nor regard them as inferior, nor revile them. Some teachers recite it as 'na ukkhipe', and the meaning is the same. 'pāragataṃ' means one who has reached the further shore of knowledge (vijjā) just as one reaches the further shore of the ocean of saṃsāra—one whose defilements are exhausted, who is endowed with the three knowledges or the six supernormal powers. One should not disturb, strike, or offend such a person. 'na ca attavaṇṇaṃ parisāsu byāhare' means one should not speak of one's own virtues and fame, or one's gains and honors, in assemblies such as those of kings, while desiring them.
425:
One should not exalt oneself through birth, learning, and so on. One should not disparage others by defining them by that noble birth, learning, and so on. Or, one should not disparage others by way of destroying their virtues. 'One should not disparage others' is connected in this way. It means one should not look down on others with the intent to criticize, nor regard them as inferior, nor revile them. Some teachers recite 'na ukkhipe', which has the same meaning as mentioned.

'Pāragataṃ' refers to one who has reached the further shore of knowledge (vijjā) as if reaching the further shore of saṃsāra—an Arahant (khīṇāsava) endowed with the three knowledges or the six supernormal powers. One should not disturb, strike, or offend such a person. 'na ca attavaṇṇaṃ parisāsu byāhare' means one should not speak of one's own praise, virtues, gains, offerings, or fame in assemblies of Khattiyas and so on, while craving them. 'Anuddhato' means being free from restlessness (uddhacca). For people do not take to heart or respect the words of one who is restless. 'Sammitabhāṇī' means one who speaks well and in a measured way; one who has the habit of speaking words connected with the goal, which are limited and reasoned, at the proper time. The words of one who speaks otherwise are not worthy of being accepted. 'Subbato' means one who is well-conducted and endowed with virtue (sīla). The verb 'siyā' (should be) should be brought in and connected.

Thus, the Elder briefly stated the characteristics of a Dhamma preacher. Realizing that those qualities existed in himself and seeing the great multitude of people who were exceedingly inspired, he spoke the second verse beginning with 'susukhumanipuṇatthadassinā' to show that 'for such a Dhamma preacher who relies on the foundation of liberation (arahattaphala), Nibbāna is not difficult; rather, it is easily attained.' The meaning of that verse has already been stated below.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Visākhapañcālaputta is Finished.

## 6. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Cūḷaka

'Nadanti morā susikhā supekhuṇā' is the verse of the Venerable Elder Cūḷaka. What is its origin? This Elder Cūḷaka also had performed special meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit that serves as a support for liberation from saṃsāra in various existences. Thirty-one aeons ago, during the time of the Blessed One Sikhī, he was born into a good family. Upon reaching maturity, he saw the Blessed One and, with a heart full of faith, offered a chattapaṇṇi fruit. Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans. In this Buddha-era, he was born into a Brahmin family in Rājagaha and received the name 'Cūḷaka'. When he came of age, he gained faith in the Blessed One who had tamed the elephant Dhanapāla and ordained. Desiring to practice the Dhamma of a monk, the Elder resided in the Indasāla Cave. One day, while sitting at the entrance of the cave, he was looking at the fields of Magadha. At that moment, a great rain of the rainy season thundered with a pleasant sound to the ear.
426:
Elder Cūḷaka, having gained faith in the Buddha and ordained, was practicing the recluse's Dhamma while residing in the Indasāla Cave. One day, while sitting at the entrance of the cave, he looked out over the fields of Magadha. At that moment, a great early-season rain cloud, with a deep and sweet sound, composed of thousands of layers, resembling a mountain of collyrium (Añjana), filled the sky and began to pour down. Groups of peacocks, hearing the thunder, became joyful and delighted; they uttered their 'kekā' cries and wandered about dancing in various places. For the Elder, too, because of the cool touch of the rain-wind inside the monastery chamber, his physical body became tranquil and healthy, free from distress. Having obtained a suitable climate (utu-sappāya), his mind became one-pointed and entered the path of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna). Realizing this, and wishing to urge himself toward meditation by praising the perfection of the season and so forth, he recited these two verses:

Peacocks cry, with beautiful crests and beautiful plumage, with beautiful blue necks, beautiful faces, and beautiful songs; this great earth is also beautiful with lush green grass, the sky is beautiful with clouds, well-spread with water.

You, of healthy appearance, meditating with a good mind, well-exerted in the well-awakened Buddha's Dispensation; touch that supreme, deathless state, which is extremely pure, subtle, and difficult to see.

—Thus he recited these two verses.

In those verses, "Nadanti morā susikhā supekhuṇā, sunīlagīvā sumukhā sugajjino" means: Those peacocks are called "susikhā" because they possess beautiful crests grown on the top of their heads. They are called "supekhuṇā" because they possess many beautiful tail-feathers of various colors. They are called "sunīlagīvā" because they possess beautiful blue necks resembling the color of a blue lotus. They are called "sumukhā" because they have beautiful beaks and faces. They are called "sugajjino" because they utter pleasant and delightful sounds. Peacocks utter their 'kekā' cries, which correspond to the 'sajja' note, and cry out.
427:
(The peacocks) utter their cries and sing. "Susaddalā cāpi mahāmahī ayaṃ" means this great earth has beautiful meadows, meadows of beautiful dark green grass. "Subyāpitambu" means that because of the newly fallen rain, water is flowing in various places, thus it is well-distributed or widespread water. There is also a variant reading "susukkatambu", meaning extremely pure water. "Suvalāhakaṃ nabhaṃ" means this sky is filled all around with beautiful clouds resembling the petals of a blue lotus.

"Sukallarūpo sumanassa jhāyataṃ" means: Now, having obtained a suitable climate, you are of healthy appearance and have a nature fit for work (kammaniya). For the meditator (yogāvacara) who has a good mind because it is not overwhelmed by the hindrances (nīvaraṇa), while meditating by way of meditation on the object (ārammaṇူpanijjhāna) and meditation on the characteristics (lakkhaṇူpanijjhāna)...

"Sunikkamo... accutaṃ padaṃ" means: While meditating and developing in this way, being one with good exertion in the Dispensation of the Well-Awakened One, the Sammāsambuddha; [touch] that supreme Nibbāna which is "extremely white" (susukka) because of extremely pure virtue, "white" (sukka) because of its pure nature and not being the range of any defilement, "subtle" (nipuṇa) because it is the range of subtle knowledge, "difficult to see" (sududdasa) because of its supreme profundity, "supreme" (uttama) because of its sublime and noble nature, and "undeviating" (accuta) because of its eternal nature. Reach it (realize it) through right practice by personal realization.

Thus, while the Elder was admonishing himself, his mind became concentrated due to obtaining a suitable climate. He intensified his insight (vipassanā) and attained Arahatship. This is stated in the Apadāna:

"I saw the Leader of the World, shining like a blossomed Kaṇikāra flower, like the full moon, and like a blazing lamp-tree."

"I offered a banana to the Teacher, holding it up. With a confident mind and joyful heart, I paid homage and departed."

"Thirty-one aeons ago from now, because of the fruit I offered then, I have not known a bad destination (duggati). This is the fruit of offering fruit."

"My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha's Dispensation has been fulfilled."
428:
Having attained the fruit of Arahantship, the Elder reviewed his own practice and, filled with joy and delight, recited once again that very verse beginning with "Nadanti morā". This verse of the Elder was indeed his declaration of final knowledge (aññābyākaraṇa).

## The Commentary on the Verses of Cūḷaka Thera is finished.

## 7. The Commentary on the Verses of Anūpama Thera

"Nandamanāgataṃ cittaṃ" and so forth is the verse of the Venerable Anūpama Thera. As for its origin—this Elder had also performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit that serves as a support for the attainment of Arahantship in various births. Thirty-one aeons ago from this present Bhadda-kappa, he was born into a respectable family. When he reached the age of discretion and wisdom, one day he saw the Paccekabuddha named Paduma walking for alms in the street. With a heart full of faith, he worshipped him with aṅkola flowers. Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans, and in this present Buddha-dispensation, he was born into a wealthy family in the Kingdom of Kosala. Because he was endowed with perfect physical beauty, he received the name Anūpama (Incomparable). When he came of age, being endowed with the necessary support for Arahantship, he renounced sense pleasures, ordained as a monk, and lived in the forest practicing Vipassanā meditation. However, his mind wandered toward external objects such as visible forms. His meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) also became unsettled. Wishing to restrain his wandering mind, the Elder admonished himself with these two verses:

"O mind, arisen with delight in sense objects, like one being impaled on a stake,
You go toward those very states where there is a stake like a birth and sense pleasures like a chopping block.

I shall speak of you, the unlucky mind; I shall speak of you, the treacherous mind.
Though a Teacher who is hard to find has been found, do not urge me toward what is harmful."

In those verses, "Nandamanāgataṃ cittaṃ" means the arising of the mind that is attached to and delights in sense objects. "Sūlamāropamānakaṃ" means the mind that is like being impaled on a stake for such a long time by means of kamma and defilements in various births, which are like stakes because they cause suffering. "Tena teneva vajasi, yena sūlaṃ kaliṅgaraṃ" means wherever...
429:
...the births known as stakes and the sense pleasures known as chopping blocks exist, there you go, O evil mind, by means of sense pleasure alone. You approach only those places and do not notice your own harm.

Because you have a nature of being heedless, I call you 'Cittakali', the one with inauspicious characteristics of mind. Because you bring harm to your own internal continuity (santāna) which is of great benefit, I shall further call you 'Cittadubbhi', the treacherous friend of the mind. Some also read it as 'Cittadubbhagā', which means one who is devoid of glory and has little merit, known as the mind.

If you ask what I say, I say: 'You have found the Teacher who is very hard to find; do not urge me toward what is harmful.' For many countless aeons, the world remains empty of Buddhas. Even when a Teacher arises, obtaining human birth, being endowed with faith, and so forth, are indeed rare. Even when human birth and such are obtained, meeting the Teacher is also difficult. Such a Teacher, who is hard to find, has now been found by you. Having found Him, do not join me with unwholesome states that bring harm and lack of benefit in the present, and bring harm and suffering in the future. Thus, the Elder, admonishing his own mind, developed Vipassanā and reached the fruit of Arahantship.

Therefore, it was said in the Apadāna:
'The Buddha named Paduma lived then on Mount Cittakūṭa. Having seen that Buddha, the Self-Enlightened, the Unconquered,

Seeing an aṅkola tree in full bloom, I then gathered the flowers, approached the Buddha, and worshipped the Victorious Paduma.

In the thirty-first aeon from now, because of the merit of worshipping with those flowers, I have not known a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.

My defilements have been burned away... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.'

## The Commentary on the Verses of Anūpama Thera is finished.
430:
## 8. The Commentary on the Verses of Vajjita Thera

"Saṃsaraṃ dīghamaddhānaṃ" and so forth is the verse of the Venerable Vajjita Thera. What is its origin? This Elder had also performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit in various births. Sixty-five aeons ago from this present Bhadda-kappa, he was born in a frontier village. When he reached the age of discretion, he became a forest-dweller. While wandering, one day he saw the Paccekabuddha named Upasanta living in a mountain cave. Seeing the peaceful faculties of that Paccekabuddha, he was filled with faith and made an offering of a campaka flower.

Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans, and in this present Buddha-dispensation, he was born into a wealthy family in the Kingdom of Kosala. From the day he was born, he would cry whenever he was placed in the hands of women. It is said that because he had passed away from the Brahma realm and come here, he could not endure the touch of women. Therefore, because of his avoidance of the touch of women, the name "Vajjita" (The One who Avoids) was given to him. When he came of age, he saw the Buddha's miraculous Twin Miracle (yamaka-pāṭihāriya) and gained faith. He ordained, established Vipassanā, and on that very day became one endowed with the six supernormal powers (abhiññā). Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

'The Buddha named Upasanta lived in the midst of the mountains. Taking a single campaka flower, I approached that Best of Men.

With a faithful heart and a joyful mind, I raised both hands and worshipped that Unconquered Great Sage (Paccekamuni).

In the sixty-fifth aeon from now, because of the merit of worshipping with that flower, I have not known a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.

My defilements have been burned away... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.'

Being one with the six supernormal powers, he recollected his own past lives and, with spiritual urgency (dhamma-saṃvega), recited these two verses:

"Wandering for a long time, I have revolved through the realms of existence,
As a blind worldling (puthujjana), not seeing the Noble Truths.

For me, who am now diligent, the rounds of saṃsāra have been destroyed,
All realms of rebirth are cut off; now there is no more renewed existence."
431:
In this verse, 'saṃsaraṃ' means wandering and roaming from one existence to another through the power of taking up and laying down the burden of the aggregates. 'Dīghamaddhānaṃ' means for a long time, for an immeasurable period in the beginningless saṃsāra. 'Gatīsu' means in happy and unhappy destinations through the power of deeds well-done and ill-done. 'Parivattaṃ' means revolving like a machine, repeatedly occurring in other existences through the power of death and rebirth. The reason for such repeated revolving is stated as: "The worldling, being blind, does not see the Noble Truths." This means not seeing the four Noble Truths, such as suffering, with the eye of wisdom, and not penetrating them. Because of this lack of knowledge, being blinded by the darkness of ignorance, and being a worldling who generates many defilements, one revolves repeatedly in the five destinations. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

"Bhikkhus, through not understanding and not penetrating the four Noble Truths, both you and I have wandered and roamed for such a long time."

For me, who was formerly a worldling in the manner described, and who now, through the method given by the Teacher, is mindful and diligent, having brought the development of Samatha and Vipassanā to its peak, 'saṃsārā vinalīkatā' means that the karmic defilements known as 'saṃsāra'—because beings wander by means of them—have been completely cut off by the Path of Arahantship, made stainless and rootless. 'Sabbā gatī samucchinnā' means that because the cycle of karma and defilements has been cleared, all destinations such as hell have been thoroughly destroyed. For this reason, there is no more renewed existence in the future. This was the elder's declaration of final knowledge (aññā).

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Vajjita is finished.

## 9. The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Sandhita

'Assatthe haritobhāse' is the verse of the Venerable Elder Sandhita. What is its origin? This elder also had performed meritorious services under previous Buddhas and, accumulating merit in various existences, was a cowherd during the time of the Blessed One Sikhī, thirty-one aeons ago. When the Teacher attained Parinibbāna, that cowherd approached an unnamed elder...
432:
Having approached the elder and heard the Dhamma concerning the qualities of the Buddha, he was inspired. When he asked, "Where is the Blessed One staying?" and heard that He had attained Parinibbāna, he gained the perception of impermanence, thinking, "Even Buddhas of such great power must follow the way of impermanence. Alas, formations are unstable; they are indeed impermanent!" That elder encouraged him to worship the Bodhi tree. From time to time, he went near the Bodhi tree, practiced Vipassanā, and paid homage to the Bodhi tree while repeatedly recollecting the qualities of the Buddha.

Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans. In this Buddha's dispensation, he was reborn in a wealthy family in the Kosala country and received the name Sandhita. Upon reaching maturity, he heard a Dhamma discourse concerning impermanence, was moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega), and went forth as a monk. Practicing Vipassanā, because his knowledge had matured, he soon became an Arahant endowed with the six supernormal powers. Recollecting his past lives, he remembered his worship of the Bodhi tree, his recollection of the Buddha, and his attainment of the perception of impermanence during the time of the Blessed One Sikhī. Wishing to manifest his attainment of distinction through that supporting condition, he spoke these two verses:

"At the Assattha tree, shining green and well-grown,
Being mindful, I gained a single perception directed toward the Buddha.
Thirty-one aeons ago, I gained that perception then;
By the power of that perception, I have reached the destruction of the taints."

In those verses, 'assatthe' means at the site of the Assattha tree. Currently, our Blessed One's Bodhi tree is an Assattha tree. At that same site, the Bodhi tree of the Blessed One Sikhī was a Puṇဍarīka tree. It is called 'assatthe' because it stood at the site of the Assattha tree. Alternatively, it is called 'assattha' because it brings relief (assāsa) to beings. Other teachers, however, say, "The elder said 'assatthe' because he sat at the foot of an Assattha tree and developed the recollection of the Buddha at that time." 'Haritobhāse' means shining with a green color like that of an emerald. 'Saṃvirūḷhamhi' means well-grown and well-established; some also say it means covered with very dense leaves, branches, and shoots. 'Pādape' means at the tree. 'Ekṃ buddhagataṃ saññaṃ alabhitthaṃ patissato' means...
433:
Because it has a single type of object, namely the Buddha, it is called 'single' (eka). I obtained the perception (saññā) associated with the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānussati), which proceeds in the manner beginning with 'Itipi so bhagavā' (Thus indeed is the Blessed One), being one who possesses mindfulness that repeatedly recollects the virtues of the Buddha because of the repeated refuge in those virtues.

Regarding when that perception was obtained and how long it took to be fulfilled, it is said: 'Thirty-one aeons ago from this [aeon],' and so forth. This occurred thirty-one aeons ago, counting upwards from this Auspicious Aeon (Bhadda-kappa). 'Yam saññam' refers to the perception associated with the recollection of the Buddha; or alternatively, having seen the impermanence of the Buddhas, and following that, I then obtained the perception of impermanence (anicca-saññā) regarding all formations of the three planes (tebhūmaka-saṅkhāra). 'By the power of that perception' means by making that aforementioned perception a causal condition and a strong support. 'I have reached the destruction of the taints' means that I have now attained the Fruition of Arahantship (arahatta-phala), which is the destruction and cessation of the four taints (āsavas). These very verses are also the Apadāna verses of this Elder Sandhita. As it is said:

'At the Bodhi tree of the Assattha species, shining with a green hue... [pe]... I have reached the destruction of the taints.
Thirteen aeons ago from now, there was a kshatriya named Dhaniṭṭha,
A Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) of great power, endowed with the seven jewels.
My defilements have been burnt away... [pe]... the teaching of the Buddha has been carried out.'

## The Commentary on the Verses of Sandhita Thera is finished.

## The Commentary on the Fifth Chapter (Vagga) is finished.

## The Commentary on the Book of Twos (Dukanipāta) is also finished.
434:
## 3. The Book of Threes (Tikanipāta)

## 1. Commentary on the Verses of Aṅgaṇikabhāradvāja Thera

In the Book of Threes, the verse beginning with 'Ayoni suddhimanvesanti' is the verse of the Venerable Aṅgaṇikabhāradvāja Thera. What is its origin? This Elder had also performed special meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and was accumulating merit that serves as a support for liberation (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) in various births. Thirty-one aeons ago from this Auspicious Aeon, in the time of the Blessed One Sikhī, he was born in a respectable family. Upon reaching maturity, one day he saw the Teacher wandering for alms. With a devoted mind, he paid homage with the five-fold prostration (pañcapatiṭṭhita) and raised his hands in salutation (añjali). Through that meritorious deed, he wandered among devas and humans, and in this Buddha-arising, he was born in the house of a wealthy Brahmin in the city named Ukkaṭṭha near the Himalayas, receiving the name Aṅgaṇikabhāradvāja. When he came of age, he became proficient in the sciences and arts. Due to his inclination toward renunciation, he went forth as a wandering ascetic (paribbājaka). While practicing 'deathless' penance and wandering from place to place, he saw the Fully Enlightened One wandering on a journey through the countryside. With a devoted mind, he heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, abandoned that false penance, and went forth in the Dispensation. While practicing the work of insight (vipassanā), he soon became one who possessed the six higher powers (chaḷabhiññā). This is stated in the Apadāna:

'The pre-eminent bull among men, the hero, the seeker of excellence, the conqueror of the five Maras,
With a devoted and joyful mind, I paid homage to the most excellent Buddha.
Thirty-one aeons ago from now, the deed I performed then,
Because of the fruit of that homage, I do not know of any miserable rebirth (duggati).
Twenty-four aeons ago, there was one named Vikatānanda,
A Universal Monarch of great power, endowed with the seven jewels.
My defilements have been burnt away... [pe]... the teaching of the Buddha has been carried out.'

Having become one with the six higher powers and dwelling in the bliss of liberation, out of compassion for his relatives, he went to his birthplace and established many relatives in the refuges and the precepts. Returning from there, in the Kuru country, at a market town named Kuṇḍiya...
435:
While dwelling in a forest in a remote area, he went to Uggārāma for some business and met with Brahmin friends who had come from the northern region (Uttarāpatha). Those Brahmins asked him, 'O Bhāradvāja, seeing what benefit did you abandon the tradition of the Brahmins and adopt this tradition?' Wishing to show them that there is no purity outside of this Buddha's Dispensation, he spoke the first verse:

'Seeking purity through improper means, I worshipped the fire in the forest.
Not knowing the path to purity, I performed penance for immortality.'

In that verse, 'ayoni' means by improper means or wrong methods. 'Suddhiṃ' means purity from the cycle of rebirth (saṃsāra) or escape from the three planes of existence. 'Anvesaṃ' means seeking. 'Aggiṃ paricariṃ vane' means that with the thought 'This is the path to purity,' he built a fire-chamber in a fire-sacrifice hall in a forest hermitage and, offering oblations, worshipped the fire-god according to the procedures mentioned in the Vedas. 'Suddhimaggaṃ ajānanto, akāsiṃ amaraṃ tapaṃ' means that not knowing the path to Nibbāna, which is true purity, he practiced self-mortification (attakilamathānuyoga) such as the five-fold fire penance (pañcatapa), just like fire-worship, thinking it to be the 'path to purity.'

Thus, the Elder showed that although he had striven through fire-worship and other Vedic rituals—like one wandering from one hermitage to another—he had not reached purity, and thus there is no purity outside the Dispensation. Now, wishing to show that 'I have attained purity in this very Dispensation,' he spoke the second verse:

'That bliss of Nibbāna has been attained through a pleasant path; behold the excellent nature of the Dhamma.
The three knowledges have been reached; the teaching of the Buddha has been carried out.'

In that verse, 'taṃ' refers to that Nibbānic bliss for the sake of which he had sought purity through fire-worship and painful penance without knowing the path; that bliss has now been attained and realized by me through the pleasant practice of Samatha and Vipassanā, without resorting to self-mortification. 'Passa dhammasudhammataṃ' means behold the excellent nature of the Dhamma of the Teacher's Dispensation...
436:
“Look at and know the nature of the Dhamma that leads out of Saṃsāra without deviation,” he says, either by way of addressing the Dhamma or by way of addressing himself. Then, wishing to show that he has attained that Dhamma, he said:

“The three knowledges have been attained; the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

This verse has the meaning already stated. Because he has attained purity in this way, wishing to show that “From this time forth, I am a Brahmin in the ultimate sense,” he spoke the third verse:

“Formerly, I was a relative of Brahmins (Brahmabandhu) by lineage alone; now I am truly a Brahmin.
I am one endowed with the three knowledges (tevijja), one who has bathed (nhātaka), a master of the scriptures (sottiya), and a knower of the Vedas (vedagū).”

The meaning of that verse is: Prior to this, I was called a ‘relative of Brahmins’ (Brahmabandhu) by the designation of Brahmins based on birth alone. But now, because I have abandoned evil and because I have attained the fruit of Arahantship, I am a true ‘Brahmin’ in the ultimate sense. Prior to this, by studying the three knowledges known as the Vedas which accumulate existence, I was a ‘Tevijja’ (possessor of three knowledges) by name alone; now, by the power of the knowledge that brings an end to existence, I have attained the three knowledges and am thus a ‘Tevijja’ in the ultimate sense. Similarly, prior to this, being attached to the pleasures of existence and completing the practice of ritual bathing, I was a ‘Nhātaka’ (one who has bathed) by name alone; now, because the stains of defilements have been well-washed away by the water of the Eightfold Path, I am a ‘Nhātaka’ in the ultimate sense. Prior to this, by contemplating the mantras that delight in unliberated existence, I was a ‘Sottiya’ (master of scriptures) by mere conventional usage; now, by contemplating the Dhamma that is free from delight in existence and well-liberated, I am a ‘Sottiya’ in the ultimate sense. Prior to this, by merely reaching the end of the Vedas which contain unabandoned evil qualities, I was named ‘Vedagū’ (knower of the Vedas); now, by the Path-knowledge known as ‘Veda,’ I have reached the far shore of the flood of Saṃsāra and the Four Noble Truths, having attained and known them, and thus I have become a ‘Vedagū’ in the ultimate sense. Hearing these words, the Brahmins expressed great faith in the Dispensation.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Aṅgaṇikabhāradvāja Thera is finished.
437:
## 2. Commentary on the Verses of Paccaya Thera

“I have been ordained for five days” is the verse of the Venerable Paccaya Thera. What is its origin? This elder also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit in various births. Ninety-one aeons ago, during the time of Vipassī Buddha, he was born into a good family. When he reached the age of discretion, one day he saw the Buddha walking along the bank of the river named Vinatā. With a mind full of faith, he plucked large, beautiful Udumbara fruits and offered them to the Buddha.

Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered only in the happy realms. In this Bhadda-kappa, when Kassapa Buddha appeared in the world, turning the noble Wheel of Dhamma and helping those who were teachable, he ordained in that Dispensation and practiced Vipassanā. One day, contemplating the suffering of Saṃsāra, he was deeply moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega). While staying in the monastery, he made a firm resolve: “I will not leave this monastery until I reach Arahantship.” Although he strove hard, because his wisdom was not yet mature, he was unable to make his Vipassanā intense.

After passing away, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans. In the time of the present Buddha, he was born into a kshatriya family in the city of Rohita and was named Paccaya. When he reached adulthood, he ascended the throne after his father’s passing. One day, he began to make a great royal offering to the four Great Kings. A great multitude of people gathered there. At that assembly, in order to inspire King Paccaya, while the multitude was watching, the Buddha sat on a jeweled lion-throne in a jeweled mansion created by Vessavaṇa in the sky and preached the Dhamma. A great number of people attained the Dhamma. Having heard that Dhamma, King Paccaya also renounced the kingdom and, urged by his past merits, ordained.

Just as he had made a promise in the time of Kassapa Buddha, he made a similar vow and entered the monastery. While developing Vipassanā, because his wisdom had matured, he attained Arahantship at that very moment. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

“By the bank of the Vinatā river, the Supreme Man (Vipassī Buddha) dwelt. I saw the Buddha, free from dust, one-pointed, and well-composed.

With a mind full of faith in Him, the washer of the stains of defilements, I took an Udumbara fruit and offered it to the Best of Buddhas.”
438:
“Because of the fruit I gave ninety-one aeons ago, I do not know any miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of offering fruit.

In this Bhadda-kappa, with a mind full of spiritual urgency, I ordained in the Dispensation of Kassapa Buddha.

Having ordained thus, I devoted myself to meditation, making the resolve: ‘I shall not leave the monastery.’

Though I had not yet reached the supreme goal then, now, through the maturity of my wisdom, I am quenched. I have reached the unshakable state, having touched the deathless goal.

My defilements are burnt up... (and so on) the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

After reaching Arahantship, wishing to inform others by way of praising his own practice, he spoke thus:

“I have been ordained for five days, a trainee (sekha) who had not yet attained the goal. When I entered the monastery, this was my heart’s resolve:

I shall not eat, I shall not drink, I shall not leave the monastery, nor shall I lie down to sleep even on one side to remove bodily fatigue, as long as the dart of craving that has pierced my heart is not pulled out.

Behold my energy and effort as I lived in this way! The three knowledges have been attained; the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

He spoke these three verses.

In those verses, “I have been ordained for five days” (pañcāhāhaṃ pabbajito) means: I have been a monk for five days; the fifth day from the day of ordination has been completed as a trainee. “A trainee who had not yet attained the goal” (sekho appattamānaso) means: he is called a trainee (sekha) because he is still training in the higher virtue, higher mind, and higher wisdom. ‘Mānasa’ refers to the fruit of Arahantship because it absolutely cuts off (samucchindati) conceit (māna); thus it means one who has not yet reached that Arahantship.
439:
One whose mind has not yet reached the fruit of Arahantship is called 'appattamānaso'. The phrase 'Vihāraṃ me paviṭṭhassa, cetaso paṇidhī ahū' means: 'When I, who was still a trainee (sekha), entered the dwelling cell of my residence, there arose a resolution of the mind in the following manner; thus was my mind directed.'

The resolution of the mind is shown by the words starting with 'Nāsiassaṃ'. In that verse, 'Nāsiassaṃ' means: 'As long as the dart of craving residing in my heart is not removed, I shall not eat any food.' This should be applied to all subsequent terms in the same way. 'Na piviassāmi' means: 'I shall not drink any beverage.' 'Vihārato na nikkhamē' means: 'I shall not leave this cell where I am now sitting.' 'Napi passaṃ nipātessaṃ' means: 'I shall not lay down even one side of my body to relieve physical fatigue; I shall not even lie down on one side.'

'Tassa mevaṃ viharato' means: 'For me, who was dwelling thus, having directed the mind and made a firm determination of energy, and practicing insight (vipassanā).' 'Vīriyaparakkamaṃ passa' means: It is called 'vīriya' (energy) because it is to be exerted in the proper way; it is called 'parakkama' (exertion) because it steps towards the highest state. See and know this effort which has become strenuous. The meaning of 'By the power of which I have attained the three knowledges and fulfilled the Buddha's teaching' is just as previously stated.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Paccaya Thera is finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Verses of Bākula Thera

The verses beginning with 'Yo pubbe karaṇīyāni' are those of the Venerable Bākula Thera. What is the background story? It is said that in the past, one hundred thousand aeons and one incalculable period (asankheyya) ago, even before the appearance of the Blessed One Anomadassī, he was born into a Brahmin family. Upon reaching maturity, he learned the three Vedas. Seeing no essence in them, he thought, 'I will seek the welfare of the hereafter,' and went forth as an ascetic. Dwelling at the foot of a mountain, he attained the five superknowledges and the eight meditative attainments. Hearing of the Buddha's arising, he went to the Teacher, heard the Dhamma, and established himself in the refuges. When the Blessed One Anomadassī suffered from an abdominal ailment, he brought medicinal herbs from the forest and cured that illness. Having performed this merit of offering medicine to cure the Buddha, he passed away and was reborn in the Brahma realm. After wandering through the happy realms for an incalculable period, he was born into a good family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. Seeing the Teacher appoint a certain monk to the foremost position (etadagga) among those of little illness (appābādha), he desired that same position and made a resolution. He accumulated merit for the rest of his life. While wandering only in the happy realms, even before the appearance of the Blessed One Vipassī, he was born into a Brahmin family in the city of Bandhumatī. As in the previous manner, he went forth as an ascetic, attained jhānas and superknowledges, and while dwelling at the foot of a mountain, he heard of the appearance of the Blessed One Vipassī...
440:
...and established himself in the refuges. When an ailment called 'grass-flower disease' (tiṇapupphaka-roga) broke out among the monks, he cured that disease. Having lived out his lifespan in that life, he passed away and was reborn in the Brahma realm.

After wandering through the realms of gods and humans for ninety-one aeons, he was born into a good family in Bārāṇasī during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa. While living the household life, he saw a large, dilapidated monastery and had all the dwellings, such as the uposatha hall, rebuilt. He provided all kinds of medicine to the Saṅgha of monks and performed meritorious deeds for the rest of his life.

After wandering through the realms of gods and humans during the interval between two Buddhas (buddhantara), even before the appearance of our Blessed One, he was born into the house of a treasurer in Kosambī. While he was being bathed in the Great Yamunā River to ensure his health, he was swallowed by a fish from the hands of his nurse. That fish fell into the hands of a fisherman and was bought by the wife of the treasurer of Bārāṇasī. When it was being cut open, he remained unharmed due to the power of his merit. She took him as her son and raised him. Hearing of this event, his biological parents came and requested, 'This is our son, give him to us.' The King decided, 'Let him belong to both families,' and appointed him as the heir to both families. Thus, he received the name 'Bākula' (meaning 'two-families'). Upon reaching maturity, he enjoyed great wealth. At the age of eighty, he heard the Dhamma from the Teacher, gained faith, and went forth as a monk. He remained a worldling (puthujjana) for only seven days, and at dawn on the eighth day, he attained Arahantship together with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā).

This is stated in the Apadāna:
'Not far from the Himalayas, there is a mountain named Sobhita. On that mountain, a well-constructed hermitage was created for me and my disciples. In that hermitage, there were many pavilions. There were also Sindhuvara trees in bloom. In that hermitage, there were many fruit trees. Jīvajีva birds sang there. In that hermitage, there were many Nigguṇḍī trees. There were also jujube and emblic myrobalan fruits.'
441:
Not far from the Himalayas, there is a mountain named Sobhita. On that mountain, there was my hermitage, well-constructed by my disciples.

In that hermitage, there were many pavilions. There were many Sindhuvāra trees in bloom, as well as wood-apple trees. Jīvajīvaka birds were also frolicking (as if in bloom).

In that place, there were many Nigguṇḍi trees. There were also jujube, myrobalan, phārusaka, and gourd plants, along with blooming white lotuses.

There were āḷaka, bael, plantain, and citron trees. There were also many mahānāma, ajjuna, and piyaṅgu trees.

Kosamba, saḷala, neem, banyan, and kapitthana trees were also there. Such was the nature of my hermitage. I lived in that hermitage together with my disciples.

The Blessed One Anomadassī, the Self-Enlightened One, the Leader of the World, seeking seclusion, came to my hermitage.

When the Great Hero Anomadassī of great fame arrived, in an instant, a wind ailment arose in the Lord of the World.

While wandering in the forest, I saw the Leader of the World. Approaching the Buddha, the Visionary of great fame—

At that time, seeing the Buddha's condition, I truly recognized and noted that an illness had arisen in the Buddha.

I quickly returned to the hermitage where my disciples were. Desiring to provide medical treatment, I then called and addressed my disciples.

Upon hearing my words, all the disciples, out of respect for me and out of respect for the Teacher, assembled together.

Quickly climbing the mountain and searching for all kinds of medicinal herbs, I prepared a medicinal drink and offered it to the Excellent Buddha.

When the Great Hero, the All-Knowing Leader of the World, had partaken of that medicine, the wind ailment of the Sugata, the Great Seer, was quickly appeased.
442:
Seeing that the distress had been appeased, the famous Anomadassī Buddha, sitting on his seat, spoke these verses:

"He who has offered medicine to me and has calmed my illness, I shall praise him; listen to my words.

For a hundred thousand aeons, he will delight in the heavenly realm. When musical instruments are played there, he will always rejoice.

When he comes to the human world, urged by the momentum of his merit, he will become a wheel-turning monarch a thousand times.

Fifty-five aeons ago, he will be a king named Anoma, a conqueror of the earth bounded by the four oceans, the lord of Jambudīpa.

Endowed with the seven treasures, a wheel-turning monarch of great power, he will even cause the Tāvatiṃsa heaven to tremble and exercise sovereignty.

Whether as a god or a human, he will be free from illness. Having abandoned grasping, he will transcend the danger of disease in the world.

In an incalculable time from this aeon, a Buddha named Gotama, born of the Okkāka clan and of the Gotama lineage, will appear in the world.

He will be an heir to that Buddha's Dhamma, a breast-born son, created by the Dhamma; fully understanding all taints (āsavas), he will attain Nibbāna, free from taints.

Having burned away the defilements, he will cross the stream of craving. He will be a disciple of the Teacher named Bākula.

Knowing all this with direct knowledge, Gotama, the Bull of the Sakyans, sitting in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks, will appoint him to the foremost position."

The Blessed One Anomadassī, the Self-Enlightened One, the Leader of the World, seeking solitude, came to my hermitage. With a confident heart, I satisfied the Great Hero, the All-Knowing Leader of the World, who had arrived, with all kinds of medicines using my own hands.

That deed of mine was a well-performed deed. It was the perfection of the seed in the Buddha, who is like a fertile field. It is impossible to exhaust the fruit of that deed. At that time, by seeing the Buddha, I performed a good deed. By the remainder of that deed, I have reached the unshakable Nibbāna.

Knowing all this with direct knowledge, Gotama, the Bull of the Sakyans, sitting in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks, appointed me to the foremost position.
