In an incalculable aeon from this Bhadda-kappa, I performed that meritorious deed. Since then, I have never known a miserable rebirth (duggati). This is the result of offering medicine. My defilements have been burned away. I have practiced the teaching of the Buddha.

Having thus attained the fruit of Arahantship, one day, when the Buddha was appointing his disciples to their respective positions in order, the Venerable Bākula, who was placed in the foremost position (Etadagga) among those with little illness, at the time near his Parinibbāna, addressed the monks in the midst of the Saṅgha, and wishing to explain further based on his advice, spoke the verses beginning with 'Yo pubbe karaṇīyāni'.
443:
That well-performed deed of mine was like the perfection of seeds in a fertile field, which is the Buddha. I am unable to exhaust that merit; at that time, I performed a well-done deed.

For me to have seen the Buddha, the supreme leader of gods and humans, is a great gain; it is a gain well-obtained. By the remainder of that wholesome karma, I have reached the unshakable state.

Having known all this with direct knowledge, Gotama, the Bull of the Sakyans, while sitting in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks, placed me in the foremost position.

In an incalculable aeon from this Bhadda Kappa, I performed that wholesome deed. Since then, I have not known a miserable rebirth. This is the fruit of offering medicine.

My defilements are burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.

Having attained Arahantship, one day, while the Teacher was assigning his disciples to their respective positions, the Venerable Bākula was placed in the foremost position of those with little illness (appābādha). At the time of his Parinibbāna, while giving an exhortation to the monks in the midst of the Saṅgha, wishing to explain another meaning, he said:

'He who wishes to do later what should have been done before, falls away from the state of happiness and later suffers repeatedly.

One should speak only of what one would do; one should not speak of what one would not do. The wise recognize the one who speaks without acting.

How very happy indeed is Nibbāna, taught by the Fully Enlightened One—sorrowless, stainless, and secure—where all suffering ceases.'

He recited these three verses.

Among them, 'Yo pubbe karaṇīyāni... kātumicchati' means: a person who, even during the time before being oppressed by old age, sickness, and so on, fails to perform wholesome deeds that bring about their own welfare and happiness due to negligence, and later wishes to do them after the proper time has passed. The word 'so' is merely a particle. At that time, however, because of being oppressed by old age, sickness, and so on, they are unable to act. Being unable, 'sukhā so dhaṃsate ṭhānā, pacchā ca manutappati' means that person falls away from the happy state of heaven and Nibbāna, or from the happy state of the celestial realm, or from Nibbāna, or from the happy place of heaven and Nibbāna. They fall away because they did not perform [the deeds]. In the later period, being oppressed by old age, sickness, and so on, they suffer repeatedly and reach a state of mental distress; this is what he intended to show.

He then spoke the second verse beginning with 'Yañhi kayirā.' In that verse, regarding the word 'parijānanti,' they recognize him, defining him as 'who is this person?' Many people do not know. They know, 'This person is one who speaks without acting.' Only one who acts as he speaks through the power of right practice is called wise. He does not speak in any other way. Why? Because he deals with things through the method of what should be done. Having shown the connection of the meaning in this way, he now spoke the third verse beginning with 'Susukhaṃ vata' to show it in its specific form. In that verse, Nibbāna—taught by the Blessed One, the Fully Enlightened One who realized the Four Noble Truths rightly and by himself—is free from all kinds of sorrow...
444:
Because one has not produced the wholesome states which are the means to the happy states of heaven and Nibbāna, one who falls away from them regrets later, thinking 'I have not done what is good,' and so on, and falls into remorse. (The letter 'm' is a euphonic junction.) Desiring to show, 'But I, having done what was to be done, speak to you thus,' he spoke the second verse beginning with 'Yañhi kayirā'. In that verse, 'parijānanti' means they know by defining, 'This person is only this much'; they do not think of him as more than he is. Indeed, by the power of right practice, one who acts as he speaks is beautiful, not otherwise. To show specifically the meaning already stated generally by way of the 'duty to be done' (karaṇīya-pariyāya), he now spoke the third verse beginning with 'Susukhaṃ vata'. The meaning of that verse is: Nibbāna is indeed very happy—Nibbāna which is peaceful (asoka) because of the total absence of causes for sorrow, stainless (viraja) because of being free from the dust of greed and so on, and secure (khema) because of not being oppressed by the four yokes (yoga)—as taught by the Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, because of his being enlightened as to all dhammas rightly by himself. Why? Because in that Nibbāna, the entire suffering of the round (vaṭṭadukkha) ceases and is utterly stilled.
## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Bakula is finished.
## 4. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Dhaniya
The verse beginning with 'Sukhañce jīvituṃ icche' belongs to the Venerable Elder Dhaniya. What is its origin? He too had performed meritorious services under previous Buddhas and, accumulating merits in various births, was reborn in a family home during the time of the Buddha Sikhi. Having reached the age of discretion, he saw the Teacher one day and, with a confident mind, made an offering of a garland of reeds (naḷamālā). Through that meritorious deed, he wandered through the worlds of gods and humans, and in this Buddha-era, he was reborn in a potter's family in Rājagaha and received the name Dhaniya. When he came of age, he made a living through the craft of pottery. At that time, the Teacher, while staying in the potter Dhaniya's shed, taught the Chadhātuvibhaṅga Sutta to the clansman Pukkusāti. Having heard it, Pukkusāti became one who had done what was to be done (an Arahant). Hearing of his Parinibbāna, Dhaniya gained faith, thinking, 'The Buddha's dispensation is indeed leading out of suffering, since even through a single night's association, one can be freed from the suffering of the round,' and he ordained.
445:
While living devoted to decorating his hut, the monk Dhaniya was rebuked by the Blessed One on account of his hut-building. Subsequently, while living in communal lodgings (saṅghika), he developed insight (vipassanā) and attained Arahatship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

'I saw the Buddha, golden-hued, the recipient of offerings brought from afar, the Leader of the World, walking through the forest.

Taking a garland of reeds and coming out at that moment, I saw the Buddha there, who had crossed the flood and was free from taints.

With a confident and joyful mind, I offered the garland of reeds to the Buddha, the worthy recipient, the Great Hero, who has compassion for the whole world.

In the thirty-first aeon from this auspicious aeon, I offered that garland; since then, I have not known the four woeful states. This is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.

My defilements have been burned away... (p) ... I have followed the teaching of the Buddha.'

Having attained Arahatship, some monks who exalted themselves through the undertaking of ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) looked down on other monks who enjoyed communal meals and such. To give them advice and to declare his attainment of Arahatship, he spoke these three verses:

'If one wishes to live happily, being regardful of recluseship, one should not despise communal robes, drinks, or food.

If one wishes to live happily, being regardful of recluseship, one should resort to lodgings as a snake resorts to a mouse hole.

If one wishes to live happily, being regardful of recluseship, one should be content with whatever is obtained and should develop the one Dhamma.'

In those verses, 'If one wishes to live happily, being regardful of recluseship' means: if one wishes to live happily by having regard for the state of a recluse and having keen respect for the training (sikkhā), and if one wishes to live with the happiness of a recluse by abandoning wrong livelihood.
446:
The meaning is: one should not despise communal property such as robes, alms-food, and requisites received from the Saṅgha. Any gain that arises for the Saṅgha is of extremely pure origin. For a monk who uses such communal gains, the happiness of recluseship is already in his hand due to the arising of purity of livelihood (ājīvapārisuddhi). This is the intention. 'As a snake resorts to a mouse hole' means one should resort to lodgings as a snake uses a hole dug by a mouse. For example, just as a snake does not make its own dwelling but lives in a dwelling made by a mouse or another creature and then goes wherever it pleases, even so, a monk should live in any place and then move on, without falling into the defilement caused by building a lodging himself. This is the meaning.

Now, wishing to show that the happiness of recluseship occurs only through contentment with whatever requisites are obtained—whether mentioned or not—and not otherwise, he said: 'One should be content with whatever is obtained.' The meaning is: one should achieve contentment with whatever requisites are received, whether they be low or excellent. 'The one Dhamma' refers to the state of diligence (appamāda). For a monk who devotedly practices that diligence, all blameless mundane and supramundane happiness is already in his hand. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'The heedful one, meditating, reaches abundant happiness.'

## The Commentary on the Verses of Dhaniya Thera is finished.

## 5. Commentary on the Verses of Mātaṅgaputta Thera

The verse beginning with 'Atisītaṃ' is that of the Venerable Mātaṅgaputta Thera. As for the circumstances of its origin: It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, this Elder was reborn as a powerful Naga king in a great Naga palace beneath the large Jātassara Lake near the Himalayas. One day, while wandering out from the Naga palace, he saw the Teacher traveling through the air. With a confident mind, he made an offering with the jewel from his head. Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, and in the time of this Buddha's arising, he was born in the Kingdom of Kosala as the son of a wealthy man named Mātaṅga...
447:
(Mātaṅgaputta) was born as the son of a wealthy man named Mātaṅga and became well-known as Mātaṅgaputta. When he reached the age of discretion, being lazy by nature, he did not perform any work and was criticized by his relatives and others. Thinking, "These recluses of the Sakyan son live a comfortable life," and desiring such a comfortable livelihood, he became acquainted with the monks. He approached the Teacher, heard the Dhamma, and having gained faith, he ordained. Seeing other monks endowed with psychic powers, he aspired to possess such powers himself. Taking a subject of meditation from the Teacher and applying himself to its cultivation, he became an Arahant endowed with the six higher knowledges (abhiññā). This account is stated in the Apadāna as follows:

The Buddha named Padumuttara, who had reached the further shore of all phenomena and desired seclusion, was traveling through the air.

Not far from the Himavanta mountains, there was a lake named Mahājātassara. There, I had a mansion associated with my meritorious deeds.

Coming out of the mansion, I saw the Lokanātha (Protector of the World). He was as beautiful as a blooming blue lotus and as radiant as a blazing fire.

Though I searched for flowers to offer to the Buddha, I found none. So, having inspired faith in my own mind, I paid homage to the Teacher.

Taking the gem from my head, I offered it to the Lokanātha. I prayed, "May the result of this offering of a gem be excellent."

The Teacher Padumuttara, the Knower of the Worlds, worthy of offerings, standing in the mid-air, spoke this verse:

"May your intention be fulfilled; may you obtain abundant happiness. Through this offering of a gem, enjoy great fame."

Having spoken thus, the Blessed One named Jalajuttama, the Supreme Buddha, departed to wherever he intended.

For sixty aeons, I exercised the sovereignty of the king of devas. And for many hundreds of times, I was a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti).

While being a deva and recollecting my former meritorious deeds, a gem would appear for me, providing me with light.

Eighty-six thousand women, who were my retinue, adorned with various garments and ornaments and wearing gem earrings, with long eyelashes, smiling faces, and slender waists, always surrounded me. Ornaments made of gold, gems, and rubies, and whatever goods I desired, came into being for me. Delightful palaces, houses, and noble beds appeared according to my desire, knowing my thoughts. For those who heard (of my story), it was the gain of a good fortune. My merit of seeing the Buddha, who is the field of merit for mankind and the medicine for all beings, was well-performed. I have been liberated from the four woeful states and have reached the stable Nibbāna. Whether born as a deva or a human, in whatever existence I reached, the seven treasures always appeared for me. There was light day and night without interruption. Because of that very offering of a gem, having enjoyed various prosperities, the light of wisdom...
448:
Eighty-six thousand women, who were my retinue, possessed various garments and ornaments and wore gem earrings.

Those women, endowed with long eyelashes, smiling faces, good perception, and slender waists, always surrounded me. This is the fruit of the offering of a gem.

Ornaments made of gold, gems, and likewise of rubies, as well as excellent goods as desired, came into being for me.

Delightful palaces, houses, and costly beds appeared according to my desire, as if they knew my thoughts.

Those who have the opportunity to hear (the Dhamma) are those who have obtained a good gain. (It is noble to see the Buddha) who is the field for planting merit for mankind and the medicine for all beings.

I, who have seen the Buddha, the pinnacle of humans and devas, have performed merit well. I have been liberated from the four woeful states and have reached the stable Nibbāna.

Whether born as a deva or a human, in whatever existence I may be, there is always light for me, day and night, at all times.

Only because of that merit of offering a gem, after enjoying all forms of prosperity and happiness, I have seen the light of wisdom and reached the stable Nibbāna.

One hundred thousand aeons ago, I offered a gem; since that time, I have never known (rebirth in) the four woeful states. This is the fruit of the offering of a gem.

My defilements are burnt away... the teaching of the Buddha has been carried out.

Being endowed with the six higher knowledges (abhiññā), censuring laziness by way of referring to a person and wishing to praise his own exertion of energy, he said this:

"It is too cold, it is too hot, it is too late in the evening"—saying thus and abandoning their work, the (auspicious) moments (khaṇa) pass by such young men.

But he who considers cold and heat as no more than a blade of grass, and performs the duties of a man, does not fall away from happiness.
449:
"I will push aside with my chest the dabba-grass, the kusa-grass, the poṭakila-grass, the usīra-grass, and the muñja and babbaja grasses, desiring to repeatedly cultivate the three kinds of seclusion (viveka)." He spoke these three verses, including this one.

In those verses, "atisītaṃ" means extremely cold due to snowfall, overcast skies, and so on; the word is brought in and connected as "this time is too cold." "Atiuṇhaṃ" means extremely hot due to the heat of summer and so on; by these two terms, he spoke of the grounds for laziness by way of the season. "Atisāyaṃ" means very late in the evening due to the passing of the day; by taking the evening, the morning is also included here; by these two, he spoke of the grounds for laziness by way of time. "Iti" means in this manner. By this statement, he includes the grounds for laziness taught as "Here, monks, a monk has work to be done," and so forth. "Vissaṭṭhakammante" means in those who have abandoned the work of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna). "Khaṇa" means the opportunities for living the holy life, such as the arising of a Buddha. "Accenti" means they pass by. "Māṇave" refers to beings. "Tiṇā bhiyyo na maññati" means he does not regard [hardships] as more than grass; regarding them just like grass, he overcomes cold and heat and performs his own task of meditation. "Karaṃ" means one who is doing. "Purisakiccāni" means the duties to be performed by a great man, namely one's own benefit and the benefit of others. "Sukhā" means from happiness, the meaning being from the happiness of Nibbāna. The meaning of the third verse has already been stated below.

## The explanation of the verses of Elder Mātaṅgaputta is finished.

## 6. Explanation of the Verses of Elder Khujjasobhita

"Those who are eloquent and learned" is the verse of the Venerable Khujjasobhita. What is the origin? It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was born in a respectable family and, upon reaching maturity, one day saw the Blessed One walking with a large Saṅgha of monks. With a devoted heart, he praised the Buddha with ten verses. Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans. In this Buddha's era, he was born into a Brahmin family in the city of Pāṭaliputta and was named "Sobhita." Because he had a slight hunchback, he was well-known only as "Khujjasobhita." When he reached maturity...
450:
...was his name. Because he had a slight hunchback, he was known only as Khujjasobhita. When he reached maturity, after the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna, he was ordained in the presence of the Elder Ānanda and became an Arahant endowed with the six supernormal powers (abhiññā). This is stated in the Apadāna:

"Who, seeing the Blessed One, the God of gods, the Bull among men, as graceful as a blooming Kakudha tree, walking on the road, would not be devoted?

"Who, seeing the Blessed One, who destroys the darkness of delusion, saves many people, and shines with the light of knowledge, would not be devoted?

"Who, seeing the Leader of the World, followed by a hundred thousand masters of their own minds, lifting many beings [from saṃsāra], would not be devoted?

"Who, seeing the Blessed One, striking the drum of Dhamma, crushing the groups of heretics, and roaring a lion's roar, would not be devoted?

"Who, seeing the Blessed One, to whom gods including Brahmas come from the Brahma realm to ask subtle questions, would not be devoted?

"Who, seeing the Blessed One, to whom those including gods pay homage with joined palms and make requests, thereby enjoying the fruits of merit, would not be devoted?

"All people gather and surround the One with Vision; though urged and requested, he remains unshaken. Who, seeing him, would not be devoted?

"When he enters a city, many drums sound and rutting elephants trumpet. Who, seeing such a Blessed One, would not be devoted?

"When he walks on the street, all splendors always shine, and uneven ground becomes level. Who, seeing such a Blessed One, would not be devoted?

"When the Buddha speaks, it is heard throughout the universe; he makes all beings understand. Who, seeing such a Blessed One, would not be devoted?

"Because of the fruit of praising the Buddha a hundred thousand aeons ago, I do not know of any rebirth in the four woeful states.

"My defilements are burnt away... [pe] ...the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled."
451:
Furthermore, that Elder, having become endowed with the six higher powers (abhiññā), at the time of the First Great Council when the Saṅgha had assembled at the Sattapaṇṇi Cave in Rājagaha, was commanded, "Invite the Venerable Ānanda." He then dived into the earth and emerged in front of the Elder Ānanda. Having conveyed the message of the Saṅgha, he himself went through the air beforehand and reached the door of the Sattapaṇṇi Cave.

At that time, a certain deity, sent by the assembly of devas to prevent Māra and his host, was standing at the door of the Sattapaṇṇi Cave. To that deity, the Elder Khujjasobhita, wishing to announce his arrival, spoke the first verse:

"Those eloquent speakers, very learned, recluses living in Pāṭaliputta; one among them, this long-lived one, Khujjasobhita, stands at the door."

In that verse, "cittakathī" means those who are habituated to giving varied Dhamma talks. It means those who have the habit of teaching the Dhamma according to the inclinations of others through various methods, such as teaching in brief, teaching in detail, making it profound, making it clear, dispelling doubts, and establishing them in the Dhamma. "Bahussutā" means they are very learned because of the fulfillment of great learning in both the scriptures (pariyatti) and realization (paṭivedha). They are "samaṇā" because of the total calming of evil. "Pāṭaliputtavāsinotesaññataro" means one among those monks who are called Pāṭaliputtavāsī because they usually reside in the city of Pāṭaliputta. "Ayaṃ āyuvā" refers to this long-lived venerable one. "Dvāre tiṭṭhati" means he stands at the door of the Sattapaṇṇi Cave to enter with the permission of the Saṅgha.

Hearing that, the deity, wishing to inform the Saṅgha of the Elder's arrival, spoke the second verse:

"Those eloquent speakers... (as before)... stands at the door, wafted by the wind (māluterito)."

In that verse, "māluterito" means wafted by the wind generated by the psychic mind; it means one who has arrived by the power of psychic potency.
452:
Thus, being informed by that deity and given permission by the Saṅgha, the Elder Khujjasobhita, while proceeding to the presence of the Saṅgha, declared his attainment of Arahantship with this third verse:

“By fighting well, by sacrificing well,
And by victory in battle,
By practicing the holy life,
This one thus attains happiness.”

In that verse, ‘suyuddhena’ means by fighting well against the defilements (kilesas) in the preliminary stage through the power of abandonment by substitution (tadaṅgapahāna) and abandonment by suppression (vikkhambhanapahāna). ‘Suyiṭṭhena’ means by having well received the suitable gift of Dhamma (dhammadāna) given from time to time by noble friends (kalyāṇamittas). ‘Saṅgāmavijayena ca’ means by obtaining victory in battle through the crushing of all defilements and volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra) by the power of abandonment by eradication (samucchedapahāna). ‘Brahmacariyānuciṇṇena’ means by the holy life of the highest path (aggamagga-brahmacariya) which has been practiced. ‘Evāyaṃ sukham edhati’ means that in the manner described, this Elder Khujjasobhita experiences and enjoys the happiness of Nibbāna and the happiness of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti).

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Khujjasobhita is Finished.

## 7. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Vāraṇa

“Whoever here among men” (Yodha koci manussesu) is the verse of the Venerable Elder Vāraṇa. What is its origin? He also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and, accumulating merit in various births, was reborn in a Brahmin family ninety-two aeons ago, even before the appearance of the Blessed One Tissa. Having reached the far shore of the Brahminical sciences and arts, he went forth as an ascetic (isi) and lived teaching the Vedas to fifty-four thousand disciples.

At that time, the Blessed One Tissa, being a Bodhisatta, passed away from the Tusita realm and descended into his mother’s womb for his final birth, causing the great earth to tremble. Seeing that earthquake, the great multitude became terrified and agitated; they approached that ascetic and asked the cause of the earthquake. He comforted them, saying, “The Great Bodhisatta has descended into his mother’s womb; because of that descent, this earth trembles. Therefore, do not be afraid.” He explained that it was a portent of the Buddha’s arising and made them experience joy (pīti) centered on the Buddha. By that meritorious deed...
453:
While wandering through the realms of devas and humans, during the time of this Buddha's appearance, he was born into a Brahmin family in the Kingdom of Kosala and received the name Vāraṇa. Upon reaching maturity, he heard the Dhamma in the presence of a certain forest-dwelling elder, gained faith, ordained, and practiced the duties of a recluse (samaṇadhamma). One day, while going to pay respects to the Blessed One, he saw a snake and a mongoose on the way that had quarreled and died. Seeing this, he thought, "These beings have reached the end of their lives due to mutual enmity," and with a mind moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega), he went to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, knowing his thoughts and wishing to give him advice suitable to his state of mind, spoke these three verses:

"Whoever among humans here harms other living beings,
That person falls away from the benefits and happiness of both worlds—this world and the next.

But whoever, with a mind of loving-kindness, has compassion for all living beings like one's own child,
Such a person, living in this way with loving-kindness, generates much merit.

One should learn the well-spoken scriptures (pariyatti), and associate with recluses who have calmed their defilements.
One should also practice dwelling alone in a secluded place and the tranquility of the mind."

He spoke these three verses.

In those verses, "yo'dha koci manussesu" means anyone in this world of humans, whether a khattiya, a brahmin, a vessa, a sudda, a householder, or a renunciant. The mention of "humans" here should be understood as indicating the highest class of beings. "Parapāṇāni hiṃsati" means killing and oppressing other beings. "Asmā lokā" means from this world, and "paramhā" means from the next world. "Ubhayā dhaṃsate" means falling away and being ruined from the benefits and happiness pertaining to both worlds. "Naro" means a being.

Having thus shown the unwholesome state characterized by the oppression of others, the Buddha now spoke the second verse beginning with "Yo ca mettena" to show the wholesome state characterized by abstaining from the oppression of others. Therein, "mettena cittena" means with a mind associated with loving-kindness, whether attained to absorption (appanā) or otherwise. "Sabbapāṇānukampatī" means developing loving-kindness toward all beings as if they were one's own children. "Bahuñhi so pasavati, puññaṃ tādisako naro" means such a person who dwells in loving-kindness obtains and attains much, not a little, merit.
454:
Now, wishing to urge him toward the practice of tranquility and insight (samatha-vipassanā) along with its components, the Buddha spoke the third verse beginning with "Subhāsitassa". Therein, "subhāsitassa sikkhetha" means one should learn the well-spoken pariyatti Dhamma, such as talks on wanting little (appicchatā-kathā), by way of hearing, retaining, and questioning. "Samaṇူpāsanassa ca" means one should learn to frequently approach and associate with recluses who are noble friends (kalyāṇamitta) and have calmed their evil, and to live near those elders through proper conduct. "Ekāsanassa ca raho cittavūpasamassa ca" means one who develops bodily seclusion by being alone without a companion should learn to dwell in a secluded place by way of devotion to meditation (kammaṭṭhāna). Thus, while devoting oneself to meditation and bringing the development (bhāvanā) to its peak, one should learn the calming of defilements and the tranquility of the mind by way of eradication (samuccheda). Through the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā) and so on, defilements are absolutely calmed and abandoned; for one who practices these trainings of the path and fruit, the mind is truly said to be absolutely tranquil. At the end of the verses, having developed insight, he attained Arahantship. This matter is stated in the Apadāna as follows:

"At that time, having entered the Himalayas, I taught the Vedas, and fifty-four thousand students attended to me."

"All the students learned the Vedas, reached the end, and attained mastery in the six limbs of the Vedas. Proud of their own knowledge, they lived in the Himalayas."

"The glorious deity, passing away from the Tusita realm, entered the mother's womb, mindful and clearly comprehending."

"When the Fully Enlightened One was conceived, the ten-thousandfold world system trembled. When the Leader of the world was conceived, the blind regained their sight."

"This entire earth trembled in every way. Hearing that thunderous sound, the great multitude of people were terrified."

"All the people gathered and came to me, asking, 'The earth has trembled; what will be the result of this?'"
455:
'I said to them then: "Do not fear, there is no danger for you. Be at ease, all of you; this arising is a sign of well-being."'
'Touched by eight causes, the earth trembles. Likewise, signs appear, and a great, vast radiance is seen.'
'Without doubt, the Excellent Buddha, the One with Vision, will arise. Having informed the people, I taught the five precepts.'
'Having heard of the five precepts and the rare arising of a Buddha, they were stirred with emotion and became joyful, glad, and delighted.'
'In the ninety-second aeon from this, I explained that sign. Due to the fruit of that explanation, I do not know any miserable rebirth.'
'My defilements are burnt... the Buddha's bidding has been done.'
## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Vāraṇa is finished.
## 8. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Vassika
The verse beginning with 'Ekopi saddho medhāvī' belongs to the Venerable Elder Vassika. As for its origin (uppatti): He too had performed special merit under previous Buddhas and did good deeds in various births. In the time of the Buddha Atthadassī, he was reborn in a good family home. Having reached the age of wisdom, he saw the Teacher one day and, with a confident heart, offered Pilakkha fruits. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered through the worlds of gods and humans, and in this Buddha-era, he was reborn in a Brahmin family in the Kosala country and was named Vassika. When he came of age, he saw the Teacher's Twin Miracle (Yamaka-pāṭihāriya), gained faith, and ordained. While practicing the recluse's duties, he became ill. Then his relatives attended to him with medicinal treatments prescribed by a physician and cured him. Having recovered from that illness, he was moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega), exerted himself in meditation, and attained the six supernormal knowledges (chalabhiññā). This is stated in the Apadāna (Ap. Thera 2.47.40-44):
456:
“Having seen the Buddha Atthadassī of great fame in the midst of the forest, with a clear and joyful heart, I offered a Pilakkha fruit.

In the eighteen hundredth aeon from now, because of that merit of offering the fruit, I have not known any rebirth in the four lower realms. This is the fruit of offering fruit.

My defilements are burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.”

Having become one possessed of the six supernormal knowledges, the elder went to his relatives through the air. Standing in the sky, he preached the Dhamma and established those relatives in the three refuges and the precepts. Among them, some who passed away were reborn in heaven because they were established in the refuges and precepts. Then, when the Venerable Vassika came to attend upon the Teacher, the Teacher asked him, “Dear Vassika, are your relatives well?” The elder, wishing to inform the Teacher of the assistance he had rendered to his relatives, spoke these three verses:

“Even a single person who is faithful and wise, established in Dhamma and endowed with virtue, is for the benefit of faithless relatives in this world.

Out of compassion, I urged and exhorted my relatives, and through the love I have for my kin, I made them make offerings to the bhikkhus.

Those relatives of mine, my mother and brothers, who have passed away, have reached the happiness of heaven; desiring sensual pleasures, they are now rejoicing.”

In those verses, the meaning of the first verse is: One who is 'faithful' (saddha) by way of faith in the fruit of kamma and faith in the Triple Gem; 'wise' (medhāvī) because of being endowed with the knowledge that kamma is one's own property (kammassakatā-ñāṇa) and so on; 'established in Dhamma' (dhammaṭṭha) because of being established in the Teacher’s teaching and the nine supramundane states; and 'endowed with virtue' (sīlasampanno) by way of virtue of conduct (ācāra-sīla), virtue of the path (magga-sīla), and virtue of the fruition (phala-sīla). Such a person, even if alone, is for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of 'relatives' (ñāti)—so called because they are known as 'ours' in this world—who are 'faithless' due to the absence of the aforementioned faith, and likewise for 'kin' (bandhu)—so called because they are bound by the bond of affection.
457:
In order to show the meaning thus stated in a general sense by applying it to himself, another verse beginning with "Niggayha" was spoken.

In that verse, "Niggayha anukampāya coditā ñātayo mayā" means: "I have admonished my relatives by restraining them, so that even now, being in a state of poverty and not having performed meritorious deeds, they may not experience suffering again in the future." Out of love for them as kin, thinking, "This person is our relative," they were unable to transgress my advice. Thus, performing meritorious deeds toward the monks with a clear and devoted mind, they made offerings of requisites such as robes and provided service, showing honor and respect to the monks. Having passed away, they have transcended this world. Furthermore, the word "te" is merely a particle. "Tidivaṃ sukhaṃ" means they reached either the happiness included in the heavenly realm or the desired heaven itself. Referring to the question, "Who are they?", he said: "My brothers and my mother, desiring sensual pleasures, are now rejoicing." The meaning is that they are enjoying themselves, being endowed with the objective sensual pleasures they desired.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Venerable Vassika is finished.

## 9. The Commentary on the Verses of Venerable Yasoja

"Kālapabbanga-saṅkāso" is the verse of the Venerable Yasoja. What is its origin? This Elder had also performed services of merit under previous Buddhas and was accumulating merits in various births. In the time of the Buddha Vipassī, he was born into a family of park-keepers. When he reached the age of discretion, one day he saw the Buddha Vipassī traveling through the air. With a devoted mind, he offered a breadfruit (labuja).

Through that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans. In the time of our Buddha's appearance, he was born as the son of a fisherman who was the head of five hundred families in a fishing village near the gate of the city of Sāvatthī. They named him Yasoja. When he came of age, he cast a net into the Aciravatī River to catch fish along with his companions, the sons of the fishermen. At that time, a large golden-colored fish entered the net. They showed that fish to King Pasenadi of Kosala. The King, thinking, "The Blessed One will know the reason for the beauty of this golden-colored fish," had the fish taken and...
458:
(The King) showed the fish to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said, "This fish, during the decline of the Dispensation of the Buddha Kassapa, became a monk but practiced wrongly, causing the Dispensation to decline, and was born in hell. After being cooked in hell for the interval between two Buddhas, he passed away from there and was born as a fish in the Aciravatī River." Having said this, the Buddha had the fish itself speak about how its sisters were born in hell and how its elder brother, a monk, had attained Parinibbāna. Based on this incident, the Buddha preached the Kapila Sutta.

Upon hearing the Buddha's teaching, Yasoja was struck with spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and ordained in the presence of the Blessed One along with his companions. While living in a suitable place, one day he went to the Jetavana Monastery with his followers to pay homage to the Blessed One. Upon their arrival, there was a loud and great noise in the monastery due to the arranging of lodgings and so forth. Hearing that, "The Blessed One dismissed Yasoja along with his followers" (Udāna 23); all should be understood according to the method mentioned in the Udāna. Having been dismissed, the Venerable Yasoja, with a mind as stirred as a noble thoroughbred horse struck by a whip, lived on the banks of the Vaggumudā River with his followers. Striving and exerting himself, he developed insight and, within that very rainy season, became a possessor of the six supernormal powers (chalabhiññā). This is stated in the Apadāna:

"In the city of Bandhumatī, I was then a park-keeper;
I saw the stainless Buddha traveling through the air.

Taking a breadfruit (labuja), I offered it to the Best of Buddhas;
The Great Famous One, standing in the air, accepted it.

Because of offering the fruit to the Buddha with a clear mind,
I gained joy that brings happiness in the present life.

At that time, I attained vast and supreme happiness;
Wherever I was born in various lives, treasures appeared.

In the ninety-one aeons since I gave that fruit,
I have not known a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of giving fruit.

My defilements have been burnt away... the Buddha's Dispensation has been fulfilled."

Thus it should be understood.
459:
The Teacher summoned the Venerable Yasoja, who possessed the six supernormal powers (chaḷabhiññā), along with his followers, and greeted them with the imperturbable attainment (āneñjasamāpatti). That elder undertook and practiced all the ascetic qualities (dhutaṅga). Because of this practice, the body of the Venerable Yasoja became thin, haggard, and of poor complexion. The Blessed One, wishing to praise him for his supreme fewness of wishes, spoke this first verse:

“Like a joint of a black creeper, thin, with veins showing, knowing moderation in food and drink, a man with an undaunted mind (is a great man).”

In that verse, ‘kālapabbangasaṅkāso’ means having a body like the joints of a black creeper (or bamboo) because his limbs were thin and poorly formed due to the absence of flesh. For that very reason, it is said, ‘kiso dhamanisanthato.’ ‘Kiso’ means having a thin body due to fulfilling the practice of a sage (moneyya-paṭipadā). ‘Dhamanisanthato’ means having a body overspread with veins; a body where the tendons and veins are prominent because of the small amount of flesh and blood. ‘Mattaññū’ means one who knows the proper measure in seeking, receiving, consuming, and discarding. ‘Adīnamānaso’ means one whose mind is not shrinking or depressed because it is not overcome by sloth and the like; one of unslothful conduct. ‘Naro’ means a man; the meaning is a leading man (purisadhoreyya) endowed with the characteristics of a man because he bears the burden of manly duties.

Thus praised by the Teacher, the Venerable Yasoja, in accordance with being so praised, wished to preach the Dhamma to the monks by way of extolling his own patient endurance, the arousal of energy, and his delight in seclusion. He recited these two verses:

“Though stung by gadflies and mosquitoes in the great forest, like a noble elephant in the heat of battle, one should endure there mindfully.

As a Brahmā is alone, so is one; as the gods are two, so are two; as a village is three, so are three; more than that is a tumult.”

In those verses, ‘nāgo saṅgāmasīseva’ means just as a noble thoroughbred elephant, having endured the strikes of swords, spears, and missiles in the circle of battle, destroys the enemy army; even so, a monk in the great forest should endure the dangers such as gadflies and the like.
460:
One should endure mindfully and with clear comprehension; and having endured, one should destroy the army of Māra by the power of meditation (bhāvanā).

“Yathā Brahmā” means just as a Brahmā lives alone, free from mental disturbance (anger) and always happy with the bliss of meditative absorption (jhāna); even so, “eko” means a monk also lives happily alone, without a companion, increasing the bliss of seclusion (viveka). Indeed, it is said that the happiness of recluseship for one who is alone is sublime. By this, he gives the instruction that a monk who lives alone is “equal to a Brahmā.” “Yathā devo tathā duve” means just as there may be occasional mental disturbances among the gods, even so, there may be friction when two monks live together. Because of living with a companion, such a monk is called “equal to a god.” In the passage “yathā gāmo tathā tayo,” the meaning is that the living together of three monks is like living in a village, and is not a secluded life. “Kolāhalaṃ tatuttariṃ” means the living together of many people beyond those three is a tumult, like a loud and great gathering of people. Therefore, the meaning is that one should be one who lives alone.

## The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Yasoja is Finished.

## 10. Sāṭimattiyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

“Ahu tuyhaṃ pure saddhā” and so forth are the verses of the Venerable Sāṭimattiya. What is the origin? This elder also had performed meritorious services under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merits in various births. In the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha, he was born in a good family, and upon reaching maturity, he saw the Teacher one day and, with a devout mind, offered a palm-leaf fan. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered among gods and humans, and in this Buddha-arising, he was born in a Brahmin family in the kingdom of Magadha and received the name Sāṭimattiya. When he reached maturity, being endowed with the necessary conditions, he went forth in the presence of forest-dwelling monks. While performing the work of insight (vipassanā), he became one who possessed the six supernormal powers. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

“I once offered a gold-decorated palm-leaf fan to the Blessed One Siddhattha. In the ninety-four aeons since I offered that palm-leaf fan, I have not known a woeful state. This is the fruit of offering a palm-leaf fan. My defilements are burnt away... (etc.) ...of the Buddha.”
461:
I offered a costly and noble palm-leaf fan, covered with jasmine flowers, to the Blessed One Siddhattha.

Ninety-four aeons ago from this auspicious aeon, I gave that palm-leaf fan. Due to that meritorious deed, I have never known a miserable rebirth. This is the fruit of offering a palm-leaf fan.

My defilements are burnt... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.

That Elder, endowed with the six supernormal knowledges (abhiññā), repeatedly instructed the monks. He preached the Dhamma to many beings and established them in the refuges and the precepts. He also inspired faith in a family that was previously faithless and uninspired. Consequently, the people of that family became very devoted to the Elder. In that house, a very beautiful and attractive young woman respectfully served the Elder with food when he entered for alms.

Then one day, Māra thought, "In this way, this Elder's fame will increase; he will become well-established." Thinking thus, he assumed the form of the Elder, went there, and took the young woman's hand. The young woman realized, "This touch is not a human touch," and made him release her hand. Seeing this, the household members lost their faith in the Elder.

On the following day, the Elder, without reflecting on the cause, went to that house again. The people there treated him with disrespect. When the Elder reflected and investigated the cause, he saw Māra's action and resolved, "Let a rotting dog carcass be fixed to that Māra's neck." He then threatened Māra, who had come to be released from the carcass, making him confess the deeds he had done the previous day, and then released him. Seeing this, the master of the house apologized, saying, "Venerable sir, please forgive my fault," and said, "From this day forward, I myself will serve you, venerable sir." The Elder, wishing to preach the Dhamma to that householder, spoke these three verses:

"O lay follower, previously you had faith; that faith does not exist in you today. Whatever is yours, let it be yours alone; there is no misconduct in me.

For faith is impermanent and unstable; so indeed it has been seen by me. People are attached and also detached; what does the Sage lose therein?

The Sage's meal is cooked little by little in every house. I will wander for alms; I have the strength of legs."

Thus he spoke these three verses.
462:
In those verses, "O lay follower, previously you had faith; that faith does not exist in you today" means: "O lay follower, before this time, you had faith in me, thinking, 'The noble one is a practitioner of Dhamma, a practitioner of evenness,' and so on. That faith of yours is not found today, at this moment." Therefore, "Whatever is yours, let it be yours alone" refers to the gift of the four requisites; let it be yours alone, I have no need for it. The intention is that a gift should be given with a truly confident mind.

Alternatively, "Whatever is yours, let it be yours alone" means that the disrespect you have shown toward me today belongs only to you; you alone must experience its fruit, not I. "There is no misconduct in me" means there is no such thing as misconduct in my continuity, because the defilements that are the causes of misconduct have been utterly cut off by the Path.

"Faith is impermanent and unstable" means that because the faith of worldlings is impermanent and not absolute, it is unstable, like a pumpkin placed on a horse's back, or like a stake driven into a heap of chaff. "So indeed it has been seen by me" means that such faith has been seen and personally known by me in you. "People are attached and also detached" means that because of that very instability, these beings sometimes become attached and show affection through friendship and intimacy, and sometimes they become detached and have a weary mind. "What does the Sage lose therein?" means: in that attachment and detachment of worldlings, what does the Sage, the renunciant, lose? What is his loss?

Showing that he should not think, "If you do not take my requisites, how will you survive?", he spoke the verse beginning with "is cooked" (paccati). Its meaning is: for the Sage, the renunciant, what is called a meal is cooked little by little, house by house, day by day; it is not cooked only in your house. "I will wander for alms; I have the strength of legs" means: I have the strength of legs; I am not one with broken legs, nor am I lame, nor do I have a foot disease. Therefore, I will wander for mixed almsfood. He shows: "I will survive by wandering for alms in the manner described by the Teacher, such as 'Just as a bee [takes nectar from] a flower...'"

## The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Sāṭimattiya is finished.
463:
## 11. Upālittheragāthāvaṇṇanā

The verse beginning with 'Saddhāya abhinikkhamma' is that of the Venerable Elder Upāli. The origin of this verse is as follows: This Venerable Elder Upāli was also born into a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of the Buddha Padumuttara. One day, while listening to the Buddha's discourse, he saw the Buddha appoint a certain monk to the foremost position among those who uphold the Vinaya. He performed an act of great merit and made an aspiration for that position. Having performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and wandering through the realms of devas and humans, he took rebirth in a barber's house during the time of this Buddha's appearance and was named Upāli.

When he came of age, he became one who inspired faith in the six princes, including Anuruddha. While the Buddha was staying at the Anupiya Mango Grove, he went forth and ordained together with the six princes who had come out to become monks. The procedure of Upāli's ordination is as it appears in the Pali (Cūḷavagga).

After ordaining and receiving full admission, he took a meditation subject from the Buddha and requested, 'Venerable Sir, please allow me to live in the forest.' The Buddha said, 'Dear monk, if you live in the forest, only one burden will increase for you. But if you live in our presence, you will fulfill both the burden of study (ganthadhura) and the burden of insight (vipassanādhura).' The Elder accepted the Buddha's words and, while practicing insight, soon attained Arahantship. This matter is stated in the Apadāna as follows:

In the city of Haṃsavatī, there was a Brahmin named Sujāta,
He had a hoard of eighty crores and was abundant in wealth and grain.

He was a reciter of the Vedas, a bearer of the Vedas, and had reached the far shore of the three Vedas,
He had reached perfection in the science of marks, the Itihāsas, and his own branch of knowledge.

At that time, wanderers, those with a single topknot,
Members of the Gotama clan, disciples of the Buddha,
Wanderers, and ascetics were traveling upon the earth.

They also surrounded me, saying, 'The Brahmin Sujāta is famous,'
Though many people honored me, I did not honor anyone.

I did not see anyone worthy of honor, so I was stiff with pride at that time,
As long as the Victorious One had not yet arisen, the word 'Buddha' did not exist.

With the passing of days and nights, the one named Padumuttara,
Having dispelled all darkness, the One with Five Eyes, the Buddha, arose in the world.
464:
When the Dispensation was widespread, known to many, and had become extensive, the Buddha then arrived at the city named Haṃsa (Haṃsavatī). For the benefit of his father, that Buddha, the One with Five Eyes, preached the Dhamma. At that time, the assembly extended for a league all around. There was an ascetic named Sunanda, who was esteemed as noble by the people. That ascetic then covered the entire assembly of the Buddha with flowers. While the Four Noble Truths were being revealed in the noble pavilion of flowers, a hundred thousand crores of beings attained the Dhamma. The Buddha, having rained down the rain of Dhamma for seven days and nights, when the eighth day arrived, the Victorious One praised the ascetic Sunanda.

'This person, wandering in the realms of devas or humans in this cycle of births, will be the most excellent of all and will wander through existences. One hundred thousand aeons from now, a Teacher named Gotama by clan, born of the Okkāka line, will arise in the world. His heir in the Dhamma, his breast-born son, created by the Dhamma, a disciple of the Teacher named Puṇṇa, the son of Mantāṇī, will come to be.'

Thus the Fully Enlightened One then praised the ascetic Sunanda, gladdening all the people and demonstrating his own power. People, with hands joined in reverence, bowed to the ascetic Sunanda. Having performed a great service to the Buddha, he purified his own destination. At that time, upon hearing the words of the Sage, the thought arose in my mind: 'I too shall perform a service so that I may see the Buddha Gotama.'

Having thought thus, I considered my own action. 'What deed shall I perform for the unsurpassed field of merit?' I thought. 'In the Dispensation of the Buddha who teaches the entire Pariyatti, this monk is placed in the foremost position in the Vinaya. I aspire to that position,' I thought.
465:
'This wealth of mine is immeasurable and vast, stable like the ocean. With that wealth, I shall create a monastery for the Buddha.'

On the eastern side of the city, I bought the grove named Sobhana for a hundred thousand pieces of money and created a Saṅghārāma.

Having constructed gabled houses, mansions, pavilions, flat-roofed mansions, caves, and well-made walkways, I created the Saṅghārāma.

Having built a hot-water bathroom, a fire-room, and also a water-stand and a bath-house, I donated them to the Saṅgha of monks.

Couches, benches, utensils, vessels, monastery attendants, and medicine—all these I donated.

Having established protection, I built a strong wall so that no one might harass those of peaceful minds, the such-like ones.

I built a dwelling in the Saṅghārāma for a hundred thousand pieces of money. Having built that extensive monastery, I offered it to the Fully Enlightened One.

'O Sage, I have completed the monastery; please accept it. O Hero, I dedicate it to you; O One with Five Eyes, please accept and reside in it.'

Padumuttara, the Knower of the World, the Receiver of Offerings, the Leader, knowing my intention, accepted it.

Knowing the acceptance of the Omniscient One, the Great Seeker of Virtue, I prepared food and announced the time for the meal.

When the time was announced, the Leader Padumuttara, along with a hundred thousand taintless ones (Arahants), came to my monastery.

Knowing the time when he was seated, I satisfied him with food and drink. Knowing the time when he had finished the meal, I spoke these words:

'O Sage, the monastery named Sobhana was bought for a hundred thousand, and it was built for that same amount. Please accept it, O Sage.'
466:
## 
By this gift of a monastery and by these intentions and aspirations, may I obtain my desired wish wherever I am reborn in the cycle of births. Having accepted the well-constructed monastery for the Saṅgha, the Buddha, seated in the midst of the community of monks, spoke these words: 'I shall praise the merit of him who gave this well-constructed monastery to the Buddha; listen to my words. A fourfold army of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry shall always surround him; this is the fruit of the gift of a monastery. Sixty thousand well-decorated drums shall always surround him; this is the fruit of the gift of a monastery. Eighty-six thousand women, adorned with various clothes and ornaments, wearing jeweled earrings, with wide eyebrows, smiling faces, good perception, and slender waists, shall always surround him; this is the fruit of the gift of a monastery. For thirty thousand aeons, he shall delight in the heavenly world; a thousand times he shall be the lord of gods (Sakka), exercising the kingship of gods. He shall obtain all that is to be attained by a king of gods; possessing undiminished wealth, he shall exercise the kingship of gods. A thousand times he shall be a Cakkavatti king in the land. He shall obtain vast kingship over the earth, beyond counting. One hundred thousand aeons from now, a Teacher named Gotama by clan, born of the Okkāka family, shall arise in the world. His heir in the Dhamma, his spiritual son, created by the Dhamma, a disciple of the Teacher named Upāli by name, shall come to be. Having reached perfection in the Vinaya, and being skilled in what is possible and impossible (ṭhānāṭhāna), he shall live without taints (anāsava), upholding the Dispensation of the Conqueror (Jina-sāsana).'
467:
The Buddha Gotama, the best of the Sakyans, knowing all this with direct knowledge, while seated in the midst of the community of monks, shall place me in the foremost rank (etadagga).

Starting from incalculable aeons, I have aspired for your Dispensation. That goal, the destruction of all fetters, I have now attained.

Just as a man tormented by royal punishment and impaled on a stake finds no pleasure on the stake but desires only liberation,

Even so, O Great Hero (Mahāvīra), I was tormented by the punishment of existence, impaled on the stake of kamma, and afflicted by the pain of thirst.

Burning with the three fires, I found no pleasure in the cycle of births; like one punished by a king, I sought liberation.

Just as a man who has consumed poison and is severely afflicted by it would seek medicine to remove the poison and preserve his life,

And while seeking, he might see the poison-destroying medicine, and by drinking it, he would be happy, being liberated from the poison,

Even so, O Great Hero, like a man struck by poison, I was severely afflicted by the poison of ignorance (avijjā) and sought the medicine of the True Dhamma (Saddhamma).

While seeking the medicine of Dhamma, I saw the Dispensation of the Sakyan Sage, which is the best of all medicines and the remover of all arrows.

Having drunk the medicine of Dhamma, I have removed all poison; I have touched and experienced Nibbāna, which is ageless, deathless, and cool.

Just as a person possessed by a spirit (bhūta), being tormented by that possession, would seek an exorcist to be liberated from the spirit,

And while seeking, he might see a physician skilled in spirit-mantras, and that exorcist would remove the spirit along with its cause and destroy it,

Even so, O Great Hero, I was tormented by the possession of the darkness of defilements; I sought the light of knowledge to be liberated from the darkness of defilements.
468: Then I saw the Sakyan Sage (Sakyamuni), the remover of the darkness of defilements; like an exorcist removing a spirit, he removed my darkness. Like an exorcist pulling it out from the root, I have cut the stream of Saṃsāra, blocked the stream of craving (taṇhā), and uprooted all existence. Just as a powerful Garuda (Garuḷa), seeing its food, a Naga, descends from the sky and agitates the great ocean for a hundred leagues around, and having seized the Naga, holding it head-downwards and harassing it, that bird flies away wherever it wishes, even so, O Great Hero, like a powerful Garuda, while seeking the Unconditioned (Asankhata), I have washed away my faults. I have seen the excellent Dhamma, the unsurpassed state of peace; carrying this excellent Dhamma, I dwell like a Garuda carrying a Naga. In the Cittalatā Grove, there grows a type of creeper named Āsāvatī. Only one fruit is produced from it every thousand years. Even though the time for fruiting is so distant, the gods attend to that creeper; that excellent Āsāvatī creeper is very dear and beloved to the gods. O Sage (Muni), I too have attended upon you for a hundred thousand aeons. Like the gods attending the Āsāvatī creeper, I always pay homage day and night. My service was not in vain, and my homage was not fruitless. Although I have come from afar, this rare occasion of a Buddha's arising (buddhupāda-khaṇa) has not failed me. Though I search through the cycle of births, I no longer see any further rebirth. Free from attachments (upadhi), liberated from defilements, and at peace, I wander. Just as a lotus blooms because of the sun's rays, even so, O Great Hero, I have bloomed because of the Buddha's rays. Among the species of cranes, there are never any males. Whenever the clouds thunder, those cranes always become pregnant.
469: As long as the thundercloud does not roar, (the cranes) carry their pregnancy for a long time; only when the rain falls are they released from that burden. While the Buddha Padumuttara was thundering with the rain of Dhamma, I took up the 'Dhamma-pregnancy' through the sound of that rain of Dhamma. For a hundred thousand aeons, I carried the 'merit-pregnancy'; I was not released from that burden because the rain of Dhamma did not thunder. O Sakyamuni, when You thundered with the rain of Dhamma in the pleasant city of Kapilavatthu, only then was I released from the burden. Thus, I gave birth to (realized) all the dhammas: the Suññata-magga, Animitta-magga, Appaṇihita-magga, and the four Fruits. For immeasurable aeons, I longed for Your teaching; that goal has been attained—the supreme state of peace (Nibbāna). I have reached the perfection in the Vinaya, like the sage Pāṭhika; there is no one equal to me; I uphold the Dispensation. In the Vinaya, the Khandhakas, the Tikaccheda, and the Pañcaka, I have no doubt, whether in the letter or the syllable. Skilled in censuring and rehabilitation, and in what is possible and impossible; I have reached perfection in all matters such as readmitting and rehabilitation. Whether in the Vinaya or the Khandhakas, having placed a word, I can explain it from both sides and delve into it by way of its essence. Very skilled in linguistics and expert in what is beneficial and what is not; having a concentrated mind in the Teacher's Dispensation, there is nothing unknown to me. Today, I am an expert in the nature of things in the Dispensation of the Sakyaputta; I dispel all doubt and cut through all uncertainty. In the word, the following word, the letter, and the syllable; in the beginning and the end; I am an expert in all things.
470: Just as a powerful king, having crushed his enemies and conquered in battle, builds a city in that place. He would have walls, moats, gate-pillars, and gate-towers built, as well as various watchtowers in the city. He would have crossroads, junctions, well-arranged shops, and a court (assembly hall) for deciding what is beneficial and what is not built there. To crush enemies, to know their weaknesses, and to protect the troops, the king appoints a general. To guard the royal treasures, he appoints a treasurer, skilled in storage, saying, 'Let my treasures not be destroyed.' To one who is devoted to the king and desires his prosperity, he gives the position of a judge to act as a friend. He appoints a chaplain who is skilled in omens, signs, and marks, and who is a reciter of mantras. One endowed with these factors is called a King (Khattiya); these factors always protect the king, just as a Cakkavāka bird protects its distressed mate. O Great Hero, likewise, You are like a king who has slain his enemies; You are called the King of Dhamma (Dhammarāja) of the world including the devas. Having subdued the heretics and conquered Māra with his army, having dispelled the darkness of delusion, You built the City of Dhamma (Dhammanagara). In that City of Dhamma, virtue is the wall; Your knowledge is the gate-tower; O Hero, Your faith is the gate-pillar; and restraint is the gatekeeper. The foundations of mindfulness are the watchtowers; O Sage, Your wisdom is the junction; the bases of power are the crossroads; the great road of Dhamma is well-constructed. The Suttanta, Abhidhamma, and the entire Vinaya—the ninefold word of the Buddha—is Your assembly hall of Dhamma.
471: The Suññata-vimokkha, Animitta-vimokkha, Appaṇihita-vimokkha, the Vihāra-dhamma, the Āneñja-samāpatti, and the Nirodha-samāpatti are Your Dhamma-shrine. The Elder named Sāriputta, who is appointed as the foremost in wisdom and is skilled in quick wit, is Your General of Dhamma. O Sage, the Elder named Kolita, who is skilled in the passing away and rebirth of beings and has reached the pinnacle of psychic power, is Your Chaplain. O Sage, the one who upholds the ancient lineage, who has fierce majesty, who is difficult to approach, and who is foremost in the quality of praising the ascetic practices (the Elder Mahākassapa), is Your Judge. O Sage, the Elder named Ānanda, who is of great learning, who upholds the Dhamma, and who can recite the entire scriptures in the Dispensation, is Your Treasurer of Dhamma. The Blessed One, having surpassed all these, compared me (in the Vinaya) and gave me the decision in the Vinaya taught to the wise. Whichever disciple of the Buddha asks a question regarding the Vinaya, I answer that very meaning without having to think about it. Excluding the Buddha, within the sphere of the Buddha, there is no one equal to me in the Vinaya; how could there be anyone superior to me? The Buddha Gotama, seated in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks, thundered thus: 'There is no one equal to Upāli in the Vinaya and the Khandhakas.' I, who am accustomed to looking at the root of the Vinaya, see that the entire ninefold Dispensation of the Teacher spoken by the Buddha is included within the Vinaya. Gotama, the Noble One of the Sakyans, remembering my deed, sat in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks and placed me in the foremost position. I have aspired for this position since a hundred thousand aeons ago. That goal has been attained, and I have reached the further shore in the Vinaya. Formerly, I was a barber who brought joy to the Sakyan princes. Having abandoned that birth, I have now become a son of the Great Sage.
472:
In the second aeon counting back from this Bhadda-kappa, there was a king named Añjasa, who possessed infinite power, incomparable retinue, great wealth, and ruled over the earth.

His son was a prince named Candana, who was arrogant and haughty due to the pride of his birth, as well as his retinue and wealth.

One hundred thousand elephants, adorned with all kinds of ornaments, being of the kind that secretes rut from three places, always surrounded me.

At that time, desiring to go to the park surrounded by my army, I mounted the elephant named Sirika and departed from the city.

The Paccekabuddha named Devala, who was accomplished in conduct, with guarded sense-doors and well-restrained faculties, came before me.

Then, I urged the elephant Sirika forward and harassed that Paccekabuddha. Because of that act, the elephant Sirika became angry and was unable to lift its feet.

Seeing the elephant in a state of anger, I in turn became angry at the Paccekabuddha. After harming and harassing that Paccekabuddha, I went to the park.

In that park, I could find no happiness; I was burned by intense anguish, like one whose head is ablaze, or like a fish that has swallowed a hook.

The entire earth, bounded by the oceans, seemed to be burning for me. Therefore, I approached my father and spoke these words:

"I have offended that Self-Enlightened Paccekabuddha, as if I had touched a provoked cobra, or as if I had touched a great mass of approaching fire, or as if I had touched a rutting tusker elephant.

I have offended that Paccekabuddha, the Conqueror (Jina) of fierce and intense austerity. Before we all perish, let us go and ask for forgiveness from that Noble Sage (Muni).

If we do not appease that Noble One, who is self-tamed and well-concentrated, my kingdom will be destroyed within seven days from now.

King Sumekhala, King Kosiya, King Siggu, and King Sattaka, having offended sages, fell into misery along with their kingdoms."
473:
When sages who are restrained in body, speech, and mind, and who practice the holy life, become angry, they can cause the destruction of the world of devas and humans, along with the oceans and mountains.

Gathering the men within three thousand yojanas, I approached the Paccekabuddha to confess my fault and ask for forgiveness.

With wet clothes and wet heads, everyone with hands joined in reverence prostrated at the feet of the Paccekabuddha and spoke these words:

"O Great Hero, please forgive us. These people appeal to you. Please dispel this burning anguish; do not let our kingdom be destroyed."

May all devas and humans, along with asuras and rakshasas, always split my head with an iron sledgehammer (if I harbor ill will).

Just as fire does not remain in water, as a seed does not grow on a rock, and as a worm does not live in medicine, even so, anger does not arise in a Paccekabuddha.

Just as the earth is unshakable, as the ocean is immeasurable, and as the sky is infinite, even so, the Buddhas (Paccekabuddhas) are imperturbable.

Those Great Heroes of austere practice are always patient and are to be forgiven. For those who are patient and forgiven, there is no (evil) destination.

Having spoken these words, the Paccekabuddha Devala, dispelling the burning anguish, flew up into the sky in the presence of the great multitude at that very moment.

O Hero, because of that karma I committed, I reached a low birth. Having fully transcended that existence, I have now entered the City of Fearlessness (Nibbāna).

O Great Hero, at that time also, you dispelled the burning anguish of me who was suffering, and you made me ask for forgiveness from the Paccekabuddha.

O Great Hero, now also, you have extinguished the three fires for me who was burning with them, and you have brought me to the state of coolness.

Let those who wish to listen with attention hear my words. I shall preach for your benefit concerning the state of Nibbāna that I have realized.
474:
Because I offended that Self-Enlightened Paccekabuddha, who was of peaceful mind and well-concentrated, I have been born today in a low caste due to that karma.

Do not let the opportune moment (of a Buddha's arising) pass you by; for those who have missed the moment truly grieve. Strive for your own benefit; the opportune moment has been provided to you.

(The Sasana) is like an emetic for some, and like a purgative for others. It is like the Halāhala poison for some, and like medicine for others.

It is the vomiting of defilements (emetic) for those established in the Path (Maggaṭṭha), and it is a purgative for those established in the Fruition (Phalaṭṭha). It is medicine for those who desire the benefit and seek the field of merit.

For those who oppose the Sasana, it is like the Halāhala poison. Just as a cobra that kills with its sight burns a person, so does the Sasana burn such a person.

Halāhala poison, once drunk, cuts off life. Having opposed the Sasana, one burns for tens of millions of aeons.

Through patience, non-violence, and a mind of loving-kindness, that Blessed Buddha saves the world of devas and humans. Therefore, one should not oppose those Buddhas.

Buddhas are not attached to gain or loss, nor to honor or dishonor. Buddhas are like the earth. Therefore, one should not oppose those Buddhas.

Towards the murderous Devadatta, the thief Aṅgulimāla, his son Rāhula, and the elephant Dhanapāla, the Sage is equal to all.

There is no resentment towards them, nor does greed exist in him. The Buddha is equal towards all—towards the murderer and towards his own son.

Even if one sees a saffron-dyed cloth (robe) discarded on the road and smeared with filth, one should place one's hands together in reverence on the head and worship that banner of the Sages (Isidhaja).

All the Buddhas of the past, the present, and the future are purified by this banner. Therefore, these robes are worthy of worship.

I carry in my heart the Vinaya, which is equal to the Teacher and provides good discipline. Worshipping the Vinaya, I shall dwell at all times.
475: The Vinaya is my abode; the Vinaya is my place for standing and walking. I dwell in the Vinaya; the Vinaya is my resort. ## O Mahāvīra, I, Upāli, who have reached the pinnacle in the Vinaya and am skilled in Samatha, pay homage to the feet of the Teacher. ## I shall wander from village to village, from city to city, paying homage to the Fully Enlightened One and knowing the excellence of the Dhamma. ## My defilements are burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled. ## Indeed, the Teacher himself taught the entire Vinaya Piṭaka to the Elder Upāli. Later, the Elder adjudicated these three cases: the Bhārukacchaka case, the Ajjuka case, and the Kumārakassapa case. At each adjudication, the Teacher uttered 'Sādhu', and based on those three adjudications, he appointed the Elder to the foremost position among those who uphold the Vinaya (Vinayadharas). Later, on an Uposatha day, while reciting the Pātimokkha, the Elder, wishing to admonish the monks, spoke these three verses: ## 'A newly ordained monk who has gone forth from the household life out of faith should associate with good friends (kalyāṇamittas) who have a pure livelihood and are not indolent. ## A newly ordained monk who has gone forth from the household life out of faith, being a monk who dwells in the Saṅgha, should be wise and train in the Vinaya. ## A newly ordained monk who has gone forth from the household life out of faith should be skilled in what is allowable and what is not, and should practice without being led by craving or views.' ## In these verses, 'saddhāya' means because of faith, not for the sake of a livelihood. Or it means having faith in the fruit of kamma and the virtues of the Triple Gem. 'Abhinikkhamma' means having departed from the household life. 'Navapabbajito' means one who has newly gone forth, having gone forth in the first stage of life. 'Navo' means one who is new and young in terms of training in the Dispensation. 'Mitte bhajeyya kalyāṇe suddhājīve atandite' means one should associate with, approach, and attend to good friends who possess the characteristics described as 'dear, respected, and venerable,' etc., those who have a pure livelihood by avoiding wrong livelihood, and those who are not indolent because they possess energetic effort; one should associate with them by receiving their advice and instructions. 'Saṅghasmiṃ viharaṃ' means (one who dwells) in the assembly of monks.
476:
One should associate with and approach those who have pure livelihood and are not lazy due to their aroused energy; one should serve them by accepting their advice and instructions. One should dwell in the Saṅgha, the community of monks, by fulfilling the major and minor duties. A wise person, being skillful in the knowledge of enlightenment, should learn the Vinaya scriptures. For the Vinaya is indeed the lifeblood of the Dispensation; as long as the Vinaya stands, the Dispensation stands. They also recite the word “Buddho” (the enlightened one); the meaning is the same. In matters of what is allowable and unallowable (kappākappesu), one should be subtle and skillful according to the Suttas and in accordance with the Suttas (suttānuloma). One should dwell without being led by craving and such, not expecting any gain from anywhere.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Upāli is Finished.

## 12. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Uttarapāla

“Though I was indeed wise” (Paṇḍitaṃ vata maṃ santaṃ) is the verse of the Venerable Elder Uttarapāla. What is its origin? This Elder also had performed special merit under previous Buddhas and, accumulating good deeds in various births, had a bridge built on the path where the Blessed One Vipassī was traveling. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, and in the time of this Buddha, he was reborn in a Brahmin family in Sāvatthī and received the name Uttarapāla. When he came of age, he saw the Twin Miracle and, gaining faith, went forth and practiced the Dhamma of a recluse. One day, due to unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra), sensual desire (kāmarāga) arose in him as he recollected an object he had previously experienced. Immediately, like catching a thief together with the stolen goods, he restrained his own mind. Struck by a sense of urgency, he suppressed the defilements through attention to the opposite (paṭipakkha-manasikāra). While performing the work of insight (vipassanā) and applying himself to meditation, he attained Arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna (Ap. ii.47.16-20):

“In the presence of the Blessed One Vipassī,
As he was walking to and fro,
With a confident and joyful heart,
I had a bridge constructed.”
477:
On the path where the Blessed One Vipassī was traveling, he had a bridge constructed. Due to the merit of donating that bridge, after wandering through the realms of devas and humans, he was reborn in a Brahmin family in Sāvatthī during the time of our Blessed One Gotama, and was named Uttarapāla. Upon reaching maturity, he witnessed the Twin Miracle (Yamaka Pāṭihāriya), gained faith, and ordained as a monk to practice the Dhamma. One day, due to improper attention (ayoniso manasikāra), the monk Uttarapāla repeatedly recollected past sensual objects he had experienced, and sensual lust (kāmarāga) arose in him. At that very moment, like catching a thief red-handed, he subdued his own mind, became struck with urgency (saṃvega), and by applying his mind to the opposing meditation subject (asubha), he removed the defilements. While striving in the practice of insight (vipassanā), he attained the fruit of Arahatship (arahattaphala). Therefore, it is stated in the Apadāna:

“Ninety-one aeons ago, I constructed a bridge; due to the merit of that gift of a bridge, I have not known a miserable rebirth.
My defilements have been burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.”

Having attained Arahatship and reflecting on his own practice, he wished to utter a lion's roar, saying:

“Though I was indeed a wise man, capable of considering what is beneficial, the five strands of sensual pleasure in the world caused me to fall (from steadiness) through delusion.
Having rushed into the realm of Māra, pierced by the firm arrow (of lust), I have been able to escape from the snare of the King of Death.
All my sensual desires are abandoned, all existences are destroyed, the wandering in the cycle of birth is exhausted, and now there is no more renewed existence.”

He uttered these three verses.

In those verses, “Paṇḍitaṃ vata maṃ santaṃ” means though being one endowed with wisdom by virtue of wisdom consisting of learning and reflection. “Alamatthavicintakaṃ” means capable of thinking of the welfare and benefit of oneself and others; or, capable and sufficient in considering the meaning; or, one who sees the meaning and is capable of destroying defilements. The Elder says all this because he is in his final existence. “Pañca kāmaguṇā” refers to the five groups of sensual objects, such as visible forms and so on. “Loke” shows the place where those sensual pleasures occur. “Sammohā” means because of the cause of delusion, which is improper attention; or, “sammohā” means from that which causes delusion or is delusive. “Pātayiṃsu” means they caused him to fall from the state of being a wise man; or the meaning is, they caused me, who wished to transcend the world, to fall back into the world.

“Pakkhando” means having entered into. “Māravisaye” means in the realm of defilements (kilesa), the place where the Māra of defilements (Kilesamāra) operates; the meaning is that he had come under its power. Or, it means having entered and stayed in the domain of Māra as a deity (Devaputta Māra). “Daḷhasallasamappito” means pierced by a firm and stable arrow, or pierced by a firm arrow; it means the heart was struck and pierced by the arrow of lust (rāga). “Asakkhiṃ maccurājassa, ahaṃ pāsa pmuccituṃ” means while pulling out the arrow of lust and so on without remainder using the pincers of the Supreme Path (aggamagga), I have been able to escape from the snare of Death, which is lust. Thus, he liberated himself.
478:
“I have been able to escape from the snares of the King of Death, known as the bond of lust; because of that, I have liberated myself.

Because of that liberation, all my sensual desires are abandoned, and all existences are destroyed. All sensual defilements (kilesa-kāma), which are of many kinds such as clothing, ornaments, and so on, have been abandoned by me through the Noble Path by way of total eradication (samuccheda-pahāna). Indeed, when sensual defilements are abandoned, objective sensuality (vatthu-kāma) is also abandoned. Likewise, all existences such as the sensual existence (kāma-bhava) and the existence of action (kamma-bhava) have been destroyed and demolished by the sword of Path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa). When the existences of action are destroyed, the existences of rebirth (upapatti-bhava) are also destroyed. Because the existences of action and so on are thus destroyed, it is said, ‘The wandering in the cycle of birth is exhausted, and now there is no more renewed existence.’ The meaning of this verse has already been explained below.
