This very verse was the Elder’s declaration of enlightenment (aññābyākaraṇa).

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Uttarapāla is finished.

## 13. The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Abhibhūta

“Listen, all kinsmen,” and so on, is the verse of the Venerable Abhibhūta Thera. What is its origin? This Elder also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit in various existences. In the time of the Blessed One Vessabhū, he was born in a good family, and upon reaching maturity, he became very devoted to the Dispensation (Sāsana) by relying on such a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitta). When the Teacher attained Parinibbāna and the great multitude was striving to take the relics, he himself was the very first to extinguish the funeral pyre (citaka) with scented water. Due to that meritorious deed, after wandering through the realms of devas and humans, he was born in the royal family of the city of Veṭhapura during the time of this Buddha’s appearance, and was named Abhibhūta. After his father’s passing, he ruled the kingdom. At that time, while the Blessed One was wandering through the countryside, he eventually reached that city. Then the King, hearing that “The Blessed One has arrived at my city,” went to the Teacher, heard the Dhamma, and on the second day, offered a great gift (mahādāna). After the Blessed One had finished his meal, he preached the Dhamma in detail, in accordance with the King’s inclination. Having heard the Dhamma and gained faith, the King renounced the kingdom, ordained, and realized Arahatship. Therefore, it is stated in the Apadāna:

“When the body of the Great Sage Vessabhū was being cremated,
I took scented water and extinguished the funeral pyre.
Thirty-one aeons ago from this auspicious aeon,
I extinguished the funeral pyre.
Due to the merit of that deed,
I have never known a miserable rebirth.
This is the fruit of donating scented water.
My defilements have been burnt away... (etc.)
The Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.”
479: Having received the name Abhibhūta, he was born and, after his father passed away, he ruled as king. At that time, the Blessed One, while wandering through the countryside, arrived at that city in due course. King Abhibhū, hearing that the Blessed One had arrived in his kingdom, went to his presence, listened to the Dhamma, and on the second day, offered a great donation. After the meal, the Blessed One gave a detailed discourse of appreciation (anumodanā) according to the King's inclination. Having heard the Dhamma, the King gained faith, renounced his royal splendor, ordained, and realized the fruit of Arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna: 'While the body of the Great Compassionate One, the Buddha Vessabhū, was being cremated, I took scented water and extinguished the funeral pyre. Thirty-one aeons ago from this present kappa, I extinguished that pyre. Due to the merit of that deed, I have never known a miserable rebirth. This is the fruit of offering scented water. My defilements are burnt away... (pe) ... I have followed the Buddha's teaching.' Having attained Arahantship and dwelling in the bliss of liberation, his relatives, ministers, attendants, and citizens from the city and countryside all gathered and lamented, 'Venerable Sir, why did you leave us helpless and ordain?' Seeing the multitude of people, led by his relatives, lamenting, the Elder wished to preach the Dhamma by explaining the reason for his ordination: 'Listen, all you relatives who have gathered here. I shall preach the Dhamma to you: birth again and again is suffering. Strive, go forth, and exert yourselves in the Buddha's teaching. Destroy the army of Death, as an elephant destroys a reed hut. Whoever dwells heedfully in this Dhamma and Discipline, having abandoned the wandering in birth (saṃsāra), shall make an end of suffering.' He spoke these three verses. Among them, 'Suṇātha' means listen; it means to pay attention to what I am about to say through the sense of hearing. 'Ñātayo' is an address to all, with relatives at the forefront. Thus he said, 'all you who have gathered here,' meaning as many as have come to this assembly or to my ordination ceremony. Now, having made the exhortation to listen with 'Suṇātha,' and promising 'I shall preach the Dhamma to you,' he began to preach with 'Birth again and again is suffering.' Therein, 'Birth again and again is suffering' means that birth is called suffering because it is the basis for various kinds of suffering, such as the initial descent into the womb and old age. That birth, occurring again and again, is extremely painful. Therefore, one should make an effort to transcend that birth. Thus, to the end of suffering...
480:
To show that effort should be made to transcend that birth, he spoke the verses beginning with "Exert yourselves." In that verse, "Exert yourselves" (ārambhatha) means to put forth the effort known as the element of initiation (ārambhadhātu). "Strive forth" (nikkamatha) means, having emerged from the side of laziness, to put forth the effort known as the element of exertion (nikkamadhātu), which is superior to that element of initiation. "Apply yourselves to the Buddha's Teaching" (yuñjatha buddhasāsane) means that for those established in these qualities—restraint in virtue, guarding the sense doors, moderation in eating, and being possessed of mindfulness and clear comprehension—the elements of initiation and exertion are fulfilled through the practice of wakefulness. Therefore, being in such a state, be intensely devoted to the Teaching of the Blessed One, which is known as serenity and insight, or the training in higher virtue and so forth. "Shatter the army of Death, as an elephant a hut of reeds" means that for those who practice in this way, because the King of Death, the lord of the three realms, leads beings into his power, you should shatter and dispel the weak mass of defilements known as his army, just as an elephant endowed with great strength destroys a hut made of reeds in an instant.

To show that for one who exerts himself in the Buddha's Teaching, the transcendence of the suffering of birth is certain, he spoke the third verse beginning with "Whoever in this..." That verse is easy to understand.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Abhibhūta is Finished.

## 14. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Gotama

The verses beginning with "Saṃsaranti" are those of the Venerable Elder Gotama. What is their origin (uppatti)? This Elder, having performed meritorious deeds of service (adhikāra) under previous Buddhas, continued to perform merits in various existences. When the Blessed One Sikhī attained Parinibbāna, while devas and humans were honoring the funeral pyre (citaka), he honored the pyre with eight campaka flowers. Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered among devas and humans, and in this Buddha-era, he was reborn in the Sakyan royal family and became well-known by his clan name, Gotama. Upon reaching maturity, he gained faith during the gathering of the Buddha's relatives, went forth as a monk, and by practicing insight meditation, became an Arahant endowed with the six direct knowledges. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

"I offered eight campaka flowers to the funeral pyre of the Blessed One Sikhī, the Friend of the World, who was absorbed in jhāna.

In the thirty-first kappa from this Bhadda-kappa, because of the power of that deed of offering flowers, I have never gone to a miserable state. This is the fruit of honoring the funeral pyre.

The defilements have been burnt away... (etc.) ... the Buddha's Teaching has been carried out."

One day, while he was dwelling in the bliss of liberation after attaining the six direct knowledges, his relatives asked him, "Why did you renounce the world and become a monk?" Wishing to show the suffering he had experienced in saṃsāra and the bliss of Nibbāna he had now attained, he preached to those relatives with three verses beginning with "Saṃsaraṃ nirayaṃ agañchiṃ, passanti meva satimā samajja-gaṃ." [Meaning:] "Wandering in saṃsāra, I have repeatedly gone to hell."
481:
## 
“I offered eight campaka flowers to the funeral pyre (citaka) of the Blessed One Sikhi, the Friend of the World, while he was in meditative absorption. Because of the power of that merit from offering flowers thirty-one aeons ago from this present aeon, I have never known a woeful state. This is the fruit of honoring the funeral pyre. My defilements are burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.”

While dwelling in the bliss of liberation (vimuttisukha), having attained the six supernormal powers (chalabhiñño), he was asked one day by his relatives: “Venerable sir, why did you leave us and go forth as a monk?” Desiring to reveal the suffering he had experienced in Saṃsāra and the bliss of Nibbāna he has now attained, he taught the Dhamma to those relatives with these three verses:

“Wandering in Saṃsāra, I went to hell; I went to the realm of hungry ghosts (peta) again and again. I also experienced suffering in the animal womb; I lived there in many ways for a long time.

Human existence was also achieved through favorable conditions; I went to the heavenly host from time to time. I stayed in the form elements (rūpadhātu), the formless elements (arūpadhātu), the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and the non-percipient realm.

Existences are well-known to be essence-less; they are conditioned, unstable, and agitated (by passion). Knowing the arising and passing of those existences, being mindful, I have attained peace (Nibbāna).”

In those verses, “saṃsaraṃ” means wandering in the beginningless Saṃsāra, repeatedly wandering through the five destinations (gati) by way of death and rebirth due to karma and defilements. “Hi” is merely a particle. “Nirayaṃ agacchissaṃ” means reaching the eight great hells such as Sañjīva and the sixteen Ussada hells such as Kukkuḷa by way of rebirth-linking. The word “punappunaṃ” (again and again) should also be applied here. “Petalokaṃ” means the realm of hungry ghosts, the various states of petas characterized by hunger and thirst...
482:
...meaning reaching the state of a hungry ghost. “Agamaṃ” means I reached or was born there by way of rebirth-linking. The word “again and again” is also applied here. I reached the realm of hungry ghosts, the various states of petas characterized by hunger and thirst. “Agamaṃ” means I reached or was born there by way of rebirth-linking. “Punappunaṃ” means repeatedly. “Dukkhamamhipi” means experiencing unbearable suffering through being struck by extremely sharp whips and prods, and through being beaten and pierced. This word “dukkhamamhipi” is spoken with a change of grammatical gender (liṅgavipallāsa). “Tiracchānayoniyaṃ” means being born in the animal womb, such as beasts and birds. “Nekadhā hi” means in many ways and many times, for a long duration, I lived as camels, oxen, donkeys, etc., and as crows, herons, hawks, etc. I continuously experienced suffering by way of having a terrified mind at all times. Because a being born in the animal womb revolves in that animal realm repeatedly for a very long time due to great delusion, the word “ciraṃ” (a long time) is used here.

“Mānusopi ca bhavobhirādhito” means that human existence was also achieved, accomplished, and attained by me through the coincidence of such wholesome karma. In this context, the Kāṇakacchapopama Sutta (The Simile of the Blind Turtle) should be cited. I went to the sense-sphere deva realm, known as the heavenly destination (saggagati), by way of being born there once in a while, from time to time. “Rūpadhātusu” means being born in the form realms which are the limit of existence for worldlings (puthujjana). “Arūpadhātusu” means being born in the formless realms. It should be understood by connecting the meaning that I reached and stayed not only in the form and formless elements and the realms with perception, but indeed also in the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and the non-percipient realm. Here, by the word “nevasaññī”, the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is taken. Although these two existences can be included within the terms form element and formless element, they are taken separately to show the wrong perception of those outside the Dispensation who have the perception of “permanence” and the perception of “liberation from existence” regarding those realms.

Thus, having shown the experience of the suffering of the round (vaṭṭadukkha) in the beginningless Saṃsāra because the root of existence—ignorance and craving—had not yet been cut with two verses, he now spoke the third verse beginning with “sambhavā” to show the experience of the bliss of the ending of the round (vivaṭṭasukha) by cutting that root of existence. In that verse, “sambhavā” means existences. Indeed, existences such as the sense-sphere existence are called “sambhavā” here because they come into being through the coincidence of causes and conditions. “Suviditā” means well-known through path-knowledge (maggapaññā) accompanied by insight-knowledge (vipassanāpaññā). The words “asārakā” etc. show the manner in which those existences are known. In that verse, “asārakā” means void of permanent essence and the like. “Saṅkhatā” means produced by the meeting of causes...
483:
Causes and conditions are combined and conditioned. 'Pacalitā' means that because they are conditioned (saṅkhata), they are particularly shaken by arising, aging, and so forth, and are unstable. 'Saderitā' means they are always shaken by dissolution (bhaṅga), lasting only for a moment, tending towards dissolution, and having a nature of breaking down.

Knowing that aforementioned conditioned nature, which is born of oneself, connected to oneself, not following the will of a creator (issara) and such, but occurring only according to its own nature, I have known it through the power of full understanding (pariññā) and penetration (abhisamaya). Being mindful with the mindfulness that accompanies the Path-knowledge (magga-paññā), I have reached the peaceful Nirvana, which is the opposite of that conditioned state; I have attained it through the development of the Noble Path (ariya-magga-bhāvanā). In this way, the Elder declared his attainment of Arahantship by means of preaching the Dhamma to his relatives.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Gotama is finished.

## 15. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Harita

The verse beginning with "Yo pubbe karaṇīyāni" is that of the Venerable Elder Harita. What is its origin? This Elder Harita was also born into a respectable family during the time of the Buddha Padumuttara. When he reached maturity and the Buddha had passed into Parinirvana, he made an offering of scents while the funeral pyre worship (citakapūjā) was being performed. Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans. In this Buddha's era, he was born into a Brahmin family in Sāvatthī and was named Harita. When he came of age, relying on his pride of birth (jātimāna), he used to address others with the word "outcast" (vasala).

Having gone to the monks and heard the Dhamma, he gained faith and ordained. However, due to long-standing habit, he could not abandon the practice of addressing others as "outcast." Then one day, after hearing the Dhamma from the Buddha, he was struck by spiritual urgency (saṃvega). While practicing insight (vipassanā) and examining his own mental process, he saw that he was oppressed by pride (māna) and restlessness (uddhacca). Abandoning them and striving in insight, he attained Arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

"While the funeral pyres were being prepared and various scents were being gathered,
With a clear and joyful mind, I worshipped with a handful of scents.

In the hundred thousandth aeon from this, I worshipped the funeral pyre;
Due to the fruit of that worship of the pyre, I do not know of any rebirth in the four woeful states.

My defilements have been burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out."
484:
That Elder Harita, having become an Arahant and experiencing the bliss of liberation (vimuttisukha), declared his attainment of Arahantship by means of giving advice to the monks through the three verses beginning with "Yo pubbe karaṇīyāni." The meaning of those verses has already been stated below.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Harita is finished.

## 16. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Vimala

The verse beginning with "Pāpamitte" is that of the Venerable Elder Vimala. What is the origin of that Elder? This Elder also had special merit performed under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit that is a supporting cause for liberation from the cycle of rebirth (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) in various lives. He was born into a good family during the time of the Buddha Padumuttara. When he reached maturity and the Buddha had passed into Parinirvana, after the days of the funeral festival had passed, while the lay devotees were carrying the Buddha's body to the place of cremation, he reflected on the virtues of the Buddha and, with a clear mind, worshipped with jasmine flowers (sumana).

Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans. When this Buddha appeared, he was born into a Brahmin family in Vārāṇasī and was named Vimala. When he came of age, relying on the Elder Somamitta, he ordained in the Dispensation. Encouraged by that Elder, he practiced insight and soon attained Arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna text:

"While the body was being carried out and the drums were being beaten,
With a clear and joyful mind, I worshipped with jasmine flowers.

In the hundred thousandth aeon from this, I worshipped with flowers;
Due to the fruit of that worship of the body, I have never reached the four woeful states.

My defilements have been burnt away... the Buddha's Dispensation has been practiced."

After reaching Arahantship, wishing to give advice to a monk who was his companion:

"Avoiding evil friends, one should associate with the supreme person;
One who desires the unshakeable happiness of Nirvana should stand in the advice of that virtuous person."
485:
"Just as one might sink in the great ocean by boarding a small log,
Even so, by relying on a lazy person, even one who lives righteously sinks.
Therefore, one should avoid that lazy person of inferior energy.

One should live together with the wise who are secluded, noble, resolute,
Meditators, and those who are always of stirred-up energy."

He spoke these three verses.

In those verses, "pāpamitte" refers to bad friends who are unvirtuous and of inferior energy. "Vivajjetvā" means avoiding them from afar by not associating with them. "Bhajeyyuttamapuggalaṃ" means one should associate with a virtuous and wise friend by accepting their advice and instruction. "Ovāde cassa tiṭṭheyya" means one should stand in the advice of that good friend by practicing according to the instruction. "Patthento" means one who desires or longs for. "Acalaṃ sukhaṃ" refers to the bliss of Nirvana and the bliss of Fruition (phala-sukha). That bliss is called "unshakeable (acala)" because it has no nature of perishing. The meaning of the remaining words is just as previously stated.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Vimala is finished.

## The Commentary on the Book of the Threes (Tikanipāta) is finished.

## The First Part is finished.
